stem:
A 72-year-old man with HFrEF (LVEF 28 percent on echo 3 months ago, NYHA II baseline) and new persistent atrial fibrillation (onset >2 months ago, rate 132 average on Holter, mildly symptomatic with exertional dyspnoea) attends a Maitland cardiology clinic. He is already on optimised guideline-directed medical therapy: bisoprolol 10 mg, sacubitril/valsartan 49/51 mg BD, spironolactone 25 mg daily, dapagliflozin 10 mg daily.

Renal function is normal (Cr 88), thyroid normal, LFT normal, no QT prolongation (QTc 420 ms). He is on apixaban 5 mg BD for AF. He has no symptomatic angina, no valvular disease beyond mild MR, no prior cardiac surgery, no history of substance use. Echo today: LV dilatation, LVEF 26 percent, LA dilated (5.2 cm), no LV thrombus.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132 AF, BP 124/76, RR 16, SpO2 97% RA. JVP not elevated.
data_table.Examination: Irregularly irregular pulse, S3 gallop, no peripheral oedema, chest clear.
data_table.Investigations: ECG AF rate 132, no LVH on voltage. Echo LVEF 26%, dilated LV, LA 5.2 cm. NT-proBNP 1240 pg/mL. Cr 88, K 4.6, TSH 1.8, LFT normal.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step for rate or rhythm control of his AF, recognising the constraints of HFrEF, optimised GDMT, and the available antiarrhythmic profile?

options.text: Add digoxin 125 microgram daily for rate control given persistent tachycardia despite maximal beta-blocker dose
Refer for catheter ablation of AF, recognising mortality and HF hospitalisation reduction in HFrEF demonstrated in CASTLE-AF
Commence flecainide 50 mg BD for rhythm control with target sinus rhythm restoration
Commence sotalol 80 mg BD for combined rate and rhythm control
Increase bisoprolol to 15 mg daily for tighter rate control

subtopic_detail: AF rhythm vs rate strategy in HFrEF with multi-comorbidity constraints

stem:
A 64-year-old woman with chronic depression on stable citalopram 40 mg daily for 6 years is admitted to Calvary Mater Newcastle with new-onset palpitations, two presyncopal episodes, and one witnessed brief loss of consciousness this morning. She had been started on azithromycin 500 mg daily for community-acquired pneumonia 4 days ago, and was started on ondansetron 8 mg TDS for the nausea associated with her infection 2 days ago.

She has no past cardiac history, no electrolyte disorder, normal renal function, no other medication changes. ECG today: sinus rhythm rate 92 with prolonged QT (QTc 580 ms), no T-wave alternans, no current torsades. Her ECG 6 months ago had QTc 440 ms.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92 sinus, BP 118/72, RR 18, SpO2 98% RA.
data_table.Examination: Alert oriented, no neurological deficit, normal heart sounds, chest mild crackles RLL.
data_table.Investigations: ECG QTc 580 ms (was 440 ms 6 months ago). K 4.1, Mg 0.82, Ca 2.32. Cr 78. Troponin negative. CXR RLL consolidation.

lead_in: Which combination of mechanisms best explains the QT prolongation, and what is the immediate management priority?

options.text: Citalopram alone is responsible; stop citalopram and accept psychiatric relapse risk

Additive QT prolongation from three QT-prolonging drugs (citalopram + azithromycin + ondansetron); admit to telemetry, stop both azithromycin (switch antibiotic to doxycycline) and ondansetron, replace IV Mg as prophylaxis
Hypokalaemia is the cause; replace IV K then continue all current medications
Cardiac ischaemia precipitating QT prolongation; cardiac catheterisation lab activation
Discharge on outpatient cardiology follow-up; QTc will normalise with antibiotic course completion

subtopic_detail: Additive drug-induced QT prolongation - time-of-onset mapping

stem: A 24-year-old woman presents to her GP with progressive cosmetic concerns over the past 9 months. She has noticed coarse facial hair growth requiring weekly waxing, gum swelling that bleeds when she brushes, and her partner has noticed she sounds slightly slurred in the evenings. She also reports new acne, intermittent diplopia at night, and unsteadiness walking down stairs. She started a new daily medication 11 months ago for a chronic condition diagnosed in adolescence. She is not on any other regular medication and is not pregnant.

data_table.Examination: Hirsutism over chin and sideburns, gingival hyperplasia covering proximal third of lower incisors with contact bleeding, mild horizontal nystagmus on lateral gaze, broad-based gait, finger-nose with end-point intention tremor.
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal, LFTs ALT 65 U/L (slightly raised), GGT 110 U/L, urinalysis negative, beta-hCG negative.

lead_in: Which medication is the single most likely cause of this constellation?

options.text: Phenytoin
Ciclosporin
Amlodipine
Sodium valproate
Topiramate

subtopic_detail: Adverse effect cluster mapping to anticonvulsant drug class

stem:
A 58-year-old retiree from the Central Coast presents to a Gosford respiratory clinic with 6 months of progressive dyspnoea, dry cough and 4 kg weight loss. He is a lifelong non-smoker. He has been retired for 5 years from his job as an aircraft mechanic. He spends most of his time at home; he keeps a small allotment vegetable garden, has two outdoor cats, and tends to the racing pigeon loft his neighbour asked him to mind during a 12-month overseas trip that began 8 months ago.

He has no occupational asbestos exposure beyond brief brake-pad work in the 1980s. There is no fever, no haemoptysis, no joint pain, no rash. Resting SpO2 96 percent room air, falling to 88 percent after a 6-minute walk test. Fine bibasal end-inspiratory crackles are heard but no clubbing. Spirometry shows a restrictive pattern with FEV1/FVC 0.84, TLC 71 percent predicted, DLCO 52 percent predicted. CT chest reports patchy ground-glass and centrilobular nodularity with mid-to-upper lobe predominance.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 deg C, HR 92, RR 22, BP 132/82, SpO2 96% room air resting (88% post 6MWT).
data_table.Examination: Fine bibasal crackles, no clubbing, no rash, no synovitis.
data_table.Investigations: Spirometry restrictive (FEV1/FVC 0.84, TLC 71%, DLCO 52%), CT chest patchy ground-glass + centrilobular nodularity, mid-upper lobe predominant. FBC, UEC, LFT, CRP all normal. ANA, ENA, ANCA negative.

lead_in: Which of the following is the single most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF)
Chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis from avian antigen exposure
Asbestos-related pleural disease
Sarcoidosis stage II
Cryptogenic organising pneumonia (COP)

subtopic_detail: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis from avian antigen exposure

stem:
A 22-year-old woman presents to a Newcastle hepatology clinic with 6 weeks of fatigue, mild jaundice and a 3 kg weight loss. She is not on any medication and denies herbal supplement use. Alcohol intake is 2 standard drinks per week. She has no risk factors for viral hepatitis on screening interview. There is a remote history of vitiligo and a paternal history of type 1 diabetes mellitus.

Bloods today show ALT 612 U/L, AST 540 U/L, ALP 142 U/L, GGT 88 U/L, total bilirubin 58 micromol/L, conjugated 41 micromol/L, INR 1.2, albumin 36 g/L, IgG 26 g/L (high). Viral hepatitis serology (HBsAg, anti-HCV, anti-HAV IgM, anti-HEV IgM) negative; HIV negative. Caeruloplasmin and alpha-1-antitrypsin normal. Iron studies show normal ferritin and transferrin saturation. Autoimmune panel: ANA 1:640 (homogeneous), anti-smooth muscle antibody (ASMA) 1:160, anti-LKM-1 negative, anti-mitochondrial antibody (AMA) negative, anti-soluble liver antigen (SLA) negative.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6, HR 78, BP 112/68, no asterixis.
data_table.Examination: Mild scleral icterus, no stigmata of chronic liver disease, soft non-tender abdomen, no hepatosplenomegaly.
data_table.Investigations: Hepatocellular pattern (ALT 612, AST 540, ALP 142). Bilirubin 58 (conj 41). IgG 26 (high). ANA 1:640 homogeneous, ASMA 1:160, anti-LKM-1 negative, AMA negative.

lead_in: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Primary biliary cholangitis
Type 1 autoimmune hepatitis
Type 2 autoimmune hepatitis
Primary sclerosing cholangitis
Wilson disease

subtopic_detail: Autoimmune hepatitis type 1 serological pattern

stem:
A 67-year-old man presents to a Maitland general practice with 5 days of progressively severe bilateral thigh and shoulder muscle pain, dark cola-coloured urine and weakness when climbing stairs. He cannot recall recent strenuous exercise or trauma. He has hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism and stable HFrEF. His regular medications are atorvastatin 40 mg, perindopril 5 mg, metformin XR 1 g BD, levothyroxine 100 micrograms, and bisoprolol 5 mg, all unchanged for over 2 years.

Two weeks ago his GP started clarithromycin 500 mg BD for a 7-day course to treat a confirmed Helicobacter pylori eradication regimen. The macrolide course finished 5 days ago. Bloods today: CK 38400 U/L, creatinine 142 micromol/L (baseline 80), K 4.1, urine dipstick blood ++++, microscopy 2 RBC per high power field, TSH 2.4.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.5, HR 78, BP 132/78, SpO2 98% room air.
data_table.Examination: Bilateral proximal muscle tenderness in shoulders and thighs, power 4/5 against resistance, reflexes preserved, no rash.
data_table.Investigations: CK 38 400 U/L; Cr 142 (baseline 80); K 4.1; urine dipstick blood ++++ but only 2 RBC/HPF on microscopy (myoglobinuria); TSH 2.4.

lead_in: Which is the single most likely precipitant for this presentation?

options.text: Hypothyroid-induced myopathy from drift in levothyroxine effect
Clarithromycin-induced atorvastatin toxicity via CYP3A4 inhibition
Idiopathic immune-mediated necrotising myopathy (anti-HMGCR)
Strenuous unrecognised exertional rhabdomyolysis
Perindopril-induced AKI causing secondary CK release

subtopic_detail: Statin-macrolide CYP3A4 interaction rhabdomyolysis

stem:
A 78-year-old man on long-term warfarin for non-valvular AF (target INR 2.0-3.0) is admitted to Calvary Mater Newcastle with community-acquired pneumonia. He is in atrial fibrillation rate 102, BP 108/68, SpO2 92% on 2 L nasal prongs. His admission bloods show creatinine 198 micromol/L (baseline 90), urea 18 mmol/L, K 5.1, INR 7.4. He had a witnessed mechanical fall yesterday with a 2x2 cm forehead haematoma but no loss of consciousness; CT brain on arrival shows no intracranial haemorrhage.

He has no active bleeding now; urinalysis no blood. Past history: hypertension, mild Alzheimer dementia, prior PE 4 years ago. Medications: warfarin 5/4 mg alternate days, perindopril 5 mg, donepezil 10 mg. He weighs 72 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.2, HR 102 AF, BP 108/68, RR 24, SpO2 92% on 2 L NP.
data_table.Examination: Forehead haematoma 2x2 cm, no active bleed, no neurological deficit. Crepitations RLL. AF irregularly irregular.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 124, Plt 220, INR 7.4. Cr 198 (baseline 90), urea 18, K 5.1. CT brain no haemorrhage. CXR RLL consolidation.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step for management of his over-anticoagulation, integrating renal function, recent fall, and continued thromboembolic risk?

options.text: Withhold warfarin only and recheck INR in 24 hours; no other intervention
Stop warfarin and give oral phytomenadione (vitamin K1) 1-2 mg PO once
Stop warfarin, give 4-factor PCC 50 IU/kg plus IV vitamin K1 10 mg
Substitute warfarin with therapeutic enoxaparin 1 mg/kg BD bridging
Continue warfarin at full dose; treat pneumonia and reassess INR after antibiotics complete

subtopic_detail: Warfarin reversal ladder in multi-organ dysfunction
Hour-1 bundle initial resuscitation
stem: You are the medical registrar called to ED to review a 72-year-old man with 2 days of dysuria, rigors and now reduced level of consciousness. He has a history of BPH and recent urinary catheterisation 1 week ago for retention. His skin is mottled and his hands are cool. He has been triaged to resus.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 86/48, HR 124, RR 28, SpO2 92% on room air, T 38.9, GCS 13
data_table.Examination: Mottled extremities, cool peripheries, mild suprapubic tenderness, no flank tenderness; chest clear, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 4.2, WCC 18.6, neutrophils 16.1, CRP 240, Cr 168 (baseline 88), urine dipstick nitrites +, leukocytes ++; ABG pH 7.28, HCO3 18; blood cultures and urine cultures collected
data_table.Medications: Tamsulosin 400 micrograms daily; finasteride 5 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic and resuscitation in the first hour?

options.text: IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg with amoxicillin 2 g and 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus over 1 hour; arrange ICU review for vasopressor
IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily with metronidazole 500 mg and 1 L crystalloid over 4 hours; arrange ward bed and senior review
IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g and 250 mL hypertonic saline bolus over 30 minutes; commence noradrenaline at 0.05 micrograms/kg/min
IV cefalexin 1 g and 500 mL crystalloid bolus over 30 minutes; defer further escalation until inpatient team reviews
IV ciprofloxacin 400 mg and 2 L crystalloid bolus over 2 hours; reassess and consider noradrenaline if BP remains below 90 systolic

subtopic_detail: Vasopressor selection in septic shock
stem: You are the ICU registrar managing a 64-year-old woman with septic shock from a perforated diverticular abscess. After 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid, her MAP is 58 mmHg and she remains tachycardic at 118. She has had source control surgery 2 hours ago and is on piperacillin-tazobactam plus gentamicin. She has a central line in situ. Her ScvO2 is 72 percent and her lactate has fallen from 4.6 to 3.2.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 92/40 (MAP 58), HR 118, RR 22 ventilated, SpO2 96% on 40% FiO2, T 37.4
data_table.Examination: Warm extremities, cap refill 3 s, urine output 0.4 mL/kg/h over last hour, no new bleeding
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 3.2 (down from 4.6), Hb 96, K 4.2, ScvO2 72%, echo bedside shows hyperdynamic LV, IVC variable
data_table.Medications: Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours; gentamicin loaded

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence dopamine at 5 micrograms/kg/min titrated to MAP 65 mmHg with arterial line monitoring in place
Commence noradrenaline at 0.05 micrograms/kg/min titrated to MAP 65 mmHg with arterial line monitoring
Commence vasopressin 0.03 units/min as monotherapy; reassess MAP after 30 minutes of stable infusion before escalation
Administer further 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus and reassess; defer vasopressor pending response to volume resuscitation
Commence adrenaline at 0.05 micrograms/kg/min; reassess MAP and lactate clearance after 2 hours of infusion at steady state

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis recognition and management
stem: You are the medical registrar called to ED to review a 42-year-old woman with Addison's disease who presents with 36 hours of vomiting and diarrhoea from suspected viral gastroenteritis. She has not taken her usual hydrocortisone for 24 hours due to vomiting. She is on hydrocortisone 20 mg morning and 10 mg afternoon and fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily.

data_table.Examination: Dry mucosa, sunken eyes, cool peripheries, hyperpigmentation of palmar creases, abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Na 124, K 5.8, glucose 2.8, Cr 142 (baseline 64), Hb 142, CRP 18, lactate 2.4, cortisol pending
data_table.Medications: Hydrocortisone 20 mg morning, 10 mg afternoon; fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Oral hydrocortisone 40 mg with ondansetron 4 mg sublingual and 500 mL crystalloid; observe over 4 hours in ED short stay
Dexamethasone 4 mg IV bolus, 1 L Hartmann's bolus, and oral glucose drinks; admit for slow-stress dosing taper
Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus, 1 L 0.9% saline bolus, and 100 mL 10% glucose bolus; admit for ongoing replacement
Fludrocortisone 200 micrograms oral, 1 L saline bolus, and oral glucose; await cortisol level before parenteral steroid
Methylprednisolone 40 mg IV bolus, 2 L 5% dextrose bolus, and noradrenaline infusion for hypotension control

subtopic_detail: Hypotension in recovery immediately after adrenalectomy
stem: A 55-year-old man is in recovery one hour after laparoscopic adrenalectomy for a catecholamine secreting adrenal tumour. He had two weeks of preoperative alpha blockade with salt and fluid loading. He is rousable and his abdomen is soft.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112 /min, blood pressure 76/44 mmHg, SpO2 98% on oxygen
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 128 g/L, unchanged; capillary glucose 5.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate step?

options.text: Give a rapid intravenous crystalloid bolus and reassess
Start a noradrenaline infusion through a central line
Return him to theatre for suspected intra-abdominal bleeding
Give intravenous hydrocortisone and start maintenance fluid
Give an intravenous metaraminol bolus and observe him

subtopic_detail: Postmenopausal osteoporosis - first line
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 68-year-old postmenopausal woman in osteoporosis clinic. She had a fragility fracture of her right wrist after a fall from standing height 6 weeks ago. Her DEXA shows L1-L4 T-score minus 2.8 and femoral neck T-score minus 2.6. She has stable hypertension on perindopril and no GI symptoms. Her eGFR is 64 mL/min/1.73m^2. She is not lactose intolerant and lives independently.

data_table.Examination: Well; no spinal tenderness; right wrist healing; no peripheral oedema; gait stable with stick
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.42, phosphate 1.0, vitamin D 64 nmol/L, Cr 88, eGFR 64, TSH 1.8, PTH 4.4 (normal), DEXA T-scores as above, beta-CTX baseline 0.62
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 5 mg daily; vitamin D 1000 IU daily; calcium 600 mg twice daily; nil PPI

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological therapy?

options.text: Strontium ranelate 2 g orally daily; review cardiovascular risk and DEXA at 12 months; continue calcium and vitamin D supplementation
Denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously every 6 months; review at 12 months with DEXA and serial beta-CTX measurements
Teriparatide 20 micrograms subcutaneously daily for 18 months; sequence to oral bisphosphonate after the course completes
Raloxifene 60 mg orally daily; advise on VTE risk; review at 12 months with DEXA and bone turnover markers
Alendronate 70 mg orally weekly; review at 12 months with DEXA and beta-CTX; continue calcium and vitamin D supplementation

subtopic_detail: SJS/TEN initial management
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 56-year-old woman with new-onset painful rash for 36 hours after starting allopurinol 100 mg daily 3 weeks ago for gout. She now has flaccid bullae over the trunk that detach with gentle pressure, oral and conjunctival erosions, and a fever. The dermatology consultant on call estimates 18 percent body surface area involvement with epidermal detachment.

data_table.Examination: Flaccid bullae trunk and arms; Nikolsky positive; oral erosions; conjunctival injection with erosions; dusky targetoid lesions
data_table.Investigations: Hb 132, WCC 6.8, Cr 142 (baseline 76), ALT 122, ALP 184, albumin 28, CRP 96; SCORTEN calculated as 3
data_table.Medications: Allopurinol 100 mg daily for 3 weeks; nil other recent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Cease allopurinol and transfer to a burns or specialised dermatology unit for supportive care and wound management
Continue allopurinol; commence oral prednisolone 50 mg daily and topical corticosteroid; review at 48 hours by dermatology
Cease allopurinol; commence ciclosporin 3 mg/kg twice daily orally with bedside isolation in the medical ward
Cease allopurinol; commence IV intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg over 4 days in current medical ward setting
Continue allopurinol; commence broad-spectrum IV antibiotics empirically and arrange skin biopsy in 48 hours for confirmation

subtopic_detail: Anticoagulation duration after unprovoked PE
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 58-year-old man in clinic 6 months after a first unprovoked submassive pulmonary embolism. He has been on apixaban 5 mg twice daily and is asymptomatic with normal exercise tolerance. He has no malignancy on age-appropriate screening and no thrombophilia screen abnormalities. He has no high bleeding risk and is keen to continue if benefit outweighs harm.

data_table.Examination: Well; no oedema; chest clear; no calf swelling
data_table.Investigations: Hb 142, platelets 240, INR not applicable; eGFR 84; LFTs normal; thrombophilia screen negative; CT chest 6 weeks ago shows resolution of PE; HAS-BLED 1
data_table.Medications: Apixaban 5 mg twice daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation strategy beyond 6 months?

options.text: Cease apixaban; arrange repeat D-dimer at 4 weeks off therapy and consider reinitiation only if D-dimer is positive
Continue apixaban at reduced dose 2.5 mg twice daily indefinitely; review annually for bleeding risk and goals of care
Switch to warfarin INR 2 to 3 indefinitely; arrange community INR monitoring weekly initially then monthly when stable
Switch to aspirin 100 mg daily; arrange GP review in 6 months and resume DOAC if recurrent VTE symptoms develop
Cease apixaban at 6 months; advise that the risk of recurrent VTE is sufficiently low after 6 months of therapy to stop

subtopic_detail: Endocarditis - Duke criteria
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 52-year-old man with 3 weeks of fever, fatigue and weight loss. He had a dental extraction 6 weeks ago. He has a history of bicuspid aortic valve. Examination reveals a new diastolic murmur, splinter haemorrhages and a tender nodule on his left index finger pulp. Echocardiography shows aortic valve vegetation 8 mm and moderate aortic regurgitation. Two of three sets of blood cultures grow viridans group streptococci.

data_table.Examination: New 2/6 diastolic decrescendo murmur LSE; splinter haemorrhages; Osler node left index finger pulp; no Janeway lesion; spleen tip palpable
data_table.Investigations: WCC 13.4, Hb 108, CRP 96, ESR 78, urine dipstick haematuria +, TTE aortic vegetation 8 mm, moderate AR; blood cultures 2 of 3 sets viridans streptococci
data_table.Medications: Nil regular

lead_in: Which best characterises the diagnostic certainty under the modified Duke criteria?

options.text: Possible endocarditis (1 major plus 1 minor criterion); commence empirical IV flucloxacillin pending further cultures
Possible endocarditis (2 minor criteria only); arrange TOE within 24 hours before commencing any antimicrobial therapy
Definite endocarditis (2 major criteria); commence IV benzylpenicillin 1.8 g 4-hourly for 4 weeks with gentamicin for the first 2 weeks
Rejected endocarditis (alternate diagnosis); arrange dental review and broad febrile workup including bone scan and PET
Definite endocarditis (3 minor criteria); commence IV vancomycin and ciprofloxacin pending speciation and sensitivities

subtopic_detail: Tension pneumothorax recognition
stem: You are the medical registrar called to a 64-year-old man with severe COPD on the respiratory ward who has acutely deteriorated. He developed sudden right-sided chest pain and severe dyspnoea 5 minutes ago. He is hypotensive, tachycardic and using accessory muscles. There is decreased breath sounds and hyperresonance on the right with tracheal deviation to the left. SpO2 is 84 percent on 15 L non-rebreather.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 78/44, HR 132, RR 36, SpO2 84% on 15 L NRB, T 36.6, GCS 13
data_table.Examination: Severe respiratory distress, accessory muscle use; trachea deviated to the left; right chest hyperresonant with absent breath sounds; distended neck veins
data_table.Investigations: Cannot wait for imaging; ECG sinus tachycardia
data_table.Medications: Tiotropium, salbutamol, prednisolone tapering

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Arrange urgent portable chest X-ray to confirm tension pneumothorax; commence non-invasive ventilation while awaiting result
Administer IV crystalloid 1 L bolus; commence noradrenaline infusion to support BP while preparing for theatre
Intubate immediately with rocuronium and ketamine; apply positive pressure ventilation to recruit collapsed lung tissue
Perform finger thoracostomy at the 5th intercostal space mid-axillary line on the right; insert intercostal catheter immediately after
Administer salbutamol 5 mg and ipratropium 500 micrograms nebulised; increase prednisolone to 50 mg orally daily

subtopic_detail: Primary hyperaldosteronism workup
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 46-year-old woman with resistant hypertension on perindopril 10 mg, amlodipine 10 mg and hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily. Despite triple therapy her BP remains 162/96. She has muscle cramps and her potassium has consistently been at the lower end (3.0 to 3.4). She has no symptoms of phaeochromocytoma. There is no family history of hypertension before age 40.

data_table.Examination: Well; no abdominal bruit; no Cushingoid features; no goitre; no neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Na 142, K 3.2, Cr 78, eGFR 78, plasma renin activity low, aldosterone elevated, ARR pending; TSH normal; HbA1c 5.6%; ECG sinus rhythm; urine ACR 2.4
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 10 mg daily; amlodipine 10 mg daily; hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test; continue current antihypertensive regimen without change before testing
24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines; correct potassium and continue all current antihypertensives during collection
Renal artery duplex ultrasound; commence empirical spironolactone 25 mg daily while awaiting the result of imaging
Late-night salivary cortisol; reduce hydrochlorothiazide to 12.5 mg daily and continue ACE inhibitor at full dose
Aldosterone-to-renin ratio screening; correct potassium and switch ACE inhibitor to verapamil before sampling for accuracy

subtopic_detail: Adult sepsis hour-1 bundle
stem: You are the medical registrar in ED reviewing a 68-year-old man with 24 hours of fever, dysuria and confusion. He has a background of well-controlled type 2 diabetes on metformin. He is hypotensive on arrival. The team has placed two large bore IV lines and a urinary catheter for output monitoring. Bloods are at the lab.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.8, HR 122, BP 84/52, RR 26, SpO2 96% on 6 L mask, GCS 13
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable; warm peripheries; suprapubic tenderness; cloudy malodorous urine; chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 4.2, WCC 18.2 (neutrophils 16.2), CRP 240, Cr 168 (baseline 95), urine dip nitrite and leukocyte positive, blood cultures pending
data_table.Medications: Metformin 1 g BD; perindopril 5 mg daily

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous noradrenaline infusion via peripheral line at 0.05 mcg/kg/min; defer fluid resuscitation pending central access
Oral co-trimoxazole 160/800 mg twice daily and oral fluids; admit to short-stay for 24 hours observation with repeat lactate
Crystalloid 30 mL/kg IV over 3 hours; IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g; blood cultures and lactate before antibiotics
Activated protein C infusion 24 mcg/kg/hour for 96 hours; broad-spectrum antibiotics after coagulopathy is excluded
Intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg as first-line therapy; defer antibiotics until cortisol response confirmed

subtopic_detail: Necrotising fasciitis recognition and LRINEC score
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 58-year-old man with 18 hours of right thigh swelling and pain disproportionate to the redness. He has type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 8.2 percent). The skin is dusky over a 12 by 8 cm area with bullae forming and crepitus on palpation. He is febrile and unwell. Vitals and bloods are back.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.0, HR 124, BP 96/58, RR 24, SpO2 96% on 4 L mask
data_table.Examination: Pain out of proportion; bullae and dusky discolouration on right thigh; crepitus palpable; reduced sensation over the central plaque
data_table.Investigations: Hb 138, WCC 22, Na 128, glucose 18.4, Cr 132, CRP 380, lactate 4.0
data_table.Medications: Metformin 1 g BD; gliclazide MR 60 mg daily; insulin glargine 18 units nocte

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Outline cellulitis with marker pen; commence IV cefazolin 2 g and observe for response over 4 hours
Bedside ultrasound to exclude deep abscess; commence oral flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily for outpatient management
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy after first dose of antibiotics; defer surgery pending response to medical therapy and hyperbaric
Urgent surgical consult for debridement; IV meropenem 1 g, vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading, clindamycin 600 mg; activate sepsis pathway
Magnetic resonance imaging of the thigh to delineate fascial involvement; defer antibiotics until imaging completed and reviewed

subtopic_detail: Latent TB diagnosis and treatment selection
stem: You are the GP registrar reviewing a 34-year-old asymptomatic nurse before commencing infliximab for rheumatoid arthritis. She was born in Australia and has no known TB contact. She did NOT have BCG as a child. She has a routine pre-biologic screen including chest x-ray and QuantiFERON Gold Plus.

data_table.Examination: No respiratory symptoms; normal chest examination; no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Chest x-ray normal; QuantiFERON Gold Plus positive (TB1 1.2 IU/mL, TB2 1.4 IU/mL); HIV negative; HBV and HCV negative; FBC, U&E, LFTs normal
data_table.Medications: Methotrexate 15 mg weekly; folic acid 5 mg weekly

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure and proceed with infliximab; treat only if active TB develops during therapy on routine monitoring
Repeat QuantiFERON in 3 months to confirm; proceed with infliximab in the interim while monitoring symptoms
Commence 6-month course of pyrazinamide and ethambutol with monthly LFTs and visual acuity assessment
Refer to public health for directly observed therapy with daily isoniazid for 24 months as an immunosuppressed patient
Commence isoniazid 5 mg/kg daily plus pyridoxine 25 mg daily for 9 months; defer infliximab until at least 4 weeks of therapy

subtopic_detail: Osteoporosis FRAX and bisphosphonate threshold
stem: You are the GP registrar reviewing a 68-year-old postmenopausal woman 6 months after a low-trauma wrist fracture. She is otherwise well, not on glucocorticoids, and her father had a hip fracture aged 78. She has had a DXA scan today. Her calcium and vitamin D are replete and her eGFR is 76 mL/min/1.73m^2. She is keen to consider preventive therapy.

data_table.Examination: No spinal tenderness; height 162 cm (lost 2 cm); BMI 24
data_table.Investigations: DXA T-score lumbar spine -2.6, femoral neck -2.4; corrected calcium 2.40, 25-OH vitamin D 78, PTH 4.2, ALP 80, Cr 76, FRAX 10-year major fracture 22%, hip fracture 6%
data_table.Medications: Vitamin D 1000 IU daily; calcium 600 mg daily; nil other

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological choice?

options.text: Alendronate 70 mg oral once weekly; continue calcium and vitamin D; reassess BMD and clinical risk at 5 years
Denosumab 60 mg subcutaneous 6-monthly indefinitely; cease calcium supplementation to avoid hypercalcaemia
Hormone replacement therapy with oral oestradiol and progesterone; bone density monitoring annually for 5 years
Teriparatide 20 mcg subcutaneous daily for 24 months as first-line agent; defer bisphosphonate during teriparatide
Raloxifene 60 mg daily; reassess BMD at 5 years and consider switch if no response on vertebral measurement

subtopic_detail: Endocarditis surgical indication
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 52-year-old man on day 3 of treatment for native aortic valve endocarditis with methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. He has new dyspnoea overnight. Echocardiogram now shows a 1.2 cm aortic vegetation, moderate to severe aortic regurgitation and a small pericardial effusion. He has bilateral fine inspiratory crackles. He has had 3 days of IV flucloxacillin and remains febrile to 38.7.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.7, BP 102/56, HR 108, RR 26, SpO2 92% on 4 L mask, JVP 5 cm
data_table.Examination: Bibasal fine crackles; soft S3; collapsing pulse; soft diastolic murmur at LSE; warm extremities
data_table.Investigations: Hb 110, WCC 14, Cr 138 (baseline 92), CRP 180, troponin 84, BNP 1200; echo aortic vegetation 12 mm, severe AR, EF 50%, no abscess yet; chest x-ray pulmonary oedema
data_table.Medications: IV flucloxacillin 2 g 4-hourly for 3 days

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue IV flucloxacillin for a further 7 days; reassess vegetation size and clinical response with echo on day 10
Urgent cardiothoracic referral for aortic valve replacement within 24 to 48 hours; continue antibiotics throughout
Add IV gentamicin 1 mg/kg every 8 hours for synergy; reassess response after 5 days before considering operative referral
Switch to IV vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading dose; defer surgery pending repeat MRI brain to exclude embolic stroke
Intravenous furosemide 40 mg with non-invasive ventilation for pulmonary oedema; cardiology review in 1 week for assessment

subtopic_detail: Cushing's syndrome first-line screening test
stem: You are the medical registrar in an outpatient clinic reviewing a 38-year-old woman with 18 months of weight gain, easy bruising, proximal muscle weakness when climbing stairs, and new-onset hypertension. Her BMI is 34 and she has wide violaceous abdominal striae. She also reports irregular menses. She is not on glucocorticoids by any route. Her sleep is good and her depression screen is negative.

data_table.Examination: Central obesity; thin extremities; proximal weakness on hip flexion; violaceous striae greater than 1 cm; supraclavicular fat pad
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 6.8 fasting, HbA1c 6.2%, K 3.4, ACTH pending; menstrual irregularity 2 to 3 months; no glucocorticoid use
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 5 mg daily; no inhaled corticosteroid

lead_in: Which screening test sequence is most appropriate?

options.text: Random morning serum cortisol and plasma ACTH; CT adrenals only if cortisol greater than 700 nmol/L
Adrenal CT alone; biochemical testing only if a mass greater than 1 cm is identified on imaging
Two of: 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test, late-night salivary cortisol, or 24-hour urinary free cortisol
Insulin tolerance test for cortisol response; pituitary MRI only if cortisol fails to rise above 500 nmol/L during test
Serum cortisol after 2 mg dexamethasone 8 mg over 2 days; pituitary MRI as first-line localisation if cortisol suppresses

subtopic_detail: Unprovoked VTE anticoagulation duration
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 58-year-old man in clinic 6 months after a first proximal lower limb DVT. He had no surgery, no immobility, no malignancy and no oestrogen use at the time. He has had a CT chest, abdomen and pelvis showing no malignancy, and is well. He has been on apixaban 5 mg twice daily. He has no bleeding history and tolerates apixaban well. He wants to know whether to continue, reduce or stop.

data_table.Examination: No leg swelling; no calf tenderness; cardiorespiratory examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Hb 142, plt 220, Cr 92, eGFR 84, INR 1.0, repeat lower limb Doppler shows residual non-occlusive thrombus; D-dimer 360 ng/mL (pending decision)
data_table.Medications: Apixaban 5 mg twice daily; nil other

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing anticoagulation plan?

options.text: Cease apixaban at 6 months; commence aspirin 100 mg daily for ongoing VTE prevention long-term
Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily indefinitely; review annually for bleeding risk and recurrence risk
Switch to warfarin with INR target 2.5 to 3.5 indefinitely; cease apixaban after 1 week of overlap with target INR
Reduce apixaban to 2.5 mg twice daily indefinitely; review annually for bleeding risk and recurrence risk
Cease apixaban at 6 months; arrange thrombophilia screen and IVC filter placement if any heritable thrombophilia is found

subtopic_detail: Type B aortic dissection acute medical therapy
stem: You are the medical registrar in ED with a 62-year-old man with sudden severe tearing interscapular back pain 2 hours ago. CT aortogram confirms an uncomplicated Stanford type B aortic dissection extending from just distal to the left subclavian artery to the iliac bifurcation. There is no organ malperfusion, no rupture, and no rapid expansion. He has a known background of hypertension. He has no asthma.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 188/108 right arm and 184/106 left arm, HR 96, RR 18, SpO2 98% RA, T 36.6
data_table.Examination: Pain 8/10 between scapulae; equal radial pulses; warm peripheries; no neurological deficit; clear chest
data_table.Investigations: Troponin negative; Cr 96; CXR widened mediastinum; CT aortogram type B dissection without malperfusion
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 8 mg daily; amlodipine 10 mg daily at home

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial blood pressure and heart rate target and first-line therapy?

options.text: Sodium nitroprusside infusion alone titrated to systolic 100 to 120 mmHg; no heart rate target during titration
Intravenous metoprolol 5 mg bolus once; no further treatment if pain settles and discharge home from ED with GP follow-up
Urgent thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) within 4 hours; defer medical therapy until anaesthetic review for surgery
Intravenous furosemide 40 mg with morphine 5 mg for pain; recheck BP at 30 minutes before further therapy
Intravenous labetalol infusion targeting systolic 100 to 120 mmHg and heart rate below 60 within 20 minutes

subtopic_detail: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction GDMT
stem: You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 64-year-old man with HFrEF (LVEF 28 percent) in clinic 3 months after admission for decompensation. He is now NYHA II symptoms on usual activity. He is on perindopril 5 mg, bisoprolol 5 mg, furosemide 40 mg and spironolactone 25 mg, all up-titrated since admission. His latest bloods and observations are stable. He has no peripheral oedema. He is not in atrial fibrillation. He has type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 6.9 percent) on metformin only. His renal function is stable.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72, HR 68 (sinus), RR 16, SpO2 98% RA, T 36.6
data_table.Examination: JVP 3 cm, no peripheral oedema, clear chest, normal heart sounds
data_table.Investigations: eGFR 62, K 4.4, Na 138, NT-proBNP 980; HbA1c 6.9; recent echo LVEF 28%
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 5 mg, bisoprolol 5 mg, furosemide 40 mg, spironolactone 25 mg, metformin 1 g BD

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase perindopril to 10 mg daily and review response in 4 weeks before any additional therapy is added
Stop spironolactone given normal potassium and stable renal function; add empagliflozin 10 mg daily as the new GDMT pillar
Add ivabradine 5 mg twice daily to slow heart rate further; defer other medication changes until heart rate is below 60
Add digoxin 125 micrograms daily for symptom control and review at 6 weeks; defer SGLT2 inhibitor and sacubitril/valsartan
Switch perindopril to sacubitril/valsartan (after 36-hour washout) and add dapagliflozin 10 mg daily for the fourth pillar of GDMT

subtopic_detail: Sepsis hour-1 bundle
stem: You are the medicine registrar in ED at 0200 reviewing a 68-year-old man with urinary symptoms for 3 days, now confused. He has a known history of BPH. His GP started oral trimethoprim yesterday. His son brought him in after he became confused this evening. On arrival his observations met sepsis criteria. Blood cultures and urine have been taken. The first set of bloods is back. Cefriaxone 2 g has just been given. He has now received 30 mL/kg crystalloid over 60 minutes. His repeat lactate is back.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.0, HR 124, RR 28, SpO2 96% on 4 L oxygen, BP 78/42 (now MAP 54 after 2.4 L crystalloid), GCS 13
data_table.Examination: Warm peripheries, dry mucous membranes, suprapubic tenderness, no rash, no meningism
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 4.2 mmol/L initial, repeat after fluid 3.8; WCC 22 (neutrophils 18), CRP 280, creatinine 168, urea 22, eGFR 38; urine dip 3+ leucocytes 3+ nitrites; ECG normal sinus
data_table.Medications: IV ceftriaxone 2 g given 25 minutes ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Switch ceftriaxone to oral ciprofloxacin once cultures return; continue conservative management while awaiting microbiology
Continue intravenous crystalloid at 1 L per hour for the next 4 hours; defer vasopressor until 6 L has been delivered
Commence noradrenaline infusion via central access (or peripheral pending central line) to target MAP 65 or above; activate critical care review
Administer intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg as a first-line therapy before considering vasopressor or critical care input
Insert an indwelling urinary catheter and observe for clinical response over the next 2 hours before any further intervention

subtopic_detail: DOAC selection in AF with chronic kidney disease
stem: You are the general medicine registrar admitting a 78-year-old woman in newly diagnosed atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. She has a CHA2DS2-VA score of 5 (hypertension, age, heart failure, female sex). She has chronic kidney disease stage 3b (eGFR 32 mL/min). She has no mechanical valve, no significant mitral stenosis and no recent bleeding. Her weight is 56 kg. She is on no anticoagulant. Liver function is normal. She has no history of intracranial bleed.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/82, HR 118 (irregular), RR 18, SpO2 97% RA, T 36.6
data_table.Examination: Irregularly irregular pulse; clear chest; no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: ECG AF rate 118; eGFR 32; creatinine 145; INR 1.0; LFT normal; Hb 124, platelets 220; TFT normal
data_table.Medications: Perindopril, furosemide, atorvastatin

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation choice?

options.text: Rivaroxaban 15 mg daily as the preferred once-daily DOAC in CKD stage 3b to improve adherence and minimise bleed risk
Warfarin to a target INR of 2.0 to 3.0 because all DOACs are contraindicated when eGFR is below 50 mL/min
Dabigatran 110 mg twice daily as the preferred DOAC in renal impairment because of available reversal with idarucizumab
Apixaban 5 mg twice daily (or 2.5 mg twice daily if 2 of 3 dose-reduction criteria are met) as the preferred DOAC in CKD stage 3b
Aspirin 100 mg daily as monotherapy because anticoagulation carries unacceptable risk in CKD stage 3b regardless of CHA2DS2-VA score

subtopic_detail: Hyperkalaemia management with ECG changes
stem: You are the medicine registrar called to ED to review a 72-year-old man with chronic kidney disease stage 4 who presents with weakness and palpitations. He is on ramipril, spironolactone and recently started trimethoprim for a UTI. He has not been able to take his medications today. He has no chest pain. Bloods returned 5 minutes ago. The ED ECG was taken urgently and is in front of you. He is haemodynamically stable. He is not in cardiac arrest.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 122/72, HR 58 (regular), RR 18, SpO2 98% RA, T 36.6
data_table.Examination: Generalised weakness, no focal neurology, no cardiac murmur, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: K 7.2 mmol/L, urea 28, creatinine 320, eGFR 16, Na 134, HCO3 17, glucose 6.8; ECG: peaked T waves, widened QRS 132 ms, no P waves
data_table.Medications: Ramipril 10 mg, spironolactone 25 mg, trimethoprim 300 mg (started 3 days ago)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management sequence?

options.text: Oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate 30 g and observe over the next 4 hours before any other intervention or further blood test review
Intravenous insulin 10 units with 50 mL of 50% dextrose alone; no calcium gluconate because the patient is haemodynamically stable currently
Intravenous calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL over 2 to 3 minutes for membrane stabilisation, then insulin/dextrose and salbutamol nebuliser
Urgent haemodialysis as the first intervention without calcium gluconate, insulin or salbutamol while waiting for vascular access placement
Furosemide 80 mg IV bolus to promote kaliuresis as the first-line intervention before considering calcium gluconate or shifting therapy

subtopic_detail: Follow up after resection of a catecholamine secreting tumour in a young adult
stem: A 28-year-old man has had a unilateral catecholamine secreting adrenal tumour removed. Histology is confirmed, his blood pressure has normalised and he has no family history of endocrine disease. He asks what happens next.

data_table.Examination: Well, normotensive, wound healing, no palpable mass
data_table.Investigations: Plasma metanephrines within the reference range six weeks after surgery

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Offer referral for germline mutation testing
Offer annual computed tomography of the abdomen
Discharge him from specialist follow up entirely
Repeat the metanephrines only if symptoms recur
Screen his parents with plasma metanephrines now

subtopic_detail: Acute ischaemic stroke thrombolysis decision
stem: You are the medicine registrar reviewing a 68-year-old man brought to ED by ambulance with right-sided weakness and expressive aphasia. His last known well time was 2 hours 30 minutes ago. He is on apixaban 5 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation, last dose 14 hours ago. He has no recent surgery, no head trauma, no known intracranial pathology and no recent bleed. His NIHSS is 14. Non-contrast CT brain shows no haemorrhage and no large established infarct; CTA shows a left middle cerebral artery M1 occlusion.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 172/96, HR 84 (irregular), RR 16, SpO2 97% RA, T 36.6, BSL 6.2
data_table.Examination: Right hemiplegia, expressive aphasia, right facial droop, NIHSS 14, GCS 14
data_table.Investigations: Non-contrast CT: no haemorrhage, ASPECTS 9; CTA: left M1 occlusion; INR 1.0; FBC, UEC normal; platelets 248
data_table.Medications: Apixaban 5 mg BD (last dose 14 hours ago); perindopril 5 mg; atorvastatin 40 mg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Administer IV alteplase 0.9 mg/kg over 1 hour and proceed to endovascular thrombectomy without delay for the proximal large vessel occlusion
Administer intravenous heparin infusion targeting an APTT of 60 to 80 seconds and monitor for clinical improvement over the next 4 hours observation
Reverse apixaban with andexanet alfa and then administer IV tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg single bolus; defer thrombectomy until thrombolysis is complete
Administer aspirin 300 mg orally and admit to stroke unit; defer mechanical thrombectomy because the time window has been exceeded for reperfusion
Withhold thrombolysis due to DOAC use within 48 hours; proceed directly to endovascular thrombectomy for the proven large vessel occlusion

subtopic_detail: Early prosthetic valve endocarditis empiric therapy
stem: You are the medical registrar admitting a 58-year-old man with two weeks of fever, malaise, anorexia and night sweats. He had a mechanical mitral valve replacement eight months ago for rheumatic mitral regurgitation. On examination he is febrile, looks unwell and has a new pansystolic murmur at the apex that was not documented at his recent valve clinic visit four weeks ago. There are no peripheral stigmata of endocarditis. He has no penicillin allergy. Blood cultures have been drawn from two separate sites and are pending.

data_table.Examination: New pansystolic murmur loudest at apex; clear lungs; no peripheral oedema; no splinter haemorrhages or Janeway lesions on inspection
data_table.Investigations: WCC 14, CRP 180, creatinine 95, lactate 1.4; transthoracic echocardiogram shows 8 mm vegetation on prosthetic mitral valve with mild paravalvular regurgitation
data_table.Medications: Warfarin INR target 2.5 to 3.5; bisoprolol 5 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin combination tailored to streptococcal and enterococcal native valve coverage with no anti-staphylococcal cover
Intravenous vancomycin combined with gentamicin and oral rifampicin to cover the staphylococcal pathogens of early prosthetic valve endocarditis
Intravenous ceftriaxone monotherapy for streptococcus viridans cover until blood culture sensitivities return to guide narrower targeted treatment
Intravenous vancomycin monotherapy without combination synergy or rifampicin while awaiting blood culture sensitivities and surgical team discussion next day
Defer empirical antibiotics until two further blood cultures and serology have returned to ensure narrowest appropriate spectrum based on confirmed organism identification

subtopic_detail: Acute pyelonephritis non-severe oral therapy
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 24-year-old non-pregnant woman with 24 hours of fever, right loin pain and dysuria. She has been able to tolerate oral fluids without vomiting and remains haemodynamically stable. She has no past medical history, no allergies, no recent antibiotics and no urological abnormality. She is sexually active and her partner has no symptoms. Urinalysis shows leucocyte esterase strongly positive, nitrites positive and microscopic haematuria. Midstream urine has been sent for culture and sensitivity.

data_table.Examination: Right costovertebral angle tenderness; abdomen otherwise soft; well perfused; chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis leucocyte++, nitrite+, blood+; serum lactate 1.4; creatinine 70, eGFR above 90; urine pregnancy test negative
data_table.Medications: Nil

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic plan?

options.text: Oral trimethoprim 300 mg once daily for three days as standard short-course empirical treatment for uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection therapy
Oral nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for five days, which is the preferred narrow-spectrum agent for upper urinary tract infection in this clinical setting
Intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily for 14 days through ambulatory care intravenous service even in haemodynamically stable patients tolerating oral fluids
Oral cefalexin 500 mg four times daily for 10 days with follow up at 48 hours to confirm clinical and biochemical improvement on therapy
Wait for the midstream urine culture sensitivity report before commencing any antibiotic to avoid inappropriate empirical therapy and selection of resistance

subtopic_detail: Refeeding syndrome prevention
stem: You are the general medical registrar admitting a 65-year-old man with alcohol use disorder who has not eaten for five days, drinking only fortified wine. He has lost 15 percent of his body weight over the past three months. He looks cachectic with temporal wasting. He is alert and orientated and his observations are stable. The nutrition team has asked you to write the initial refeeding plan and electrolyte replacement orders before any oral or enteral nutrition is commenced on the ward today.

data_table.Examination: Cachectic with temporal wasting; soft abdomen; no peripheral oedema; alert and orientated
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.2, magnesium 0.65, phosphate 0.75, sodium 138, glucose 4.2, albumin 28, INR 1.2
data_table.Medications: Nil regular on admission; pabrinex prescribed pending decision on timing

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial refeeding plan?

options.text: Give intravenous thiamine, correct potassium, magnesium and phosphate, then commence nutrition at 10 kcal/kg/day with daily electrolyte monitoring and slow titration
Commence a standard 1500 kilocalorie oral diet immediately and replace electrolytes only if levels fall below the laboratory reference range during ward observation
Use 10 percent dextrose intravenously as the sole nutritional source for the first 72 hours and defer enteral feeding until biochemistry has fully normalised after admission
Insert a nasogastric tube and run full-strength polymeric feed at 80 mL per hour from day one to meet his estimated full caloric requirement immediately on the ward
Defer all nutrition for a further five days while focusing solely on alcohol withdrawal management and hydration before any oral or enteral feeding plan is restarted

subtopic_detail: Cushing's syndrome first-line screening
stem: You are the endocrinology registrar reviewing a 45-year-old woman with a six-month history of progressive central weight gain, easy bruising on the forearms, proximal muscle weakness on standing from a chair, and new-onset hypertension requiring two antihypertensive medications. She has facial plethora and purple abdominal striae 1.5 cm wide. She has no exogenous corticosteroid use confirmed on pharmacy records. She takes no medications likely to affect cortisol metabolism. She is keen to know what tests will confirm or exclude hypercortisolism today.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 158/96 on two agents, HR 80, weight 92 kg, BMI 33
data_table.Examination: Moon facies; supraclavicular fat pad; purple striae over abdomen and thighs; proximal weakness in hip flexion grade 4/5
data_table.Investigations: HbA1c 7.2 percent, fasting glucose 8.1; FBC and UEC unremarkable; ACTH and a.m. cortisol not yet performed
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 5 mg daily; amlodipine 5 mg daily; nil corticosteroids confirmed by pharmacy record

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line screening test?

options.text: Random midday serum cortisol drawn during the next clinic visit as the initial screening test before considering further dynamic investigations of the axis
Serum adrenocorticotrophic hormone level at 09:00 as the single first-line test that distinguishes ACTH-dependent and ACTH-independent forms of Cushing syndrome
Late-night salivary cortisol on two consecutive nights collected at home with point-of-collection swabs and laboratory cortisol measurement on the samples
Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary gland with gadolinium contrast performed prior to any biochemical screening to identify a pituitary corticotroph adenoma
Insulin tolerance test performed in the endocrine day-stay unit as the first-line dynamic screening method to assess hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis function

subtopic_detail: Primary aldosteronism confirmatory testing
stem: You are the medical registrar in the hypertension clinic reviewing a 38-year-old man with three-drug resistant hypertension and persistent hypokalaemia despite oral potassium replacement. His aldosterone to renin ratio screening test taken in the morning after his usual antihypertensives were optimised to non-interfering agents has returned strongly positive. He has no headaches, palpitations or sweating. CT of the adrenal glands has not yet been arranged and he is keen to know what comes next before any imaging or surgical opinion is sought.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 162/100 on three drugs, HR 76, BMI 28, no orthostatic drop
data_table.Examination: Cardiovascular examination unremarkable; no abdominal bruit; no Cushingoid features; reflexes brisk symmetric
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.1 (on supplements 40 mmol daily), sodium 142, creatinine 80; aldosterone:renin ratio 110 (normal under 30); morning aldosterone 720 pmol/L, plasma renin 6.5 mU/L
data_table.Medications: Doxazosin 4 mg daily; verapamil 240 mg daily; hydralazine 50 mg three times daily; potassium chloride 40 mmol daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Proceed directly to CT scan of the adrenal glands today to identify a unilateral adenoma before any confirmatory dynamic biochemical testing has been completed
Refer immediately for adrenal vein sampling for lateralisation of aldosterone secretion before any dynamic confirmation of autonomous aldosterone production is undertaken
Commence empirical spironolactone 100 mg daily as therapeutic confirmation without further biochemical or radiological investigation in this resistant hypertension setting
Repeat the aldosterone:renin ratio test in three months on the same medications without confirmation testing and review the trend before any further escalation occurs
Perform saline suppression testing under medical supervision in the day-stay unit to confirm autonomous aldosterone secretion before any imaging or surgical consultation

subtopic_detail: Apixaban major intracerebral haemorrhage reversal
stem: You are the medical registrar called to ED to assess a 78-year-old woman on apixaban 5 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation who has presented with three hours of sudden headache, right hemiparesis and reduced consciousness following a fall at home. CT brain shows a 28 mL left basal ganglia haemorrhage with intraventricular extension. Her last apixaban dose was four hours ago according to her dosette. She has no current anti-fibrinolytic or platelet inhibitor in addition to her DOAC. Her renal function is stable from clinic two weeks ago.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 178/102, HR 78, RR 18, SpO2 96 percent RA, GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5), T 36.6
data_table.Examination: Right hemiparesis 2/5; right facial droop; dysarthria; left pupil 3 mm reactive; chest clear
data_table.Investigations: CT 28 mL left basal ganglia haemorrhage with intraventricular extension; INR 1.1; APTT 38; creatinine 90 (eGFR 56); Hb 124; platelets 220
data_table.Medications: Apixaban 5 mg twice daily; metoprolol 25 mg twice daily; rosuvastatin 20 mg nocte

lead_in: What is the most appropriate reversal agent?

options.text: Intravenous idarucizumab 5 g given as two consecutive 2.5 g boluses as the targeted reversal antibody binding the active anticoagulant directly in the circulation
Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate 25 to 50 units/kg intravenously as the reversal option when andexanet alfa is unavailable in the local hospital
Vitamin K 10 mg intravenously combined with fresh frozen plasma four units transfused over four hours through a peripheral large-bore intravenous access
Protamine sulfate 50 mg intravenously over 10 minutes administered as the recommended reversal agent for any factor Xa inhibitor major bleeding presentation
Activated charcoal 50 g orally via nasogastric tube after intubation as the sole intervention to reduce ongoing absorption of the most recent apixaban dose

subtopic_detail: Hour-1 bundle in septic shock
stem: A 68-year-old man is brought to your emergency department from his nursing home with 24 hours of fevers, confusion and reduced oral intake. He has type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and previously had a transurethral prostatectomy. On arrival he is hypotensive, tachycardic, and confused. He is unable to provide a coherent history. The triage nurse has placed two large-bore peripheral cannulas. You are the ED registrar leading the resuscitation.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.9, BP 88/52, HR 118, RR 26, SpO2 92 percent RA, GCS 13 (E3V4M6)
data_table.Examination: Confused, mottled lower limbs, mild suprapubic tenderness; chest clear; warm peripheries
data_table.Investigations: Bedside lactate 4.2 mmol/L; VBG pH 7.30, bicarbonate 17; finger-prick glucose 11.4 mmol/L
data_table.Medications: Metformin, perindopril, atorvastatin, tamsulosin

lead_in: Within the first hour, what is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Obtain blood cultures, administer 30 mL/kg crystalloid, and commence empiric intravenous antibiotics only once culture results return
Obtain blood and urine cultures, give empiric intravenous antibiotics within an hour, administer 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid, and recheck lactate at 2 hours
Commence peripheral noradrenaline infusion without initial fluid resuscitation given the hypotension and rising lactate today
Administer a 1 L crystalloid fluid challenge and reassess the need for intravenous antibiotics only after blood pressure normalises
Insert a urinary catheter for source control, perform CT abdomen pelvis, and commence antibiotics only after imaging confirms the source

subtopic_detail: Empiric antibiotic regimen in IVDU native valve IE
stem: A 38-year-old man presents to your emergency department with 2 weeks of fevers, night sweats, and weight loss. He uses intravenous heroin and admits to recent injecting through the femoral vein. Examination shows a new pansystolic murmur loudest at the lower left sternal edge, splinter haemorrhages on two fingernails, and bilateral basal crackles. You suspect infective endocarditis and are awaiting an urgent transthoracic echocardiogram. Three sets of blood cultures from separate sites have been drawn.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.6, BP 110/72, HR 108, RR 22, SpO2 94 percent RA
data_table.Examination: New PSM 3/6 at LLSE, splinter haemorrhages, JVP elevated 5 cm, bibasal crackles
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18.4 (neutrophils 14.2), CRP 220, Hb 102, platelets 145, creatinine 95; ECG sinus tachycardia; CXR pulmonary congestion with small bilateral effusions; troponin 24 (mildly raised); blood cultures pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empiric antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin alone pending culture results and consideration of surgical management
Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate while awaiting echocardiogram and definitive blood culture results
Intravenous flucloxacillin plus intravenous gentamicin pending culture results and echocardiogram
Intravenous ceftriaxone alone with no additional empirical gram-positive coverage at this stage
Intravenous vancomycin alone with no additional empirical gram-negative coverage at this stage

subtopic_detail: Guillain-Barre syndrome first-line immunotherapy
stem: A 42-year-old man presents to your emergency department with 5 days of progressive bilateral leg weakness that started in his calves and has ascended to his thighs. He now reports tingling in both hands. He had a brief gastroenteritis illness 2 weeks ago. On examination he has symmetric proximal and distal leg weakness 3/5, areflexia in lower limbs and reduced upper-limb reflexes. He can still walk slowly with assistance. Forced vital capacity is 28 mL/kg. Sensation is intact.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/78, HR 88, RR 18, SpO2 99 percent RA, T 36.8, FVC 28 mL/kg
data_table.Examination: Symmetric flaccid lower limb weakness 3/5; areflexia LL; reduced UL reflexes; no bulbar signs; no autonomic features yet
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal; UEC normal; CK 220; CSF protein 1.4 g/L, WCC 2 x10^6/L; nerve conduction studies show demyelinating pattern; MRI spine pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line disease-modifying treatment?

options.text: High-dose intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days as initial immunomodulation
Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily with proton pump inhibitor cover and slow taper over 12 weeks
Therapeutic plasma exchange as the most cost-effective Australian first-line treatment for this presentation
Intravenous immunoglobulin 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 consecutive days targeting a total dose of 2 g/kg
Pyridostigmine 30 mg every 6 hours with regular cardiopulmonary monitoring during titration

subtopic_detail: Intravenous iron when oral fails with time-limited surgical window
stem: A 48-year-old woman presents to your GP clinic with 3 months of fatigue and breathlessness on exertion. She has heavy menstrual bleeding for 18 months, takes ibuprofen frequently for dysmenorrhoea, and has tried oral ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily for the past 8 weeks. She reports nausea and constipation on the oral iron and intermittent adherence. Her gynaecologist has referred her for endometrial ablation but the procedure is 6 weeks away.

data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae; no koilonychia; cardiovascular and respiratory examinations normal; mild ankle oedema
data_table.Investigations: Hb 88 g/L, MCV 70 fL, ferritin 8 mcg/L, transferrin saturation 7 percent, CRP 4; UEC normal; LFTs normal; coeliac serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue oral ferrous sulfate for another 12 weeks and recheck full blood count then
Switch to oral iron polymaltose complex 100 mg daily and review tolerance after 4 weeks
Arrange packed red cell transfusion of 2 units to correct the anaemia rapidly before surgery
Commence erythropoietin-stimulating agent subcutaneously 4-weekly until ferritin normalises
Arrange intravenous ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg infusion at the general practice infusion clinic

subtopic_detail: Giant cell arteritis with visual symptoms
stem: A 74-year-old woman presents to your ED with 2 weeks of new bilateral temporal headache and 2 days of intermittent transient monocular vision loss in the right eye lasting a few minutes each episode. She has 3 weeks of jaw claudication. She was diagnosed with polymyalgia rheumatica 6 months ago and is on prednisolone 5 mg daily. She has no diplopia and no focal neurological deficit. Fundoscopy is normal.

data_table.Examination: Tender thickened right temporal artery; reduced pulsation; visual acuity 6/6 both eyes; pupils equal reactive; visual fields intact at this moment; tongue normal
data_table.Investigations: ESR 110 mm/hr, CRP 96 mg/L; Hb 108, platelets 412; LFTs ALP mildly raised at 142; UEC normal; CT brain normal; carotid Doppler arranged
data_table.Medications: Prednisolone 5 mg daily; metformin; atorvastatin

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Administer intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days and arrange temporal artery biopsy within 14 days
Defer steroid escalation until the temporal artery biopsy result is available to avoid masking diagnosis
Increase oral prednisolone to 40 mg daily and arrange temporal artery biopsy within 4 weeks at the next available slot
Commence aspirin 100 mg daily without altering current prednisolone, and refer to ophthalmology outpatients
Arrange ultrasound of the temporal arteries as the sole confirmatory test and treat empirically based on the ultrasound alone

subtopic_detail: Acute adrenal crisis management in primary adrenal insufficiency
stem: A 58-year-old woman with known primary adrenal insufficiency presents to your ED with 24 hours of fever, vomiting, abdominal pain and lethargy. She has not been able to take her usual hydrocortisone 20 mg morning and 10 mg evening due to vomiting. She has type 1 diabetes, hypothyroidism, and a daughter with coeliac disease. She is hypotensive, drowsy and warm peripherally.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4, BP 78/45, HR 122, RR 24, SpO2 96 percent RA, GCS 13 (E3V4M6), BSL 3.2 mmol/L
data_table.Examination: Hyperpigmented skin and buccal mucosa, dry mucous membranes, soft non-peritonitic abdomen with mild epigastric tenderness; chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Na 124, K 5.8, glucose 3.2; creatinine 110 (baseline 70); CRP 84; lactate 3.2; FBC WCC 14.0; cortisol pending; urine ketones positive; CXR clear
data_table.Medications: Hydrocortisone 20/10, fludrocortisone 100 mcg, levothyroxine, insulin

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Withhold steroids until a random cortisol level is back to confirm the diagnosis before commencing therapy
Administer intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg stat plus intravenous 0.9 percent saline 1 L bolus and supplemental dextrose
Administer prednisolone 50 mg via nasogastric tube and commence intravenous saline once the prednisolone is absorbed
Administer intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg stat because it does not interfere with subsequent cortisol assay sampling
Commence noradrenaline infusion centrally before any glucocorticoid replacement to support blood pressure

subtopic_detail: Migraine prophylaxis with pregnancy planning
stem: A 36-year-old woman presents to your GP clinic for migraine prevention. She has had migraine with aura for 12 years, currently 6 attacks per month each lasting 8-12 hours. She had reasonable benefit from propranolol 40 mg twice daily for 3 months (cutting frequency to 3 per month) but stopped 4 weeks ago after fainting once during a 5 km run and developing exertional bradycardia. She has well-controlled asthma on Symbicort. She is planning pregnancy in the next 12 months.

data_table.Examination: Normal neurological examination including fundi; no focal deficit
data_table.Investigations: Recent thyroid normal; ECG sinus bradycardia 52 bpm without QT prolongation; FBC normal; pregnancy test negative
data_table.Medications: Stopped propranolol 4 weeks ago; using sumatriptan 50 mg PRN

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next preventive treatment?

options.text: Restart propranolol at a reduced dose of 20 mg twice daily and recommend avoidance of strenuous exercise altogether
Commence amitriptyline 25 mg nocte with explicit anti-cholinergic side effect counselling before her planned conception
Commence sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily as an effective and well-tolerated long-term preventive option
Commence topiramate 25 mg nocte with planned titration to 50 mg twice daily and pregnancy counselling
Commence verapamil 80 mg three times daily as an effective option for migraine with aura prevention

subtopic_detail: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes and trimethoprim trigger
stem: A 67-year-old man presents to your ED with palpitations and weakness for 12 hours. He has stage 4 CKD (baseline eGFR 22), heart failure with reduced EF, and type 2 diabetes. He takes ramipril 10 mg, spironolactone 25 mg, furosemide 40 mg, and metformin. He was recently started on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a UTI. Triage ECG shows tall peaked T waves and widening QRS.

data_table.Examination: Mild peripheral oedema; chest with bibasal crackles
data_table.Investigations: K 7.2 mmol/L, Na 138, urea 18, creatinine 320 (baseline 220), bicarbonate 18, glucose 6.4; VBG pH 7.30; ECG: tall peaked T waves V2-V6, QRS 132 ms, no P waves visible

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate first step?

options.text: Administer intravenous insulin 10 units in 50 percent dextrose 50 mL to shift potassium intracellularly
Administer salbutamol 10 mg nebulised over 10 minutes to shift potassium intracellularly via beta-2 receptors
Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol over 30 minutes to shift potassium intracellularly
Administer intravenous calcium gluconate 10 percent 10 mL over 2-5 minutes to stabilise the myocardial membrane
Administer sodium polystyrene sulfonate 30 g orally as the most effective first measure for total body potassium

subtopic_detail: Antibiotic choice for moderate COPD exacerbation in ED
stem: You are the medical registrar in the emergency department with a 68-year-old man presenting with 48 hours of worsening dyspnoea, increased sputum volume, and sputum purulence on a background of GOLD stage 3 COPD. He has had 2 exacerbations in the last year. He takes a long-acting bronchodilator and inhaled corticosteroid daily. He has no penicillin allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.2, HR 102, RR 24, SpO2 88 percent on air rising to 92 percent on 2 L/min nasal prongs, BP 138/82
data_table.Examination: Bilateral wheeze, accessory muscle use, no focal consolidation
data_table.Investigations: ABG on 2 L pH 7.36, PaCO2 50, PaO2 70, HCO3 28; CXR no consolidation; CRP 38; FBC normal
data_table.Medications: Tiotropium plus formoterol budesonide combined inhaler daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empiric antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Withhold antibiotics and treat with prednisolone 50 mg daily for 5 days alone given absence of fever
Oral azithromycin 500 mg daily for 5 days alongside oral prednisolone 50 mg daily for 5 days
Oral amoxicillin clavulanate 875 plus 125 mg twice daily for 5 days alongside oral prednisolone 50 mg daily for 5 days
Oral moxifloxacin 400 mg daily for 5 days alongside oral prednisolone 50 mg daily for 5 days
Oral amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 5 days alongside oral prednisolone 50 mg daily for 5 days

subtopic_detail: Occupational HIV postexposure prophylaxis timing and regimen
stem: You are the staff health registrar reviewing a 28-year-old nurse 2 hours after a deep needlestick injury from a hollow bore needle used on a patient who is HIV positive on antiretroviral therapy with a viral load over 50000 copies/mL. The nurse has no chronic illness and is currently well. The source patient is also hepatitis B and C negative.

data_table.Examination: Wound puncture to right index finger; no active bleeding now
data_table.Investigations: Baseline HIV antibody pending; baseline UEC, LFTs, FBC, beta-hCG normal; hepatitis B antibody titre 120 IU/L; source HIV viral load over 50000, hepatitis B and C negative
data_table.Medications: Combined oral contraceptive; baseline HIV testing in progress

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start a 28 day course of tenofovir disoproxil emtricitabine plus dolutegravir as recommended PEP within 72 hours of exposure
Defer PEP until source patient viral load is confirmed below 200 copies/mL by repeat testing within 24 hours
Start a 28 day course of zidovudine plus lamivudine as the recommended dual NRTI backbone in AU guidance
Provide written advice on signs of seroconversion without antiretroviral prophylaxis given the use of source antiretroviral therapy
Test source for HIV drug resistance before commencing any antiretroviral postexposure prophylaxis regimen

subtopic_detail: BP reduction target and agent in hypertensive emergency with end-organ damage
stem: You are the medical registrar in ED reviewing a 58-year-old man with severe headache, blurred vision, and acute breathlessness over 6 hours. His BP is 232/132 with no prior diagnosis of hypertension. He has bibasal crackles, a third heart sound, troponin elevation, and pulmonary oedema on chest X-ray.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 232/132, HR 118, RR 30, SpO2 92 percent on 4 L/min
data_table.Examination: Bibasal crackles, S3, raised JVP, no focal neurology, fundi show flame haemorrhages and papilloedema
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia, LV strain pattern; CXR pulmonary oedema; troponin 0.18 (upper limit 0.04); creatinine 142; urinalysis 2+ protein; CT brain unremarkable
data_table.Medications: Nil regular; today: IV furosemide 80 mg and nitrate sublingual given

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial BP reduction strategy?

options.text: Withhold further antihypertensive therapy until troponin trend confirms or excludes acute myocardial infarction
Reduce systolic BP to under 140 within the first hour with rapid bolus dosing of intravenous antihypertensive agents
Reduce systolic BP to under 100 over the next 4 hours using sodium nitroprusside at high titration step infusion
Start oral amlodipine 10 mg now and reassess at 1 hour expecting a stepwise reduction over the next 6 hours
Reduce mean arterial pressure by 20 to 25 percent over the first hour using an intravenous agent then aim 160/100 over the next several hours

subtopic_detail: Hour-1 bundle interventions in septic shock from urinary source
stem: You are the medical registrar called to the ward at 23 minutes after midnight to assess a 74-year-old woman day 1 admission for pyelonephritis. She has rigors, mottling, and altered mental state. Initial empirical antibiotics for pyelonephritis were given 3 hours ago but her condition has deteriorated.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.2, HR 132, RR 32, SpO2 94 percent on 4 L/min, BP 78/42
data_table.Examination: Mottled peripheries, cool, confused (GCS 13), right flank tenderness
data_table.Investigations: VBG lactate 4.8 pH 7.28 BE -8; WCC 21, neutrophils 18; CRP 280; creatinine 162 (baseline 78); urinalysis 4+ leucocytes, 3+ nitrites; blood cultures taken on admission and now
data_table.Medications: IV ceftriaxone 2 g daily started 3 hours ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next set of immediate interventions in the first hour from recognition of septic shock?

options.text: Crystalloid 10 mL/kg bolus and reassess; defer antibiotic broadening until repeat blood culture results are available tomorrow
Crystalloid 30 mL/kg bolus over the first hour, repeat blood cultures and lactate, broaden antibiotics, start vasopressor for MAP under 65
Transfer to ICU for invasive line placement before any fluid or antibiotic action is taken now on the ward
Administer hydrocortisone 200 mg IV before fluid bolus as first step in shock from any source in older adults
Start noradrenaline infusion immediately as first step before any fluid resuscitation in the setting of MAP under 65

subtopic_detail: Identifying the underlying mechanism of metabolic alkalosis with hypokalaemia
stem: You are the general medical registrar reviewing a 56-year-old woman with resistant hypertension despite three agents who has been intermittently using furosemide tablets sourced from her sister. She presents with weakness and muscle cramps over 1 week. She is normovolaemic on examination. She denies vomiting, laxative use, or recent diarrhoea.

data_table.Examination: Normal volume status, no oedema, no abdominal mass
data_table.Investigations: Na 138, K 2.6, Cl 88, HCO3 36, urea 6.8, creatinine 78; ABG pH 7.52 PaCO2 49 HCO3 36; urine chloride 32 mmol/L; urine sodium 64; renin and aldosterone pending
data_table.Medications: Perindopril, amlodipine, hydrochlorothiazide, and intermittent furosemide

lead_in: What is the most likely mechanism contributing to her metabolic alkalosis with hypokalaemia?

options.text: Primary hyperaldosteronism with autonomous adrenal aldosterone production driving the entire biochemical picture
Diuretic induced chloride and potassium loss producing a saline responsive chloride low metabolic alkalosis
Surreptitious vomiting with gastric acid loss producing chloride low metabolic alkalosis with low urine chloride
Bartter syndrome with congenital tubular dysfunction producing chronic chloride and potassium losses
Acute respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation accounting for the elevated bicarbonate and PaCO2

subtopic_detail: Induction therapy choice for newly diagnosed ANCA-associated vasculitis with renal involvement
stem: You are the general medical registrar admitting a 62-year-old man with 6 weeks of weight loss, sinusitis with crusting, haemoptysis, and progressive renal impairment over 3 weeks. He has no infection and is haemodynamically stable. ANCA testing is strongly positive for PR3. Renal biopsy shows pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis. He has a stable haemoglobin and no requirement for dialysis at present.

data_table.Examination: Nasal crusting; bilateral basal crackles; lower limb purpura sparse
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 320 (baseline 90), eGFR 18, urine red cell casts; PR3-ANCA strongly positive; chest CT pulmonary nodules; renal biopsy crescentic GN
data_table.Medications: Nil regular

lead_in: What is the most appropriate induction regimen?

options.text: Azathioprine plus oral prednisolone as the initial induction regimen with cyclophosphamide reserved for relapse only
Plasma exchange alone as primary induction therapy when renal involvement and pulmonary haemorrhage are present
Pulse methylprednisolone monotherapy at 1 g IV daily for 3 days as adequate induction therapy in renal involvement
Rituximab plus high dose glucocorticoid as induction therapy with rapid steroid tapering protocol over the next several months
Mycophenolate mofetil plus oral prednisolone as the recommended first-line induction therapy in PR3 positive AAV
