subtopic_detail: Correction rate in chronic hyponatraemia with mild neurological symptoms
stem: You are the medical registrar admitting a 72-year-old woman with 2 weeks of progressive nausea, gait unsteadiness, and a fall today. She has been on a thiazide for 6 months and recently started taking sertraline 2 weeks ago. She has no seizure, no severe headache, and remains alert. She is clinically euvolaemic and well hydrated.

data_table.Examination: Alert, ataxic gait, no focal neurology, euvolaemic mucous membranes
data_table.Investigations: Na 116, K 3.6, urea 4.2, creatinine 78, glucose 5.4, TSH normal, cortisol AM 320; urine osmolality 480, urine sodium 64, plasma osmolality 248
data_table.Medications: Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily; sertraline 50 mg daily (started 2 weeks ago); calcium and vitamin D

lead_in: What is the most appropriate correction strategy over the next 24 hours?

options.text: Aim to raise serum sodium by 4 to 6 mmol/L in the first 6 hours then no more than 10 mmol/L over 24 hours with frequent reassessment
Restrict fluids to 800 mL daily without changing existing medications and reassess sodium tomorrow morning
Start hypertonic saline infusion targeting a serum sodium rise of 1 to 2 mmol/L per hour throughout the next 12 hours
Aim to normalise serum sodium to over 135 mmol/L within the first 24 hours using 3 percent hypertonic saline boluses
Withhold all fluid replacement and observe with hourly neurological assessment for the next 24 hours

subtopic_detail: Preoperative pharmacological preparation for phaeochromocytoma
stem: You are the endocrinology registrar planning preoperative care for a 48-year-old woman with confirmed adrenal phaeochromocytoma on biochemistry (24 hour fractionated metanephrines 5 times upper limit) and a 5 cm right adrenal mass on CT. She has episodic headache, palpitations, and sweating. Her resting BP is 158/92 with paroxysms to 220/120. She has had no cardiac events and her echocardiogram shows normal LV function.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 158/92 with paroxysms to 220/120; HR 90 baseline, 130 during paroxysm
data_table.Examination: No tremor at rest; no thyroid enlargement; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: 24 hour fractionated metanephrines 5 times upper limit; CT adrenal 5 cm right mass; ECG sinus rhythm; echocardiogram normal
data_table.Medications: Nil regular cardiovascular medications

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step in preoperative preparation?

options.text: Commence phenoxybenzamine and titrate over 2 to 3 weeks before introducing a beta blocker if tachycardia persists
Commence amlodipine 5 mg daily as a calcium channel blocker first-line before considering more specific therapy
Proceed to surgical resection within the next week without further pharmacological preoperative preparation today
Commence labetalol 100 mg twice daily as a combined alpha and beta blocker for outpatient preoperative preparation
Commence atenolol 50 mg daily first to control the resting tachycardia and add alpha blocker if BP control is incomplete

subtopic_detail: Differentiating ectopic ACTH from pituitary Cushing disease using dynamic and imaging tests
stem: You are the endocrinology registrar reviewing a 51-year-old man with 8 weeks of rapidly progressive proximal weakness, central weight gain, refractory hypokalaemia, glucose intolerance, and now bilateral lower limb oedema. He has a 40 pack-year smoking history. His skin is hyperpigmented but he has no thin skin or purple striae. Initial screening confirms ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome. He has commenced ketoconazole while workup proceeds.

data_table.Examination: Central adiposity; hyperpigmentation of palmar creases; bilateral oedema; no abdominal striae
data_table.Investigations: 24 hour urine cortisol 5 times upper limit; midnight salivary cortisol elevated; ACTH 280 (normal under 50); 8 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression: cortisol 980 (under 50 percent suppression); pituitary MRI no adenoma; CT chest 18 mm left lower lobe nodule; potassium 2.6 on supplementation
data_table.Medications: Ketoconazole 200 mg twice daily; potassium chloride 600 mg twice daily; perindopril 10 mg daily

lead_in: Which feature most strongly favours ectopic ACTH syndrome rather than pituitary Cushing disease as the cause?

options.text: Absence of a visible pituitary lesion on MRI of the sella reliably rules out pituitary Cushing disease entirely
Hyperpigmentation of palmar creases without other findings is itself diagnostic of ectopic ACTH syndrome in adults
A 24 hour urine cortisol level of more than 4 times the upper limit reliably distinguishes ectopic from pituitary disease
Failure of cortisol to suppress below 50 percent after high dose dexamethasone in combination with marked hypokalaemia and rapid onset
ACTH level over 100 picograms/mL is itself characteristic of pituitary Cushing rather than ectopic ACTH syndrome

subtopic_detail: First-line imaging for suspected ureteric calculus in adult with single haematuria episode
stem: You are the ED registrar reviewing a 40-year-old man with acute left flank pain radiating to the groin, microscopic haematuria, and no fever. He has no prior stone history. His eGFR is 88 mL/min/1.73 m2 and bedside ultrasound shows mild left hydronephrosis. He is otherwise well, normotensive, and tolerating oral fluids.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8, HR 92, RR 18, BP 124/76, SpO2 99 percent
data_table.Examination: Left flank tenderness, no rebound, no palpable mass, no peritonism
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis 2+ blood, no nitrites, no leucocytes; WCC 8.6; eGFR 88; bedside US mild left hydronephrosis
data_table.Medications: Nil regular

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line definitive imaging?

options.text: Plain KUB film alone, sufficient to confirm a radiopaque calculus and guide initial treatment now
Magnetic resonance urogram, providing accurate stone detection without any ionising radiation exposure
Intravenous urogram with contrast, providing functional and anatomical imaging in a single examination
Repeat formal radiology renal ultrasound with full bladder views and Doppler resistive index measurement
Non-contrast low-dose CT KUB, the first-line investigation for adult suspected ureteric calculus disease

subtopic_detail: First-line pharmacotherapy for newly diagnosed trigeminal neuralgia in 58-year-old woman
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 58-year-old woman with two months of brief electric shock pains in the right cheek triggered by chewing and brushing teeth. Episodes last seconds and resolve completely between attacks. She has no facial numbness, no weakness, and a normal neurological examination. She has no liver disease, normal renal function, and no allergy to anticonvulsants. MRI brain reported as no demyelination and a normal trigeminal nerve.

data_table.Examination: Trigger zone right cheek to light touch, no sensory deficit, normal corneal reflex, normal jaw jerk
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain: no demyelination, no vascular loop on trigeminal nerve; LFTs ALT 22; eGFR 90; Na 138
data_table.Past history: Nil regular medication; no Asian heritage HLA-B*1502 risk; no allergy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Gabapentin 300 mg three times daily titrated up over two weeks against pain and sedation tolerance
Amitriptyline 25 mg at night titrated upwards as needed for trigeminal neuralgia symptomatic relief
Carbamazepine 100 mg twice daily titrated up against symptoms with sodium and LFT monitoring
Oral paracetamol modified release 1330 mg three times daily as the first-line analgesic regimen
Refer for microvascular decompression surgery before any pharmacological trial as definitive treatment

subtopic_detail: Diagnostic confirmation manoeuvre and treatment for posterior canal BPPV in 62-year-old
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 62-year-old man with three weeks of brief positional vertigo on rolling over in bed and looking up. Episodes last around 30 seconds, resolve completely, and are accompanied by nausea. He has no hearing loss, no tinnitus, no continuous unsteadiness, and no neurological deficit. His cervical spine has no rotational restriction and he has no significant carotid disease.

data_table.Examination: Cranial nerves normal, no nystagmus at rest, no cerebellar signs, normal gait, no lateralising neurological signs
data_table.Investigations: Routine bloods normal; no imaging performed; audiometry not yet done
data_table.Past history: Hypertension on ramipril; no recent head injury

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next combined diagnostic and therapeutic manoeuvre?

options.text: Order MRI internal auditory meatus to exclude vestibular schwannoma and review imaging report
Trial regular oral prochlorperazine 5 mg three times daily for two weeks for vestibular sedation
Refer to ENT for diagnostic vestibular testing including videonystagmography and rotational chair tests
Perform Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre and if positive then apply Epley canalith repositioning manoeuvre
Prescribe vestibular rehabilitation home exercise program alone and review four weeks later in clinic

subtopic_detail: Saddle anaesthesia and urinary retention with new lower back pain requires urgent imaging
stem: You are the ED registrar reviewing a 48-year-old man with three days of severe lower back pain after lifting at work. He now describes new perineal numbness, difficulty initiating urination, and reduced erection. Bladder scan shows 700 mL post-void residual. Examination confirms saddle anaesthesia, reduced anal tone, and bilateral leg weakness. Reflexes are reduced at the ankles. He has no fever and no systemic illness.

data_table.Examination: Saddle anaesthesia, reduced anal tone, bilateral leg weakness power 4/5, absent ankle jerks, normal plantars
data_table.Investigations: Bladder scan 700 mL post-void residual; WCC 9.2; CRP 6; no fever
data_table.Setting: Tertiary hospital with MRI 24/7 available; spinal team on call

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Outpatient lumbar spine X-ray with flexion and extension views to assess instability and review in clinic
Lumbar puncture with measurement of opening pressure and cell count and biochemistry analysis
Outpatient CT lumbar spine within 48 hours, scheduled through GP referral pathway after discharge
Outpatient nerve conduction studies in two weeks to assess for peripheral neuropathy or radiculopathy
Urgent whole lumbosacral spine MRI within hours to confirm cauda equina compression for surgery

subtopic_detail: Single attack of monocular vision loss with pain on eye movement and normal fundoscopy
stem: You are the ED registrar reviewing a 28-year-old woman with two days of progressive blurred vision in the right eye with pain on eye movement. Visual acuity is 6/24 right and 6/6 left with a right relative afferent pupillary defect. Fundoscopy is normal in both eyes. There is no headache, no fever, and no systemic symptoms. She has no prior neurological episodes and is otherwise well.

data_table.Examination: Right RAPD, reduced colour vision right, normal fundoscopy bilaterally, normal cranial nerves otherwise, no cerebellar or long tract signs
data_table.Investigations: Routine bloods unremarkable; OCT not yet performed
data_table.Past history: Nil regular medication; no prior optic or neurological event

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Visual field testing with Humphrey perimetry in outpatient clinic in two weeks alongside OCT
Urgent CT brain with contrast to exclude intracranial mass lesion as the diagnostic next step
MRI brain and orbits with contrast to assess for demyelinating lesions and confirm optic neuritis
Routine outpatient ophthalmology review in six weeks with no imaging pending symptom progression
Empiric oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 14 days as immediate treatment without imaging input

subtopic_detail: Pharmacological management of acute idiopathic facial nerve palsy at 36 hours of onset
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 36-year-old man with 36 hours of right-sided facial weakness affecting forehead, eyelid, and corner of mouth. He cannot fully close the right eye and has subjective hyperacusis. There is no vesicular rash on the ear or palate, no hearing loss, and no other neurological deficit. He is otherwise well, has no diabetes, no immunosuppression, and is not pregnant.

data_table.Examination: House-Brackmann grade IV right LMN facial palsy, intact corneal reflex, no vesicles, normal otoscopy bilaterally, normal taste anteriorly
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 5.8 mmol/L; HbA1c not yet done; no further imaging
data_table.Past history: Nil regular medication; no recent zoster or VZV exposure

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological management?

options.text: Topical aciclovir cream to the affected side three times daily for two weeks as antiviral monotherapy
Oral valaciclovir 1 g three times daily for one week as antiviral monotherapy and outpatient review
Intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for three days inpatient with cardiac monitoring after admission
Oral prednisolone 50 mg daily for 10 days commenced within 72 hours of symptom onset with eye care
Combined oral prednisolone 50 mg daily plus oral aciclovir 800 mg five times daily for 10 days now

subtopic_detail: Choice of biologic for severe eosinophilic asthma uncontrolled on triple inhaled therapy in adult
stem: You are the respiratory registrar reviewing a 42-year-old non-smoking woman with severe asthma referred from her GP. She remains symptomatic with two hospitalisations in 12 months despite high-dose ICS-LABA plus tiotropium and good adherence. Blood eosinophils are 540 cells/microL, FeNO 65 ppb, total IgE 110 IU/mL, and she has nasal polyps. No specific aeroallergen sensitisation is documented. She has no parasitic infection risk and is not pregnant.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8, HR 80, RR 18, BP 124/78, SpO2 98 percent
data_table.Examination: Mild end-expiratory wheeze, nasal polyps on rhinoscopy, no clubbing
data_table.Investigations: Blood eosinophils 540 cells/microL; FeNO 65 ppb; total IgE 110 IU/mL; spirometry FEV1 62 percent predicted; specific IgE panel negative for perennial allergens
data_table.Medications: ICS-LABA 1000 mcg/250 mcg twice daily, tiotropium 5 mcg daily, montelukast 10 mg daily

lead_in: Which biologic is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Omalizumab subcutaneous monthly dosed by weight and total IgE level as anti-IgE biologic first choice
Mepolizumab subcutaneous 100 mg every four weeks as IL-5 biologic monotherapy ongoing
Reslizumab IV monthly weight-based dosing for severe eosinophilic asthma as the next step now
Benralizumab subcutaneous every eight weeks after loading as IL-5 receptor antibody monotherapy
Dupilumab subcutaneous every two weeks for severe type 2 asthma with nasal polyps as combined indication

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing isolated polymyalgia rheumatica from giant cell arteritis overlap on presentation
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 72-year-old woman with three weeks of bilateral shoulder and hip girdle pain with morning stiffness over an hour. She also describes a new bitemporal headache that has worsened over five days, jaw claudication after eating tough foods, and a single brief episode of right monocular blurred vision two days ago. There is no rash, no fever, and no joint swelling. ESR is 102 and CRP is 88.

data_table.Examination: Limited shoulder and hip range with pain, no synovitis, mild bitemporal scalp tenderness, no visual deficit on examination, palpable temporal arteries with reduced pulsation right
data_table.Investigations: ESR 102 mm/hr; CRP 88 mg/L; Hb 112; platelets 410; LFTs ALP 180 with normal bilirubin; eGFR 78
data_table.Past history: Nil regular medication; no recent infection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 15 mg daily for PMR symptoms with rapid taper over six weeks as monotherapy outpatient
Oral NSAID such as celecoxib 200 mg twice daily and book temporal artery biopsy in two weeks for diagnosis
Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily and arrange temporal artery biopsy within 14 days of treatment start
Arrange outpatient rheumatology referral within four weeks without initiating any steroid before assessment
Intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for three days for monocular visual loss already established prior

subtopic_detail: Empiric antibiotic choice for suspected prosthetic valve endocarditis
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 64-year-old man with 3 weeks of fevers, weight loss, and night sweats. He had a mechanical aortic valve replacement 14 months ago. Two sets of blood cultures taken 30 minutes apart are pending. His observations are stable and there is no peripheral stigmata of endocarditis. A transthoracic echocardiogram shows a possible 6 mm vegetation on the prosthetic aortic valve and trivial regurgitation. He has no penicillin allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.6, HR 96, BP 124/68 mmHg, SpO2 98 percent
data_table.Bloods: WCC 12.4 x10^9/L, CRP 88 mg/L, creatinine 92 micromol/L
data_table.Examination: Mechanical second heart sound, no peripheral stigmata, no embolic phenomena
data_table.Imaging: TTE: possible 6 mm vegetation on prosthetic aortic valve, trivial AR, normal LV function

lead_in: Which empiric antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.8 g 4-hourly plus gentamicin 1 mg/kg 8-hourly as initial therapy
Intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g 4-hourly plus benzylpenicillin 1.8 g 4-hourly plus gentamicin
Intravenous vancomycin plus gentamicin plus rifampicin pending blood culture and susceptibility
Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily monotherapy until blood cultures result and adjust thereafter
Oral linezolid 600 mg twice daily monotherapy with outpatient transthoracic review in 1 week

subtopic_detail: Application of the sepsis hour-1 bundle in suspected community-acquired sepsis
stem: You are the emergency registrar reviewing a 58-year-old woman with 24 hours of dysuria, loin pain, and rigors. She presents looking unwell, mottled peripheries, capillary refill 3 seconds. Her observations on triage 15 minutes ago triggered an emergency response, and no antibiotics or fluids have yet been given. She is fully alert. She has no documented antibiotic allergy and her usual medications are amlodipine and metformin.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.1, HR 124, BP 86/52 mmHg, RR 24, SpO2 95 percent room air
data_table.Bloods: WCC 18.6 x10^9/L, lactate 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 168 micromol/L (baseline 90)
data_table.Examination: Tender right flank, no peritonism, peripheries mottled, mentation intact

lead_in: Within the first hour, which action is most important to perform first?

options.text: Administer empiric intravenous gentamicin and ampicillin within 1 hour after taking blood cultures
Order computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis before any further escalation or therapy
Wait for urine culture susceptibility results before commencing any empiric antibiotic therapy
Commence intravenous noradrenaline immediately at 0.1 microgram/kg/min as first-line resuscitation
Provide 1 L of 5 percent dextrose intravenously as bolus over 30 minutes for volume expansion

subtopic_detail: Recognition and surgical urgency of necrotising fasciitis using clinical and LRINEC features
stem: You are the surgical registrar called to the emergency department to review a 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes who has 18 hours of severe pain in the right leg out of proportion to the limited erythema. He has had two previous episodes of cellulitis treated with oral antibiotics. He is increasingly distressed by the pain and his observations are deteriorating. There is a small skin break over the shin from a gardening injury 2 days ago.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.0, HR 130, BP 92/58 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 96 percent
data_table.Bloods: WCC 22 x10^9/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, glucose 16 mmol/L, CRP 220 mg/L, creatinine 152 micromol/L, haemoglobin 132 g/L
data_table.Examination: Localised erythema 5 cm proximal to ankle, exquisite tenderness extending 15 cm proximally, no crepitus, no bullae yet
data_table.Imaging: Plain radiograph shows no soft tissue gas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence oral cefalexin 500 mg every 6 hours and review the response in the emergency department in 2 hours
Order urgent magnetic resonance imaging before any decision on surgical exploration is made
Refer for orthopaedic review next day to plan elective wound debridement in the operating room
Activate emergency operating theatre booking for surgical exploration plus empiric meropenem and clindamycin
Admit for observation on the medical ward and intravenous flucloxacillin alone for severe cellulitis

subtopic_detail: Treatment selection after minimal trauma vertebral fracture in postmenopausal woman
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 72-year-old postmenopausal woman 6 weeks after a thoracic vertebral compression fracture sustained when she stepped down from a kerb. She has had no other fractures. She takes alendronate 70 mg weekly correctly for 5 years and a daily calcium and vitamin D supplement. Recent investigations are back. Her renal function is preserved and there is no history of oesophageal disease.

data_table.DXA: Lumbar spine T score -3.2, femoral neck T score -2.9, total hip -2.7
data_table.Bloods: 25-OH vitamin D 78 nmol/L, corrected calcium 2.32 mmol/L, eGFR 78 mL/min/1.73m^2, TSH 1.4 mIU/L
data_table.Other: PTH 4.6 pmol/L, normal SPEP, no malignant features

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next change in management?

options.text: Continue current alendronate at the same dose and review again with repeat DXA in 2 years
Switch alendronate to teriparatide 20 mcg subcutaneously daily for 18 months under specialist review
Add daily high-dose calcitriol 0.5 micrograms to current alendronate to improve fracture healing
Switch alendronate to oral risedronate 35 mg weekly as an alternative oral bisphosphonate option
Switch alendronate to raloxifene 60 mg daily as a selective oestrogen receptor modulator

subtopic_detail: Workup for suspected acute HIV seroconversion in a man with febrile illness and mucosal ulcers
stem: You are the registrar in a sexual health clinic reviewing a 26-year-old man with 10 days of fevers, sore throat, malaise, painful oral ulcers, a generalised maculopapular rash on the trunk, and tender cervical lymphadenopathy. He had condomless receptive anal sex with a new partner 5 weeks ago. He has not previously been on pre-exposure prophylaxis. His last HIV test was negative 6 months ago.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4, HR 96, BP 118/70 mmHg, SpO2 98 percent
data_table.Bloods: WCC 4.2 x10^9/L (lymphopenia), platelets 116 x10^9/L, ALT 88 U/L, CRP 32 mg/L
data_table.Examination: Oropharyngeal ulcers, tender bilateral posterior cervical lymph nodes, truncal maculopapular rash, no genital ulcers
data_table.STI history: Last negative HIV 4th generation test 6 months ago, no PrEP, single recent exposure

lead_in: Which test most reliably establishes acute HIV infection at this stage?

options.text: Standard 3rd generation HIV antibody test from a venous blood sample as the first investigation
Rapid point-of-care fingerprick antibody test as a definitive single test for acute infection
Anti-HIV western blot performed on a serum sample collected today to confirm acute infection
Quantitative chest computed tomography to assess for opportunistic infection complicating seroconversion
HIV RNA viral load polymerase chain reaction alongside a 4th generation antigen antibody combination test

subtopic_detail: Diagnostic sequence for suspected Cushing syndrome in a woman with central obesity and hypertension
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 42-year-old woman with 18 months of progressive central weight gain, easy bruising, proximal muscle weakness in climbing stairs, and new hypertension. She does not take exogenous corticosteroids and denies herbal preparations. She has type 2 diabetes diagnosed last year and her BP is 158/96 mmHg on amlodipine. Her menstrual cycles have become irregular and acne has worsened.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 158/96 mmHg, HR 84
data_table.Examination: Central obesity, supraclavicular fat pads, dorsocervical fat pad, violaceous abdominal striae, proximal hip and shoulder weakness
data_table.Bloods: HbA1c 7.6 percent, potassium 3.4 mmol/L, fasting glucose 8.4 mmol/L
data_table.Medications: Amlodipine 10 mg daily, metformin 1 g twice daily; no glucocorticoids or herbal supplements

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next diagnostic test?

options.text: Random serum cortisol level taken between 08:00 and 10:00 as the first screening investigation
Immediate adrenal computed tomography to identify a primary adrenal source of hypercortisolism
Overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test or late-night salivary cortisol or 24-hour urinary free cortisol
Serum adrenocorticotrophic hormone level alone as the first investigation to localise hypercortisolism
Inferior petrosal sinus sampling to localise an ACTH-secreting pituitary microadenoma at this stage

subtopic_detail: Recognition of Miller Fisher variant of Guillain-Barre syndrome in a returned traveller
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 36-year-old man with 4 days of progressively worsening unsteady gait, double vision, and difficulty reading. He returned from Vietnam 3 weeks ago, where he had 24 hours of watery diarrhoea that resolved without treatment. He has no significant past medical history and takes no regular medications. He is fully alert with normal language and cognition.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7, HR 84, BP 122/74 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99 percent
data_table.Examination: Bilateral abducens palsy, broad-based ataxic gait, absent ankle and knee reflexes, normal limb power, sensation intact
data_table.Investigations: Pending CSF, normal CT brain, normal FBC and electrolytes, ECG normal
data_table.Travel and exposure: Returned 3 weeks ago from Vietnam; self-limiting gastroenteritis 4 weeks ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Order high-resolution MRI of the brainstem to investigate suspected acute disseminated encephalomyelitis
Send GQ1b antibody serology and provide reassurance pending the result with outpatient review
Commence high-dose oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 5 days as first-line therapy
Admit to a monitored bed with respiratory observation and commence IVIG 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days
Order Tensilon test to differentiate from myasthenia gravis before any further treatment is started

subtopic_detail: Latent tuberculosis screening
stem: A 38-year-old woman with newly diagnosed rheumatoid arthritis is planned to commence adalimumab through your rheumatology clinic. She was born in Vietnam, arrived in Australia six years ago, and received BCG vaccination as a child. She has had no known TB contacts and no respiratory symptoms. She has no chronic liver disease and her bloods are normal. The rheumatologist asks you to organise pre-biologic latent tuberculosis screening.

data_table.Examination: BCG scar present; chest clear; no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: FBC, LFTs, renal function within reference range; CXR pending
data_table.Medications: Methotrexate 15 mg weekly, folate 5 mg weekly

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate screening test for latent TB before starting a TNF-alpha inhibitor?

options.text: Tuberculin skin test (Mantoux) alone using a 5 mm threshold for positivity in this immunosuppressed cohort
QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus interferon-gamma release assay together with a baseline plain chest radiograph
Three serial induced-sputum smears for acid-fast bacilli over consecutive mornings as the principal screen
High-resolution CT of the chest as the primary screen for asymptomatic latent tuberculosis before biologic therapy
Total serum IgE and peripheral blood absolute eosinophil count to risk-stratify for mycobacterial disease activity

subtopic_detail: Parkinson's disease initial therapy
stem:
A 72-year-old retired teacher is referred to your geriatric clinic with a six-month history of asymmetric rest tremor of the right hand, micrographia, slowed gait with reduced right arm swing, and difficulty turning in bed. He has fallen once. He has well-controlled hypertension and stage 3 chronic kidney disease. Examination confirms cogwheel rigidity right greater than left, bradykinesia and a positive pull test for postural instability.

There is no early autonomic failure and no cognitive complaint. He scores 28/30 on MoCA. MRI brain is unremarkable. He asks about treatment options to maintain independence.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 68, BP 128/76 supine to 124/74 standing; no postural drop
data_table.Examination: Asymmetric rest tremor right hand, cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia, postural instability; UPDRS motor moderate
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain unremarkable; eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73m2
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 5 mg daily

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Pramipexole modified release titrated to 1.5 mg daily as initial dopamine agonist monotherapy for motor symptoms
Levodopa with carbidopa (Sinemet) 100/25 mg three times daily titrated upward to motor response over weeks
Trihexyphenidyl 2 mg twice daily as initial anticholinergic monotherapy directed primarily at his rest tremor
Amantadine 100 mg twice daily as oral monotherapy for combined bradykinesia, rigidity and rest tremor relief
Rasagiline 1 mg daily as MAO-B inhibitor monotherapy aiming for modest symptomatic effect in early disease

subtopic_detail: RA early DMARD initiation
stem:
A 46-year-old retail manager presents to your rheumatology outpatient clinic with progressive symmetrical polyarthritis affecting the MCP and PIP joints of both hands and wrists for the past three months, with morning stiffness of 90 minutes and difficulty opening jars. She has no chest, eye or skin symptoms. There is no family history of inflammatory arthritis. She does not smoke.

Her bloods are listed below. Hand x-rays show periarticular osteopenia of MCP joints without erosions. She has no liver disease, no plan to become pregnant, and has had varicella infection in childhood.

data_table.Examination: Synovitis at bilateral MCP 2-5 and PIP 2-3; wrist tenderness; no rheumatoid nodules
data_table.Investigations: CRP 32 mg/L, ESR 48 mm/hr; anti-CCP strongly positive at 180 U/mL; RF positive at 1:160; FBC, UEC, LFTs normal; Hep B and Hep C negative; varicella IgG positive
data_table.Medications: Paracetamol 1 g qid

lead_in: Which initial DMARD strategy best matches Australian guidance?

options.text: Hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily as solitary DMARD monotherapy for a planned six-month treatment trial
Tofacitinib 5 mg twice daily as initial targeted synthetic DMARD therapy ahead of conventional synthetic agents
Methotrexate titrating to 15-25 mg weekly with folic acid plus short bridging low-dose oral prednisolone over weeks
Indefinite NSAID monotherapy with daily ibuprofen for sustained symptomatic control of inflammatory joint pain
Adalimumab 40 mg subcutaneously every 14 days as initial biologic monotherapy without prior conventional DMARDs

subtopic_detail: Acute aortic dissection workup
stem: You are the ED resident assessing a 62-year-old man with sudden severe interscapular tearing pain that started 45 minutes ago while gardening. He is sweaty, anxious, and rates pain 10/10. Past history includes hypertension (often unmonitored) and bicuspid aortic valve. Right arm BP is 178/96 and left arm BP is 142/72. Femoral pulses are present and equal. Cardiac examination reveals a soft early diastolic murmur. The chest is clear. ECG shows sinus rhythm with non-specific lateral T wave changes and no ST elevation. CXR shows a widened mediastinum.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96 sinus, BP right 178/96, BP left 142/72, RR 22, SpO2 96%, Temp 36.8
data_table.Examination: Sweaty, distressed, soft early diastolic murmur left sternal edge, no focal neurology, equal femoral pulses
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus, lateral T wave changes; CXR widened mediastinum; hs-troponin 18 ng/L (no rise expected at 45 min); D-dimer pending
data_table.Medications: Irregular perindopril use

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Urgent CT aortogram from the neck through to the femoral bifurcation acquired with arterial-phase contrast
Bedside transthoracic echocardiogram by ED clinician as the sole definitive investigation before specialty referral
Coronary angiography to exclude STEMI before any further imaging or treatment decisions are made for this patient
Exercise stress test once analgesia controls his pain to risk-stratify before further investigation choices are made
Outpatient transoesophageal echocardiogram within 24 hours after admission to a chest-pain short-stay observation unit

subtopic_detail: Multiple sclerosis - McDonald criteria
stem:
You are the neurology registrar reviewing a 31-year-old woman who presents with a four-day history of right eye pain on movement and blurring of central vision. She had a self-limited bout of left-sided sensory loss in the leg six months ago lasting two weeks that she did not seek care for. Visual acuity is 6/18 right and 6/6 left with a right RAPD.

Fundus examination shows mild right optic disc swelling. MRI brain shows three T2 hyperintense lesions: one periventricular, one juxtacortical and one infratentorial, with one demonstrating contrast enhancement. MRI of the spinal cord shows a single non-enhancing cervical T2 lesion. CSF analysis is pending.

data_table.Examination: Right RAPD, right central scotoma, otherwise normal neurological examination
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain: 3 T2 hyperintense lesions (periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial), one enhancing. MRI cord: cervical T2 lesion non-enhancing. VEP delayed right
data_table.Medications: Nil

lead_in: Which statement best applies the 2017 McDonald criteria here?

options.text: Diagnosis requires a second clinical attack before multiple sclerosis can be confirmed even with current MRI findings
DIS is met by MRI but dissemination in time requires repeat MRI in three months before MS can be formally diagnosed
DIS and DIT are met on a single MRI but CSF oligoclonal bands are required before MS diagnosis can be formally made
Diagnosis cannot be made without first confirming negative aquaporin-4 antibodies plus complete CSF analysis results
CIS with DIS and DIT satisfied on single MRI fulfils 2017 McDonald criteria allowing diagnosis after exclusion of mimics

subtopic_detail: Dementia with Lewy bodies - antipsychotic sensitivity
stem: A 78-year-old man with a 14-month history of fluctuating cognition, recurrent vivid visual hallucinations of small animals, mild bradykinesia and REM sleep behaviour disorder is admitted under your geriatrics team with new agitation overnight after a urinary tract infection has been identified. The night staff request a sedating medication. He is not a danger to himself. He is normally on rivastigmine 9.5 mg patch daily and trimethoprim was started six hours ago. He has had no benzodiazepines or antipsychotics previously.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP 122/76, RR 18, SpO2 95% on room air, Temp 37.6
data_table.Examination: Disoriented to time and place, mild bradykinesia, no focal neurology, visual hallucinations of cats in the corner
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick leucocytes +++, nitrites positive; FBC, UEC, LFTs within usual range; CXR clear
data_table.Medications: Rivastigmine 9.5 mg/24 h patch; trimethoprim 300 mg started 6 h ago

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate medication choice for sedation tonight?

options.text: Haloperidol 0.5 mg orally as required for agitation overnight with hourly nursing observations of motor status
Risperidone 0.5 mg orally as required overnight aiming to reduce hallucinations and agitation during the night shift
Olanzapine 5 mg orally as required overnight as the sedating atypical antipsychotic of choice for nocturnal agitation
Address reversible delirium triggers with non-pharmacological measures, reserving low-dose quetiapine for refractory severe distress
Diazepam 5 mg orally as required overnight for sedation as the standard first-line agent in agitated older inpatients

subtopic_detail: VTE duration of anticoagulation
stem: A 56-year-old woman who works as a school administrator is reviewed in your haematology clinic three months after a first unprovoked segmental pulmonary embolism. She presented at the time with breathlessness on exertion and was treated with apixaban with full clinical and radiological recovery. There is no personal or family history of malignancy, no recent surgery, immobilisation or pregnancy, and no oestrogen-containing therapy. A thrombophilia screen at three months shows no high-risk hereditary thrombophilia. Her HAS-BLED score is 1.

data_table.Examination: No leg swelling, no signs of bleeding, normal cardiopulmonary examination
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, coagulation profile normal; thrombophilia screen negative; D-dimer not indicated for treatment decision
data_table.Medications: Apixaban 5 mg twice daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for ongoing anticoagulation?

options.text: Stop apixaban now at the three-month mark with no ongoing oral anticoagulation or antiplatelet substitution prescribed
Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily for a further nine months and then stop without further haematology review of risk
Continue extended indefinite anticoagulation with apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily with annual bleeding and recurrence review
Switch to aspirin 100 mg daily as ongoing long-term secondary prevention against recurrent venous thromboembolic events
Switch to warfarin with target INR 2.0-3.0 because of well-established long-term safety data and lower drug acquisition cost

subtopic_detail: Tension pneumothorax under mechanical ventilation
stem:
You are the ICU registrar called urgently to bed 4. A 64-year-old man intubated for ARDS secondary to community-acquired pneumonia three days ago suddenly becomes haemodynamically unstable. He is on volume-controlled ventilation with tidal volume 6 mL/kg, PEEP 12 cm H2O, FiO2 0.6. Over the past three minutes, peak airway pressures have risen from 28 to 46 cm H2O, plateau pressures from 22 to 38 cm H2O, BP has fallen from 118/72 to 70/40, HR has risen from 96 to 138 sinus, and SpO2 has dropped from 94% to 80%.

The trachea appears deviated to the left, the right hemithorax is hyperresonant with absent breath sounds, and there is distended neck veins. He is on noradrenaline 0.15 mcg/kg/min already.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138 sinus, BP 70/40, SpO2 80%, peak airway pressure 46 cm H2O, plateau 38 cm H2O
data_table.Examination: Tracheal deviation left, hyperresonant right hemithorax, absent right breath sounds, distended neck veins, mottled peripheries
data_table.Investigations: ABG pH 7.18, PaO2 55, PaCO2 64, HCO3 22, lactate 4.6; CXR not yet taken
data_table.Medications: Noradrenaline 0.15 mcg/kg/min, propofol, fentanyl, atracurium infusions

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next intervention?

options.text: Immediate finger or needle thoracostomy in the right 4th-5th intercostal space anterior axillary line followed by ICC
Briefly disconnect the ventilator and manually bag-mask ventilate to confirm tension pneumothorax before any decompression
Obtain an urgent portable supine chest radiograph for tension pneumothorax confirmation before any decompression is performed
Increase noradrenaline infusion to 0.5 mcg/kg/min and add vasopressin while continuing current ventilator settings unchanged
Increase PEEP to 18 cm H2O and perform a sustained-inflation lung recruitment manoeuvre on the affected hemithorax

subtopic_detail: Infective endocarditis Duke criteria
stem:
A 52-year-old man presents to your emergency department with three weeks of fever, anorexia and a 4 kg unintentional weight loss. He had a bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement nine months ago for severe aortic regurgitation. On examination he is febrile, has a soft early diastolic murmur unchanged from baseline, splinter haemorrhages on two fingers and tender nodules on his left finger pad.

Two sets of blood cultures drawn at separate venepuncture sites 12 hours apart have grown Streptococcus gallolyticus (formerly S. bovis biotype I). Transthoracic echo shows no clear vegetation but limited views.

data_table.Examination: Early diastolic murmur unchanged; Janeway lesions, Osler nodes; no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Two sets blood cultures positive Streptococcus gallolyticus; CRP 96; WCC 13.2; TTE limited
data_table.Medications: Aspirin 100 mg daily; perindopril 5 mg daily

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Transoesophageal echocardiography to evaluate prosthetic valve and assess for vegetations, abscess, or new regurgitation now
Cardiac CT angiography with delayed-phase imaging as a first-line replacement for echocardiography to detect vegetations and abscess formation
Cardiac MRI as a first-line imaging modality to evaluate vegetations and associated annular or myocardial extension at presentation
Repeat transthoracic echocardiography in 48 hours with intravenous contrast to improve windows and revisit vegetation question
PET-CT with FDG to localise an occult source of bacteraemia before considering further cardiac imaging in this prosthetic valve patient today

subtopic_detail: Cushing's syndrome workup
stem: A 44-year-old woman presents to your general practice clinic with new-onset hypertension (BP 162/96 today), 9 kg weight gain over six months, easy bruising, proximal muscle weakness climbing stairs, and oligomenorrhoea. On examination she has central adiposity, supraclavicular fat pads, violaceous abdominal striae greater than 1 cm wide, and thin skin. She drinks two standard drinks weekly and takes no glucocorticoids including inhaled, intra-articular, or topical products. She is otherwise well. You suspect endogenous Cushing's syndrome and need to choose an initial screening investigation.

data_table.Examination: BMI 33; supraclavicular fat pads; wide violaceous striae; proximal weakness
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 8.4 mmol/L (random); K 3.4; HbA1c 7.1%; normal TSH
data_table.Medications: Nil glucocorticoids; nil current antihypertensive

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate initial screening test?

options.text: Random morning serum cortisol with simultaneous ACTH measurement on a single clinic visit for initial screening at first presentation
Overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test with 8 am cortisol on the following morning after the patient takes 1 mg at bedtime
Pituitary MRI with contrast as the initial test to identify a corticotroph adenoma before any biochemical confirmation of hypercortisolism
Bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling as the screening investigation to confirm pituitary versus ectopic ACTH source at first review today
CT adrenals with contrast as an initial test to identify a primary adrenal tumour before any biochemical confirmation of cortisol excess present

subtopic_detail: Septic shock hour-1 vasopressor
stem: A 68-year-old man is brought to your emergency department by ambulance with fever, rigors and confusion. He has urinary frequency for three days and known benign prostatic hyperplasia. After 30 mL/kg of crystalloid over the first hour, his blood pressure remains 84/48 mmHg with MAP 60 mmHg and his lactate has risen from 3.6 to 4.2 mmol/L. Blood cultures and a urine culture have been collected and broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics have been administered. There is no current contraindication to central venous access and central venous access can be obtained within 30 minutes.

data_table.Examination: Cool peripheries; capillary refill 4 seconds; mildly confused; tender suprapubic area
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 4.2 (was 3.6); WCC 18.2; Cr 142 (baseline 90); urine cloudy, leucocytes 3+
data_table.Medications: Tamsulosin 400 micrograms daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next vasoactive therapy?

options.text: Start intravenous dopamine infusion at 5 micrograms per kilogram per minute as first-line vasoactive therapy via reliable peripheral access today
Administer further 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus over the next hour as primary therapy before initiating any vasopressor infusion today
Commence intravenous noradrenaline infusion via reliable access targeting mean arterial pressure 65 mmHg and initiate central access
Administer intravenous metaraminol boluses to titrate blood pressure rather than initiating any continuous vasopressor infusion at this time today
Withhold vasopressor and re-resuscitate with 1 litre of 4% albumin instead of further crystalloid before reassessment of his perfusion status

subtopic_detail: Hypercalcaemia differentiation
stem: A 62-year-old woman is referred to your general medical clinic after incidental hypercalcaemia on a routine panel. She is asymptomatic but admits to mild constipation. She has osteopenia on a recent bone density scan. She takes no thiazide diuretics, lithium or calcium supplements and does not smoke. Family history includes her sister having a renal stone in her thirties. On examination she is well, with no lymphadenopathy and a normal respiratory and abdominal examination. Repeat fasting bloods on a separate day confirm the abnormality. The result pattern points to a single biochemical category before further imaging.

data_table.Examination: Well; no lymphadenopathy; abdomen soft non-tender; no bony tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Corrected Ca 2.85 (RR 2.10-2.55) mmol/L; PTH 8.6 (RR 1.5-6.5) pmol/L; phosphate 0.74; 25-OH vit D 62; Cr 78; 24h urine Ca/Cr ratio 0.018
data_table.Medications: Colecalciferol 1000 IU daily; aspirin 100 mg daily

lead_in: Which diagnosis best fits this biochemical pattern?

options.text: Vitamin D toxicity from prolonged supplementation with appropriately suppressed PTH and hyperphosphataemia from gut calcium absorption excess and bone resorption
Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia given inherited calcium-sensing receptor mutation with similar PTH elevation and benign clinical course over years
Humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy from PTH-related peptide secretion with suppressed PTH driving phosphate wasting in the renal tubule
Primary hyperparathyroidism with PTH-driven hypercalcaemia and normocalciuric phosphate-lowering profile consistent with autonomous parathyroid adenoma typically
Sarcoidosis driving 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity in granulomas with suppressed PTH and elevated 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D in a patient with subclinical disease

subtopic_detail: Cellulitis vs necrotising fasciitis
stem:
A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents to your emergency department with severe pain in his left lower leg that began yesterday after a minor garden scratch. The pain is dramatically out of proportion to the modest erythema seen on examination. Over six hours in the department the erythema has crept upward and a single haemorrhagic bulla has formed.

He is febrile and tachycardic. His bloods show neutrophil leucocytosis, sodium 130 mmol/L, creatinine 142 micromol/L (baseline 78), glucose 14 mmol/L, CRP 320 mg/L and lactate 3.2 mmol/L. Wound swab is pending.

data_table.Examination: Severe pain disproportionate to redness; haemorrhagic bulla; cool peripheries
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22; Na 130; Cr 142 (baseline 78); glucose 14; CRP 320; Hb 132; lactate 3.2; LRINEC 9
data_table.Medications: Metformin 1000 mg BD; perindopril 5 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Hyperbaric oxygen referral as first-line therapy in suspected necrotising soft tissue infection with planning of operative debridement only afterwards
Intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g six-hourly for presumed simple cellulitis and reassess clinical progression of the affected limb in 12 hours
MRI of the lower limb to confirm fascial involvement before any surgical consultation or empirical antibiotic escalation initiated in the department
Intravenous immunoglobulin alone for streptococcal toxic shock syndrome cover without immediate surgical consultation or any antibiotic escalation today
Urgent surgical consultation for operative debridement combined with intravenous meropenem plus clindamycin while resuscitating from sepsis

subtopic_detail: Acute HIV seroconversion
stem: A 31-year-old man presents to your sexual health clinic with a one-week history of fever, sore throat, generalised lymphadenopathy and a faint truncal rash. He reports a high-risk condomless receptive anal intercourse exposure approximately 18 days ago with a partner of unknown serostatus. He took no post-exposure prophylaxis. His fourth-generation HIV combination antigen and antibody test today is negative. He has no other infections identified on EBV serology, throat swab or chest imaging. He asks how confident you are in excluding HIV based on the current result alone today.

data_table.Examination: Cervical lymphadenopathy; mild pharyngeal erythema; truncal maculopapular rash
data_table.Investigations: 4th-gen Ag/Ab HIV: negative; EBV IgM neg; monospot neg; CRP 56
data_table.Medications: Paracetamol PRN

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: HIV-1 RNA viral load by NAAT now to detect acute seroconversion within the eclipse and window phase before antibody seroconversion completes
Repeat 4th-generation HIV Ag/Ab combination test in three months to definitively exclude infection without any further testing required today
Western blot HIV antibody confirmatory test to override the screening negative and detect early seroconverting antibody bands before clinical resolution
Commence empirical antiretroviral therapy now without further testing given the high pretest probability of acute HIV in this clinical presentation today
CD4 cell count immediately to identify acute HIV-related lymphopenia as evidence of active infection before any further screening or molecular testing

subtopic_detail: DOAC bleeding reversal
stem: A 78-year-old man on apixaban 5 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation presents to your emergency department six hours after a witnessed unwitnessed fall at home. CT brain demonstrates a 12 mm right frontal acute subdural haematoma with 4 mm of midline shift. His last apixaban dose was four hours before his fall and his renal function is normal. The neurosurgical registrar advises operative evacuation in the next two hours. His weight is 78 kg, he has no history of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, and there are no contraindications to specific factor Xa inhibitor reversal.

data_table.Examination: Mild left arm weakness 4/5; PEARL; no other focal deficit
data_table.Investigations: Hb 122; platelets 188; INR 1.2; Cr 78 (eGFR 78); CT: 12 mm SDH, 4 mm midline shift
data_table.Medications: Apixaban 5 mg BD; perindopril 5 mg daily

lead_in: Which reversal strategy is most appropriate before surgery?

options.text: Administer 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) 50 units per kilogram intravenously as the only available reversal in many Australian hospital sites
Administer andexanet alfa via the high-dose intravenous bolus and infusion regimen because last apixaban dose was within eight hours of intracranial haemorrhage
Administer fresh frozen plasma 15 mL per kilogram intravenously to dilute circulating apixaban and provide some non-specific factor replacement support
Administer intravenous vitamin K 10 mg slowly with platelet transfusion to enhance clotting in the face of an ongoing acute intracranial haemorrhage now
Administer idarucizumab 5 g intravenously as a single dose to reverse direct anticoagulant activity prior to neurosurgical intervention proceeding

subtopic_detail: Phaeochromocytoma alpha block sequencing
stem:
A 41-year-old man is referred to your endocrine inpatient team with episodic severe headache, palpitations and diaphoresis over six months, now with sustained hypertension. He has been resistant to standard agents. He is awake, alert and currently haemodynamically stable. Plasma metanephrines are markedly elevated and CT abdomen shows a 4.5 cm right adrenal mass with classic imaging features. The surgical registrar suggests starting metoprolol now for the tachycardia.

He has no current angina, no asthma, and good background renal function. He is reviewed today for medical preparation prior to laparoscopic adrenalectomy in three weeks.

data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic; otherwise well; no orthostasis on standing today
data_table.Investigations: Plasma metanephrines markedly elevated; CT 4.5 cm right adrenal mass with washout pattern; eGFR 88
data_table.Medications: Amlodipine 5 mg daily; perindopril 5 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate medical preparation strategy now?

options.text: Commence amlodipine dose escalation and add an angiotensin receptor blocker alone without any specific catecholamine-targeted pharmacological preparation prior to surgery
Commence metoprolol now to control the tachycardia and add prazosin in two weeks once heart rate is consistently below 80 beats per minute on review
Commence phenoxybenzamine alpha-blockade titrated to mild orthostatic hypotension; introduce beta-blockade only after adequate alpha-blockade is established
Proceed directly to laparoscopic adrenalectomy within 48 hours without any specific preoperative pharmacological preparation in a young patient at lower operative risk
Commence labetalol monotherapy as a combined alpha- and beta-blocker for preoperative preparation given its dual receptor activity simplifying medication titration logistics

subtopic_detail: Sepsis hour-1 bundle
stem:
A 64-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by ambulance with 24 hours of rigors and confusion. He has a history of type 2 diabetes on metformin and a recent dental abscess treated with oral amoxicillin 3 days ago. He is now disoriented to time. The triage nurse documents a quick SOFA score of 3 (altered mentation, RR 28, BP 88/50).

Venous blood gas shows lactate 4.1 mmol/L. Blood cultures have been drawn through a peripheral cannula. No imaging has been performed yet and no source of infection beyond the dental history is clear on initial examination.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 124, BP 88/50, RR 28, SpO2 95% room air, Temp 39.0
data_table.Examination: Confused, dry mucous membranes; mild tenderness over right mandible; no rash; clear chest
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 4.1, WCC 18.4, CRP 295, creatinine 168 (baseline 90), glucose 14.1

lead_in: What is the single most important next action within the hour-1 bundle?

options.text: Order a contrast-enhanced CT of the head, chest, abdomen and pelvis to identify the source before antibiotic administration
Insert a central venous catheter for noradrenaline before any antibiotic administration to avoid extravasation
Administer broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, give a 30 mL per kg crystalloid bolus, and start vasopressors if MAP remains below 65
Repeat blood cultures from a second site before any antibiotic administration to maximise culture yield
Administer 100 mg of hydrocortisone immediately as the priority over fluid resuscitation and antibiotic delivery

subtopic_detail: Necrotising fasciitis recognition
stem:
A 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents with 24 hours of escalating left lower-leg pain, warmth, and a poorly demarcated erythematous patch above the medial malleolus. He is now systemically unwell with rigors. His pain is markedly out of proportion to the visual changes and he describes a numb central zone. There are no obvious skin breaks, no bullae yet, and no necrosis on inspection.

He has not travelled and has not had recent saltwater exposure. He has not had surgery. He uses metformin and atorvastatin and has no known allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 124, BP 92/56, RR 26, SpO2 95% room air, Temp 39.2
data_table.Examination: Erythema ill-defined; severe pain on light palpation; central anaesthesia; no crepitus; no bullae yet
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22.4, Na 132, glucose 18, creatinine 158, CRP 320, Hb 132, lactate 3.4; LRINEC 9

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence oral flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily and outpatient review in 24 hours for a moderate cellulitis
Admit for intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g 6 hourly with limb elevation and re-image at 24 hours
Activate immediate surgical review for debridement, give intravenous meropenem plus clindamycin, and resuscitate with fluids
Order an urgent MRI of the lower limb and defer surgical consultation until imaging confirms fascial involvement
Commence intravenous vancomycin alone empirically pending culture results from initial blood cultures and skin swab

subtopic_detail: Uncomplicated UTI in non-pregnant women
stem:
A 32-year-old non-pregnant woman attends her general practice clinic with 36 hours of dysuria, urinary frequency, and suprapubic discomfort. She has no fever, no flank pain, no nausea and no vaginal discharge. She has no history of antibiotic use in the past 6 months and no recent travel. She is otherwise well, sexually active in a stable relationship, and uses combined oral contraception.

A urine dipstick in the surgery is positive for nitrites and leucocyte esterase. There is no history of recurrent UTIs and she has normal renal function.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 80, BP 118/72, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.7
data_table.Examination: Mild suprapubic tenderness, no flank tenderness, no signs of systemic illness
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick positive for nitrites and leucocyte esterase; urine MCS not routinely required

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 3 days targeting common urinary tract gram-negative pathogen profiles
Oral amoxicillin clavulanate 500 mg three times daily for 5 days as a broad-spectrum first-line agent for cystitis
Oral trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 3 days or nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for 5 days as first-line therapy
Oral cefalexin 500 mg twice daily for 5 days based on patient preference and reported convenient twice daily dosing
Oral fosfomycin 3 g as a single dose plus phenazopyridine 200 mg three times daily for symptomatic relief over 48 hours

subtopic_detail: Influenza antiviral indication
stem:
A 72-year-old man with stable congestive heart failure and type 2 diabetes presents to his general practitioner with 36 hours of fever, cough, myalgia and fatigue. There is high influenza activity in the community. He has no chest pain, no haemoptysis, no significant shortness of breath, and his observations are stable. He is fully vaccinated this season. His chest examination is clear.

Nasopharyngeal swab PCR confirms influenza A. He has not been hospitalised this year and lives independently with his wife. His current medications include perindopril, carvedilol, furosemide, metformin and atorvastatin.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP 132/82, RR 18, SpO2 96% room air, Temp 38.4
data_table.Examination: Mildly fatigued; chest clear; no peripheral oedema; no signs of respiratory distress
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal swab PCR positive for influenza A; chest examination clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management decision?

options.text: Reassure, recommend rest and oral fluids, and review only if symptoms worsen significantly over coming days
Prescribe oral amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 5 days for likely bacterial co-infection given his comorbidities
Prescribe inhaled zanamivir 10 mg twice daily for 5 days as the preferred neuraminidase inhibitor for older adults
Prescribe oral oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days starting today as treatment within 48 hours of symptom onset
Recommend baloxavir marboxil single oral dose for first-line treatment in older adults with influenza A confirmed on PCR

subtopic_detail: Spontaneous pneumothorax management
stem: A 24-year-old tall thin male university student presents to the emergency department with 4 hours of sudden right-sided pleuritic chest pain and mild dyspnoea while sitting in a lecture. He has no past medical history, does not smoke, and takes no medications. He is haemodynamically stable, breathing comfortably and able to speak in full sentences. His chest radiograph shows a right apical pneumothorax measuring 3 cm from the chest wall at the level of the hilum. The remainder of the chest is unremarkable. There is no tension physiology and no underlying lung disease evident.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 90, BP 122/78, RR 18, SpO2 96% room air, Temp 36.7
data_table.Examination: Reduced breath sounds right apex, mildly hyperresonant percussion right side, trachea midline
data_table.Investigations: Chest radiograph right apical pneumothorax 3 cm at hilum; no underlying parenchymal disease

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Insert a 28 French intercostal catheter immediately for definitive drainage and admit under cardiothoracic surgery for observation
Reassure, discharge with simple analgesia and outpatient respiratory review in 4 weeks without any acute intervention
Perform needle thoracostomy at the second intercostal space midclavicular line emergently before any definitive imaging
Commence non-invasive positive pressure ventilation to accelerate re-expansion of the visceral pleural defect noted today
Perform needle aspiration with a 16G catheter and reassess radiologically; if unsuccessful insert a small-bore intercostal drain

subtopic_detail: Myasthenic crisis acute management
stem: A 52-year-old woman with anti-acetylcholine receptor positive myasthenia gravis presents to the emergency department with worsening dyspnoea and dysphagia. She has had a vomiting illness for 36 hours and has missed her last three doses of pyridostigmine. On examination she has bilateral ptosis, a weak head lift, soft voice, paradoxical abdominal breathing, and weak cough. Her forced vital capacity at the bedside is 14 mL/kg and falling. She is alert and orientated but distressed.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 110, RR 28 shallow, SpO2 96% on 4 L nasal prongs, BP 138/82, Temp 36.8
data_table.Examination: Bilateral ptosis; weak head lift; paradoxical abdominal breathing; weak cough; clear chest
data_table.Investigations: Bedside FVC 14 mL/kg; ABG: pH 7.32, PaCO2 52, PaO2 80, HCO3 26; CXR clear; CK normal

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Administer high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g and admit to a high-dependency bed for monitoring
Increase the home pyridostigmine dose and treat the underlying vomiting with intravenous ondansetron
Trial bilevel non-invasive ventilation overnight while continuing pyridostigmine at maintenance dose
Intubate now with a non-depolarising relaxant avoided, then commence intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange
Give intravenous edrophonium as a diagnostic challenge and titrate further therapy to the response

subtopic_detail: Bronchiectasis infective exacerbation
stem: A 58-year-old woman with non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis attributable to childhood whooping cough presents to her general practice with 5 days of increased sputum volume, change to thicker yellow-green sputum, low-grade fever, and worsening exertional breathlessness compared with her usual baseline. Her routine sputum cultures over the past 2 years have grown Haemophilus influenzae only. She has not required hospital admission for 3 years and is otherwise well, taking azithromycin three times weekly as maintenance.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96, RR 22, SpO2 95% room air, BP 128/76, Temp 37.6
data_table.Examination: Coarse crackles at the right base; mild end-expiratory wheeze; no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: CXR ordered today; previous sputum cultures show Haemophilus influenzae; no Pseudomonas history

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in her antibiotic management?

options.text: Admit for intravenous ceftriaxone and switch to oral therapy after 48 hours of clinical improvement
Prescribe oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 5 days and review with sputum culture in 1 week
Continue azithromycin only, reinforce airway clearance technique, and review in 7 days
Commence nebulised tobramycin twice daily as monotherapy and review with sputum culture at 48 hours
Send a sputum culture today and commence oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily for 14 days

subtopic_detail: Latent tuberculosis treatment
stem:
A 26-year-old woman who recently arrived from Papua New Guinea attends a refugee health clinic for routine screening. She is asymptomatic, has no cough, no fevers, and no weight loss. Her chest X-ray is reported as normal with no apical scarring or cavitation. A QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus assay returns positive. She is HIV negative on rapid testing and not pregnant.

Her vaccination history includes BCG in infancy. She is not currently taking any medications and her sputum culture cannot be collected as she has no productive cough.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78, BP 118/72, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.7
data_table.Examination: Well; chest clear; no lymphadenopathy; no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: CXR: normal lung fields; QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus: positive; HIV: negative; LFTs normal

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: No treatment is needed because she has had BCG and a positive QuantiFERON likely reflects vaccination
Commence empirical four-drug therapy with rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol
Prescribe isoniazid 300 mg daily for 9 months with pyridoxine 25 mg daily and monthly LFT monitoring
Repeat the QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus in 3 months and treat only if the result remains positive
Refer for bronchoscopy and bronchoalveolar lavage to obtain a definitive microbiological diagnosis

subtopic_detail: Parkinson disease initial pharmacotherapy
stem:
A 68-year-old retired carpenter is referred to neurology with a 12 month history of progressive right hand tremor at rest, micrographia, and slowing of fine finger movements. Examination shows asymmetric resting tremor, cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia of right hand finger tapping, and a slowed gait with reduced right arm swing. There is no postural instability and no autonomic or cognitive impairment.

An MRI brain has excluded a structural cause. He continues part-time consultancy and reports that his tremor is interfering with this work. His UPDRS motor score is 22.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 72, BP 138/82 lying with no postural drop, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.7
data_table.Examination: Asymmetric resting tremor right > left; cogwheel rigidity; bradykinesia; reduced right arm swing; no postural instability
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain: normal; thyroid function normal; copper studies normal; UPDRS-III 22

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Commence carbidopa-levodopa at a low dose with gradual titration to control symptoms while maintaining function
Initiate the dopamine agonist pramipexole and titrate as tolerated to minimise long-term motor fluctuations
Start the MAO-B inhibitor rasagiline as monotherapy and defer dopamine therapy until functional impairment increases
Commence amantadine 100 mg twice daily as initial therapy with neurology review in 6 weeks
Defer all medication and refer for structured exercise therapy as the sole intervention for 6 months

subtopic_detail: Pleural effusion Light criteria
stem: A 62-year-old man with a 20 pack-year smoking history presents with 3 weeks of progressive right-sided breathlessness and a dry cough. He has lost 4 kg unintentionally. Chest X-ray shows a moderate right pleural effusion with no other parenchymal abnormality. A diagnostic thoracentesis is performed under ultrasound guidance. The pleural fluid is straw coloured. Pleural protein is 38 g/L, pleural lactate dehydrogenase is 280 U/L, pleural glucose is 4.2 mmol/L, and pleural pH is 7.42. Serum protein is 68 g/L and serum LDH is 200 U/L.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, RR 22, SpO2 94% room air, BP 128/76, Temp 36.8
data_table.Examination: Stony dullness, reduced breath sounds, and reduced vocal resonance over the right base; no clubbing or lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Pleural protein 38 g/L, LDH 280 U/L; serum protein 68 g/L, LDH 200 U/L; pleural glucose 4.2, pH 7.42

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate interpretation and next step?

options.text: Transudate consistent with cardiac failure; commence furosemide and arrange outpatient echocardiogram
Transudate consistent with hypoalbuminaemia; commence albumin replacement and review with nutrition
Equivocal sample; repeat thoracentesis in 48 hours and review with results of a paired serum sample
Chylothorax most likely; check pleural triglycerides and consider lymphatic imaging before further workup
Exudate by Light criteria; arrange contrast CT chest and discuss with respiratory for further investigation

subtopic_detail: Type B aortic dissection blood pressure target
stem: A 56-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension presents to the emergency department with sudden severe tearing interscapular and chest pain 90 minutes ago. He is diaphoretic, distressed, and complains of a heavy feeling in both legs. His right arm blood pressure is 198/108 and his left arm is 162/92. ECG is in sinus rhythm with no ischaemic changes. A bedside contrast computed tomography aortogram confirms a type B aortic dissection beginning distal to the left subclavian artery with no end-organ malperfusion. He is otherwise haemodynamically stable.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96, BP right arm 198/108, left arm 162/92, SpO2 98% room air, RR 22, Temp 36.7
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic; equal radial pulses; bilateral leg heaviness without weakness; clear chest; no peritonitis
data_table.Investigations: CT aortogram: type B dissection distal to left subclavian; troponin negative; lactate 1.4; UEC normal

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Commence intravenous glyceryl trinitrate as monotherapy targeting a systolic blood pressure below 120 mmHg
Administer intravenous nicardipine as monotherapy and titrate to systolic blood pressure 100 to 120 mmHg
Administer thrombolysis with intravenous tenecteplase for presumed inferior myocardial infarction
Commence intravenous esmolol or labetalol to a heart rate below 60 then add nitroprusside if needed
Refer for emergency open surgical repair as definitive management of all uncomplicated type B dissections

subtopic_detail: Acute pyelonephritis empirical antibiotics
stem: A 45-year-old previously well woman presents to the emergency department with 36 hours of right flank pain, fever, rigors, dysuria, and three episodes of vomiting. She has no history of urinary tract infection and is not pregnant. Examination reveals right costovertebral angle tenderness and a soft non-peritonitic abdomen. Urinalysis shows leucocytes 3+, nitrites positive, and blood 1+. Bloods show a white cell count of 18.5, lactate of 2.4, and creatinine of 95. A urine culture has been sent. She is unable to tolerate oral fluids.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, BP 96/58, SpO2 98% room air, Temp 39.2, RR 22
data_table.Examination: Right costovertebral angle tenderness; soft non-peritonitic abdomen; warm peripheries
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis: leucocytes 3+, nitrites positive; WCC 18.5; lactate 2.4; creatinine 95; urine culture sent; beta-hCG negative

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous amoxicillin 2 g 6-hourly plus gentamicin 5 mg/kg daily after senior review of risks
Oral trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 14 days with outpatient follow-up of urine culture
Intravenous vancomycin 1.5 g loading dose targeting MRSA cover for community-acquired sepsis
Intravenous metronidazole 500 mg 8-hourly with intravenous fluconazole pending culture results
Oral nitrofurantoin 100 mg 6-hourly for 7 days with intravenous fluid resuscitation for vomiting

subtopic_detail: Multiple sclerosis clinically isolated syndrome
stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with 2 weeks of progressive painful loss of central vision in the right eye and a relative afferent pupillary defect. Six months ago she had transient left-sided weakness and numbness that resolved spontaneously over 3 weeks without medical assessment. MRI brain today shows multiple T2 hyperintense lesions in the periventricular and juxtacortical white matter, one of which enhances with gadolinium, plus a non-enhancing lesion in the cervical spinal cord. Cerebrospinal fluid shows two oligoclonal bands not present in serum. She is otherwise well and has no family history of demyelinating disease.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 72, BP 118/72, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.6
data_table.Examination: Right relative afferent pupillary defect; reduced colour vision; otherwise normal neurological examination
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain: multiple T2 lesions, one gadolinium enhancing; MRI spine: non-enhancing cervical lesion; CSF: 2 unique oligoclonal bands

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Defer all immunomodulatory therapy until a second clinical relapse confirms relapsing-remitting disease
Commence intravenous immunoglobulin as a maintenance disease-modifying therapy with quarterly infusions
Prescribe oral prednisolone 50 mg daily for 6 months as long-term immunosuppression for relapse prevention
Plan whole brain irradiation as definitive management of inflammatory demyelinating disease activity
Treat acute optic neuritis with pulse methylprednisolone and initiate disease-modifying therapy promptly

subtopic_detail: Adult anaphylaxis immediate IM adrenaline dose
stem: A 38-year-old man presents to the emergency department after 15 minutes of progressive lip and tongue swelling, audible wheeze, and lightheadedness during a restaurant meal. He has a known allergy to tree nuts and forgot to bring his autoinjector. On arrival he is anxious, generalised urticaria is visible, his tongue is swollen but he is still phonating, and his peripheries are cool. He weighs 78 kg. He has no other medical conditions and is on no regular medications.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, RR 28, SpO2 92% room air, BP 86/52, Temp 36.5
data_table.Examination: Generalised urticaria; tongue swelling without stridor; bilateral wheeze; CRT 4 seconds; alert
data_table.Investigations: Not performed; allergy referral after stabilisation

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 0.5 mg of 1:1000 solution into the anterolateral mid-thigh and prompt reassessment cycle
Intravenous adrenaline 1 mg of 1:10000 solution given as a slow push under continuous cardiac monitoring
Intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg with intravenous promethazine 25 mg as initial pharmacological treatment given
Nebulised adrenaline 5 mg with high-flow oxygen 15 L per minute and a 1 litre crystalloid bolus through wide cannula
Subcutaneous adrenaline 0.5 mg from a 1:1000 ampoule given into the upper arm with airway adjunct preparation

subtopic_detail: Infective endocarditis modified Duke criteria
stem: A 56-year-old man with a bioprosthetic aortic valve replaced 14 months ago presents with three weeks of fever, weight loss, and night sweats. He has had two intervening dental procedures without prophylaxis. His blood cultures from two separate venepuncture sites taken 12 hours apart have grown viridans group streptococci. A transthoracic echocardiogram is poor quality and inconclusive. A transoesophageal echo is awaited. The patient is otherwise haemodynamically stable on the ward.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 102, BP 118/72, RR 20, SpO2 96% room air, Temp 38.4
data_table.Examination: Soft early diastolic murmur at left sternal edge; nil splinter haemorrhages or Janeway lesions noted today
data_table.Investigations: WCC 14.2 x10^9/L, CRP 102 mg/L, Hb 105 g/L, Cr 92 micromol/L; ECG sinus tachycardia, no new conduction; TTE non-diagnostic

lead_in: How is this patient classified under the modified Duke criteria at present?

options.text: Definite infective endocarditis on the strength of pathological criteria from histology and microbiology already
Possible infective endocarditis pending transoesophageal echo result and a documented new regurgitant murmur
Definite infective endocarditis fulfilled by two clinical major criteria from typical organism and new regurgitation
Rejected diagnosis because transthoracic echocardiogram failed to visualise vegetations and patient remains stable
Definite infective endocarditis based on one major criterion only with multiple supportive minor criteria currently

subtopic_detail: ANCA-associated vasculitis pattern recognition
stem: A 64-year-old woman presents to her general practitioner with 6 weeks of progressive nasal crusting, recurrent epistaxis, hearing loss, and intermittent haemoptysis. Over the past week she has noticed dark urine. Her bloods are remarkable for raised inflammatory markers and a rising creatinine. Urinalysis shows red cell casts and proteinuria. She is afebrile, alert, and her chest x-ray shows multiple non-cavitating peripheral nodules. ANCA testing has been requested. She is referred urgently to medical assessment.

data_table.Examination: Crusting nasal septum; saddle-nose deformity early; conductive hearing loss; no focal neurology; chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Cr 168 micromol/L (baseline 78); urine PCR 280 mg/mmol, RBCs and casts; CRP 92 mg/L; ANCA pending; CXR with multiple non-cavitating peripheral nodules

lead_in: What is the most likely ANCA pattern in this presentation?

options.text: Anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody (anti-GBM) positivity without ANCA positivity in the typical case
Cytoplasmic ANCA pattern targeting proteinase-3 (PR3-ANCA), classically associated with granulomatosis with polyangiitis
Perinuclear ANCA pattern targeting myeloperoxidase, classically associated with eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis
Atypical ANCA pattern with no recognised target antigen, classically associated with secondary drug-induced vasculitis
Negative ANCA testing with positive cryoglobulins and reduced complement levels, classically suggesting cryoglobulinaemia

subtopic_detail: Stevens-Johnson syndrome / TEN early recognition
stem: A 32-year-old man on day 14 of carbamazepine for newly diagnosed epilepsy presents with 24 hours of malaise, fever, and a painful pink macular rash on his torso. By the time he reaches the emergency department, he has developed early painful blistering of the oral mucosa, conjunctival hyperaemia, and Nikolsky-positive areas covering an estimated 12 percent of his body surface area. He is haemodynamically stable but visibly uncomfortable. His other medications include paracetamol PRN and a probiotic. There is no preceding upper respiratory infection.

data_table.Examination: Pink macular rash on trunk and limbs; Nikolsky positive on shoulder; lip and oral mucosal erosions; bilateral conjunctival injection
