data_table.Investigations: Hb 138 g/L, WCC 11.2 x10^9/L, CRP 64 mg/L, Cr 84 micromol/L, ALT 92 U/L; urea 5.2; bicarbonate 22

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management plan?

options.text: Cease the carbamazepine and arrange urgent transfer to a tertiary burns unit with multidisciplinary support
Continue carbamazepine because of seizure risk and treat the rash with potent topical corticosteroids and emollients
Start empirical intravenous flucloxacillin for presumed staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome until cultures available
Admit under dermatology to the general ward and commence high-dose oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg for skin involvement
Wait 48 hours to see whether erythema multiforme resolves spontaneously before triggering specialty referral pathways

subtopic_detail: DVT 2-level Wells score and pathway
stem: A 58-year-old woman presents to her general practice with 4 days of left calf swelling, pain, and tenderness. She returned from a 12-hour flight from Singapore 6 days ago. She has a history of stage II breast cancer 18 months ago treated with lumpectomy and tamoxifen, but no active disease. Her left calf is 4.5 cm larger than her right and she has pitting oedema. There is no evidence of an alternative diagnosis on examination. She is haemodynamically stable and walks unaided. She has no history of bleeding.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 84, BP 124/76, RR 16, SpO2 98% RA, Temp 36.8
data_table.Examination: Left calf 4.5 cm > right; pitting oedema; tenderness along deep venous system; superficial veins not prominent; no cellulitis
data_table.Investigations: FBC and renal function normal; D-dimer pending

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange D-dimer first and proceed to ultrasound only if positive without calculating a Wells probability score
Refer immediately for inferior vena cava filter placement to prevent pulmonary embolism while diagnosis is being confirmed
Discharge with leg elevation and a compression stocking and review in 1 week if symptoms have not resolved fully
Calculate Wells score; if DVT likely, arrange same-day proximal compression ultrasound and consider therapeutic anticoagulation pending result
Commence empirical oral flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily for presumed cellulitis given calf erythema and warmth

subtopic_detail: Hypertension diagnosis confirmation with ABPM
stem: A 48-year-old woman attends her general practice for a routine review. Three separate in-clinic blood pressure readings over 6 weeks have been 152/94, 148/92, and 156/96 using a calibrated upper-arm device. She is asymptomatic, has no diabetes, and has no end-organ damage on initial screening. Her lipids and ECG are unremarkable. Her absolute cardiovascular risk is calculated as moderate. She is keen to know whether she has hypertension that warrants pharmacotherapy or whether further confirmation is appropriate before treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: Clinic BP 152/94 (today), HR 76, BMI 26
data_table.Examination: No end-organ examination findings; cardiovascular and respiratory examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus rhythm with no LVH criteria; eGFR 92 mL/min; urinary ACR 1.2 mg/mmol; lipids HDL 1.3, LDL 3.4, TG 1.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start perindopril 4 mg daily today based on consistent in-clinic readings above the threshold for stage 1 hypertension
Repeat clinic blood pressure measurement in 12 months without confirmatory home or ambulatory blood pressure assessment
Arrange polysomnography for obstructive sleep apnoea screening before any further diagnostic blood pressure measurement
Refer to endocrinology for plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio testing to exclude primary hyperaldosteronism before treatment
Arrange 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring or 7-day home BP averages, treating if daytime average above 135/85

subtopic_detail: Pleural effusion Light's criteria interpretation
stem: A 67-year-old man presents with 2 weeks of progressive dyspnoea and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. He has a 40 pack-year smoking history and recently lost 5 kg unintentionally. Chest x-ray shows a large right pleural effusion and CT chest demonstrates pleural thickening with no obvious mass. Diagnostic thoracentesis is performed. The serum LDH is 220 U/L (upper limit of normal 240) and serum protein 68 g/L. The pleural fluid analysis is shown. He is afebrile.

data_table.Examination: Right basal stony dullness; reduced breath sounds; no consolidation; no peripheral oedema; JVP not raised
data_table.Investigations: Pleural fluid: protein 38 g/L, LDH 220 U/L, glucose 4.2 mmol/L, pH 7.36; cytology pending; AFB and culture sent. Serum LDH 220 U/L (ULN 240), serum protein 68 g/L

lead_in: How is this pleural effusion best classified using Light's criteria?

options.text: Transudate because the pleural fluid LDH is below the upper limit of normal serum LDH despite raised protein
Transudate consistent with cardiac failure because the patient has a smoking history and dyspnoea on exertion
Exudate, but only if pleural fluid LDH exceeds two thirds of the upper limit of normal serum LDH for laboratory comparison
Transudate based on the pleural fluid to serum LDH ratio being below 0.6 and otherwise unremarkable biochemistry
Exudate because the pleural fluid to serum protein ratio exceeds 0.5, requiring investigation for cause including malignancy

subtopic_detail: Glycaemic target in frail elderly with hypoglycaemia history
stem:
An 84-year-old man with type 2 diabetes (diagnosed 22 years ago), background mild cognitive impairment, stage 3a CKD (eGFR 48), polypharmacy and one fall in the past month attends his GP for diabetic review. He lives alone with home care twice daily. His current HbA1c is 6.5 percent (48 mmol/mol). He has had two episodes of symptomatic hypoglycaemia (BSL under 3.5 mmol/L) in the past 6 weeks, one requiring family call-out.

His treatment is metformin 500 mg BD, gliclazide MR 60 mg daily, and basal insulin glargine 14 units nocte. He has no known retinopathy and his most recent foot check was satisfactory.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 76, BP 132/78, BMI 24, weight 68 kg
data_table.Examination: Frail appearance, normal cardiorespiratory, no peripheral oedema, intact monofilament sensation feet, gait slow with frame indoors
data_table.Investigations: HbA1c 6.5 percent (48 mmol/mol); eGFR 48; ACR 8 mg/mmol; LFT normal; B12 240 pmol/L; lipids LDL 1.9
data_table.Medications: Metformin 500 mg BD, gliclazide MR 60 mg daily, insulin glargine 14 units nocte, perindopril 4 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in glycaemic management?

options.text: Continue current regimen but add a continuous glucose monitor for 14 days then reassess with the family at the next routine clinic visit
Aim for tighter HbA1c at 6 percent (42 mmol/mol) by intensifying basal insulin and adding prandial insulin to reduce risk of long-term diabetic complications
Cease metformin first to reduce gastrointestinal side effects then review the rest of his diabetes regimen in 6 weeks at the next routine appointment
Switch gliclazide to a daily SGLT2 inhibitor for cardiorenal benefit and continue insulin and metformin at the same doses with weekly home checks
Cease gliclazide and reduce insulin glargine by 2 units, targeting HbA1c 7.5 to 8.5 percent (58 to 69 mmol/mol) appropriate for a frail older adult at risk

subtopic_detail: Severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes acute treatment
stem: A 62-year-old man with stage 4 CKD (baseline creatinine 280, eGFR 18) on long-term perindopril and spironolactone presents to ED with 2 days of vomiting, diarrhoea, and now muscle weakness and palpitations. He has not been eating but has continued his usual medications. He looks unwell, mildly hypovolaemic and dyspnoeic. On examination he is alert. The bedside ECG taken 5 minutes ago shows broad-based QRS at 152 ms with tall symmetrical peaked T waves in all precordial leads and absent P waves. Urgent VBG shows potassium 7.4 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 58, BP 102/64, RR 22, SpO2 96% air, T 36.4, weight 78 kg
data_table.Examination: Sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes, JVP not seen, chest clear, no focal neurology, generalised proximal weakness
data_table.Investigations: VBG K 7.4, Na 134, HCO3 16, lactate 1.9, ionised Ca 1.10. Creatinine 412, eGFR 12; ECG: peaked T, broad QRS 152 ms, absent P
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 8 mg, spironolactone 25 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, furosemide 40 mg, paracetamol PRN

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate first step in management?

options.text: Intravenous 10 percent calcium gluconate 10 mL over 2 to 3 minutes by slow push with continuous cardiac monitoring throughout the administration
Activate the renal registrar for emergency haemodialysis as the first definitive treatment while no other temporising measure is attempted yet
Sodium polystyrene sulfonate 30 g orally as a one-off dose to remove potassium from the gut while awaiting renal replacement therapy review
Intravenous actrapid (soluble) insulin 10 units in 50 mL of 50 percent dextrose over 15 minutes as the first intervention before any other therapy
Salbutamol 10 mg nebulised over 10 minutes as a single agent treatment while ECG monitoring continues with bedside cardiac team

subtopic_detail: Sacubitril-valsartan initiation after ACE inhibitor in HFrEF
stem:
A 64-year-old man with chronic HFrEF (LVEF 28 percent on most recent echo) attends cardiology for review. He has been on optimal guideline-directed medical therapy with perindopril 8 mg daily, bisoprolol 10 mg daily, spironolactone 25 mg daily, dapagliflozin 10 mg daily, and furosemide 40 mg daily for 4 months. He remains NYHA class II with mild exertional breathlessness on hills.

There has been no hospitalisation. His BP and renal function are stable. He has no symptomatic hypotension. The cardiologist has agreed with him to switch to sacubitril-valsartan for additional mortality benefit.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 64, BP 122/74, RR 14, SpO2 97% air, weight 84 kg
data_table.Examination: Apex non-displaced, soft S3, no JVP elevation, clear chest, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 138, potassium 4.2, urea 8.2, creatinine 102 (eGFR 64), NT-proBNP 1860 pg/mL, K stable, no recent hypotension or syncope, eGFR stable
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 8 mg, bisoprolol 10 mg, spironolactone 25 mg, dapagliflozin 10 mg, furosemide 40 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, aspirin 100 mg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initiation regimen for sacubitril-valsartan?

options.text: Continue perindopril 8 mg and add sacubitril-valsartan 24/26 mg twice daily for the first 4 weeks then taper perindopril off over the following month
Switch perindopril to candesartan 16 mg first, achieve stable ARB dose for 4 weeks, then change candesartan to sacubitril-valsartan with no washout required
Stop perindopril and start sacubitril-valsartan 24/26 mg twice daily the same evening, doubling every 2 to 4 weeks as tolerated to target dose
Cease perindopril and bisoprolol simultaneously, wait 36 hours, then start sacubitril-valsartan 49/51 mg twice daily and reintroduce beta-blocker later
Cease perindopril, wait 36 hours, then start sacubitril-valsartan 49/51 mg twice daily and uptitrate to 97/103 mg twice daily over 2 to 4 weeks

subtopic_detail: Antibiotic indication in COPD exacerbation using Anthonisen criteria
stem:
A 71-year-old woman with severe COPD (FEV1 38 percent predicted, GOLD group D, two exacerbations in the past year) presents to her GP with 5 days of increased breathlessness, increased cough productive of yellow-green sputum (previously clear), and a sense of greater volume of sputum than usual. There is no fever, chest pain, or haemoptysis. She is using her salbutamol inhaler hourly and her usual budesonide-formoterol twice daily.

She tolerates short walks indoors. She has had no recent travel or sick contacts. She has been triple-therapy inhaler optimised for the past 6 months and her routine sputum culture last admission grew Haemophilus influenzae.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96, BP 138/82, RR 22, SpO2 92% air (baseline 94%), T 36.8
data_table.Examination: Pursed-lip breathing, mild accessory muscle use, prolonged expiration, expiratory wheeze bilaterally, no focal consolidation, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: CXR no consolidation, FBC normal, CRP 32, electrolytes normal, BSL 6.2
data_table.Medications: Budesonide/formoterol 400/12 BD, salbutamol PRN, tiotropium 18 micrograms daily, atorvastatin 40 mg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 50 mg daily for 5 days alone with watchful waiting for the green sputum to resolve and review in 48 hours by phone
Add roflumilast 500 micrograms daily to current therapy and continue inhalers without commencing antibiotics or corticosteroids at this time
Hospital admission for intravenous hydrocortisone, intravenous ceftriaxone, and continuous nebulised salbutamol with NIV standby in the medical assessment unit
Switch budesonide-formoterol to fluticasone-vilanterol-umeclidinium triple therapy as a single inhaler and add oral mucolytic with planned review in one week
Oral prednisolone 50 mg daily for 5 days plus oral amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 5 days and outpatient review in 48 hours by GP or nurse

subtopic_detail: New Graves disease initial pharmacotherapy
stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with 8 weeks of palpitations, 7 kg weight loss despite increased appetite, heat intolerance, tremor, anxiety, frequent loose stools, and mild bilateral exophthalmos with lid lag. She has a diffusely enlarged smooth thyroid with a soft bruit. She is not pregnant and uses condoms with her partner. There is no proximal weakness, no atrial fibrillation, and no thyroid storm features. She is otherwise well. Investigations come back with overt biochemical hyperthyroidism and positive TSH-receptor antibodies. She is willing to start treatment today.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 116 regular, BP 138/68, RR 16, SpO2 99%, T 36.8, weight 56 kg
data_table.Examination: Fine tremor, sweaty palms, lid lag, mild proptosis, smooth goitre with bruit, ECG sinus tachycardia, regular rhythm
data_table.Investigations: TSH <0.01 mU/L, free T4 48 pmol/L, free T3 18 pmol/L, TSH receptor antibodies positive at 12 IU/L, FBC normal, LFT mild ALT rise 56, beta-hCG negative
data_table.Medications: Combined oral contraceptive (suspends), no other regular medication

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological management?

options.text: Atenolol 50 mg daily as monotherapy without thionamide, with reassessment of TFTs in 6 weeks to plan definitive treatment options
Refer for radioactive iodine therapy as definitive treatment without preceding thionamide trial, given the moderate biochemistry and ophthalmic features
Carbimazole 30 mg daily for symptom control and beta-blockade with propranolol 20 mg three times daily until thyroid function normalises
Refer urgently to endocrine surgery for total thyroidectomy as the safest definitive treatment in young women with thyroid eye disease and reproductive plans
Propylthiouracil 100 mg three times daily as the preferred first-line thionamide for all new Graves disease cases in non-pregnant patients

subtopic_detail: Subarachnoid haemorrhage CT-LP investigation pathway for thunderclap headache
stem:
A 46-year-old woman presents to ED 9 hours after a sudden severe headache that reached maximal intensity within 30 seconds while lifting weights at the gym. The headache is now 8 of 10, occipital and band-like, with nausea but no vomiting, no neck stiffness, no photophobia, no focal neurology, and GCS 15. She has hypertension treated with amlodipine. She had no preceding aura, no fever, no recent trauma, and no migraine history.

Non-contrast CT brain performed 30 minutes after arrival (at 9 hours 30 minutes from headache onset) by an experienced neuroradiologist is reported as normal with no haemorrhage and normal grey-white differentiation.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, BP 156/92, RR 16, SpO2 99% air, T 36.6, weight 72 kg, GCS 15
data_table.Examination: No meningism, cranial nerves intact, normal fundi (no papilloedema), no focal weakness or sensory deficit, gait normal, no carotid bruits
data_table.Investigations: Non-contrast CT brain at 9.5 h: no haemorrhage. FBC, electrolytes, coagulation, glucose normal. ECG sinus rhythm
data_table.Medications: Amlodipine 5 mg daily; nil other

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat non-contrast CT brain in 24 hours to detect any progression and discharge home in the interim if symptoms remain stable and there are no new neurological signs
Discharge with reassurance and paracetamol because non-contrast CT within 6 hours has greater than 99 percent sensitivity for subarachnoid haemorrhage in a thunderclap headache presentation
Lumbar puncture at the bedside looking for xanthochromia by spectrophotometry on cerebrospinal fluid collected at least 12 hours after headache onset
Trial sumatriptan 6 mg subcutaneously and admit overnight for migraine observation given the gym onset suggesting an exertional migraine attack
Commence nimodipine 60 mg six-hourly empirically for presumed reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome and admit to the stroke unit for observation

subtopic_detail: Suspected pulmonary embolism in pregnancy diagnostic pathway
stem: A 32-year-old G2P1 at 28 weeks gestation presents to ED with sudden right pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness over 4 hours. She has mild swelling of the right calf with tenderness along the saphenous vein. She is haemodynamically stable, with no haemoptysis. She has no personal or family VTE history. Bedside echocardiogram shows no right heart strain. CXR is unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 108, BP 116/72, RR 22, SpO2 96% air, T 36.8, weight 78 kg
data_table.Examination: Mild right calf tenderness, no obvious unilateral swelling difference, gravid uterus, fetal heart 142 reactive, no S1Q3T3
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal, D-dimer not done (low utility in pregnancy), troponin negative, ECG sinus tachycardia, CXR clear
data_table.Medications: Pregnancy multivitamin, iron supplement

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next diagnostic investigation?

options.text: CT pulmonary angiography as the first-line investigation because it has the highest sensitivity and specificity for pulmonary embolism in all patients
Ventilation perfusion (V/Q) scan as the first-line investigation in pregnancy because of reduced fetal radiation compared to CT pulmonary angiography
Quantitative D-dimer interpreted against trimester-adjusted age-stratified pregnancy-specific cutoffs to rule out venous thromboembolism in pregnancy
Bilateral lower limb compression ultrasound first to look for proximal deep vein thrombosis before any chest imaging in the pregnant patient
Empirical therapeutic dose enoxaparin without imaging while booking outpatient ultrasound and arranging follow-up cardiology and obstetric review

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis management in known Addison disease
stem: A 38-year-old woman with established autoimmune Addison disease (diagnosed 5 years ago) presents to ED with 36 hours of vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain and weakness after attending a friend's wedding. She last took her morning hydrocortisone 20 mg yesterday but has vomited subsequent doses. She normally takes hydrocortisone 20 mg morning, 10 mg lunch, 5 mg evening, and fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily. She wears a medic-alert bracelet. She looks unwell, drowsy but rousable, and is hypotensive.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 124, BP 76/44, RR 22, SpO2 97% air, T 37.4, weight 56 kg, capillary glucose 3.1
data_table.Examination: Pale, dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes, JVP not seen, abdomen soft mildly diffusely tender, no peritonism, increased pigmentation creases and gums
data_table.Investigations: Na 124, K 6.0, urea 14.2, creatinine 132, glucose 3.1, lactate 3.8, troponin negative, beta-hCG negative, FBC normal, blood cultures sent
data_table.Medications: Hydrocortisone 20/10/5, fludrocortisone 100 micrograms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Continue her usual oral hydrocortisone regimen at increased dose 40 mg morning then 20 mg lunch, with ondansetron and intravenous saline rehydration overnight
Intravenous fludrocortisone 0.1 mg stat as the primary corticosteroid replacement for adrenal crisis along with one litre of isotonic saline boluses
Defer corticosteroid administration until a short Synacthen test is performed and cortisol baseline is documented to confirm the diagnosis
Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg stat plus rapid 1 litre intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride bolus and intravenous 50 mL of 50 percent dextrose for hypoglycaemia
Oral dexamethasone 4 mg dispersible tablet with rapid intravenous saline rehydration while awaiting cortisol and ACTH results before commencing further therapy

subtopic_detail: Adult asthma uncontrolled on ICS-LABA step-up
stem: A 42-year-old woman with adult-onset asthma reports daily symptoms requiring her salbutamol 4 times a day, two night-time awakenings per week, and has used three prednisolone courses in the past year. She is fully adherent with budesonide-formoterol 200/6 mcg twice daily plus reliever and has good inhaler technique demonstrated in clinic today. She does not smoke. Spirometry shows FEV1 of 68 percent predicted with 14 percent reversibility post-bronchodilator.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/78, HR 78, RR 16, SpO2 98 percent
data_table.Examination: Scattered end-expiratory wheeze, no clubbing
data_table.Investigations: FEV1 68 percent predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.65, eosinophils 0.35, IgE 88
data_table.Medications: Budesonide-formoterol 200/6 BID, salbutamol PRN

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next medication change?

options.text: Add oral montelukast 10 mg daily to current ICS-LABA as third controller for symptom control
Add a long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) inhaler as a third controller to current ICS-LABA
Refer immediately for omalizumab biologic therapy without further inhaled corticosteroid trials given symptoms
Commence maintenance oral prednisolone 10 mg daily until symptoms have resolved completely
Double the dose of inhaled corticosteroid component within current ICS-LABA combination

subtopic_detail: Notification and partner notification duties after a new HIV diagnosis
stem: You confirm a new HIV diagnosis in a 27-year-old man at your Sydney general practice. He is well and has accepted referral to an s100 prescriber. He asks who else will be told, and says he has had three regular male partners this year.

data_table.Results: Reactive screening immunoassay with positive confirmatory testing; CD4 540 cells per microlitre
data_table.Examination: No rash, oral thrush, lymphadenopathy or weight loss

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Notify the public health unit and offer help with contact tracing
Telephone his named partners today without discussing it with him
Withhold notification because the result is confidential clinical data
Notify only if he declines to tell his partners himself
Leave notification to the laboratory and take no further action

subtopic_detail: Latent tuberculosis - QuantiFERON-Plus interpretation
stem: A 34-year-old woman from Vietnam who immigrated to Australia 6 years ago is being assessed before commencing infliximab for inflammatory bowel disease. She has no respiratory symptoms, no contact with anyone with tuberculosis and a normal chest x-ray. She received BCG vaccination in childhood. She is asymptomatic with normal observations.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7, HR 72, BP 118/70, SpO2 99 percent room air
data_table.Examination: Chest clear, no lymphadenopathy, well
data_table.Investigations: Chest x-ray reported as normal, QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus positive with both TB1 and TB2 antigen tubes above cut-off, sputum unable to be obtained
data_table.Medications: Mesalazine, prednisolone 10 mg daily, planned infliximab

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence infliximab immediately because the positive QuantiFERON likely represents BCG vaccination from childhood, not true latent infection
Begin a 9-month course of isoniazid 5 mg/kg daily with monthly liver function tests and proceed with infliximab in parallel without further evaluation
Repeat QuantiFERON in 12 weeks to confirm persistent positivity before deciding whether to delay biologic initiation in a symptom-free patient
Confirm absence of active tuberculosis with sputum induction and CT chest, then treat latent TB with isoniazid plus pyridoxine for 9 months before commencing infliximab
Refer for directly observed RIPE four-drug therapy as latent TB treatment standard before biologic initiation in this high-risk patient population

subtopic_detail: Necrotising soft tissue infection - recognition and management
stem: A 54-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes presents with 36 hours of severe progressively worsening left lower leg pain following a minor garden injury. The pain is out of proportion to the modest erythema seen at the wound. There is dusky discolouration over a 10 cm area with one tense fluid-filled bulla. He is febrile with tachycardia and feels unwell. He has had paracetamol with no relief.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.9, HR 124, BP 96/58, RR 26, SpO2 96 percent room air
data_table.Examination: Lower limb erythema, dusky 10 cm area, tense haemorrhagic bulla, crepitus to palpation, exquisite pain on light touch
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22, neutrophils 19, Na 128, creatinine 142, glucose 16, CRP 320, lactate 4.6, CK 8400, hb 132
data_table.Medications: Metformin, gliclazide, perindopril

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Plain x-ray of the left lower limb followed by venous duplex ultrasound to exclude deep vein thrombosis prior to antibiotic selection
Admit for intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g every 6 hours and reassess in 24 hours if symptoms have not improved before considering surgical referral
Immediate fluid resuscitation, intravenous meropenem plus vancomycin plus clindamycin, and emergent surgical debridement without delay for imaging
Compute LRINEC score using laboratory values and observe in resuscitation area for 6 hours before deciding on surgical exploration if score is below 6
Apply topical mupirocin to the wound, elevate the limb and arrange outpatient surgical review for early necrotising fasciitis with negative blood cultures

subtopic_detail: Septic shock - hour 1 bundle priorities
stem: A 72-year-old man presents to the emergency department from his nursing home with 6 hours of fever, confusion and reduced urine output. He is normally independent in basic care and lives in the community. He has a history of well-controlled type 2 diabetes and benign prostatic hypertrophy. On arrival he is drowsy and disoriented in time. The triage nurse has applied oxygen and obtained intravenous access.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.7, HR 124, BP 84/52, RR 28, SpO2 92 percent on 2 L nasal prongs
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, cool peripheries, capillary refill 4 seconds, abdomen soft, suprapubic tenderness, no meningism
data_table.Investigations: Bedside lactate 4.2, glucose 14, urinalysis nitrites and leucocytes positive, ECG sinus tachycardia, qSOFA 3
data_table.Medications: Metformin, perindopril, tamsulosin

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step within the first hour of resuscitation?

options.text: Send blood cultures and obtain CT abdomen and pelvis before starting antibiotics to identify the urinary source and exclude obstruction first
Administer oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg single dose while awaiting intravenous access then transfer to a ward bed for ongoing care
Draw blood cultures, give intravenous gentamicin plus piperacillin-tazobactam within 1 hour and start 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid resuscitation guided by clinical response
Defer all antibiotic therapy until cultures return positive in 24 to 48 hours to ensure susceptibility-targeted treatment with the narrowest agent
Commence noradrenaline infusion via peripheral cannula at 0.05 microgram/kg/min before any intravenous fluid resuscitation is given to maintain organ perfusion

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis - recognition and stress dose steroids
stem: A 42-year-old woman with known Addison's disease on hydrocortisone 20 mg morning and 10 mg afternoon plus fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily presents to the emergency department with 24 hours of vomiting from gastroenteritis. She has not been able to keep down her morning hydrocortisone dose. She is drowsy with cool peripheries and looks unwell. She normally carries an emergency steroid card and self-injectable hydrocortisone but did not take it.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4, HR 124, BP 86/52, RR 22, SpO2 98 percent room air
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, dry mucosa, cool peripheries, capillary refill 3 seconds, soft abdomen with mild generalised tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Na 124, K 5.6, glucose 3.1, creatinine 142, lactate 2.4, CRP 18, hb 138, WCC 11
data_table.Medications: Hydrocortisone 20/10 mg, fludrocortisone 100 micrograms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg stat, intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride 1 L over 30 minutes, intravenous dextrose for hypoglycaemia, then hydrocortisone 50 mg every 6 hours
Oral prednisolone 50 mg stat with antiemetic ondansetron 4 mg intravenously and admit to ward for observation with hourly blood pressure and oral fluid replacement
Intravenous dexamethasone 4 mg stat without further hydrocortisone so that subsequent ACTH stimulation testing can be performed within the next 24 hours for confirmation
Intravenous noradrenaline infusion via peripheral cannula at 0.05 microgram/kg/min to address hypotension prior to any glucocorticoid replacement therapy
Intravenous fludrocortisone 200 micrograms stat replacement with intravenous bicarbonate to correct mild metabolic acidosis prior to any other interventions

subtopic_detail: Acute pyelonephritis - empiric therapy
stem: A 42-year-old non-pregnant woman presents to the emergency department with a 36-hour history of fever, rigors, right flank pain and frequency and dysuria. She has no significant medical history. She has been unable to keep down sips of water for the last 6 hours. Examination demonstrates right loin tenderness and percussion tenderness. She has no allergies. Her vital signs reveal sepsis without shock.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.0, HR 112, BP 108/70, RR 22, SpO2 98 percent room air
data_table.Examination: Right loin tenderness, costovertebral angle tenderness, abdomen soft, no peritonism
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis nitrites and leucocytes positive, WCC 14, neutrophils 12, CRP 86, creatinine 88, lactate 1.4, urine culture pending
data_table.Medications: Nil

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empiric therapy?

options.text: Intravenous gentamicin 5 mg/kg single dose followed by oral trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 7 days after discharge with primary care follow-up
Oral nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for 5 days as outpatient management for community-acquired urinary tract infection with mild upper tract features
Intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 6 hours as broad-spectrum empiric therapy for hospitalised community-acquired pyelonephritis with sepsis
Intravenous ampicillin 2 g every 6 hours plus gentamicin 5 mg/kg daily until clinically improved, then oral antibiotics directed by urine culture susceptibility
Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 10 days at home as first-line empiric therapy for community-acquired pyelonephritis in a non-pregnant adult

subtopic_detail: Cushing's syndrome - screening tests
stem: A 38-year-old woman presents with 12 months of progressive weight gain centred on her trunk, easy bruising, proximal muscle weakness when climbing stairs, irregular periods and newly diagnosed hypertension and impaired glucose tolerance. She takes no glucocorticoid medication. She has wide purple striae on her abdomen and a rounded plethoric face. Her GP has referred her for assessment of suspected Cushing's syndrome.

data_table.Examination: Moon facies, supraclavicular and dorsocervical fat pads, central obesity, purple abdominal striae more than 1 cm wide, proximal weakness 4 of 5
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 8.2 fasting, HbA1c 7.2 percent, K 3.4, ALT normal, eGFR 96, ECG sinus rhythm with LVH
data_table.Medications: Perindopril, nil glucocorticoids

lead_in: Which set of investigations is the most appropriate initial screening?

options.text: Plasma morning ACTH at 09:00 with a paired serum cortisol level as a single measurement combined with an FBC and serum electrolytes panel screen
Random 24-hour urinary catecholamines and plasma metanephrines as the initial assessment for secondary causes of hypertension in this 38-year-old woman
MRI pituitary as the first-line investigation to identify a 4-6 mm adenoma, followed by inferior petrosal sinus sampling if no adenoma is seen on imaging today
Insulin tolerance test using 0.1 unit/kg insulin with measurement of cortisol and growth hormone responses to demonstrate adrenal axis activity in this case
At least two of the following: 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test, two 24-hour urinary free cortisol collections, and two late-night salivary cortisol samples

subtopic_detail: Influenza - antiviral indication in high-risk adult
stem: A 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, ischaemic heart disease and COPD on long-acting bronchodilators presents to the general practice with 28 hours of fever, dry cough, myalgia and headache. He had his annual influenza vaccination this year. Nasal swab influenza PCR is positive for influenza A. He is well enough to be managed in the community and has no respiratory distress or hypoxaemia today. He is otherwise stable.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4, HR 96, BP 134/80, RR 18, SpO2 95 percent room air
data_table.Examination: Mild rhinorrhoea, chest with mild expiratory wheeze unchanged from baseline, no consolidation, normal sensorium
data_table.Investigations: Nasal swab influenza A positive, RSV negative, COVID negative, point-of-care CRP 24
data_table.Medications: Tiotropium, salmeterol-fluticasone, metformin, atorvastatin, aspirin, perindopril

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence oral oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days starting today and provide written sick-day advice including return precautions for any deterioration
Reassure that influenza is self-limiting, recommend paracetamol and increased oral fluids, with no role for antivirals when symptom onset is greater than 24 hours ago
Empirical oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily for 5 days for community-acquired bacterial superinfection given his chronic respiratory comorbidity and current viral illness
Increase fluticasone propionate metered dose inhaler dose to 500 micrograms twice daily and prescribe a 5-day course of oral prednisolone 30 mg daily for COPD exacerbation
Refer to hospital for intravenous remdesivir as recommended antiviral therapy for confirmed influenza A in adults with multiple chronic disease comorbidities

subtopic_detail: Primary aldosteronism - aldosterone renin ratio interpretation
stem: A 46-year-old woman is referred for evaluation of resistant hypertension. She is on perindopril, amlodipine and indapamide and her clinic blood pressure remains 168/96. She has spontaneous hypokalaemia and a maternal aunt who had a unilateral adrenal adenoma in her 50s. Her primary care doctor has stopped indapamide for 6 weeks and is considering further investigation before referral. She has had no recent caffeine or strenuous activity before testing.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 168/96 confirmed, HR 76, BMI 28
data_table.Examination: Clinically euvolaemic, no abdominal bruit, no cushingoid features
data_table.Investigations: Na 142, K 3.0, bicarbonate 30, creatinine 78, eGFR 78, ECG sinus rhythm with U waves
data_table.Medications: Perindopril, amlodipine

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Twenty-four hour urinary fractionated metanephrines collected over 24 hours with parallel plasma metanephrines to screen for an underlying phaeochromocytoma diagnosis
Renal artery duplex ultrasound to exclude renovascular hypertension secondary to fibromuscular dysplasia as a treatable cause of her resistant blood pressure pattern
Empirical commencement of spironolactone 25 mg daily and clinical reassessment of blood pressure at 6 weeks without measuring the aldosterone or renin first
Morning paired plasma aldosterone and renin to calculate aldosterone to renin ratio after replacing potassium and substituting interfering antihypertensives
Overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test to assess cortisol axis and exclude subclinical Cushing syndrome as cause of resistant hypertension and metabolic disturbance

subtopic_detail: Postmenopausal osteoporosis - pharmacological initiation
stem: A 68-year-old postmenopausal woman attends the general practice for review after a low-trauma wrist fracture following a fall from standing height 6 weeks ago. She had a previous Colles fracture 2 years ago. Her mother had a hip fracture aged 78. She is on no current bone-affecting medications. Her DXA shows lumbar spine T-score minus 2.6 and femoral neck T-score minus 2.4. Her calcium and vitamin D levels are within range and her renal function is normal.

data_table.Examination: Healing wrist fracture, height loss 2 cm over past decade, no kyphosis, no spinal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.34, phosphate 1.1, 25-OH vitamin D 78, ALP 88, eGFR 78, PTH 4.2, TSH 1.6
data_table.Medications: Calcium 600 mg with vitamin D 1000 IU daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue calcium and vitamin D supplementation alone with annual DXA scanning and lifestyle advice for the next 12 months without pharmacological bone therapy
Commence raloxifene 60 mg orally daily as a selective oestrogen receptor modulator for postmenopausal spinal osteoporosis with prior fragility fracture
Initiate transdermal estradiol patch 50 micrograms twice weekly with a progestogen for endometrial protection as primary therapy for postmenopausal bone loss
Refer for teriparatide 20 micrograms subcutaneously daily as first-line anabolic therapy for high fracture risk postmenopausal osteoporosis with a recent fragility fracture
Commence oral alendronate 70 mg weekly with calcium and vitamin D and arrange dental review before starting given the risk of medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw

subtopic_detail: HSV encephalitis - empirical management
stem: A 56-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his partner with 3 days of progressive headache, confusion, fever and one witnessed generalised seizure today. He has no significant medical history and is up to date with his vaccinations. He is drowsy with GCS 13, disoriented, has slow word-finding speech and no focal neurology. There is no rash and no neck stiffness on examination. He has had no recent travel or sick contacts.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.6, HR 102, BP 138/86, RR 18, SpO2 97 percent room air
data_table.Examination: GCS 13 (E3V4M6), disoriented, no meningism, no focal weakness, no rash, no papilloedema
data_table.Investigations: WCC 10, CRP 32, Na 132, glucose 6.4, creatinine 82, ECG sinus rhythm
data_table.Medications: Nil

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Commence intravenous aciclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours empirically before any imaging or lumbar puncture is performed for suspected herpes simplex viral encephalitis
Perform urgent lumbar puncture for CSF analysis and viral PCR before any therapy is commenced to confirm the diagnosis and identify the responsible pathogen accurately
Order urgent non-contrast CT brain and EEG, then commence ceftriaxone 4 g daily plus dexamethasone for bacterial meningitis cover pending further results from investigations
Administer intravenous levetiracetam 1500 mg loading dose for seizure control and observe with neurological observation until brain imaging and CSF results return for review
Treat with intravenous foscarnet 60 mg/kg every 12 hours as first-line antiviral therapy for adult viral encephalitis given the higher potency over standard aciclovir options

subtopic_detail: Adult bacterial meningitis - empiric therapy with dexamethasone
stem: A 32-year-old previously well woman presents with 18 hours of severe headache, fever, neck stiffness, photophobia and one episode of vomiting. She is alert. Examination demonstrates positive Brudzinski sign and significant neck stiffness. She has no rash. She has no allergies and is not pregnant. The CT brain has been arranged but is delayed and a lumbar puncture has not yet been done. She is haemodynamically stable.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.1, HR 108, BP 128/76, RR 18, SpO2 98 percent room air
data_table.Examination: Alert, severe neck stiffness, positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs, no rash, no focal neurology, GCS 15
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18, neutrophils 16, CRP 240, lactate 1.6, Na 138, glucose 7.2, coags normal, blood cultures sent
data_table.Medications: Nil

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate empirical therapy?

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g every 12 hours without adjunctive corticosteroid because steroids have inconclusive benefit in adult community-acquired bacterial meningitis
Defer all antibiotic therapy until non-contrast CT brain excludes raised intracranial pressure followed by diagnostic lumbar puncture for CSF analysis and culture
Oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily with paracetamol as outpatient management for community-acquired meningitis in a well-appearing patient without focal neurology
Intravenous vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading dose monotherapy and proceed directly to lumbar puncture for CSF testing without empirical beta-lactam coverage first today
Intravenous dexamethasone 10 mg immediately followed by ceftriaxone 2 g every 12 hours with benzylpenicillin 1.8 g every 4 hours pending CSF results

subtopic_detail: Suspected giant cell arteritis - initiation of treatment
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 74-year-old woman with 3 days of severe right-sided temporal headache, jaw claudication after a few minutes of chewing, and a brief episode of blurred vision in her right eye that resolved after 30 minutes this morning. She has been generally fatigued for 6 weeks. Past history includes hypertension and osteoporosis on alendronate. Examination reveals tenderness over the right temporal artery, which is non-pulsatile and feels thickened. Visual acuity is currently 6/6 bilaterally and fundoscopy is normal.

data_table.Examination: Right temporal artery tender, thickened, pulseless; no proximal limb weakness, no scalp necrosis, neuro exam normal, fundoscopy normal
data_table.Investigations: Hb 116, platelets 444, WCC 9.8, ESR 92, CRP 78, ALP normal, creatinine 74
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 5 mg daily; alendronate 70 mg weekly; calcium 600 mg, vitamin D 1000 IU daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 60 mg daily immediately, refer urgently for temporal artery biopsy within 1 week, and arrange ophthalmology review the same day for visual symptom assessment
Arrange temporal artery biopsy first to confirm the diagnosis histologically before commencing any corticosteroid therapy that might confound interpretation of the histological vessel inflammation
Prescribe oral aspirin 100 mg daily, refer for urgent vascular ultrasound of the temporal artery, and review the result before deciding on initiation of corticosteroid therapy at a later date
Prescribe paracetamol regularly for headache, arrange GP review in 1 week with repeat inflammatory markers, and refer to general medicine if the clinical features have not settled by then
Commence oral prednisolone 15 mg daily and refer to rheumatology outpatients for assessment within 4 weeks, providing patient information about polymyalgia rheumatica and steroid management plan

subtopic_detail: Adult cellulitis - empirical antibiotic selection
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 56-year-old man with a 2-day history of a painful, hot, expanding erythematous area over his left shin since gardening barefoot last week. There is no systemic upset, no fever, and no diabetes. He has had no previous cellulitis. He has no penicillin allergy. The erythema is sharply demarcated, warm and tender, with no fluctuance, no necrotic centre, and no skin breakdown beyond a small healed abrasion. He is able to weight-bear and there is no joint involvement. He is otherwise well.

data_table.Examination: Sharply demarcated erythema 12 cm diameter over left anterior shin, warm and tender, no fluctuance, no lymphangitis, small healed abrasion centrally, inguinal nodes not enlarged
data_table.Investigations: Not routinely required for uncomplicated cellulitis
data_table.Medications: Nil

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic?

options.text: Oral cefalexin 500 mg orally four times daily for 5 days, with arm or leg elevation, demarcating the leading edge in pen, and review at 48 hours to ensure clinical improvement
Oral amoxicillin clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily for 7 days as broad spectrum cover including Gram negatives, with anti-inflammatory cover using oral ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily
Oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days to cover community-associated MRSA, accepting that doxycycline gives suboptimal Streptococcus cover compared to a beta lactam antibiotic
Intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g six hourly via outpatient parenteral antibiotic service for 5 days, with daily nurse review and observation for failure of erythema demarcation to improve
Oral phenoxymethylpenicillin 500 mg four times daily for 10 days as targeted streptococcal cover, with topical mupirocin to the abrasion site to address the likely entry portal

subtopic_detail: Hyperthyroidism in pregnancy - first trimester management
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 29-year-old G2P1 at 9 weeks gestation referred by the GP for thyroid abnormalities found on routine bloods. She has tremor, palpitations, heat intolerance and a 3 kg weight loss despite a good appetite. There is no family history of thyroid disease. She has no eye signs. She is not currently taking any medication.

Her previous pregnancy was uncomplicated. The midwife notes a goitre is palpable. The infant's heart rate is 158 on Doppler. There is no neck pain or recent viral illness.

data_table.Examination: Fine tremor, smooth diffuse goitre 2x normal size, no nodules palpable, no exophthalmos, no lid lag, no pretibial myxoedema, hyperreflexia
data_table.Investigations: TSH less than 0.01, free T4 38, free T3 12.4, TSH receptor antibodies positive, beta-hCG 90000, viability scan 9+2
data_table.Medications: Nil

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence carbimazole 15 mg daily and titrate based on monthly free T4, refer to endocrinology and high-risk obstetrics, and aim for free T4 in the upper third of the non-pregnant reference range
Commence propylthiouracil 100 mg three times daily, refer to endocrinology and high-risk obstetrics, switch to carbimazole at start of second trimester, and monitor free T4 monthly
Reassure as transient gestational hyperthyroidism, recheck thyroid function at 16 weeks, and reserve antithyroid drug therapy for persistent biochemical abnormality at the second trimester review
Arrange radioactive iodine ablation now to permanently resolve the hyperthyroid state and prevent fetal exposure to antithyroid drugs through the placenta over the remainder of the pregnancy
Commence propranolol 20 mg three times daily as monotherapy for symptom control, defer definitive antithyroid drug therapy until after delivery to avoid placental transfer to the developing fetus

subtopic_detail: Lewy body dementia - antipsychotic avoidance
stem: You are the geriatric medicine registrar reviewing a 73-year-old man in the rehab ward with a 12-month progressive cognitive decline characterised by fluctuating attention, recurrent vivid visual hallucinations of small animals, and bradykinesia with a shuffling gait. His wife reports he acts out his dreams at night. Cognition fluctuates from near-normal to disoriented over hours. He has been agitated overnight on the ward and the after-hours doctor is considering a sedating antipsychotic to manage the night-time disturbance for the rest of the admission.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6, HR 78, BP 124/72 lying, BP 102/64 standing, RR 16, SpO2 98%
data_table.Examination: Bradykinesia, mild cogwheel rigidity bilaterally, MMSE 22/30 with marked fluctuation across the assessment, no focal neurology, no seizure activity
data_table.Investigations: Hb 132, UEC normal, TSH 1.9, B12 320, glucose 5.4, CT brain age-related atrophy, MRI excluded vascular dementia, DaTscan reduced striatal uptake
data_table.Medications: Donepezil 5 mg nocte (recently started)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of his nocturnal behavioural disturbance?

options.text: Commence olanzapine 5 mg at night for behavioural disturbance, with reassessment in 1 week to assess for sedation, parkinsonism worsening, or any other adverse effects on motor function
Stop the donepezil because cholinesterase inhibitors may aggravate behavioural disturbance, and substitute with quetiapine 25 mg at night for sedation and management of visual hallucinations
Commence haloperidol 0.5 mg at night for hallucinations and behavioural disturbance, accepting the small risk of extrapyramidal side effects in older patients with cognitive impairment

Optimise non-pharmacological interventions, exclude delirium triggers (infection, constipation, urinary retention, pain), continue cholinesterase inhibitor, and consider low-dose melatonin for sleep regulation
Commence levodopa-carbidopa 100/25 mg three times daily to address the parkinsonism, accepting that this may worsen hallucinations but provides motor benefit for the patient's gait disturbance

subtopic_detail: Provoked VTE - duration of anticoagulation
stem: You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 58-year-old man for outpatient follow-up after a confirmed right lower limb deep vein thrombosis 3 months ago. The DVT followed elective right total knee replacement and was diagnosed at day 5 postoperatively. He is on apixaban 5 mg twice daily after a loading dose at presentation. He is otherwise well, has had no symptoms since the event, has no personal or family history of VTE, and is not on hormones. He is back to his usual activity level and his postoperative recovery is otherwise excellent.

data_table.Examination: Knee well healed, no calf swelling, no tenderness, no chest signs, no new neurology
data_table.Investigations: FBE normal, UEC creatinine 78, LFTs normal, INR baseline 1.0, repeat duplex ultrasound shows residual non-occlusive thrombus, no recurrence
data_table.Medications: Apixaban 5 mg BD; paracetamol PRN for occasional knee pain

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing anticoagulation plan?

options.text: Stop apixaban and commence aspirin 100 mg daily indefinitely for secondary prevention against recurrent venous thromboembolism, with review by haematology before any future major surgery
Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily indefinitely because residual thrombus on ultrasound indicates ongoing prothrombotic state and conveys a high risk of recurrence without long-term anticoagulation
Reduce apixaban to 2.5 mg twice daily and continue indefinitely for extended secondary prevention, with annual review of bleeding risk and renal function to maintain ongoing anticoagulation safety
Switch from apixaban to warfarin with INR target 2 to 3 for ongoing therapy and arrange thrombophilia screening including factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene mutation and lupus anticoagulant
Stop apixaban now at the standard 3 months and provide written advice on VTE recurrence symptoms with safety net advice for return if any new chest, leg or breathlessness symptoms develop

subtopic_detail: Aortic dissection - diagnostic imaging selection
stem:
You are the ED registrar called to see a 62-year-old man with sudden onset severe ripping interscapular and chest pain that began 1 hour ago at rest. He has a history of poorly controlled hypertension. On examination there is a 28 mmHg difference between arms with the right side higher, an early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge that was not previously documented, and reduced left radial pulse volume.

ECG shows sinus rhythm with left ventricular hypertrophy and no ST elevation. He is alert and his pain remains severe despite 5 mg of intravenous morphine.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7, HR 92, BP right arm 178/96, BP left arm 150/90, RR 22, SpO2 97%
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, early diastolic murmur LSE, reduced left radial volume, no focal neurology, chest clear, abdomen soft non-tender
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus LVH no ST elevation, troponin 28 (mildly raised), chest x-ray widened mediastinum 9 cm, D-dimer 4.8, creatinine 92, lactate 1.6
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 4 mg daily; amlodipine 5 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Commence aspirin 300 mg and ticagrelor 180 mg, give a heparin bolus then infusion, and refer to cardiology for emergent percutaneous intervention for likely NSTEMI complicated by acute aortic regurgitation
Arrange transthoracic echocardiogram on the ward first to confirm the diagnosis before any CT imaging is performed, with cardiology consult once visualisation of the aortic root has been obtained

Administer thrombolysis with tenecteplase weight-adjusted bolus immediately based on the chest pain and elevated D-dimer, accepting that primary PCI is not available within the standard 120-minute window
Commence sodium nitroprusside infusion to rapidly lower blood pressure to target systolic 120, with intravenous morphine for analgesia and observation for spontaneous resolution of pain
Commence intravenous esmolol infusion to target heart rate under 60 and systolic BP under 120, give intravenous opioid for analgesia, and arrange immediate contrast CT aortogram with surgical consult

subtopic_detail: STEMI without immediate PCI access
stem: You are the ED registrar in a regional hospital 220 km from the nearest cardiac catheterisation laboratory. A 58-year-old man arrives with 80 minutes of central crushing chest pain radiating to his left arm. He has hypertension and dyslipidaemia and is a current smoker. He took aspirin 300 mg on the ambulance and is haemodynamically stable. The nearest PCI service has confirmed a minimum 150-minute door-to-balloon time including air transfer.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/86 mmHg, HR 92 bpm, RR 18, SpO2 96% on room air, T 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, chest clear, normal heart sounds, no murmur, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: 12-lead ECG: 2 mm ST elevation V2-V4 with reciprocal changes in II, III, aVF; troponin pending; no prior ECG available

lead_in: What is the most appropriate reperfusion strategy?

options.text: Commence intravenous metoprolol 5 mg three times to slow heart rate and defer reperfusion until troponin returns
Administer intravenous heparin alone and arrange transfer for primary PCI on arrival 150 minutes after first medical contact
Continue oral aspirin 300 mg only and arrange transfer for angiography within 24 hours without acute reperfusion
Administer oral ticagrelor 180 mg load and observe in the coronary care unit without further reperfusion therapy
Administer intravenous tenecteplase weight-based bolus plus clopidogrel and enoxaparin then transfer for early angiography within 24 hours

subtopic_detail: Severe acute pancreatitis
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 54-year-old man admitted overnight with epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea and vomiting. He drinks 80 g of alcohol most evenings. He has been started on intravenous fluids and morphine. At 24 hours after admission you are asked to reassess him because he has become more tachypnoeic, his urine output has fallen and he feels worse. He has no history of cardiac or renal disease.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 102/64 mmHg, HR 116 bpm, RR 28, SpO2 92% on 4 L oxygen via nasal prongs, T 38.2°C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen diffusely tender with guarding, no peritonism, no rebound, no rash, no jaundice, urine output 18 mL/hour over the last 3 hours
data_table.Investigations: Lipase 1820 U/L, calcium 1.92 mmol/L, glucose 11.4 mmol/L, urea 14.6 mmol/L, WCC 18.4 x10^9/L, LDH 480 U/L, AST 220 U/L, PaO2 on arterial gas 58 mmHg on supplemental oxygen

lead_in: Which severity stratification action is most appropriate now?

options.text: Apply Ranson criteria at 48 hours and continue current ward-level management until that time point
Commence intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics prophylactically to prevent infected necrosis
Continue ward-level care with intravenous fluids and morphine and review at 48 hours with repeat lipase
Arrange urgent endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography to relieve presumed gallstone obstruction
Transfer urgently to a high-dependency unit because the patient meets organ failure criteria for severe acute pancreatitis

subtopic_detail: Carotid endarterectomy timing
stem: You are the neurology registrar reviewing a 68-year-old man in the stroke clinic 3 days after a transient ischaemic attack of right-sided weakness and aphasia lasting 30 minutes that resolved spontaneously. He has hypertension, hyperlipidaemia and is a former smoker. He is on aspirin 100 mg daily and has been started on atorvastatin 80 mg daily. He has no atrial fibrillation on Holter monitoring. His ABCD2 score is 5.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/82 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, T 36.7°C, sinus rhythm
data_table.Examination: Normal neurological examination, no carotid bruits audible, no signs of cardiac failure
data_table.Investigations: Carotid duplex: 80% stenosis left internal carotid artery, MRI brain DWI shows small acute left frontal infarct, no haemorrhage, lipids LDL 1.8 mmol/L on statin, HbA1c 6.0%

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Add clopidogrel 75 mg daily as long-term dual antiplatelet therapy without carotid surgical or stenting intervention
Continue medical management alone with aspirin and atorvastatin and arrange surveillance carotid duplex in 6 months
Refer for carotid endarterectomy ideally within 2 weeks of the symptomatic event with ongoing aspirin and statin therapy
Refer for carotid endarterectomy electively in 3 to 6 months once the patient has fully recovered from the TIA event
Refer for carotid artery stenting as first-line intervention in this 68-year-old man with high-grade symptomatic stenosis

subtopic_detail: HFrEF GDMT in low-BP patient
stem: You are the cardiology registrar reviewing a 68-year-old man with newly diagnosed heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. His echocardiogram shows LVEF 28% and a moderately dilated left ventricle. He has type 2 diabetes, hypertension and chronic kidney disease stage 3a. He is currently on ramipril 5 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily and metformin 1 g twice daily. He has been improving over 3 days of hospital admission and is now euvolaemic.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 98/58 mmHg seated, HR 72 bpm, RR 16, SpO2 97% on room air, T 36.6°C
data_table.Examination: JVP not raised, no peripheral oedema, lungs clear, mild left ventricular heave, no murmur
data_table.Investigations: K 4.6 mmol/L, creatinine 142 micromol/L (eGFR 46 mL/min/1.73 m^2), HbA1c 7.2%, NT-proBNP 1800 pg/mL

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next medication adjustment?

options.text: Increase ramipril to 10 mg daily aiming for maximum tolerated ACE inhibitor dose
Switch ramipril to sacubitril-valsartan 24/26 mg twice daily today
Add spironolactone 25 mg daily today as the next pillar of guideline-directed therapy
Add empagliflozin 10 mg daily and continue ramipril 5 mg daily without dose changes
Add ivabradine 5 mg twice daily for heart rate control alongside the current therapy

subtopic_detail: HIV with cryptococcal antigen positive
stem: You are the infectious diseases registrar reviewing a 38-year-old man newly diagnosed with HIV through community testing. He has a CD4 count of 78 cells/microL and viral load of 350,000 copies/mL. He has no current symptoms of headache, fever or visual changes. As part of baseline workup his serum cryptococcal antigen has returned positive at a titre of 1:160. He has not commenced antiretroviral therapy yet. He has no medication allergies and is not on any current medications.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/74 mmHg, HR 76 bpm, T 36.7°C, weight 72 kg
data_table.Examination: No meningism, no focal neurology, normal fundoscopy, no skin lesions, no oral candidiasis, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Serum cryptococcal antigen positive 1:160, lumbar puncture pending, MRI brain pending, FBC, UEC, LFTs within normal limits, hepatitis serology negative, tuberculin IGRA negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Defer all interventions and repeat serum CrAg in 4 weeks to see if the titre declines spontaneously
Commence antiretroviral therapy with bictegravir-emtricitabine-tenofovir alafenamide and review in 4 weeks
Commence oral fluconazole 800 mg daily for 2 weeks then start ART without lumbar puncture
Perform lumbar puncture today to exclude cryptococcal meningitis before any treatment decision
Refer for primary prophylaxis with oral itraconazole 200 mg daily without further investigation

subtopic_detail: Status epilepticus second-line
stem: You are the medical registrar in resus seeing a 28-year-old woman with known generalised epilepsy on lamotrigine, brought in with a generalised tonic-clonic seizure that started 12 minutes before arrival and has continued. Paramedics gave 10 mg intramuscular midazolam without termination. On arrival she received a further intravenous 4 mg lorazepam without effect. She is not pregnant on point-of-care testing. Her airway is patent on a jaw thrust and she has IV access.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 168/96 mmHg, HR 138 bpm, RR 24, SpO2 94% on 15 L oxygen via non-rebreather, T 37.8°C, BSL 5.8 mmol/L
data_table.Examination: Ongoing generalised tonic-clonic seizure, no focal neurology, no rash, no head injury, no needle marks
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.22 with metabolic acidosis, lactate 6.8 mmol/L, Na 138 mmol/L, lamotrigine level pending, urine drug screen pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Intravenous levetiracetam 60 mg/kg infused over 5 to 10 minutes with cardiac monitoring
Intravenous phenytoin 20 mg/kg infused over 30 minutes with cardiac monitoring
Intravenous propofol 2 mg/kg bolus and infusion to induce general anaesthesia immediately
Intravenous sodium valproate 40 mg/kg infused over 10 minutes with electrolyte monitoring
Intravenous midazolam 0.2 mg/kg as a third benzodiazepine dose to attempt termination

subtopic_detail: Contrast-associated AKI prevention
stem: You are the medical registrar planning a non-emergency CT coronary angiogram in a 74-year-old man with stable angina to clarify the cause of his recurrent chest pain. He has type 2 diabetes, chronic kidney disease stage 3b with stable eGFR 32, and well-controlled hypertension. He is on perindopril, furosemide 40 mg daily, atorvastatin and metformin. He is not in acute heart failure and has had no recent illness. The cardiologist has requested your input on peri-procedural medication.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 128/74 mmHg, HR 68 bpm, T 36.6°C, weight 84 kg
data_table.Examination: JVP not raised, no peripheral oedema, lungs clear, no abdominal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 168 micromol/L, eGFR 32 mL/min/1.73 m^2, K 4.4 mmol/L, HbA1c 6.8%, urine ACR 14 mg/mmol

lead_in: Which combination of peri-procedural strategies is most appropriate?

options.text: Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1.4% at 3 mL/kg/hour for 1 hour pre-procedure as the sole preventive intervention
Withhold metformin permanently and give oral N-acetylcysteine 1200 mg twice daily for 24 hours pre- and post-procedure
Continue all current medications including perindopril, furosemide and metformin without peri-procedural changes
Withhold metformin for 48 hours from morning of procedure, give intravenous sodium chloride 0.9% at 1 mL/kg/hour pre and post
Administer prophylactic intravenous loop diuretic 80 mg immediately pre-contrast to enhance contrast clearance

subtopic_detail: Phaeochromocytoma preoperative alpha-blockade
stem: You are the endocrine registrar planning the surgical preparation for a 47-year-old woman with a 5.2 cm right adrenal mass producing markedly elevated 24-hour fractionated metanephrines. She has paroxysmal severe headaches with palpitations and pallor. Her resting blood pressure is 168/108 mmHg with episodes recorded to 220/120 mmHg during paroxysms. Her HbA1c is 6.4% and she is not on any current medications. Cardiology review showed normal left ventricular function. Surgery is planned for 14 days from now.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 168/108 mmHg average over the last day, HR 96 bpm, RR 16, T 36.6°C, weight 64 kg
data_table.Examination: Patient anxious, mild diaphoresis at rest, no signs of cardiac failure, no abdominal mass palpable
data_table.Investigations: Plasma metanephrines markedly elevated, 24-hour urinary metanephrines elevated, K 3.6 mmol/L, Mg 0.78 mmol/L, ECG sinus tachycardia, MRI confirms 5.2 cm right adrenal lesion

lead_in: Which preoperative regimen is most appropriate?

options.text: Phenoxybenzamine 10 mg twice daily titrated against orthostatic BP, add atenolol 25 mg daily after 7 days, high salt diet
Atenolol 25 mg daily first to control heart rate then add phenoxybenzamine 10 mg twice daily after 5 days, normal salt diet
Amlodipine 5 mg daily titrated to control blood pressure as the sole preoperative agent for 14 days before surgery
Proceed directly to surgery without preoperative blockade because the patient has been asymptomatic between paroxysms
Intravenous magnesium sulfate infusion alone for 14 days before surgery as the sole preoperative blockade agent

subtopic_detail: DOAC choice in atrial fibrillation with CKD stage 3
stem: You are the GP seeing a 78-year-old woman with newly diagnosed paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. Her CHA2DS2-VA score is 4 (age over 75, hypertension, prior TIA, female sex not counted in CHA2DS2-VA). Her HAS-BLED is 2. Her eGFR is 38 mL/min/1.73m2 (CKD G3b) and serum creatinine 145 micromol/L. She has no liver disease, no recent bleeding and weighs 62 kg. She is hesitant about warfarin because she cannot easily attend frequent INR checks.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6°C, HR 88 irregular, RR 14, BP 138/82
data_table.Examination: Irregularly irregular pulse, no peripheral oedema, no murmurs, no neurology
data_table.Investigations: ECG AF, eGFR 38, Cr 145, Hb 128, LFTs normal, INR 1.0

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulant strategy?

options.text: Dabigatran 150 mg twice daily titrated against renal function with trough drug sampling
Warfarin titrated to INR 2.0 to 3.0 with weekly point-of-care monitoring at her local clinic
Long-term aspirin 100 mg daily as monotherapy for stroke prophylaxis in atrial fibrillation
Apixaban 5 mg twice daily, dose-reduce if two of age 80, weight 60 kg, Cr 133 micromol/L
Defer anticoagulation until Holter confirms at least six hours per day of AF burden

subtopic_detail: Hypertensive emergency BP target
stem: You are the ED registrar seeing a 56-year-old man with severe occipital headache, blurred vision and nausea for 6 hours. His BP at triage is 222/128 mmHg. He has a background of long-standing untreated hypertension and is normally well. Fundoscopy shows bilateral flame haemorrhages and a single cotton wool spot. He has new mild confusion and his ECG shows LVH with strain. He has no chest pain, no neurological deficit and no recent stroke. The renal function is mildly impaired with creatinine 145 micromol/L.

data_table.Examination: Mildly drowsy, GCS 14, no lateralising signs, fundoscopy as above
data_table.Investigations: Cr 145 micromol/L, K 3.9, troponin negative, ECG LVH strain pattern, CT head no acute haemorrhage

lead_in: What is the most appropriate blood pressure target and agent in the next hour?

options.text: Discharge home on oral perindopril 5 mg with GP review in 48 hours of presentation
Lower the mean arterial pressure by 20 to 25 percent in the first hour with IV labetalol
Defer pharmacological treatment until ambulatory monitoring confirms sustained elevation
Commence oral hydralazine plus oral clonidine simultaneously aiming for fast normotension
Bring BP to 140/90 mmHg within the first 30 minutes using sublingual nifedipine capsules

subtopic_detail: TIA ABCD2 risk stratification and admission threshold
stem: You are the ED registrar reviewing a 72-year-old man with a 25-minute episode of right-sided weakness and dysarthria that resolved 1 hour ago. He has hypertension, diabetes and is in sinus rhythm. CT brain is normal. He has no atrial fibrillation on telemetry. He is on perindopril, metformin and atorvastatin. Carotid Doppler ultrasound is available the next morning at the same site. He has no contraindication to antiplatelet therapy.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 162/92, HR 78, RR 16, T 36.5 °C, SpO2 98% room air, BSL 8.2
data_table.Examination: Normal neurological examination now, no carotid bruit, no facial droop, no dysarthria currently
data_table.Investigations: CT brain unremarkable, ECG sinus rhythm, troponin negative; carotid Doppler tomorrow morning

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Admit for inpatient stroke workup, start aspirin 300 mg today and arrange carotid imaging today
Discharge home with aspirin 100 mg daily and a routine outpatient carotid Doppler in two weeks' time
Commence apixaban 5 mg twice daily today and arrange carotid Doppler tomorrow morning as planned
Arrange urgent MRI brain with diffusion weighting prior to commencing any antiplatelet therapy today
Refer to outpatient TIA clinic in 7 days without commencing any new medication today at all

subtopic_detail: AF cardioversion timing and DOAC anticoagulation
stem: You are the ED registrar managing a 64-year-old man with new symptomatic atrial fibrillation. Onset was 18 hours ago by his account during exertion. He has hypertension, diabetes and a CHA2DS2-VA score of 4. He is haemodynamically stable. He has no history of bleeding and no contraindication to anticoagulation. Transthoracic echocardiogram shows normal left ventricular function and no thrombus visualised. He prefers rhythm control if safe and you have decided cardioversion is appropriate.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/82, HR 138 irregular, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air, T 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Irregularly irregular pulse, no chest pain, no signs of heart failure, no carotid bruit
data_table.Investigations: Hb 142, U&E normal, INR 1.0, ECG atrial fibrillation 132 bpm, TTE LVEF 60% no thrombus, TFTs normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation plan around DC cardioversion?

options.text: Defer cardioversion until 3 weeks of therapeutic apixaban 5 mg twice daily have been completed
Start apixaban 5 mg twice daily now, cardiovert today and continue anticoagulation for at least 4 weeks
Cardiovert immediately without anticoagulation because no thrombus was seen on the transthoracic echo today
Bridge with intravenous unfractionated heparin and cardiovert in 7 days after admission to coronary care
Cardiovert without anticoagulation now and start aspirin 100 mg daily for long-term thromboprophylaxis

subtopic_detail: Hour-1 bundle and vasopressor choice in septic shock
stem: You are the ED registrar reviewing a 58-year-old woman with two days of dysuria, fever and rigors. She is hypotensive with cool peripheries. She has no allergies and no chronic disease. Initial intravenous crystalloid 30 mL/kg has been given over the past hour but her mean arterial pressure remains 58 mmHg. Lactate is 4.6 mmol/L. Urine, blood cultures and a chest X-ray have been completed. Empirical antibiotics for severe urosepsis are being prepared.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.2 °C, HR 122, BP 86/52, MAP 58, RR 24, SpO2 96% room air, UO 0.3 mL/kg/h
data_table.Examination: Warm flushed centrally, cool peripheries, no focal chest signs, suprapubic tenderness, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 4.6 mmol/L, CRP 220, creatinine 138, WCC 18 x10^9/L, urinalysis leucocytes and nitrites positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in haemodynamic management?

options.text: Continue further intravenous crystalloid up to 50 mL/kg before commencing any vasopressor support
Commence intravenous noradrenaline infusion via large-bore peripheral line targeting MAP 65 mmHg
Administer intravenous adrenaline 1 mg bolus and commence infusion targeting systolic above 100 mmHg
Commence dopamine 5 micrograms/kg/min infusion as the recommended first-line vasopressor in septic shock
Defer vasopressor and add intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg per day for refractory hypotension now

subtopic_detail: Aortic dissection imaging and initial pharmacotherapy
stem: You are the ED registrar at a tertiary hospital seeing a 64-year-old man with sudden severe tearing interscapular pain. BP is 184/108 in the right arm and 142/82 in the left arm. He has a long history of hypertension and is on perindopril. He is now diaphoretic but alert. Pulses are present in all four limbs. ECG shows sinus rhythm with LVH but no ischaemic changes. He has no contrast allergy and creatinine is 92 micromol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 184/108 right arm, 142/82 left arm, HR 92, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air, T 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, alert, palpable pulses all four limbs, no focal neurological deficit, no abdominal pain
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus rhythm LVH, CXR widened mediastinum, troponin negative, creatinine 92, D-dimer 3.8 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Send for urgent transthoracic echocardiogram as the definitive first-line diagnostic test for aortic dissection
Commence intravenous heparin infusion empirically until CT pulmonary angiogram has excluded clot
Start intravenous nitroprusside infusion first without beta blocker to drop SBP under 110 mmHg fast
Arrange CT angiography of the aorta and start IV esmolol then sodium nitroprusside to control BP
Discharge home with oral perindopril increase to 8 mg daily once routine bloodwork is unremarkable

subtopic_detail: Dabigatran reversal with idarucizumab in major bleeding
stem: You are the ED registrar reviewing a 78-year-old woman with a confirmed traumatic intracerebral haemorrhage of 30 mL on CT after a fall. She takes dabigatran 150 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation. Her last dose was 4 hours ago. She has a GCS of 12 and is being prepared for neurosurgical input. She has no other medications and no chronic kidney disease. The hospital pharmacy stocks idarucizumab, prothrombin complex concentrate and tranexamic acid.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 174/96, HR 78, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air, T 36.6 °C, GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5)
data_table.Examination: Right hemiparesis MRC 3/5, slurred speech, no other focal deficit, pupils equal reactive
data_table.Investigations: Hb 124 g/L, platelets 220, creatinine 85, INR 1.3, dTT pending, CT brain 30 mL right thalamic haematoma

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Administer prothrombin complex concentrate 25 IU/kg now and recheck the INR after 30 minutes
Administer intravenous idarucizumab 5 g as two 2.5 g boluses given 15 minutes apart now urgently
Give intravenous vitamin K 10 mg and fresh frozen plasma 15 mL/kg to correct her coagulopathy quickly
Commence intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes as the sole haemostatic agent for ICH now
Arrange urgent haemodialysis to remove dabigatran prior to commencing any specific reversal therapy

subtopic_detail: Giant cell arteritis biopsy and steroid timing
stem: You are the ED registrar seeing a 76-year-old woman with two weeks of new daily temporal headache, jaw claudication after a few bites, and a tender thickened right temporal artery. Vision is currently normal. She has had no transient visual loss and no diplopia. She has had no prior steroid use and has no diabetes. She has an enlarged thyroid but is biochemically euthyroid. Her ESR is 92 mm/h and CRP is 110 mg/L. The vascular team can perform temporal artery biopsy within 7 days.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/82, HR 76, RR 16, T 36.7 °C, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Examination: Tender thickened right temporal artery, no pulses; visual acuity 6/9 bilaterally, no relative afferent pupillary defect
data_table.Investigations: ESR 92 mm/h, CRP 110 mg/L, FBC normal, platelets 380, no anaemia, eye fundoscopy normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management plan?

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg today and arrange temporal artery biopsy within the next week
Defer all steroid therapy until temporal artery biopsy histology has confirmed the underlying diagnosis
Start intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days only for any patient with suspected GCA
Commence indometacin 50 mg three times daily and review again with ESR result in two weeks' time
Commence low-dose prednisolone 15 mg daily and arrange same-day temporal artery duplex ultrasound study

subtopic_detail: Phaeochromocytoma crisis alpha then beta blockade
stem: You are the ED registrar managing a 44-year-old man with episodic severe headaches, palpitations and sweating. His BP today is 218/124 with HR 124. He has had no antihypertensive therapy. Recent imaging from an outside hospital showed a 5 cm adrenal mass on CT. Plasma free metanephrines from a prior workup were markedly elevated. He has had no prior cardiovascular events. He is now in the resuscitation cubicle with arterial line and ICU is aware. Endocrine surgery has been contacted.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 218/124, HR 124, RR 22, SpO2 97% room air, T 36.8 °C, BSL 9.2
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, alert, no focal neurology, no chest pain currently, mild tremor
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia LVH; plasma normetanephrine markedly elevated; CT 5 cm right adrenal mass; troponin negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate pharmacological management?

options.text: Start intravenous metoprolol 5 mg now and add phenoxybenzamine after rate control has been achieved
Give intravenous hydralazine 10 mg as a single bolus to lower the blood pressure rapidly first now
Begin intravenous labetalol 20 mg bolus to provide combined alpha and beta blockade in one rapid step
Commence intravenous phentolamine 5 mg boluses and titrated infusion, defer beta blocker until alpha block is established
Administer intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g as a single bolus then continue infusion in lieu of any alpha blocker
