subtopic_detail: Rhabdomyolysis fluid resuscitation and hyperkalaemia management
stem: You are the ED registrar reviewing a 24-year-old man brought in after 18 hours immobile on the floor following a methamphetamine binge. He has dark urine, swollen tender thighs and is oliguric. His CK is 86,000 IU/L. He has had no prior renal disease. He is alert but distressed by limb pain. Trauma has been excluded by primary and secondary survey. He has no medications. The intensive care registrar has been contacted regarding admission.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/82, HR 102, RR 22, SpO2 99% room air, T 36.9 °C, UO 0.2 mL/kg/h
data_table.Examination: Tense tender swollen thighs bilaterally, sensation intact, distal pulses intact, no compartment syndrome features yet
data_table.Investigations: CK 86,000 IU/L, K 6.4 mmol/L, creatinine 280, urea 18, pH 7.28, bicarbonate 16, urinalysis blood 3+ no RBC, ECG peaked T waves V2-V4

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Administer intravenous insulin 10 units with dextrose 25 g only and reassess potassium after 30 minutes today
Give intravenous furosemide 80 mg bolus to drive forced diuresis as the cornerstone of myoglobin clearance
Commence haemodialysis empirically to remove myoglobin and lower the serum creatine kinase fast
Begin intravenous mannitol 1 g/kg as the recommended renal-protective osmotic diuretic in rhabdomyolysis
Administer intravenous calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10% solution and start aggressive isotonic crystalloid fluid

subtopic_detail: Empirical antibiotic therapy for native-valve right-sided endocarditis
stem: You are the medical registrar admitting a 38-year-old man with 4 weeks of fevers, sweats and a 6 kg weight loss. He has injected heroin daily for 4 years. On examination there is a new pansystolic murmur loudest at the lower left sternal edge. Two sets of peripheral blood cultures taken 12 hours apart have already grown methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. Transthoracic echo shows an 8 mm tricuspid vegetation. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4 °C, HR 110, BP 118/72, RR 22, SpO2 96% room air
data_table.Examination: New pansystolic murmur at LLSE louder on inspiration; multiple injection sites on forearms; no peripheral stigmata; clear chest; soft abdomen
data_table.Investigations: Blood cultures: MSSA in 2 of 2 sets at 12 h apart; TTE: 8 mm tricuspid vegetation, preserved LV function; FBC and U&E unremarkable; HIV non-reactive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antimicrobial therapy?

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin alone for 6 weeks dosed to target trough 15-20 mg/L
Intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g every 4 hours for at least 4 weeks with daily review
Intravenous amoxicillin and gentamicin combination for 6 weeks with daily monitoring
Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g once daily as monotherapy for 6 weeks under outpatient OPAT
Oral cefalexin 1 g four times daily with outpatient cardiology review next week

subtopic_detail: Vasopressor initiation in fluid-refractory septic shock
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 72-year-old man transferred from the ward 48 hours after admission for community-acquired pneumonia. He has now had 2 litres of intravenous crystalloid in the last hour with no improvement. Blood cultures were drawn and intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam was administered 30 minutes ago. He is confused and looks unwell. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.9 °C, HR 124, BP 78/40, RR 28, SpO2 92% on 4 L oxygen, GCS 13
data_table.Examination: Cool peripheries with capillary refill 5 seconds; coarse crackles right base; warm core; oliguria for 2 hours
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 4.2 mmol/L, WCC 21 x10^9/L, CRP 280 mg/L, creatinine 162 micromol/L (baseline 90), procalcitonin elevated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next intervention?

options.text: Continue with a further 2 L crystalloid bolus before considering vasopressor support
Commence dopamine infusion as a first-line vasopressor through a peripheral line first
Give intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg before starting any vasopressor infusion now
Commence noradrenaline infusion through central or large peripheral access targeting MAP ≥65
Defer further antibiotic doses until repeat blood cultures and sensitivities are available

subtopic_detail: Empirical therapy for adult bacterial meningitis with Listeria cover
stem: You are the medical registrar in the emergency department reviewing a 65-year-old man with 12 hours of fever, severe headache, photophobia and neck stiffness. GCS is 13. No focal neurology. No skin rash. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. He takes no immunosuppressants. Lumbar puncture has been performed and the CSF analysis is back.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.5 °C, HR 116, BP 132/82, RR 22, SpO2 96% room air, GCS 13
data_table.Examination: Marked neck stiffness; positive Kernig sign; no focal deficit; no skin rash; clear chest
data_table.Investigations: CSF: WCC 1200/microL (90 percent neutrophils), protein 3.2 g/L, glucose 1.2 mmol/L (paired BSL 6.4 mmol/L), Gram stain pending; FBC and U&E unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g 12-hourly as the sole antibiotic until cultures return
Intravenous amoxicillin and gentamicin only awaiting culture and sensitivity results
Ceftriaxone with benzylpenicillin Listeria cover and dexamethasone at standard adult doses
Intravenous vancomycin alone with a target trough of 15-20 mg/L pending sensitivities
Defer all antibiotics until Gram stain and culture results are available later today

subtopic_detail: Acute HIV seroconversion diagnosis with negative antibody screen
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 28-year-old man who has sex with men with a 10-day history of fever, sore throat, generalised lymphadenopathy and a maculopapular rash on the trunk. He reports unprotected receptive anal intercourse with a new partner 3 weeks ago. He has had no recent travel. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. Fourth-generation HIV combined antigen and antibody assay is negative. Streptococcal throat swab, EBV serology and CMV serology are all negative.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.6 °C, HR 96, BP 122/76, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Examination: Maculopapular rash on trunk; cervical, axillary and inguinal lymphadenopathy; mild pharyngeal erythema; no oral ulceration; no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: HIV combined Ag/Ab fourth generation: negative; EBV IgM negative; CMV IgM negative; throat swab negative for strep; FBC: lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat the HIV combined Ag/Ab test in 12 weeks for a definitive negative result
Order HIV RNA viral load PCR now to detect early infection within the window period
Send CD4 count alone to assess immune status before deciding on next investigations
Commence empirical antiretrovirals immediately without diagnostic confirmation now
Discharge with reassurance and review in 4 weeks if symptoms have not resolved

subtopic_detail: Necrotising soft tissue infection time-critical surgical referral
stem: You are the medical registrar in the emergency department reviewing a 55-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes who presents with 12 hours of rapidly progressive, severely painful swelling of the left lower leg following trivial garden trauma. He looks toxic with rigors. The leg has dusky erythema with two haemorrhagic bullae and a small area of crepitus over the medial calf. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. He has no documented antibiotic allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.2 °C, HR 124, BP 96/58, RR 24, SpO2 95% room air
data_table.Examination: Dusky erythema with two haemorrhagic bullae; crepitus over medial calf; pain out of proportion; brisk capillary refill becomes sluggish at edges
data_table.Investigations: CRP 380 mg/L, WCC 24 x10^9/L, Hb 110 g/L, sodium 128 mmol/L, creatinine 180 micromol/L, glucose 18 mmol/L, lactate 3.8 mmol/L; LRINEC score 11

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Outpatient oral cefalexin 500 mg four times daily with review in primary care in 48 hours
Intravenous cefazolin 2 g 8-hourly as monotherapy without referral for surgical exploration
Arrange punch skin biopsy first to confirm the diagnosis prior to any surgical consultation
Magnetic resonance imaging of the affected leg before any surgical exploration takes place
Urgent surgical exploration with debridement plus IV piperacillin-tazobactam, clindamycin and vancomycin

subtopic_detail: Pharmacotherapy initiation in older-onset Parkinson disease
stem: You are the neurology registrar reviewing a 68-year-old retired teacher with an 18-month history of right-hand resting tremor, bradykinesia, mild rigidity, mild gait shuffle and difficulty with handwriting that is interfering with daily activities. There are no falls, no orthostasis, no early visual hallucinations and no cognitive impairment on MoCA (28/30). He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 128/76 supine, 124/74 standing; HR 70
data_table.Examination: Right-hand resting tremor 4 Hz; cogwheel rigidity at wrist; mild hypomimia; bradykinesia on finger taps; mild shuffling gait; no postural instability; MoCA 28/30
data_table.Investigations: TFTs, B12 and folate normal; FBC and U&E unremarkable; DAT-SPECT abnormal asymmetric nigrostriatal uptake

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Rasagiline 1 mg daily as monotherapy aiming to defer levodopa for at least 12 months
Pramipexole 0.125 mg three times daily titrating to symptom control with no levodopa
Amantadine 100 mg twice daily alone for symptom control over the next 6-12 months
Levodopa with peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor titrated from low dose to symptom control
Refer for deep brain stimulation now before any oral pharmacotherapy is initiated

subtopic_detail: Outpatient anticoagulation for provoked deep venous thrombosis
stem: You are the emergency department resident reviewing a 56-year-old man with a 5-day history of swelling and aching in the right leg. He returned 10 days ago from a 24-hour international flight. He has no chest pain or breathlessness. He has no personal or family history of clotting or bleeding. He is on no regular medications and has no allergies. His weight is 88 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 °C, HR 86, BP 124/78, RR 16, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Examination: Swollen erythematous right calf, tender along medial calf, asymmetric calf measurement 38 vs 35 cm, palpable distal pulses, no chest signs
data_table.Investigations: Whole-leg compression ultrasound: non-compressible right popliteal vein with extension to the femoral vein. FBC, U&E and LFTs unremarkable. eGFR 92 mL/min/1.73 m^2.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Admit for intravenous unfractionated heparin titrated to APTT 60 to 80 seconds and bridge to warfarin maintaining INR 2 to 3 over the following days of admission
Commence apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily for at least 3 months and arrange general practitioner follow-up to plan total duration of anticoagulation
Refer urgently for thrombolysis with intravenous alteplase 100 mg over two hours to clear the venous thrombus and prevent post-thrombotic syndrome at long-term follow-up
Place an inferior vena cava filter and start apixaban 5 mg twice daily without a lead-in phase to prevent pulmonary embolism in his routine outpatient anticoagulation pathway
Defer anticoagulation and arrange weekly compression ultrasounds for the next month to monitor whether the thrombus extends proximally before any treatment is initiated for him

subtopic_detail: Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease corticosteroid duration
stem: You are the general medical registrar admitting a 68-year-old man with a 3-day worsening of his usual breathlessness and a productive cough with purulent sputum. He has known COPD on tiotropium and salbutamol with two exacerbations in the last 12 months. He is afebrile and able to speak in short sentences. He has no diabetes and no recent antibiotics. His baseline FEV1 is 52% predicted.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.0 °C, HR 102, BP 138/82, RR 26, SpO2 90% room air, rising to 94% on 2 L nasal prongs
data_table.Examination: Bilateral wheeze, use of accessory muscles, no consolidation, no peripheral oedema, calves soft
data_table.Investigations: Chest x-ray: hyperinflation, no consolidation. ABG on 2 L: pH 7.36, pCO2 52 mmHg, pO2 68 mmHg, HCO3 28 mmol/L. CRP 38 mg/L, WCC 12.4 x10^9/L.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate course of systemic corticosteroid?

options.text: Administer a single intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg dose only with no oral corticosteroid follow-on therapy planned at discharge from the emergency department
Prescribe oral prednisolone 50 mg daily for 14 days with weekly clinic review during the taper and a brief intravenous methylprednisolone bridge to commence treatment
Order intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg every 6 hours for 72 hours and convert to ongoing oral maintenance prednisolone 10 mg daily on discharge for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease control
Continue inhaled corticosteroid as currently prescribed with no oral course because this exacerbation is sufficiently mild and self-limiting and additional steroid will not change outcomes
Start oral prednisolone 30 to 50 mg daily for 5 days without taper and add empirical amoxicillin or doxycycline based on the purulent sputum profile during this exacerbation

subtopic_detail: Metformin initiation in newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes
stem: You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 58-year-old woman with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes confirmed by two fasting glucose readings and an HbA1c. She has no symptoms of polyuria or weight loss. She has hypertension on perindopril. She does not smoke and drinks one glass of wine on weekends. She has no chronic kidney disease history and no acute cardiovascular events. Her body mass index is 31 kg/m^2.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 31 kg/m^2, no peripheral oedema, foot examination intact, fundi unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: HbA1c 7.8%, fasting glucose 9.2 mmol/L, eGFR 68 mL/min/1.73 m^2, creatinine 86 micromol/L, LFTs normal, urine albumin:creatinine ratio 2.4 mg/mmol

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological step?

options.text: Start basal insulin 10 units at night and uptitrate by 2 units every 3 days targeting a fasting glucose below 6.0 mmol/L without using any oral hypoglycaemic agent first
Commence empagliflozin 10 mg daily as initial monotherapy and arrange a follow-up appointment in three months for a repeat HbA1c and dose review with a structured plan
Recommend lifestyle measures only and review the HbA1c in 6 months before starting any glucose-lowering medication, regardless of her starting HbA1c or other clinical risk profile
Start metformin 500 mg daily with food, uptitrate over 4 weeks to 1 g twice daily as tolerated and review HbA1c and renal function at 3 months
Initiate gliclazide modified-release 30 mg daily with breakfast and aim for an HbA1c below 6.5% over the next six months without using any other glucose-lowering therapy

subtopic_detail: Rate control of new-onset atrial fibrillation without heart failure
stem: You are the general medical resident reviewing a 64-year-old man brought in with palpitations and mild exertional breathlessness over 24 hours. He has hypertension on perindopril. He has no chest pain and no history of heart failure or asthma. He has had no fevers, recent surgery or alcohol binge. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. He is comfortable at rest and the symptoms are not currently distressing.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 °C, HR 132 irregularly irregular, BP 138/86, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Examination: Chest clear, JVP not elevated, no peripheral oedema, no murmurs, calves soft
data_table.Investigations: ECG: atrial fibrillation, ventricular rate 130s, no ischaemic changes. TSH 1.8 mIU/L, electrolytes normal, troponin not elevated. Bedside echo: preserved left ventricular ejection fraction. CHA2DS2-VA score 2.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial rate-control agent?

options.text: Start oral digoxin 250 micrograms twice daily for 48 hours then a maintenance dose of 125 micrograms daily as first-line rate control monotherapy in this stable presentation
Commence oral metoprolol tartrate 25 mg twice daily and arrange anticoagulation with apixaban 5 mg twice daily for stroke prevention given his CHA2DS2-VA score
Refer for direct current cardioversion under sedation today within 48 hours of estimated onset, without prior anticoagulation, to restore sinus rhythm as the primary management strategy
Start oral amiodarone 200 mg three times daily for one week and then 200 mg daily ongoing as long-term combined rate and rhythm control in this stable patient with preserved function
Commence intravenous verapamil 5 mg over 5 minutes and arrange oral diltiazem maintenance therapy alongside apixaban for ongoing rate control in this clinically stable patient

subtopic_detail: Diagnostic workup of suspected pulmonary tuberculosis
stem: You are the infectious diseases registrar reviewing a 41-year-old man who arrived from Vietnam six months ago. He has had a 6-week productive cough with night sweats and 4 kg of weight loss. He has had two episodes of streaks of blood in his sputum. He has no chronic medical conditions and is on no medications. He has had no known sick contacts within his immediate household at present.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.6 °C, HR 96, BP 122/78, RR 18, SpO2 96% room air
data_table.Examination: Thin man, no clubbing, fine crackles in the right upper zone, no lymphadenopathy, normal cardiac examination
data_table.Investigations: Chest x-ray: right upper lobe cavitating consolidation with fibronodular changes. HIV antibody negative. FBC: Hb 124 g/L, WCC 8.4 x10^9/L, lymphocytes 1.6 x10^9/L. ESR 68 mm/h. CRP 56 mg/L.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?

options.text: Start empirical anti-tuberculosis therapy with rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol immediately and obtain microbiological samples after a 14-day clinical response review at the clinic
Place a tuberculin skin test now and proceed to start empirical anti-tuberculosis therapy only if it shows induration above 10 mm at the 48 to 72 hour reading
Arrange a single QuantiFERON-TB Gold-Plus interferon gamma release assay test, place him in airborne isolation pending the assay result and avoid further sputum sampling testing
Place him in single-room airborne isolation and collect 3 sputum specimens for acid-fast smear, Xpert MTB/RIF nucleic acid amplification and mycobacterial culture before commencing therapy
Order a chest computed tomography scan and bronchoscopy as the first investigation to obtain bronchoalveolar lavage samples for cytology and routine microbiological cultures upfront

subtopic_detail: Massive pulmonary embolism with haemodynamic compromise
stem: You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 64-year-old woman 8 days after right hip arthroplasty. She has sudden severe breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain. She is on prophylactic enoxaparin 40 mg daily. She has no major bleeding risk factors and no recent stroke or surgery to neck or central nervous system. She has not been thrombolysed for any other condition recently.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 °C, HR 124, BP 86/54, RR 32, SpO2 88% on 10 L Hudson mask
data_table.Examination: Pale, cold peripheries, capillary refill 4 seconds, raised jugular venous pulse, clear chest, right calf 4 cm larger than left
data_table.Investigations: CT pulmonary angiogram: bilateral central pulmonary emboli with right ventricular dilation, septal bowing. Troponin elevated. ECG: sinus tachycardia, S1Q3T3 pattern.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Start a continuous enoxaparin infusion at 1 mg/kg twice daily and admit for observation and serial echocardiography to assess for right ventricular recovery over the next 24 to 48 hours
Insert an inferior vena cava filter via the femoral vein under fluoroscopic guidance as the initial intervention before considering further escalation of anticoagulation or reperfusion
Resuscitate with intravenous fluids and noradrenaline targeting MAP above 65 mmHg, give intravenous unfractionated heparin and administer alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours
Switch to oral apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily and discharge home in 24 hours for outpatient follow-up with general practitioner and physiotherapy
Arrange immediate transfer for surgical pulmonary embolectomy as the first-line reperfusion strategy without prior thrombolysis or anticoagulation in this haemodynamically compromised patient

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis precipitated by intercurrent illness in a patient on long-term steroids
stem: You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 52-year-old woman with primary adrenal insufficiency, presenting with 36 hours of vomiting, abdominal pain and progressive drowsiness. She normally takes hydrocortisone 10 mg morning, 5 mg afternoon and fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily. She has not taken her steroids in the last 24 hours because of vomiting. She has not received intramuscular hydrocortisone at home and is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.2 °C, HR 124, BP 78/46, RR 24, SpO2 97% room air, capillary refill 4 seconds
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, dry mucous membranes, hyperpigmented palmar creases, mild abdominal tenderness, no peritonism
data_table.Investigations: Na 122 mmol/L, K 5.8 mmol/L, glucose 3.0 mmol/L, creatinine 124 micromol/L, urea 14 mmol/L. ABG: pH 7.30, HCO3 18 mmol/L. ECG sinus tachycardia. CRP 84 mg/L.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Administer intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg once and arrange transfer to the medical ward for ongoing rehydration with crystalloid fluid resuscitation and broad-spectrum antibiotics
Triple her oral hydrocortisone dose to 30 mg morning and 15 mg afternoon, give an oral glucose drink and arrange admission for serial monitoring of electrolytes and observation
Restrict fluids to 1 L per 24 hours, give intravenous hypertonic saline 3% for the hyponatraemia and observe for clinical response before commencing any specific steroid therapy
Withhold any steroid until a random cortisol level has been processed by the laboratory and the result is available, then dose based on the measured cortisol level result
Give intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg stat, commence intravenous 0.9% saline with dextrose 5% and start an empirical sepsis workup with broad-spectrum antibiotic cover

subtopic_detail: Discriminating SIADH from hypovolaemic hyponatraemia in a hospitalised patient
stem: You are the general medical registrar reviewing a 72-year-old woman on day 4 of admission with community-acquired pneumonia. She is on oral amoxicillin and clarithromycin. She had been improving but is now mildly confused and has had three falls overnight. She has been drinking freely from the water jug. She has no diuretics and no recent vomiting. She has not received intravenous fluids in the past 24 hours. Her chest is clearing on examination.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 °C, HR 84, BP 124/76, RR 16, SpO2 96% room air, no postural drop documented
data_table.Examination: Moist mucous membranes, no peripheral oedema, JVP not elevated, abdomen soft, capillary refill under 2 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Na 122 mmol/L (admission 138), K 4.2 mmol/L, urea 3.4 mmol/L, creatinine 60 micromol/L, glucose 5.4 mmol/L, plasma osmolality 256 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 480 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 56 mmol/L. TSH 1.6 mIU/L. Cortisol 412 nmol/L.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer 100 mL of 3% hypertonic saline as a single bolus, recheck sodium in 1 hour and limit total correction to 10 mmol/L in 24 hours and 18 mmol/L in 48 hours
Commence intravenous 0.9% saline at 100 mL/hour and check the sodium every 4 hours for the first 24 hours and adjust the infusion rate accordingly based on the trajectory
Continue current management without specific sodium intervention and recheck serum sodium and clinical state in 24 hours because the result is likely a pseudohyponatraemia laboratory artefact
Restrict free water to 1 L per 24 hours, cease the clarithromycin which is contributing to free water retention and recheck the sodium in 24 hours after these measures are in place
Start oral tolvaptan 15 mg daily and recheck the sodium every 6 hours over the next 24 hours, withholding additional treatment if the sodium rises by more than 10 mmol/L in that period

subtopic_detail: STEMI presenting within PCI window
stem: You are the emergency registrar in a metropolitan hospital with onsite primary percutaneous coronary intervention service. A 58-year-old non-Aboriginal man presents 50 minutes after the onset of central crushing chest pain radiating to his left arm. He has been given aspirin 300 mg orally by the paramedics. He has no contraindications to dual antiplatelet therapy and no bleeding diathesis. His pain is now 7 out of 10 and he is diaphoretic.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 °C, HR 96, BP 138/82, RR 20, SpO2 96% room air
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, chest clear, heart sounds dual without murmur, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: ECG: 2 mm ST elevation V2 to V5 with reciprocal inferior depression, troponin pending, FBE and U&E normal, INR 1.0

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence tenecteplase weight-adjusted intravenous bolus and admit to the coronary care unit with rescue percutaneous coronary intervention if no resolution at 90 minutes
Administer aspirin 300 mg, an additional oral P2Y12 inhibitor and arrange transfer for elective angiography within 24 hours during normal working hours
Loading dose ticagrelor 180 mg orally, intravenous heparin and immediate activation of the cardiac catheter laboratory for primary PCI within 90 minutes of first contact
Order CT coronary angiogram to confirm the diagnosis before deciding on revascularisation strategy, given that troponin has not yet been reported back as elevated
Manage medically with intravenous beta-blocker, statin and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor in the coronary care unit and reassess for invasive strategy in 72 hours

subtopic_detail: Community acquired pneumonia outpatient antibiotic
stem: You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 42-year-old non-Aboriginal woman with three days of productive cough, fever and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. She has no significant past medical history and no recent hospital admission. She is not pregnant. She lives independently and her partner can supervise her at home. Her SMART-COP score is 0. She is up to date with COVID-19 and influenza vaccinations.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.6 °C, HR 96, BP 124/74, RR 20, SpO2 96% room air
data_table.Examination: Right lower zone crackles and bronchial breath sounds, no oxygen requirement, normal mental state, no signs of dehydration
data_table.Investigations: Chest x-ray: right lower lobe consolidation; rapid antigen testing for SARS-CoV-2 and influenza negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic?

options.text: Oral azithromycin 500 mg once daily for three days as monotherapy for atypical and typical coverage in the outpatient setting
Oral cefalexin 500 mg four times daily for 7 days because it provides broad-spectrum cover for both Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae
Oral moxifloxacin 400 mg daily for seven days as broad-spectrum coverage including atypical pathogens in the community setting given the productive cough
Oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily for five days with general practice review at 48 hours and safety netting for worsening breathlessness or systemic features
Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily for seven days because of broader beta-lactamase coverage given right lower lobe consolidation on imaging

subtopic_detail: New atrial fibrillation rate versus rhythm control
stem: You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 68-year-old non-Aboriginal man with palpitations and breathlessness for three weeks. He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes. He has had no chest pain or syncope. His exercise tolerance has fallen from 1 km to 200 m. His CHA2DS2-VA score is 4 and he has no bleeding risk factors. He has no history of heart failure or asthma.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132 irregular, BP 138/84, RR 18, SpO2 97% room air
data_table.Examination: Irregularly irregular pulse, chest clear, no peripheral oedema, no thyroid swelling, no carotid bruit
data_table.Investigations: ECG atrial fibrillation rate 130, TSH normal, echocardiogram pending, electrolytes normal, troponin normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management strategy?

options.text: Immediate DC cardioversion in the emergency department under conscious sedation and discharge on aspirin 100 mg daily without anticoagulation
Commence oral amiodarone 200 mg three times daily for one week then 200 mg daily and start aspirin 100 mg with cardiology outpatient review in three months
Start digoxin 125 micrograms daily for rate control and aspirin 100 mg daily for stroke prevention with review in two weeks to assess heart rate and symptoms
Commence apixaban 5 mg twice daily, metoprolol 25 mg twice daily titrated for rate control and arrange cardiology review for rhythm-control consideration
Refer for urgent electrophysiology study and pulmonary vein isolation ablation without commencing anticoagulation in the interim while awaiting the procedure

subtopic_detail: Moderate adult asthma exacerbation
stem: You are the emergency registrar reviewing a 28-year-old non-Aboriginal woman with a four hour history of worsening breathlessness and wheeze on a background of asthma. She has used 12 puffs of salbutamol at home in the last hour without much relief. She is able to speak in short phrases. She has not required steroids in the last six months. She has no penicillin allergy and is up to date with her influenza vaccine.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 °C, HR 116, BP 124/76, RR 26, SpO2 93% room air
data_table.Examination: Bilateral expiratory wheeze, mild accessory muscle use, able to complete short sentences, no cyanosis
data_table.Investigations: Peak expiratory flow 200 L/min (personal best 420 L/min), chest x-ray clear, no fever

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 0.5 mg, nebulised ipratropium and oral antibiotics empirically for presumed lower respiratory tract infection driving the exacerbation
Inhaled fluticasone-formoterol four puffs via spacer and discharge home with an updated written asthma action plan after 30 minutes of observation in the department
Intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg, intravenous aminophylline loading infusion and admission to high dependency for continuous cardiac and respiratory monitoring
Salbutamol 12 puffs via spacer (or 5 mg nebulised) every 20 minutes for one hour, oral prednisolone 50 mg, oxygen titrated to SpO2 of 93 to 95%, and reassess at one hour
Heliox-driven salbutamol nebulisation with immediate intubation if no response, and intravenous magnesium sulfate 10 g infused over 30 minutes as first-line therapy

subtopic_detail: Severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes
stem: You are the medical registrar urgently reviewing a 72-year-old non-Aboriginal man with chronic kidney disease stage 4 brought in by his wife with weakness and nausea. He takes ramipril, spironolactone, metformin and trimethoprim for a recent urinary tract infection. He missed his haemodialysis-free clinic review last week. He has had no chest pain. He has no contraindication to insulin therapy.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6 °C, HR 48, BP 110/68, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Examination: Alert, normal mental state, no peripheral oedema, soft abdomen
data_table.Investigations: K 7.4 mmol/L, Na 136, urea 23.1, creatinine 358 micromol/L, bicarbonate 18, glucose 6.8; ECG sinus bradycardia 48 with peaked T waves, PR 220 ms, broad QRS 124 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Intravenous sodium polystyrene sulfonate (resonium) 30 g and oral sodium bicarbonate 1 g three times daily while awaiting renal review later today
Intravenous furosemide 80 mg, oral salbutamol 8 mg and arrange a fast track to outpatient haemodialysis later today via the renal registrar on call team
Insulin actrapid 10 units in 50 mL 50% dextrose intravenously and reassess potassium and ECG at 30 minutes without giving any calcium because the patient is haemodynamically stable
Activate the medical emergency team and prepare for intubation given the bradycardia and broad QRS, with definitive cardiac pacing and central venous access before any drug therapy is administered
Intravenous calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10% solution over 5 minutes for cardiac membrane stabilisation, then insulin-dextrose and nebulised salbutamol, and urgent dialysis referral

subtopic_detail: Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia with seizure
stem: You are the medical registrar called urgently to assess a 65-year-old non-Aboriginal woman who has had a witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure on the ward. She was admitted three days ago for an exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and given intravenous fluids. She drinks no alcohol and is on no diuretics. She is now post-ictal but rousable. Her serum sodium on admission was 138 mmol/L and is now 116 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6 °C, HR 92, BP 132/78, RR 18, SpO2 96% on 1 L oxygen via nasal prongs
data_table.Examination: Post-ictal, GCS 12, no focal neurological deficit, soft abdomen, no oedema
data_table.Investigations: Na 116 mmol/L, K 4.0, urea 4.2, creatinine 76 micromol/L, serum osmolality 248, urine osmolality 510, urine sodium 68, TSH normal, cortisol normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride 1000 mL infusion over 4 hours and restrict free water intake to under 1 L per 24 hours with daily electrolyte review for 3 days
Oral fluid restriction to 800 mL per day combined with oral sodium chloride 1 g three times daily and reassess sodium in 12 hours with intravenous fluids ceased
Demeclocycline 300 mg twice daily orally for one week and continue current intravenous fluids and supportive care without active sodium correction in the next 6 hours
Oral tolvaptan 15 mg single dose now with serial sodium measurements at 2 hours and admission to high dependency for cardiac and respiratory monitoring
Intravenous 3% sodium chloride 150 mL bolus over 10 minutes, repeat to a maximum of three boluses, with sodium target rise of 4 to 6 mmol/L in the first hour and capped at 10 mmol/L per 24 hours

subtopic_detail: Acute on chronic respiratory acidosis interpretation
stem: You are the respiratory registrar reviewing a 70-year-old non-Aboriginal man with a 60 pack-year smoking history presenting with three days of worsening breathlessness and increased sputum production. He has known severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and was given controlled oxygen by the paramedics. He is drowsy but rousable to voice. He has been on home oxygen 1 L overnight only. He has no chest pain.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.4 °C, HR 110, BP 138/82, RR 26, SpO2 92% on 28% Venturi mask
data_table.Examination: Pursed lip breathing, accessory muscle use, asterixis, expiratory wheeze and prolonged expiratory phase, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: ABG on 28%: pH 7.28, paCO2 70, paO2 62, HCO3 32, base excess +6; chest x-ray hyperinflated with no infiltrate; CRP 42, WCC 12.4

lead_in: Which interpretation of the arterial blood gas is most accurate?

options.text: Acute respiratory acidosis with normal bicarbonate consistent with a primary new pulmonary embolism rather than a chronic obstructive pulmonary disease exacerbation today
Compensated chronic respiratory acidosis at baseline because the pH is only mildly low and the bicarbonate is elevated, requiring no escalation in current ventilation support
Primary metabolic alkalosis with secondary hyperventilation as compensation, suggesting overuse of bicarbonate-containing antacids or recent vomiting as the dominant disturbance
Hyperoxic hypercapnia from oxygen toxicity alone, which would correct with cessation of supplemental oxygen and switching to room air without ventilation support
Acute on chronic respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation; non-invasive bilevel ventilation is indicated and oxygen should be titrated to a target saturation of 88 to 92%

subtopic_detail: Hypertensive emergency with end-organ damage
stem: You are the emergency registrar reviewing a 56-year-old non-Aboriginal man with new severe headache and blurred vision for 6 hours. He has hypertension treated with poorly compliant amlodipine 10 mg daily. He has had no chest pain and no focal limb weakness. He is alert and oriented. His urinalysis is positive for protein and blood. Fundoscopy reveals flame haemorrhages and cotton wool spots.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 °C, HR 88, BP 224/132, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Examination: Alert, no focal neurological deficit, no carotid bruit, chest clear, no peripheral oedema, fundoscopy with flame haemorrhages and cotton wool spots
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 142 micromol/L (baseline 88), urea 9.4, urinalysis protein 2+ blood 1+, troponin normal, ECG sinus rhythm with voltage criteria for LV hypertrophy, CT brain no haemorrhage

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial blood pressure management?

options.text: Oral captopril 25 mg sublingually with target blood pressure under 140/90 in the first hour and discharge home once below target on the same antihypertensive regimen
Sublingual nifedipine 10 mg every 15 minutes until pressure is below 140/90, then commence oral perindopril and arrange general practice review the following week
Intravenous furosemide 80 mg bolus and oral metoprolol 100 mg with target pressure under 140/90 in one hour and admission to the general medical ward for observation
Increase his amlodipine to 20 mg daily and add irbesartan 300 mg orally with home blood pressure monitoring; arrange cardiology outpatient review within 4 weeks
Intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion titrated in a monitored bed targeting a mean arterial pressure reduction of 20 to 25% in the first hour, then to 160/100 over 6 hours

subtopic_detail: Cellulitis versus necrotising fasciitis discrimination
stem: You are the emergency medicine registrar reviewing a 62-year-old non-Aboriginal man with type 2 diabetes who presents with 18 hours of worsening lower leg pain disproportionate to the visible cellulitis. He is febrile and tachycardic. His pain has progressed despite paracetamol. He has had no recent injury, IV drug use or travel. His diabetes is poorly controlled with an HbA1c of 9.5%. He takes metformin and gliclazide.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.9 °C, HR 124, RR 24, BP 96/54 mmHg, SpO2 96% room air
data_table.Examination: Right lower leg with patchy violaceous discolouration, two small skin blisters, exquisite tenderness extending beyond the area of erythema, crepitus on palpation, mild lower leg oedema
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22 x10^9/L, CRP 280 mg/L, lactate 4.1 mmol/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, glucose 16.8 mmol/L, creatinine 142 micromol/L, Hb 122 g/L, LRINEC score 9, plain X-ray shows soft tissue gas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange MRI of the lower leg before deciding management, withhold antibiotics until diagnosis is confirmed, and reassess in 4 hours for repeat clinical examination by the team
Admit to the medical ward, commence intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g every 6 hours, mark the erythema boundary and review in 12 hours for response assessment by the medical team
Urgent surgical consultation for theatre debridement, commence broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics including meropenem and clindamycin, and resuscitate with intravenous crystalloid
Discharge home on oral cefalexin 500 mg four times daily, advise elevation and arrange community nurse review in 24 hours for clinical reassessment of progression
Commence intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg as primary treatment for streptococcal toxic shock syndrome and continue current ward observation pending surgical review in the morning

subtopic_detail: Adult bacterial meningitis empirical therapy
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 48-year-old non-Aboriginal woman in ED with 12 hours of high fever, severe headache, photophobia and confusion. She has been previously well, with no recent travel or immunosuppression. She has had two episodes of vomiting. There is no rash. She works as a primary school teacher.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.4 °C, HR 122, RR 22, SpO2 97% room air, BP 110/68 mmHg
data_table.Examination: GCS 13, neck stiffness present, no focal neurology, Kernig and Brudzinski positive, no skin rash, no papilloedema
data_table.Investigations: FBC WCC 22 x10^9/L (neutrophils 19), CRP 240 mg/L, lactate 2.6 mmol/L, sodium 135 mmol/L, glucose 6.8 mmol/L, INR 1.1, platelets 215 x10^9/L, blood cultures taken; CT brain pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform a lumbar puncture immediately without CT given the absence of focal neurology and papilloedema, send all CSF tubes for analysis, and commence antibiotics after the procedure
Defer antibiotics until lumbar puncture results are available, administer paracetamol 1 g intravenously and dexamethasone 10 mg, and reassess after CSF microscopy
Administer intravenous vancomycin 1.5 g and meropenem 2 g as first-line empirical therapy, given the severity of presentation and risk of cephalosporin-resistant pneumococcus in Australia
Administer intravenous dexamethasone 10 mg with the first dose of ceftriaxone 2 g and benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV, then proceed to lumbar puncture once CT is clear
Administer intravenous aciclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours empirically with ceftriaxone, withhold dexamethasone given the uncertain pathogen, and arrange a lumbar puncture in 6 hours

subtopic_detail: Warfarin reversal in supratherapeutic INR without bleeding
stem: You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 76-year-old non-Aboriginal man with atrial fibrillation on warfarin for stroke prevention. He attends the anticoagulant clinic for a routine INR check after starting trimethoprim 5 days ago for a urinary tract infection. He has no signs of bleeding and feels well. He has no recent falls or head injury. His warfarin target range is 2.0 to 3.0. His other medications are bisoprolol and atorvastatin.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/78 mmHg, HR 72, RR 14, T 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: No bruising, gums not bleeding, no haematuria visually, neurologically intact, no flank tenderness
data_table.Investigations: INR 9.4 (target 2.0 to 3.0), Hb 134 g/L, platelets 215 x10^9/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L, urinalysis nil blood, faecal occult blood not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Withhold warfarin, administer oral vitamin K 1 to 2 mg, repeat INR in 24 hours, and review for the need to continue trimethoprim or substitute alternative antibiotic
Withhold warfarin alone for 48 hours, recheck the INR at that point, and continue trimethoprim until urinary culture results return at follow-up in the clinic
Administer intravenous vitamin K 10 mg and Prothrombinex-VF 50 units/kg now, admit to a monitored bed, and recheck the INR at 1 hour after the infusion has completed
Administer fresh frozen plasma 4 units intravenously over 4 hours and recheck the INR immediately afterwards, with rewarfarinisation planned the following day in clinic
Continue current warfarin dose, advise to avoid contact activity, and arrange routine INR review at the next scheduled appointment in 7 days at the clinic

subtopic_detail: Tension pneumothorax recognition and decompression
stem: You are the medical registrar called urgently to the ward for a 68-year-old non-Aboriginal man with COPD whose dyspnoea has acutely worsened 2 hours after a CT-guided lung biopsy. He is anxious and clammy with marked respiratory distress. He has been on his usual COPD medications and just received nebulised salbutamol with no improvement. His oxygen saturation has fallen rapidly over the last 15 minutes. His ECG is not yet available.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 °C, HR 138, RR 38, SpO2 84% on 8 L/min via Hudson mask, BP 88/52 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Distressed, sweaty, tracheal deviation to the left, absent breath sounds on the right with hyperresonant percussion, raised jugular venous pressure, no peripheral oedema, no flail segment
data_table.Investigations: Bedside ultrasound shows absent lung sliding on the right, ABG pH 7.30 pCO2 56 mmHg pO2 56 mmHg lactate 3.4 mmol/L, ECG pending

lead_in: What is the single best initial intervention?

options.text: Arrange an urgent portable chest X-ray to confirm the diagnosis, escalate to ICU, and prepare for chest drain insertion once imaging has been formally reported by radiology
Perform immediate needle thoracostomy at the right 5th intercostal space anterior axillary line, then proceed to intercostal catheter insertion after decompression confirmed by clinical improvement
Commence non-invasive ventilation with bilevel positive airway pressure at 15/5 cm H2O and increase the inspired oxygen fraction, reassess the response in 15 minutes by the team
Administer intravenous fluid bolus 1 litre, increase oxygen flow to 15 L/min via non-rebreather mask, and arrange immediate echocardiogram to exclude cardiac tamponade as the alternative cause
Administer intravenous adrenaline 50 micrograms boluses titrated to blood pressure response, intubate immediately and ventilate with high tidal volumes to recruit lung units

subtopic_detail: Cushing syndrome screening with 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test
stem: You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 42-year-old non-Aboriginal woman referred from primary care with a 12-month history of progressive central weight gain, easy bruising, proximal muscle weakness and new-onset hypertension. She has stretch marks on her abdomen and her HbA1c has risen from 5.4% to 6.6% over 12 months. She takes no glucocorticoid medication and has not used over-the-counter creams. There is no recent stress or major illness.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 158/96 mmHg, HR 84, RR 16, T 36.7 °C, BMI 32 kg/m2 (up from 27)
data_table.Examination: Moon facies, supraclavicular fat pads, abdominal striae 1 cm wide and purple, proximal lower limb weakness Medical Research Council grade 4 of 5, multiple bruises on forearms
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 142 mmol/L, potassium 3.4 mmol/L, fasting glucose 6.4 mmol/L, HbA1c 6.6%, ALT 28 U/L, TSH 1.5 mIU/L, urine drug screen negative, no exogenous steroid use disclosed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Order a single random morning serum cortisol with paired ACTH, and refer to endocrinology if the cortisol is greater than 550 nmol/L on that specimen
Order a high-dose 8 mg dexamethasone suppression test to differentiate pituitary from ectopic ACTH-driven Cushing syndrome before confirming hypercortisolism with any other screening test
Arrange overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test and a 24-hour urinary free cortisol, with a confirmatory second test before endocrinology referral and further imaging
Order an MRI pituitary as the first investigation given the clinical features of central weight gain and striae, with endocrine biochemistry to be added once the imaging result is available
Commence empirical metyrapone 250 mg three times daily while awaiting investigations, with cardiovascular monitoring and review by endocrinology within 2 weeks for further plan

subtopic_detail: Hypercalcaemia of malignancy
stem: You are the oncology medicine registrar called to see a 67-year-old non-Aboriginal woman with metastatic breast cancer admitted with 4 days of progressive confusion, polyuria and constipation. Her primary cancer was diagnosed 2 years ago with bone metastases. She has been on letrozole and palbociclib. There is no recent infection or thiazide use. She has had no falls and no head injury.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 102/64 mmHg lying, 86/52 mmHg standing, HR 102, RR 18, T 36.8 °C, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Examination: Confused and dehydrated, dry mucous membranes, no focal neurology, no signs of fluid overload, normal cardiovascular examination
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 3.4 mmol/L (normal 2.10 to 2.55), phosphate 0.8 mmol/L, creatinine 142 micromol/L (baseline 78), urea 15 mmol/L, albumin 30 g/L, ECG short QT interval, PTH less than 0.5 pmol/L (suppressed), 25-hydroxy vitamin D 60 nmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence calcitonin 4 units/kg subcutaneously every 12 hours as primary treatment, withhold intravenous fluid in view of the hypotension and dehydration documented
Administer cinacalcet 30 mg orally twice daily as initial therapy and arrange repeat corrected calcium in 24 hours, with further management based on the response to the initial dose given

Administer 0.9% sodium chloride 4 to 6 litres over 24 hours with cautious monitoring for fluid overload, give intravenous zoledronic acid 4 mg over 15 minutes once euvolaemic and renal function stabilises
Administer intravenous furosemide 40 mg with concurrent crystalloid replacement to promote calciuresis, withhold bisphosphonates pending an MRI spine to characterise the bone metastases
Administer denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously without preceding intravenous fluid resuscitation, with the rationale that denosumab is the preferred agent regardless of renal function

subtopic_detail: Severe community-acquired influenza pneumonia
stem: You are the medical registrar called to ED for a 58-year-old non-Aboriginal woman with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease (eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73m2) presenting with 3 days of fever, myalgia, dyspnoea and productive cough during a documented community influenza A outbreak. She works at the local primary school where multiple staff have tested positive for influenza. Her usual medications are metformin and atorvastatin. She has not received this year's influenza vaccine. She lives independently and is otherwise functionally intact.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.2 °C, HR 124, RR 30, SpO2 90% on 6 L/min via face mask, BP 96/58 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Toxic appearance, bilateral basal crackles, no rash, no peripheral oedema, GCS 14, capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Investigations: FBC WCC 14 x10^9/L, CRP 220 mg/L, procalcitonin 1.8 micrograms/L, sodium 128 mmol/L, urea 14 mmol/L, creatinine 168 micromol/L, lactate 3.2 mmol/L, chest X-ray bilateral patchy consolidation, nasopharyngeal PCR pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antimicrobial plan?

options.text: Commence oseltamivir 30 mg twice daily with renal dose adjustment, ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, send nasopharyngeal PCR, and admit to a monitored bed
Commence ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily alone, withhold oseltamivir pending nasopharyngeal PCR confirmation, and admit to ED short stay for monitoring over the next 12 hours
Commence oseltamivir 75 mg IV every 12 hours, intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 4 hours, escalate oxygen and admit to ICU on the basis of CURB-65 score 3 and the lactate
Commence oseltamivir 75 mg orally twice daily, ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, escalate to ICU for severe community-acquired pneumonia and continue oxygen support
Commence dexamethasone 6 mg daily as empirical therapy for inflammatory pneumonitis, withhold antiviral therapy in the setting of bacterial co-infection, and admit to a monitored ward bed

subtopic_detail: Hour-1 sepsis bundle initial management
stem: You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 68-year-old man brought in by ambulance with 12 hours of fever, dysuria, flank pain and rigors. He has a history of benign prostatic hyperplasia and an indwelling catheter inserted 3 weeks ago for retention. He has been unable to keep down oral fluids overnight. His Glasgow Coma Scale is 14. He looks unwell with cool peripheries and mottled knees.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.2 °C, HR 124, RR 28, SpO2 94% room air, BP 92/56 mmHg, capillary refill 4 seconds, urine output 10 mL last hour
data_table.Examination: Reduced peripheral perfusion, mottled lower legs, soft tender suprapubic region, right costovertebral angle tenderness, indwelling urinary catheter in situ with cloudy urine
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 3.6 mmol/L, FBC WCC 18.4 x10^9/L neutrophils 16.0, CRP 268 mg/L, creatinine 152 micromol/L (baseline 90), urinalysis pyuria nitrites positive, blood cultures and urine culture pending, chest radiograph clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Start oral trimethoprim 300 mg as a single stat dose plus 7-day course at home with general practitioner follow-up tomorrow morning, arrange community nursing for catheter change and oral fluid rehydration overnight

Send blood cultures only after the patient has received the first dose of intravenous antibiotics to maximise yield and avoid delaying antimicrobial therapy in the initial hour of sepsis bundle delivery in the department

Wait for blood culture and urine culture results before commencing any antimicrobial therapy because empirical broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure may delay identification of the responsible organism and select for further resistance

Send blood and urine cultures, administer 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid intravenously within 3 hours, give intravenous gentamicin plus amoxicillin or piperacillin-tazobactam empirically within 1 hour, monitor lactate clearance and start vasopressors if hypotension persists

Start non-invasive ventilation with continuous positive airway pressure, give intravenous noradrenaline 0.1 micrograms/kg/min and intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g, and admit for source control work up tomorrow on the morning ward round

subtopic_detail: Pulmonary embolism Wells score and age-adjusted D-dimer
stem: You are the emergency medicine registrar reviewing a 72-year-old non-Aboriginal woman with 24 hours of dyspnoea and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. She had a right total knee replacement 2 weeks ago and has been mostly bedbound at home. There is no haemoptysis, no calf swelling and no syncope. She has a past history of well-controlled hypertension on perindopril. She is afebrile and clinically stable.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 °C, HR 102, RR 22, SpO2 94% room air, BP 138/82 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Mild tachypnoea, normal heart sounds, clear chest, calves symmetrical and non-tender, no signs of right heart strain
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia rate 102 no S1Q3T3 or right strain, chest radiograph clear, FBC and UEC within reference ranges, troponin not elevated, D-dimer 720 ng/mL (laboratory cut-off 500 ng/mL)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge home with oral apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily for 3 months because empirical treatment is more time-efficient than imaging given high pre-test probability and likely VTE in this clinical context

Reassure that pulmonary embolism is unlikely because the chest radiograph is clear and the ECG shows no evidence of right heart strain or S1Q3T3 pattern and reassess at general practitioner clinic in 48 hours

Repeat the D-dimer in 24 hours and admit for observation overnight with serial troponin and ECG monitoring before deciding on definitive imaging or empirical therapeutic anticoagulation in the morning ward round

Calculate the Wells score (recent surgery within 4 weeks 1.5, tachycardia 1.5, PE most likely diagnosis 3 equals 6, high probability) and apply the age-adjusted D-dimer cut-off only if Wells is low or moderate before imaging

Calculate the Wells score, determine the patient is at moderate risk, apply age-adjusted D-dimer cut-off (age x 10 ng/mL = 720), find it exceeded and arrange computed tomography pulmonary angiography for diagnostic confirmation

subtopic_detail: Acute kidney injury KDIGO staging and management
stem: You are the medical registrar admitting a 76-year-old non-Aboriginal man with a 5-day history of fever, productive cough and reduced oral intake. He has community-acquired pneumonia confirmed on chest radiograph and has been on ramipril 10 mg daily and rosuvastatin 20 mg daily for cardiovascular prevention. His baseline creatinine 4 months ago was 95 micromol/L. He has been unable to drink for the past 24 hours.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.6 °C, HR 110, RR 24, SpO2 92% on 4 L nasal prongs, BP 102/64 mmHg, capillary refill 3 seconds, urine output 0.4 mL/kg/hour over 6 hours
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, jugular venous pressure not visible at 30 degrees, focal coarse crackles right base, no peripheral oedema, normal heart sounds
data_table.Investigations: Na 134 K 4.8 urea 14.2 mmol/L creatinine 198 micromol/L eGFR 28, FBC WCC 17 x10^9/L Hb 132 platelets 268, urinalysis no blood no protein, urine osmolality 620 mOsm/kg, fractional excretion of sodium 0.6%

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Continue ramipril for renoprotection given the patient's cardiovascular risk profile and proteinuria history, and add intravenous furosemide 40 mg to maintain urine output above 0.5 mL/kg/hour during the acute illness

Commence intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg every 6 hours empirically for relative adrenal insufficiency in addition to broad-spectrum antibiotics and continue ramipril at the current dose while monitoring renal function trend

Arrange immediate haemodialysis given the rise in creatinine to over 2 times baseline meeting KDIGO stage 2 criteria with oliguria and pulmonary involvement to prevent further deterioration of renal function and clinical status

Arrange an urgent renal tract ultrasound to exclude obstruction, withhold ramipril and rosuvastatin temporarily and commence intravenous N-acetylcysteine to attenuate any contrast or sepsis-related acute tubular necrosis insult

Diagnose KDIGO stage 2 acute kidney injury, withhold ramipril and rosuvastatin, give a 500 mL bolus of balanced crystalloid then 1 mL/kg/hour, treat the pneumonia, monitor urine output and reassess fluid status hourly

subtopic_detail: SIADH workup and management of euvolaemic hyponatraemia
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 68-year-old non-Aboriginal man with newly diagnosed small-cell lung cancer admitted for chemotherapy planning. He has had a single fall at home, mild headache and mild nausea over the last week. He has no peripheral oedema, normal jugular venous pressure and mucous membranes appear moist. His weight has not changed. He takes amlodipine for hypertension but no diuretics or antidepressants.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 °C, HR 76, RR 14, SpO2 96% room air, BP 124/78 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Mild dehydration not evident, no peripheral oedema, normal heart sounds, breath sounds reduced right base, no focal neurology, GCS 15
data_table.Investigations: Na 118 K 4.2 urea 3.4 mmol/L creatinine 78 micromol/L, serum osmolality 248 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 480 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 56 mmol/L, TSH 1.8 mU/L, 9 am cortisol 480 nmol/L, glucose 5.0 mmol/L, no current diuretic or SSRI

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence intravenous 3% hypertonic saline 150 mL bolus over 20 minutes targeting a sodium rise of 4 to 6 mmol/L in the first hour and continue hourly boluses to restore sodium to within normal range over 12 hours of monitoring

Diagnose syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion, commence fluid restriction to 800 mL/24 hours, treat the underlying malignancy and target sodium correction at no more than 10 mmol/L in 24 hours

Commence intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride at 125 mL/hour for 24 hours alongside intravenous demeclocycline and arrange a cosyntropin stimulation test if sodium has not improved within 48 hours from admission

Commence oral tolvaptan 15 mg daily as first-line therapy with daily sodium monitoring and rapid up-titration to 60 mg daily over 1 week if sodium has not improved by 8 mmol/L within the first 48 hours of treatment

Commence oral salt tablets 1 g three times daily, encourage free fluid intake to thirst and arrange outpatient endocrinology review in 2 weeks once the underlying malignancy is being treated definitively with combination chemotherapy

subtopic_detail: Acute pancreatitis severity stratification Modified Glasgow
stem: You are the medical registrar admitting a 58-year-old non-Aboriginal man with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back over the past 12 hours after a heavy alcohol bout. He has nausea and four episodes of vomiting since onset. He is haemodynamically stable but in significant pain. He has a 30-year history of heavy alcohol use and is not on any regular medications. He has been admitted twice previously with episodes of acute pancreatitis.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4 °C, HR 112, RR 24, SpO2 92% room air, BP 118/76 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Tender epigastrium with voluntary guarding, no rebound, no Cullen or Grey-Turner signs, bowel sounds reduced but present, jaundice not present
data_table.Investigations: Lipase 1800 U/L, FBC WCC 16.4 x10^9/L Hb 142 platelets 280, Na 136 K 3.8 urea 11.2 creatinine 96 micromol/L glucose 11.6 mmol/L, calcium 1.92 mmol/L corrected, ALT 88 ALP 110 albumin 30 g/L LDH 480 U/L, ABG pH 7.34 pCO2 32 pO2 58 mmHg HCO3 18, CRP 220 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Commence oral hydration with electrolyte solution at 100 mL/hour, prescribe oxycodone immediate release 5 mg every 4 hours as needed and arrange ultrasound abdomen within 24 hours to assess for gallstone aetiology

Commence parenteral nutrition immediately to rest the pancreas, give intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics with piperacillin-tazobactam empirically and arrange MRCP within 24 hours of admission for biliary evaluation

Diagnose severe acute pancreatitis, admit to high-dependency care, commence aggressive intravenous Hartmann's resuscitation, provide opioid analgesia, monitor urine output and arrange contrast-enhanced CT abdomen at 72-96 hours

Arrange urgent endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography within 6 hours of admission for sphincterotomy and ductal clearance because of the high lipase and significant systemic inflammatory response in this patient

Arrange immediate laparotomy with surgical drainage of pancreatic necrosis and intra-abdominal sepsis source control given the elevated white cell count, raised CRP and clinical features of systemic inflammatory response

subtopic_detail: Infective endocarditis empirical therapy native valve
stem: You are the medical registrar admitting a 52-year-old non-Aboriginal man with a 2-week history of fevers, night sweats, fatigue and 3 kg weight loss. He has a known bicuspid aortic valve under cardiology surveillance and recently had a routine dental cleaning without antibiotic prophylaxis. On examination he has new splinter haemorrhages, two Janeway lesions on the soles and a new early diastolic murmur. He has no penicillin allergy and no recent intravenous drug use.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.9 °C, HR 104, RR 18, SpO2 97% room air, BP 132/56 mmHg with wide pulse pressure
data_table.Examination: New early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge, splinter haemorrhages on three fingernails, two Janeway lesions on the right sole, no Osler nodes, no Roth spots on fundoscopy, no neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: FBC WCC 14.2 x10^9/L Hb 116 platelets 220, CRP 168 mg/L ESR 88 mm/h, UEC creatinine 102 micromol/L, blood cultures (3 sets from separate venipunctures over 1 hour pending), transthoracic echocardiogram shows aortic regurgitation with a 12 mm vegetation on the aortic valve

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical intravenous antibiotic regimen pending cultures?

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g once daily monotherapy adjusted to culture results when available, continued for a total of 4 weeks of intravenous therapy with follow-up echocardiography at 2 and 6 weeks from initiation of antimicrobial cover

Intravenous vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading then 15 mg/kg every 12 hours, intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g every 4 hours and intravenous gentamicin 3 mg/kg once daily until culture and sensitivity results are reported by microbiology

Intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.8 g every 4 hours, intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g every 4 hours, intravenous gentamicin 1 mg/kg every 8 hours and a single 1 g dose of intravenous vancomycin upfront for rapid coverage prior to confirmatory blood cultures

Intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.8 g every 4 hours, intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g every 4 hours and intravenous gentamicin 1 mg/kg every 8 hours for an Australian native valve empirical regimen pending culture identification

Intravenous meropenem 1 g every 8 hours as broad-spectrum monotherapy and arrange transoesophageal echocardiography within 24 hours for vegetation characterisation and complication assessment before further antibiotic adjustment

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis recognition and hydrocortisone dosing
stem: You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 42-year-old non-Aboriginal woman known to have primary adrenal insufficiency on regular hydrocortisone 20 mg in the morning and 10 mg at midday and fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily. She has had 24 hours of fever, vomiting and diarrhoea and was unable to take her morning hydrocortisone dose today. She looks unwell, drowsy and hypotensive. Her family is with her and confirms she is fully adherent normally.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.6 °C, HR 124, RR 24, SpO2 97% room air, BP 82/48 mmHg, capillary refill 4 seconds, capillary glucose 3.0 mmol/L
data_table.Examination: Drowsy GCS 13, dry mucous membranes, abdomen soft non-tender, no focal neurology, hyperpigmentation of palmar creases consistent with her known underlying condition
data_table.Investigations: Na 128 K 5.8 urea 9.2 mmol/L creatinine 132 micromol/L glucose 3.0 mmol/L, FBC WCC 12.4 x10^9/L, ECG no hyperkalaemic changes, blood cultures sent, urinalysis no nitrites

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give intramuscular adrenaline 0.5 mg, commence intravenous adrenaline infusion 0.1 microgram/kg/min and arrange immediate intensive care admission for ongoing support of shock with vasopressors and inotropes as needed
Increase her oral hydrocortisone to 30 mg three times daily for the duration of illness, arrange community follow-up tomorrow and provide oral fluid replacement with electrolyte solution overnight

Administer intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately as a bolus, commence intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride 1 L over the first hour, give intravenous dextrose for hypoglycaemia and continue intravenous hydrocortisone 50 mg every 6 hours

Administer intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg as an alternative to hydrocortisone so that a short Synacthen test can be performed within the next 24 hours of admission to confirm the diagnosis of primary adrenal insufficiency

Administer intravenous fludrocortisone 200 micrograms as a single dose to correct mineralocorticoid deficiency contributing to hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia and continue her regular oral hydrocortisone schedule

subtopic_detail: VTE provoked vs unprovoked anticoagulation duration
stem: You are the general practitioner reviewing a 56-year-old non-Aboriginal man 3 months after a confirmed proximal lower limb deep vein thrombosis. He has been on apixaban since diagnosis. He has no past or family history of thromboembolism, no known thrombophilia and no current malignancy on age-appropriate screening. The DVT occurred 2 weeks after a 12 hour transcontinental flight. He has not had any bleeding complications on apixaban and is keen to discuss duration of treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 °C, HR 72, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, BP 124/78 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Resolved calf swelling, no new oedema, no respiratory or cardiac signs of recurrent disease, no signs of malignancy
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC and LFT within reference ranges, d-dimer 380 ng/mL after 4 weeks off anticoagulation simulation not yet performed, age-appropriate cancer screening up to date, thrombophilia screen not performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation plan?

options.text: Stop apixaban now at 3 months because this was a provoked deep vein thrombosis with a transient risk factor (long-haul flight), discuss recurrence risk and provide VTE prevention advice for future air travel and immobilisation

Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily indefinitely because all proximal deep vein thromboses regardless of provoking factor benefit from indefinite anticoagulation based on observational evidence of recurrence reduction without bleeding risk increase

Continue apixaban at the reduced dose of 2.5 mg twice daily indefinitely as extended-duration secondary prevention because all transcontinental flight-related deep vein thromboses recur at higher rates than other transient provoked thromboses

Stop apixaban at 6 months and arrange thrombophilia screening before discontinuation to identify any inherited thrombophilia that would justify ongoing anticoagulation regardless of the transient nature of the provoking risk factor present

Switch to aspirin 100 mg daily indefinitely as extended secondary prevention because aspirin has shown a meaningful reduction in recurrent VTE risk with a lower bleeding profile than ongoing direct oral anticoagulant therapy in this group

subtopic_detail: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension recognition and lumbar puncture opening pressure
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the assessment unit reviewing a 26-year-old woman with 6 weeks of progressively worsening daily headache, retro-orbital pressure, pulsatile tinnitus and transient visual obscurations on standing. She has gained 8 kg over 6 months and her BMI is now 32. She is on no regular medication. She has no history of head trauma, neoplasia or immunosuppression.

Fundoscopy shows bilateral papilloedema with peripapillary haemorrhages. MRI brain with venography is normal with no mass, hydrocephalus or sinus thrombosis. Cranial nerve examination shows a bilateral abducens nerve weakness with normal visual acuity.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/76 mmHg, HR 78, T 36.7 °C, BMI 32
data_table.Examination: Bilateral papilloedema with peripapillary haemorrhages, bilateral CN VI weakness, otherwise normal cranial nerves and limb examination
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain with venography normal; bloods FBC, UEC, LFTs, B12, TSH normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Lumbar puncture in the lateral decubitus position with measurement of opening pressure and CSF studies including cell count, glucose and protein to confirm idiopathic intracranial hypertension before initiating treatment

Initiate acetazolamide 250 mg twice daily empirically and arrange follow-up in 2 weeks for review of papilloedema and visual fields without further diagnostic investigation given the typical clinical pattern of IIH

Arrange CT venogram or MR venogram to exclude cerebral venous sinus thrombosis as the primary cause of raised intracranial pressure given the clinical features and presence of papilloedema and CN VI palsy

Refer urgently to neurosurgery for consideration of optic nerve sheath fenestration and ventriculoperitoneal shunting given the bilateral papilloedema and risk of permanent visual loss without immediate decompression

Send a lumbar CSF for autoimmune encephalitis and paraneoplastic antibody panels and arrange whole-body PET-CT to look for occult malignancy given the subacute course and weight gain over the last 6 months

subtopic_detail: AECOPD ventilatory failure and BiPAP threshold
stem: You are the medical registrar in the emergency department reviewing a 72-year-old former smoker (75 pack-years) with severe COPD (FEV1 35 percent predicted, GOLD D) presenting with 3 days of increased dyspnoea, purulent sputum and reduced exercise tolerance. He uses tiotropium and salbutamol. On arrival he is using accessory muscles and is drowsy but rousable. He has had nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium plus 40 mg oral prednisolone in the department. Current oxygen is 4 L/min via nasal prongs.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.6, HR 112, BP 142/82, RR 32, SpO2 92% on 4 L/min nasal prongs
data_table.Examination: Pursed-lip breathing, audible polyphonic wheeze and prolonged expiration bilaterally, drowsy but rousable, no asterixis yet, no focal chest signs of consolidation
data_table.Investigations: ABG (on 4 L/min): pH 7.26, pCO2 78 mmHg, pO2 62 mmHg, HCO3 30 mmol/L, base excess +4; FBC WCC 12.4, CRP 84, U+E normal, chest X-ray hyperinflation no infiltrate

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Proceed directly to endotracheal intubation and invasive mechanical ventilation without trial of non-invasive ventilation because NIV is contraindicated when the patient has a depressed level of consciousness and a pCO2 over 70 mmHg

Increase the oxygen to 8 L/min via non-rebreather mask to achieve saturations above 95 percent and continue back-to-back nebulised salbutamol plus ipratropium without commencing non-invasive ventilation at this stage

Reduce oxygen to titrate SpO2 88 to 92 percent via Venturi mask and commence bilevel non-invasive ventilation (IPAP 14 cmH2O EPAP 5 cmH2O) for hypercapnic respiratory failure, with reassessment of ABG in 1 hour

Administer intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes and intravenous aminophylline 5 mg/kg loading followed by an infusion of 0.5 mg/kg/hr without commencing NIV at this stage and reassess clinical response in 1 hour

Commence oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily and continued nebulised bronchodilators on the ward, deferring any ventilatory support because the chest X-ray shows no consolidation to indicate severe infective exacerbation

subtopic_detail: Acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema first-line management
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the resuscitation bay reviewing a 68-year-old man with known HFrEF (LVEF 28 percent), previous anterior MI 4 years ago, and hypertension. He has had 6 hours of progressive dyspnoea, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea and pink frothy sputum. He is sitting upright, distressed and unable to complete a sentence. His usual medications are perindopril 5 mg, bisoprolol 5 mg, spironolactone 25 mg, furosemide 40 mg twice daily and atorvastatin 40 mg.

He has not been adherent for the last 3 days. He has no chest pain. The 12-lead ECG shows sinus tachycardia and known left bundle branch block without acute ischaemic changes.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 184/112, HR 124 sinus, RR 36, SpO2 87% air rising to 92% on 15 L NRB, T 36.6
data_table.Examination: Tripod posture, accessory muscle use, fine bibasal crackles to mid-zones, raised JVP, pitting peripheral oedema to knees, peripheral perfusion warm
data_table.Investigations: Chest X-ray: cardiomegaly with bilateral perihilar opacities and Kerley B lines; troponin pending; BNP 1842 ng/L; UEC creatinine 110 (baseline 102), K 4.0; ABG pH 7.32 pCO2 48 pO2 60 on NRB

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Administer intravenous adrenaline 50 mcg as a slow push, intubate immediately and commence noradrenaline infusion at 0.05 mcg/kg/min as first-line therapy for cardiogenic shock pending arrival of the cardiology consult team

Commence high-dose intravenous beta blocker with metoprolol 5 mg slow push every 5 minutes and continue current oral diuretic at home dose, deferring nitrate or non-invasive ventilation until heart rate has been controlled below 100

Administer intravenous morphine 5 mg, an intravenous bolus of 500 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride to support cardiac output, and continue home oral diuretic dose pending observation over the next 4 hours of inpatient management

Sit upright, commence non-invasive bilevel positive airway pressure ventilation, give sublingual glyceryl trinitrate 600 mcg and start an intravenous nitrate infusion titrated to BP, and administer intravenous furosemide 80 mg as initial diuretic dose

Cease all chronic heart failure medications including perindopril and bisoprolol now to avoid contributing to acute decompensation, and start oral metolazone 5 mg in combination with continuing oral furosemide as first-line acute therapy

subtopic_detail: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes - first-line cardioprotection
stem: You are the medical registrar in a busy emergency department called by the resuscitation nurse with a critical potassium result on a 69-year-old man with stage 4 chronic kidney disease (baseline eGFR 22) who presented 2 hours ago with worsening lethargy and reduced urine output for 3 days. He takes perindopril 8 mg, spironolactone 25 mg and furosemide 80 mg daily. He started a high-dose oral potassium chloride supplement from a friend last week. He has no chest pain. Routine bloods are back.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/82, HR 48 bradycardic, RR 16, SpO2 98% air, T 36.6
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, normal cardiovascular exam apart from bradycardia, no peripheral oedema, mild abdominal discomfort, no flank tenderness
data_table.Investigations: K 7.4 mmol/L, Na 136, urea 28, creatinine 280 micromol/L (baseline 220), bicarbonate 18, calcium 2.18, glucose 6.0; ECG: peaked T waves, broad QRS to 140 ms, P waves attenuated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Insert a vascular dialysis catheter and arrange urgent haemodialysis as the sole initial intervention because pharmacological measures are unreliable in chronic kidney disease and only dialysis removes the potassium load definitively

Administer 30 g of oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate (resonium) as first-line therapy because it removes potassium definitively over the next 2 hours and obviates the need for intravenous calcium or insulin-dextrose shift therapy

Commence intravenous furosemide 80 mg bolus and 1000 mL of 5% dextrose over 2 hours as initial therapy because forced diuresis with isotonic dextrose acts as both potassium shift and excretion in this oliguric kidney patient

Administer 50 mL of 8.4% sodium bicarbonate as a slow intravenous push as first-line therapy because acidosis-correction shifts potassium intracellularly more rapidly than any other available pharmacological measure

Administer 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate intravenously over 2 to 5 minutes for cardiac membrane stabilisation, then 10 units of intravenous short-acting insulin in 50 mL of 50% dextrose to shift potassium intracellularly, with continuous cardiac monitoring
