subtopic_detail: Necrotising soft tissue infection recognition and management
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 8.9 percent) admitted overnight with a left leg cellulitis from a minor garden injury 3 days ago. Despite intravenous flucloxacillin he has clinically worsened over 8 hours with pain disproportionate to the visible erythema, dusky discolouration extending beyond the marked margin, and new dark haemorrhagic blisters along the medial calf. He is more tachycardic, looks toxic and confused. He has had two intravenous fluid boluses without improvement.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4, HR 132, BP 92/58, RR 28, SpO2 95% on 2 L/min, GCS 14, lactate 4.6
data_table.Examination: Confused but rousable, left medial calf swollen tense skin with dusky purpuric discolouration spreading beyond marked margin, two new haemorrhagic bullae, marked tenderness disproportionate to appearance, decreased sensation centrally over the lesion, crepitus on palpation
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22.4 x10^9/L (neutrophils 19.8), Hb 122, platelets 165, Na 132, glucose 16.2 mmol/L, creatinine 162, CRP 380 mg/L, lactate 4.6 mmol/L, INR 1.4, LRINEC score calculated as 9

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Continue intravenous flucloxacillin at the current dose, add intravenous gentamicin 5 mg/kg daily and arrange routine elective surgical review on the next routine list in 24 to 48 hours pending repeat blood cultures and clinical reassessment

Initiate sepsis bundle with intravenous fluid resuscitation, blood cultures, broad-spectrum intravenous meropenem plus clindamycin plus vancomycin and arrange immediate surgical consultation for urgent operative debridement in theatre

Arrange urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the limb to confirm necrotising fasciitis before any change in antibiotic therapy or surgical decision making because imaging is required to distinguish soft tissue infection from cellulitis

Apply a topical silver sulfadiazine dressing to the bullae, mark the erythema margins with a black pen and continue intravenous flucloxacillin while observing for response over the next 12 hours of inpatient management

Commence intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg as monotherapy for streptococcal toxic shock syndrome and observe for 12 hours before considering antibiotic broadening or surgical referral if no clinical improvement has occurred

subtopic_detail: Septic shock hour-1 bundle and vasopressor selection
stem: You are the medical registrar in the resuscitation area reviewing a 64-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes admitted with dysuria, frank haematuria and right loin pain progressing over 36 hours. On arrival she is confused, peripherally cool with prolonged capillary refill, and breathing rapidly. She has received 30 mL/kg of intravenous Hartmann's over 90 minutes without improvement. Blood cultures and a urine culture were obtained on arrival. She has been given intravenous ceftriaxone and gentamicin.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 78/40, MAP 53, HR 132 sinus, RR 32, T 39.2, SpO2 96% on 4 L/min, GCS 14, lactate 5.4
data_table.Examination: Confused, cool peripheries, mottled knees, right renal angle tender, no abdominal peritonism, no rash
data_table.Investigations: WCC 19.8 (neutrophils 17.0), CRP 240, creatinine 192 (baseline 88), Na 130, K 4.6, glucose 16.4, ABG pH 7.28 pCO2 30 pO2 90 HCO3 16 BE -8, lactate 5.4 mmol/L, urine dipstick 3+ blood 3+ leucocytes 2+ nitrites

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer a further 30 mL/kg of intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride over 30 minutes and reassess MAP before considering vasopressors, because all sepsis patients need at least 60 mL/kg of resuscitation fluid in the first hour to maximise preload

Commence an intravenous noradrenaline infusion via peripheral cannula at 0.05 mcg/kg/min targeting a mean arterial pressure of at least 65 mmHg, arrange immediate intensive care review, repeat serum lactate at 2 hours and image the renal tract for obstruction

Commence intravenous adrenaline 1 mcg/kg/min as first-line vasoactive therapy for septic shock because adrenaline provides both inotropic and vasopressor support and is recommended ahead of noradrenaline in current Australian intensive care guidelines

Administer intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg as initial monotherapy for refractory septic shock before commencing any vasopressor therapy because corticosteroids alone often reverse hypotension by restoring vascular tone

Switch antibiotic therapy to piperacillin tazobactam 4.5 g intravenously and meropenem 1 g intravenously as combination Gram-negative cover and observe response over 4 hours before any vasopressor or further fluid resuscitation is started

subtopic_detail: Acute type A aortic dissection diagnosis and BP control
stem: You are the medical registrar in resuscitation reviewing a 62-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension (home BP often 170/100) and a 30 pack-year smoking history who presents with sudden onset severe tearing chest pain radiating through to the interscapular area, starting 40 minutes ago. He looks pale and diaphoretic. On examination there is an early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge new since last documented review, a 25 mmHg differential between his right and left arms, and weak right radial pulse. ECG shows sinus tachycardia and old left ventricular hypertrophy. Bedside chest X-ray shows a widened mediastinum.

data_table.Vital signs: BP right arm 172/108, left arm 144/86, HR 108, RR 20, SpO2 97% air, T 36.6
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, soft early diastolic murmur left sternal edge, weak right radial pulse, normal left radial pulse, no focal neurology, abdomen soft, no leg pulse asymmetry
data_table.Investigations: Troponin marginally raised at 78 ng/L (URL 14), creatinine 102, INR 1.0, lactate 1.8; ECG sinus tachycardia LVH no acute ST changes; CXR widened mediastinum

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Refer to the catheter lab for urgent invasive coronary angiography under the suspicion of left main acute coronary syndrome because dissection rarely causes a 25 mmHg interarm differential and the murmur is more likely chronic

Administer 300 mg of aspirin orally and 600 mg of clopidogrel as a dual antiplatelet load and arrange urgent coronary angiography because the marginally elevated troponin and chest pain are most consistent with acute coronary syndrome

Commence an intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion at 50 mcg/min as initial monotherapy aiming for blood pressure under 120 mmHg without a beta blocker because vasodilator-first management reduces wall shear stress most rapidly in dissection

Administer therapeutic-dose enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily and arrange CT pulmonary angiography urgently for suspected acute pulmonary embolism with right ventricular strain that explains the murmur and asymmetric pulses

Commence intravenous esmolol or labetalol infusion targeting heart rate 60 to 80 and systolic blood pressure 100 to 120 mmHg, manage pain with intravenous opioid, and arrange urgent CT angiogram of the aorta with cardiothoracic surgical consultation in parallel

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis with intercurrent illness - immediate management
stem: You are the medical registrar at the resuscitation bay reviewing a 38-year-old woman with known primary autoimmune adrenal insufficiency since age 19 on hydrocortisone 10/5/5 mg and fludrocortisone 100 mcg daily. She has had 36 hours of vomiting from gastroenteritis. She told her mother she could not keep her medications down but did not double-dose with sick-day rules. On arrival she is profoundly hypotensive, drowsy, peripherally cool and has been given 1 L of intravenous Hartmann's en route by paramedics. Her partner is reading her steroid emergency card. The endocrine consultant is being paged.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 72/40, HR 130 sinus, RR 24, T 36.4, SpO2 97% air, GCS 13, BSL 3.4
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, mucous membranes dry, capillary refill 4 sec, generalised hyperpigmentation including palmar creases, no focal neurology, no abdominal peritonism
data_table.Investigations: Na 124 mmol/L, K 6.2, urea 14.8, creatinine 142, glucose 3.4, calcium corrected 2.42, cortisol on arrival drawn at 0830 hours is 84 nmol/L (subnormal); VBG pH 7.30 HCO3 16, lactate 3.2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Administer 100 mg of intravenous hydrocortisone immediately, commence intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride 1 L bolus and 10% dextrose to correct the hypoglycaemia, and start continuous hydrocortisone 200 mg over 24 hours pending source identification of the precipitating illness

Administer intravenous fludrocortisone 200 mcg as the priority steroid for the mineralocorticoid deficiency and the hyperkalaemia, and defer hydrocortisone until urgent ACTH stimulation testing has confirmed the adrenal pathway is unresponsive

Administer intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg as the first-line glucocorticoid because dexamethasone does not interfere with subsequent cortisol assays and avoids cross-reactivity in the urgent diagnostic ACTH stimulation testing pathway

Insert a central venous access catheter and commence intravenous noradrenaline 0.05 mcg/kg/min titrated to mean arterial pressure 65 mmHg as the first-line haemodynamic support with intravenous hydrocortisone added only after stable blood pressure is achieved

Administer intravenous calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10% for the hyperkalaemia and intravenous insulin-dextrose for potassium shift while she continues her usual oral hydrocortisone dose once vomiting has settled with intravenous ondansetron antiemetic

subtopic_detail: Anticoagulation duration after unprovoked pulmonary embolism
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 58-year-old man at his 3-month follow-up after an unprovoked submassive pulmonary embolism initially treated with rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily for 21 days followed by 20 mg daily ongoing. He has had no recurrent venous thromboembolism, no significant bleeding episodes, normal renal function, no active malignancy, no antiphospholipid antibodies, and a normal first-degree family history.

His current symptoms have resolved and he has returned to full-time work. His PESA-style bleeding risk assessment is low. He understands the recurrence risk discussion and asks about whether to stop his anticoagulation now that 3 months have passed without any complications during the initial treatment course.

data_table.Examination: Cardiovascular and respiratory examination unremarkable, no calf swelling or tenderness, oxygen saturations 98% in air at rest
data_table.Investigations: eGFR 88, Hb 142, platelets 220 x10^9/L; thrombophilia screen negative; CT chest at 3 months shows partial clot resolution

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing anticoagulation plan?

options.text: Switch from rivaroxaban to warfarin with a target international normalised ratio of 2.0 to 3.0 for indefinite anticoagulation and arrange weekly INR monitoring until the patient is stable on the new anticoagulant regimen

Continue rivaroxaban at the reduced extended dose of 10 mg once daily indefinitely with annual review of bleeding risk, renal function and the ongoing balance of recurrence risk against bleeding risk to inform continuation

Cease all anticoagulation at 3 months and provide a written plan to recommence rivaroxaban if there are any new symptoms suggesting recurrence, with annual D-dimer testing as a surveillance strategy for asymptomatic recurrence

Stop rivaroxaban now and prescribe aspirin 100 mg daily as secondary prevention for the next 12 months, with a planned VTE recurrence review at 12 months to determine whether further intervention is required at that time

Continue rivaroxaban 20 mg once daily indefinitely without dose reduction and arrange follow-up CT pulmonary angiography in 12 months to assess for chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension and adjust treatment accordingly

subtopic_detail: Early rheumatoid arthritis DMARD initiation with methotrexate
stem:
You are the rheumatology registrar in clinic reviewing a 46-year-old woman with 10 weeks of progressive symmetrical polyarthritis of the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints and wrists, with 90 minutes of early morning stiffness. She has no prior medical history, takes no regular medications, and is up to date with cervical screening. Her bloods show a markedly elevated rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibody, raised inflammatory markers, normal renal and liver function, and a normal full blood count.

Plain hand films are without bony erosion at this point. She is keen to start treatment, lives within 30 minutes of the clinic, has reliable transport, has no plans for pregnancy in the next 12 months and is willing to use reliable contraception during treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 122/76, HR 76, T 37.0 degrees C, BMI 25
data_table.Examination: Bilateral symmetrical MCP and PIP synovitis, both wrists synovitic, no nodules, no extra-articular features, no skin rash
data_table.Investigations: RF 320 IU/mL (RR under 15), anti-CCP 198 U/mL (RR under 20), ESR 64, CRP 38; normal Hb, WCC, platelets, eGFR, LFTs; HBV/HCV/HIV serology negative, latent TB screen negative, varicella immune

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug regimen?

options.text: Commence long-term prednisolone 15 mg daily as monotherapy with calcium and vitamin D and a bisphosphonate for bone protection, with plans for slow gradual taper over the next 12 to 24 months as her symptoms improve over time

Defer DMARD therapy and commence celecoxib 200 mg twice daily with regular paracetamol 1 g four times daily, plan a 6-month review with a repeat clinical assessment before any decision about disease-modifying therapy is made

Commence subcutaneous adalimumab 40 mg fortnightly as first-line biologic monotherapy given her highly seropositive disease and the elevated inflammatory markers to maximise rapid suppression of the inflammatory disease burden

Commence triple oral therapy with hydroxychloroquine 400 mg daily, sulfasalazine 1 g twice daily and leflunomide 20 mg daily from the outset to maximise control of disease activity in this newly diagnosed early polyarthritis case

Commence oral methotrexate starting at 10 mg weekly with uptitration to 20 to 25 mg weekly over 8 weeks, prescribe folic acid 5 mg weekly on a non-methotrexate day, and bridge with a short prednisolone taper for symptom control

subtopic_detail: T2DM HbA1c 8.5% second-line therapy with SGLT2 inhibitor
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 62-year-old man with a 5-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus on metformin 1 g twice daily for the past 18 months. He has stable albuminuric chronic kidney disease (eGFR 56, urine ACR 38 mg/mmol), well-controlled hypertension on perindopril, established cardiovascular disease with a previous percutaneous coronary intervention 3 years ago, and is on aspirin and high-intensity atorvastatin.

His current HbA1c is 8.5% (target under 7.0%), BMI 29, blood pressure 132/82, no symptomatic hyperglycaemia. He has been adherent with metformin and has implemented dietary changes through dietitian referral for the past 6 months. He has no recent genital or urinary tract infections and no history of diabetic ketoacidosis.

data_table.Examination: No peripheral oedema, palpable foot pulses, no diabetic foot ulceration, normal cardiovascular and respiratory examination
data_table.Investigations: HbA1c 8.5% (RR under 7.0% target), eGFR 56 (RR over 90), urine ACR 38 mg/mmol, LDL 1.8, BP 132/82, no acute clinical infections

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next addition to his diabetes therapy?

options.text: Commence basal insulin glargine 10 units at night and titrate by 2 units every 3 days according to fasting blood glucose with a target fasting glucose between 5 and 7 mmol/L and ongoing review of the dose with his GP

Add gliclazide modified release 60 mg daily as second-line therapy and arrange diabetes nurse follow-up for self-monitoring of blood glucose and education about hypoglycaemia symptoms with this newly added sulfonylurea agent

Add sitagliptin 100 mg daily as a DPP-4 inhibitor for its neutral cardiovascular safety profile and lack of weight gain, with monitoring for any pancreatitis-type symptoms and renal function in the months following the addition

Increase metformin to 1 g three times daily as the only intensification step at this point and review his HbA1c in 3 months before considering the addition of any second-line agent to his current diabetes regimen

Add empagliflozin 10 mg once daily as an SGLT2 inhibitor for cardiorenal protection in this man with established cardiovascular disease and albuminuric CKD, and arrange short-interval review of his BP, eGFR and ketones

subtopic_detail: Latent tuberculosis infection household contact management
stem:
You are the infectious diseases registrar reviewing a 34-year-old asymptomatic Vietnamese-born woman who has lived in Australia for 6 months. She is a contact of her brother, who has just been diagnosed with smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis, and they have been sharing a 2-bedroom flat together. She is well, with no cough, fever, night sweats, or weight loss. Her HIV serology is negative; she is not pregnant and is using effective contraception.

Her chest x-ray is clear with no upper-lobe scarring or cavitation. A QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus assay returns positive with normal mitogen and negative nil tubes. Her routine bloods including LFTs and FBC are normal. She drinks no alcohol and takes no regular medications.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/74, HR 76, T 36.8 degrees C, BMI 22, SpO2 99% in air
data_table.Examination: No respiratory or systemic symptoms, no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, chest clear on auscultation, no hepatomegaly
data_table.Investigations: CXR clear; QFT-Plus positive (mitogen and nil normal); HIV negative; LFTs and FBC within normal limits; sputum not produced

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Provide reassurance and arrange surveillance with annual chest x-rays for 5 years given her low individual risk of progression to active disease and the side effect burden of isoniazid in an asymptomatic young woman

Repeat the QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus assay in 8 weeks and only commence treatment if the second test remains positive, given the possibility of an early false positive in a recently arrived migrant from a high-prevalence country

Commence full quadruple anti-tuberculous therapy with rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for 2 months followed by rifampicin and isoniazid for 4 months given the high transmission risk and her recent contact

Refer her to a respiratory clinic for induced sputum and bronchoalveolar lavage for tuberculosis culture and nucleic acid amplification testing before commencing latent TB therapy, with no treatment until those microbiology results are available

Commence daily oral isoniazid 5 mg/kg up to 300 mg with pyridoxine 25 mg for 6 to 9 months under the state TB service, with monthly clinical and biochemical review and confirmation of active disease exclusion before therapy commences

subtopic_detail: Acute HIV seroconversion testing with 4th generation immunoassay
stem:
You are the GP registrar reviewing a 28-year-old man with 6 days of fever, sore throat, generalised maculopapular rash, painful mouth ulcers, marked fatigue and tender cervical and inguinal lymphadenopathy. He reports condomless receptive anal intercourse with a new male partner 18 days ago. He has not been on HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis. He has had no other recent illnesses, no travel and no medications.

Routine testing shows lymphopenia, transient transaminitis, and a 4th-generation HIV-1/2 antigen-antibody combination immunoassay returns positive today with a low signal-to-cutoff ratio; the supplemental Western blot is indeterminate. Syphilis serology, hepatitis B and C serology and gonorrhoea NAAT are negative. His past sexual health screening was negative 6 months ago.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 122/76, HR 96, T 38.4 degrees C, SpO2 99% in air
data_table.Examination: Maculopapular rash on trunk, tender cervical and inguinal lymphadenopathy, painful aphthous oral ulcers, no meningism
data_table.Investigations: 4th gen HIV Ag/Ab assay positive (low S/CO), Western blot indeterminate; lymphopenia 0.8 x10^9/L; AST 78, ALT 92; syphilis/HBV/HCV/GC negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Commence post-exposure prophylaxis with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate plus emtricitabine plus dolutegravir empirically for 4 weeks given the recent exposure 18 days ago and reassess his testing situation at the end of the prophylaxis course

Send an HIV-1 RNA viral load assay urgently as the confirmatory test for acute HIV seroconversion, refer to a sexual health or infectious diseases physician for prompt antiretroviral therapy initiation, and arrange partner notification

Order a CD4 count alone today as the confirmatory test for acute HIV infection and only commence antiretroviral therapy once the CD4 count is below 500 cells per microlitre and confirmation of seroconversion has occurred

Arrange supportive care alone with paracetamol and oral fluids and rebook for HIV serology in 12 weeks, since most acute seroconversion presentations are self-limiting and the diagnostic uncertainty makes ART premature at this stage of testing

Repeat the 4th-generation HIV Ag/Ab combination immunoassay in 4 weeks before any decision about commencing antiretroviral therapy, since the present indeterminate Western blot does not confirm an HIV-positive result at the present time

subtopic_detail: Abdominal aortic aneurysm 5.5 cm asymptomatic surgical threshold
stem:
You are the vascular surgery registrar reviewing a 72-year-old asymptomatic ex-smoker man (50 pack-year history quit 4 years ago) in clinic after a routine ultrasound surveillance scan demonstrated a 5.6 cm infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm, up from 4.8 cm 12 months ago. He has well-controlled hypertension on perindopril, an LDL of 2.0 on atorvastatin, no diabetes, no significant ischaemic heart disease on stress imaging 2 years ago, and an exercise tolerance limited only by mild osteoarthritis.

He has no family history of aortic disease, no Marfan or vascular Ehlers-Danlos features, and the aneurysm morphology is suitable for endovascular repair with a long infrarenal neck of 25 mm and no significant tortuosity.

data_table.Examination: No abdominal tenderness, pulsatile non-tender central abdominal mass, palpable femoral and pedal pulses bilaterally, no distal embolic signs
data_table.Investigations: Abdominal ultrasound: infrarenal AAA 5.6 cm (was 4.8 cm 12 months ago); CT angiogram: 5.6 cm with 25 mm infrarenal neck suitable for EVAR; eGFR 62; LDL 2.0; HbA1c 5.8%

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Defer surgery and arrange repeat surveillance ultrasound in 3 months given the absence of symptoms and the satisfactory exercise tolerance, with intervention only if the aneurysm exceeds 6 cm at the next surveillance scan in 3 months

Continue 6-monthly ultrasound surveillance and intensify his medical therapy with the addition of a beta blocker and an angiotensin receptor blocker to slow further aneurysm expansion below the threshold for surgery in the medium term

Refer for open surgical repair via midline laparotomy as the most durable repair option given his young age and good fitness, with planned admission for around 7 to 10 days of inpatient recovery and pre-operative renal optimisation

Refer for elective endovascular aneurysm repair within the next 1 to 2 months, confirm cardiac fitness for intervention, continue strict blood pressure and lipid control and arrange smoking cessation follow-up given his history of past tobacco use

Refer for emergency endovascular aneurysm repair within the next 24 hours as the aneurysm exceeds the 5.5 cm threshold and any further delay would substantially increase his risk of imminent and catastrophic aortic rupture

subtopic_detail: Phaeochromocytoma preoperative alpha-then-beta blockade sequencing
stem:
You are the endocrinology registrar reviewing a 48-year-old woman with biochemically and radiologically confirmed unilateral 4 cm right adrenal phaeochromocytoma. She presented 3 weeks ago with paroxysmal hypertension to 220/120, headache, palpitations and pallor. Investigations now show plasma free metanephrines 12 times the upper limit of normal, 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines 8 times normal, and a 4 cm right adrenal lesion on MRI with high T2 signal and avid uptake on 68Ga-DOTATATE PET.

She is scheduled for laparoscopic right adrenalectomy in 2 weeks. She has not yet been commenced on any antihypertensive therapy. There is no family history of MEN, neurofibromatosis or von Hippel-Lindau syndrome, and genetic testing has been requested.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 168/108 lying, drop on standing 18 mmHg systolic; HR 96
data_table.Examination: Normal cardiovascular and respiratory examination, no carotid bruits, no abdominal mass palpable, no neurofibromas or cafe au lait macules
data_table.Investigations: Plasma free metanephrines x12 ULN, 24h urinary fractionated metanephrines x8 ULN, MRI: 4 cm right adrenal lesion high T2, 68Ga-DOTATATE PET avid; eGFR 92, K 4.0

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate pharmacological management before surgery?

options.text: Commence phenoxybenzamine 10 mg twice daily titrated upward over 10 to 14 days targeting nasal stuffiness and mild postural hypotension, encourage high salt and fluid intake, then add a beta blocker only after adequate alpha blockade is achieved

Commence metoprolol 25 mg twice daily as initial therapy to control her resting tachycardia and to lower her blood pressure before surgery, then add an alpha blocker once her heart rate has been brought below 80 beats per minute

Commence labetalol 100 mg twice daily titrated up over 7 days as a combined alpha and beta blocker as a single-agent strategy and proceed to surgery once she is normotensive on the highest tolerated dose of labetalol

Proceed immediately to laparoscopic right adrenalectomy without further pharmacological preparation given the moderate size of the lesion and the relatively short interval until the scheduled surgical procedure in two weeks' time

Commence amlodipine 5 mg daily for blood pressure control and proceed to surgery within 7 days, since calcium channel blockade alone is sufficient pre-operative preparation for laparoscopic adrenalectomy in a haemodynamically stable patient at this time

subtopic_detail: Acute pyelonephritis empiric antibiotic choice when vomiting
stem: You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 28-year-old woman with 24 hours of right loin pain, fever to 39 degrees, rigors, dysuria and three episodes of vomiting today. She is not pregnant (negative urinary beta-hCG), has no diabetes mellitus, no known renal tract abnormalities and is not immunosuppressed. She has had two prior episodes of uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection three years apart, both successfully treated with oral trimethoprim. Today she has been unable to keep down oral fluids or paracetamol since this morning and last passed urine four hours ago.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.9, HR 108, BP 108/68, RR 20, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Right renal angle tenderness, soft abdomen, no peritonism, normal pelvic examination
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick LE++ nit+ blood+; urine MCS sent; bHCG negative; CRP 142, WCC 14.8, Cr 88, eGFR >90; blood cultures sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empiric antibiotic plan?

options.text: Oral trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 7 days with paracetamol as required and discharge with advice to drink at least two litres of clear fluid daily and review in general practice in three days

Admit for IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg daily plus IV ampicillin 2 g six-hourly with antiemetic and IV fluid resuscitation, narrowing therapy when urine and blood culture sensitivities are available within 48-72 hours

Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 7 days commenced in the emergency department with discharge to home if she can tolerate two doses, and outpatient follow-up by her general practitioner within 24 hours

Admit for IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g eight-hourly with vasopressor on standby and HDU admission given the severity of presentation and to ensure broad coverage of all likely uropathogens including resistant organisms

Oral nitrofurantoin 100 mg six-hourly for 5 days with discharge after a single dose of IM ceftriaxone in the emergency department and outpatient antibiotic service follow-up in 24 to 48 hours for assessment

subtopic_detail: Necrotising fasciitis recognition with LRINEC and urgent surgical referral
stem: You are the surgical registrar called to a 65-year-old man admitted 24 hours ago with presumed cellulitis of the left calf treated with IV cefazolin. He is now describing pain markedly out of proportion to examination, has dusky discolouration extending proximally past the original margin marked overnight, and you palpate crepitus at the calf. His T2DM is poorly controlled with HbA1c 9.1 percent and his current observations show septic physiology. The leg has tense bullae that were not present on admission. He had a minor laceration cleaning his garden five days before admission.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.9, HR 124, BP 96/58, RR 26, SpO2 95% room air, GCS 14
data_table.Examination: Tense haemorrhagic bullae over anterolateral left calf, crepitus, dusky skin extending beyond marked margin, exquisite tenderness on light palpation, absent dorsalis pedis pulse on Doppler
data_table.Investigations: WCC 19.4, CRP 295, Hb 138, Na 131, glucose 14.3, Cr 145, lactate 4.1, LRINEC score 9

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Urgent operating theatre for surgical exploration and debridement of fascia, with concurrent IV piperacillin-tazobactam plus IV vancomycin plus IV clindamycin for toxin suppression, and aggressive fluid resuscitation in resus

Urgent CT of the lower limb with intravenous contrast to confirm fascial gas and the extent of involvement before booking the operating theatre, with continuation of intravenous cefazolin while awaiting imaging and surgical review

Continue IV cefazolin and add IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg daily, mark the new margin in pen with hourly re-assessment, and reconsider operative debridement only if the patient deteriorates further over the next 6 to 12 hours

Transfer the patient to a hyperbaric oxygen unit at the tertiary centre for adjunctive therapy as the first intervention given the high LRINEC score, with antibiotics continued during the transfer and surgical exploration planned on arrival

MRI of the leg with contrast to delineate the extent of fascial involvement and guide surgical planning, with antibiotics escalated to meropenem 1 g eight-hourly while awaiting access to MRI within four to six hours in business hours

subtopic_detail: Empiric antibiotic choice for native valve infective endocarditis in IVDU
stem: You are the medical registrar admitting a 42-year-old man with a 5-day history of fever, malaise and night sweats. He has been injecting drugs intravenously for 6 years and currently injects daily, most recently in the right antecubital fossa. Examination reveals a new diastolic murmur loudest at the left sternal edge, splinter haemorrhages on three nail beds, a 3-mm tender lesion on the pulp of the left index finger, and no peripheral oedema. Three sets of peripheral blood cultures have been drawn from separate sites within the past hour and transthoracic echocardiography is being arranged today.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.5, HR 108, BP 122/68, RR 18, SpO2 97% room air
data_table.Examination: New diastolic murmur LSE, splinter haemorrhages, Osler node on left index finger pulp, no pulmonary oedema, injection sites visible at antecubital fossa
data_table.Investigations: Hb 105, WCC 16, CRP 280, Cr 110, lactate 1.6, blood cultures x 3 drawn, ECG sinus rhythm with first-degree AV block, urine dipstick microhaematuria

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empiric antibiotic regimen while awaiting culture results?

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily as monotherapy with reassessment when blood cultures are available at 48 to 72 hours, given the broad spectrum of coverage including most likely organisms for native valve endocarditis in this patient population

Intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g 4-hourly plus IV gentamicin 1 mg/kg 8-hourly empirically without MRSA cover, with planned addition of vancomycin only if cultures grow MRSA in the next 48 to 72 hours after drawing samples today

Intravenous vancomycin (loaded then dosed by TDM) plus IV flucloxacillin 2 g 4-hourly plus IV gentamicin 1 mg/kg 8-hourly synergistically, awaiting culture and sensitivity results with daily renal function and aminoglycoside trough monitoring

Intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.8 g 4-hourly as monotherapy until streptococcal endocarditis confirmed on culture, given that viridans streptococci remain the most common organism overall in native valve infective endocarditis across populations

Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg twice daily with discharge on outpatient parenteral antibiotic therapy after a single dose of IV ceftriaxone in the emergency department and outpatient antibiotic service review the next day

subtopic_detail: Plasma ACTH measurement after positive screening for Cushing syndrome
stem: You are the endocrinology registrar reviewing a 45-year-old woman with 12 months of progressive central weight gain (18 kg), purple abdominal striae, easy bruising, proximal muscle weakness (difficulty rising from a chair), new hypertension at 158/95, and newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes with HbA1c 7.4 percent. Her initial 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test showed a morning cortisol of 195 nmol/L (suppressed less than 50), and a 24-hour urinary free cortisol is elevated at twice the upper limit of normal on two separate collections. There is no exogenous glucocorticoid exposure (no inhaled, topical or injected steroid).

data_table.Examination: Central adiposity, dorsocervical fat pad, supraclavicular fullness, purple abdominal striae over 1 cm wide, multiple bruises, proximal myopathy
data_table.Investigations: Morning cortisol after 1 mg dexamethasone 195 nmol/L (suppressed if <50), 24 h urinary free cortisol 2x ULN on two collections, late-night salivary cortisol elevated, HbA1c 7.4%, K 3.4, BP 158/95

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: High-dose dexamethasone suppression test with 8 mg dexamethasone overnight and morning cortisol measurement to distinguish Cushing disease from ectopic ACTH source, with concurrent CRH stimulation if available at the tertiary endocrinology service

Plasma ACTH measurement on an early-morning sample with appropriate handling on ice, repeated on a separate day to confirm, to distinguish ACTH-dependent from ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome and guide subsequent localisation imaging

Dedicated pituitary MRI with gadolinium contrast as the next diagnostic step to identify a microadenoma causing Cushing disease, given the higher prevalence of pituitary corticotroph adenomas compared with other causes of endogenous Cushing syndrome

Adrenal CT with adrenal protocol (non-contrast and delayed washout phases) to identify an adrenal adenoma causing ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome before plasma ACTH is measured, given the presence of biochemical confirmation

Inferior petrosal sinus sampling with CRH stimulation under interventional radiology guidance to localise the corticotroph source as a definitive next step in the diagnostic algorithm for Cushing syndrome with both screening tests positive

subtopic_detail: Hypertensive emergency with target end-organ damage and gradual BP reduction
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 58-year-old man in the emergency department with a severe occipital headache for 2 hours, blurred vision and one episode of vomiting. His BP is 220/130 in both arms with a regular pulse. Fundoscopy demonstrates bilateral flame-shaped haemorrhages and papilloedema. Creatinine has risen from baseline 90 to 180 with new microscopic haematuria and 2+ proteinuria.

He has no chest pain, focal neurological deficit, or pulmonary oedema, and the GCS is 15. ECG shows sinus rhythm with LVH by voltage criteria. He has not taken his usual amlodipine or perindopril for one week.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 220/130 both arms, HR 88, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air, GCS 15, T 36.8
data_table.Examination: Bilateral flame haemorrhages and papilloedema, no focal neurology, no carotid bruit, no chest signs, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Cr 180 (baseline 90), urine microscopic haematuria with 2+ proteinuria, ECG sinus rhythm with LVH voltage criteria, CXR no pulmonary oedema, troponin within normal range

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit to HDU and commence intravenous labetalol infusion titrated to reduce mean arterial pressure by about 25 percent in the first hour, then to BP around 160/100 over the next 6 hours, while investigating for end-organ damage

Commence IV sodium nitroprusside infusion targeting normalisation of BP to 120/80 within the first hour to minimise the risk of further hypertensive end-organ injury, with arterial line monitoring and cyanide level checking after 24 hours

Restart oral amlodipine 10 mg and perindopril 8 mg in the emergency department, allow an oral observation period of 4 to 6 hours and discharge home with general practitioner review in 24 hours for ongoing medication compliance

Administer sublingual nifedipine 10 mg now and again in 30 minutes if BP remains elevated above 180/110 with bedside continuous monitoring, then transition to oral amlodipine therapy for ongoing maintenance once stable

Administer GTN spray 0.4 mg sublingually as needed for symptom control, with repeat as required, alongside oral metoprolol 25 mg as monotherapy in the emergency department before bed-based ward admission for further blood pressure observation

subtopic_detail: Levodopa first-line for symptomatic functional impact in older-onset Parkinson disease
stem:
You are the general physician reviewing a 68-year-old retired accountant referred by his GP with 12 months of progressive bradykinesia, an asymmetric right-hand rest tremor, micrographia, and stiffness most evident on his right side. Examination shows cogwheel rigidity at the right wrist, reduced right-arm swing, no postural instability, normal vertical eye movements, and no cerebellar signs. An empirical low-dose levodopa challenge produced a 50 percent reduction in his UPDRS motor score.

He is functionally impaired (struggling with shoelaces and handwriting his usual diary entries), has no cognitive impairment on MoCA 27/30, and has no orthostatic, urinary or REM-sleep behavioural symptoms.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/78 lying, 128/76 standing, HR 68, MoCA 27/30
data_table.Examination: Asymmetric right rest tremor, cogwheel rigidity right wrist, micrographia, reduced right arm swing, no postural instability, normal vertical eye movements, no cerebellar signs
data_table.Investigations: Levodopa challenge produced 50% UPDRS motor improvement, MRI brain unremarkable for age, B12 and TSH normal, no medication-induced cause identified

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Rasagiline 1 mg daily as monotherapy MAO-B inhibitor providing modest symptomatic benefit and good tolerability for early Parkinson disease with minimal functional impact, deferring levodopa until functional decline progresses further

Pramipexole 0.125 mg three times daily titrated weekly as dopamine agonist monotherapy in order to delay levodopa exposure and reduce the long-term risk of dyskinesia, with monitoring for impulse control disorder and somnolence

Amantadine 100 mg twice daily as monotherapy for symptomatic improvement of bradykinesia and tremor in early Parkinson disease, with later addition of levodopa if symptoms progress beyond what can be controlled by amantadine alone

Defer all pharmacotherapy and refer to a physiotherapist and occupational therapist with movement disorders interest for tailored exercise program, with neurology review in 6 months to reassess and consider levodopa at that time only if needed

Levodopa-carbidopa 100/25 mg three times daily titrated to symptoms as first-line therapy, given functional impact, older age, and good response to levodopa challenge, with monitoring for nausea, orthostasis, and later motor fluctuations

subtopic_detail: Immediate needle decompression for tension pneumothorax in trauma
stem: You are the emergency department registrar at a level 1 trauma centre receiving a 32-year-old man brought in by ambulance after a high-speed motor vehicle collision 25 minutes ago. He sustained blunt right chest trauma against the steering wheel. He is in severe respiratory distress, agitated and diaphoretic. Trachea is deviated to the left, breath sounds are absent on the right with hyper-resonance to percussion, JVP is markedly elevated, and he is profoundly hypotensive despite a 500 mL crystalloid bolus en route. No chest X-ray has yet been performed and the resuscitation team is in attendance.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.4, HR 132, BP 78/42, RR 38, SpO2 86% on 15 L non-rebreather mask, GCS 14
data_table.Examination: Tracheal deviation to left, absent right breath sounds, hyper-resonance to percussion right hemithorax, JVP raised, distended neck veins, no pelvic instability, no obvious external haemorrhage
data_table.Investigations: No CXR or CT yet performed, bedside ultrasound shows absent right lung sliding with lung point at mid-axillary line, FAST otherwise negative, no obvious pericardial effusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Urgent CT chest with intravenous contrast to confirm the diagnosis of tension pneumothorax and characterise other associated thoracic injuries such as haemothorax, lung contusion, or great vessel injury before any procedural intervention

Continue high-flow oxygen via non-rebreather mask and observe for response over the next 5 to 10 minutes, with reassessment of breath sounds and saturations before any invasive procedure is considered to avoid iatrogenic harm

Perform rapid sequence intubation with positive pressure ventilation now using ketamine and rocuronium, before chest decompression, in order to secure the airway given the GCS 14 and ongoing respiratory failure with progressive desaturation

Immediate needle decompression with a large-bore cannula at the 4th-5th intercostal space anterior axillary line on the right (or 2nd intercostal space mid-clavicular line if 5th IC anatomy precludes), followed by definitive intercostal catheter insertion

Emergency pericardiocentesis via subxiphoid approach with bedside ultrasound guidance as the haemodynamic compromise with raised JVP is most likely due to cardiac tamponade from blunt cardiac injury rather than tension pneumothorax

subtopic_detail: Mixed cardiogenic and septic shock with line-related bacteraemia post-STEMI
stem:
You are the ICU registrar reviewing a 72-year-old woman day 3 post-large anterior STEMI treated with primary PCI to the LAD. She is now hypotensive on noradrenaline 0.4 mcg/kg/min, with a new fever (38.9) since this morning. WCC is 19, lactate 4.8 (up from 2.1 on day 2). Bedside echo shows severe LV systolic dysfunction (EF 25 percent), no tamponade, no new regional wall motion abnormality.

CVP 18, ScvO2 55 percent, cardiac index by PiCCO 1.6 L/min/m squared, urine output 10 mL/hr over the last 2 hours. Blood cultures from the femoral central line (in situ 4 days) are growing a gram-negative bacillus identified provisionally as E. coli.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.9, HR 124 sinus tachycardia, BP 78/45 on noradrenaline 0.4 mcg/kg/min, RR 26, SpO2 95% on FiO2 0.5
data_table.Examination: Cool peripheries, mottled knees, raised JVP, bibasal crackles, S3 gallop, femoral central line in situ day 4 with mild erythema at site
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 4.8, ScvO2 55%, CVP 18, CI 1.6 L/min/m sq, EF 25% on echo, no tamponade, blood cultures growing GNB from femoral line and peripheral; urine output 10 mL/hr

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next haemodynamic intervention?

options.text: Increase noradrenaline to 1.0 mcg/kg/min and give a 1 litre Hartmann bolus over 30 minutes to support BP and intravascular volume, with continued current antibiotic regimen and review of inotrope after the fluid bolus

Switch noradrenaline to vasopressin 0.04 units/min as monotherapy and add hydrocortisone 50 mg every 6 hours, without addressing inotropy or source control, while continuing the current empirical antibiotic regimen unchanged

Diurese aggressively with furosemide 80 mg IV bolus and ongoing infusion targeting negative balance of 1 to 2 litres in 24 hours given the high CVP 18 and bibasal crackles representing pulmonary oedema and fluid overload

Add an inotrope (dobutamine 2.5-5 mcg/kg/min targeting CI >2.2), broaden antibiotics to piperacillin-tazobactam plus vancomycin pending sensitivities, remove and replace the infected femoral line, and refer to cardiothoracics for IABP or Impella consideration

Defer all changes pending insertion of a pulmonary artery catheter to fully characterise the haemodynamic profile before commencing or modifying any therapy, given the diagnostic uncertainty between predominantly cardiogenic and septic components

subtopic_detail: Native valve endocarditis empirical therapy with benzylpenicillin, flucloxacillin and gentamicin
stem:
You are the general medical registrar admitting a 45-year-old previously well man with 3 weeks of fevers, night sweats and progressive exertional dyspnoea. He has lost 4 kg, has new finger clubbing, and a recently noted soft early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge. He has no intravenous drug use, no prosthetic valves, no recent dental procedure and no central venous access.

His chest X-ray is unremarkable. Echocardiography has been requested urgently and three sets of blood cultures have been collected at least 30 minutes apart in the emergency department prior to any antibiotic exposure. He is haemodynamically stable but has signs suggestive of mild congestive cardiac failure on examination today.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.2, HR 104, BP 124/68, RR 20, SpO2 96% room air, BMI 24
data_table.Examination: Soft early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge grade 2/6, splinter haemorrhages bilateral fingernails, bilateral basal fine inspiratory crackles, hepatomegaly, no peripheral oedema, normal neurological examination, no Janeway lesions or Osler nodes
data_table.Investigations: WCC 13.6 neutrophilic, CRP 138, Hb 102 normocytic, urinalysis dipstick +2 protein and microscopic haematuria, ECG sinus tachycardia, chest X-ray clear; three sets of blood cultures sent; echocardiography requested urgently

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily for 2 weeks pending echocardiography results and blood culture sensitivities, with planned admission for definitive intravenous therapy only if echocardiography confirms vegetations on the valves

Intravenous vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading dose then dose-adjusted monotherapy targeting a trough level of 15 to 20 mg/L, providing broad gram-positive cover including methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and viridans group streptococci pending culture results

Intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.8 g four-hourly plus flucloxacillin 2 g four-hourly plus gentamicin 1 mg/kg eight-hourly, with continued cultures, urgent echocardiogram and infectious diseases consultation, narrowing on culture and sensitivity data

Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily monotherapy until culture results are available, given the broad gram-positive and gram-negative cover and convenient dosing schedule, with reassessment based on the formal echocardiogram and the eventual organism identified

Hold all antibiotics pending the echocardiogram and blood culture results in 48 hours, since premature empirical therapy may reduce the diagnostic yield of cultures and complicate identification of the responsible organism in subacute endocarditis presentations

subtopic_detail: Acute HIV seroconversion diagnosis HIV RNA when fourth-generation antigen antibody is negative
stem:
You are the sexual health clinic registrar reviewing a 32-year-old man with a 5-day history of fevers, sore throat, generalised lymphadenopathy, a non-pruritic maculopapular truncal rash and oral ulcers. He had condomless receptive anal intercourse with a new male partner 3 weeks ago. He has no previous diagnosis of HIV. Same-day point-of-care fourth-generation antigen-antibody HIV test is negative today. He has had no other recent illnesses and has had no other medications.

He is otherwise systemically well, haemodynamically stable, and not on any antiretroviral therapy currently. He has had no exposure to post-exposure prophylaxis in the past month and is keen to confirm or exclude HIV diagnosis today.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.0, HR 92, BP 122/76, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Pharyngeal erythema with bilateral tonsillar exudate, generalised non-tender lymphadenopathy, fine non-blanching truncal maculopapular rash, oral aphthous ulcers, soft non-tender abdomen, no neurology deficit
data_table.Investigations: Point-of-care fourth-generation HIV antigen-antibody negative; FBC mild leucopenia 3.4 with mild thrombocytopenia 132; LFTs mildly elevated ALT 78; EBV serology and CMV pending; chlamydia, gonorrhoea NAAT and syphilis serology sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation to confirm or exclude acute HIV seroconversion?

options.text: Reassure that the negative fourth-generation antigen-antibody test 3 weeks post-exposure effectively excludes HIV given that the p24 antigen detection window opens within 2 weeks, and discharge with safer-sex counselling and routine STI follow-up in 3 months

Send Epstein-Barr virus and cytomegalovirus serology and a heterophile antibody test to confirm acute infectious mononucleosis as a more probable diagnosis given the lymphadenopathy and pharyngitis, with planned outpatient follow-up in 7 days

Treat empirically for secondary syphilis with intramuscular benzathine penicillin 1.8 g stat given the rash and the high-risk exposure, with planned outpatient infectious diseases follow-up to confirm with syphilis serology and consider HIV testing in 3 months

Commence empirical post-exposure prophylaxis with tenofovir/emtricitabine and dolutegravir for 28 days given the high-risk exposure profile and the clinically suspected seroconversion, with planned repeat HIV testing at week 4 to confirm or exclude

Send quantitative HIV RNA viral load testing along with fourth-generation antigen-antibody confirmation, refer urgently to specialist HIV outpatients for confirmation and ART initiation if positive, and counsel on partner notification and testing

subtopic_detail: Septic shock hour-1 bundle blood cultures antibiotics fluids lactate
stem: You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 68-year-old man brought by ambulance with rigors, confusion and hypotension. He has a 2-day history of urinary frequency, dysuria and flank pain. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus on metformin and a history of benign prostatic hyperplasia. He is alert but disoriented, has dry mucous membranes and warm peripheries. There are no signs of obvious surgical abdomen, no obvious focal infection elsewhere, and no recent hospitalisation, urological instrumentation or known antibiotic-resistant organism colonisation. Three sets of blood cultures have been drawn and a peripheral large-bore intravenous line has been placed. His weight is 80 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.6, HR 122, BP 85/45, RR 26, SpO2 95% room air, GCS 14
data_table.Examination: Warm peripheries, capillary refill 3 seconds, mildly tender right flank, soft abdomen, no peritonism, dry mucous membranes, no neurological focal deficit
data_table.Investigations: Venous lactate 5.2 mmol/L, WCC 19.4, CRP 256, creatinine 168 (baseline 88), urine dipstick LE+++ nit+ blood+, blood cultures sent, urine MCS sent, chest X-ray no consolidation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management within the first hour?

options.text: Commence intravenous noradrenaline infusion through a central venous catheter at 5 micrograms per minute targeting a mean arterial pressure of 65 mmHg before commencing fluid resuscitation, with admission to the intensive care unit for ongoing management

Arrange urgent contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis to identify the source of infection and any complicating obstructive uropathy or perinephric abscess prior to commencing antibiotic therapy or significant fluid resuscitation

Prescribe oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for suspected uncomplicated urinary tract infection and discharge home with safety-net advice if blood pressure improves on a single litre normal saline bolus, with general practice review in 24 hours

Hold antibiotics and fluids pending urine and blood culture sensitivities to avoid premature empirical antibiotic exposure that may compromise the bacteriological yield from cultures and broaden the patient's antibiotic resistance profile longer term

Commence intravenous antibiotics within 1 hour (gentamicin 5 mg/kg plus ampicillin 2 g for suspected urosepsis), administer 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid bolus over 1 to 3 hours, repeat lactate within 2 hours, source control planning and ICU referral

subtopic_detail: B12 deficiency with neurological involvement parenteral hydroxocobalamin
stem:
You are the general medical registrar reviewing a 70-year-old woman with 4 months of progressive lower-limb paraesthesias, an unsteady gait, mild memory disturbance, and exertional dyspnoea. She has no history of bowel surgery, has had a long-standing diagnosis of atrophic gastritis, has never been a vegetarian, and is otherwise self-caring at home. She has not been on metformin or proton pump inhibitor therapy chronically.

On examination she has reduced vibration and proprioception in both lower limbs with brisk knee reflexes and absent ankle reflexes, and a positive Romberg test. She has no jaundice, no glossitis on examination today, and no pancytopenia.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7, HR 88, BP 122/74, RR 16, SpO2 97% room air
data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae, no jaundice, no glossitis, neurology with reduced vibration and proprioception lower limbs bilaterally, absent ankle reflexes, brisk knee reflexes, positive Romberg, no focal cortical deficit
data_table.Investigations: Hb 96 normocytic transitioning to macrocytic with MCV 108, WCC 4.2, platelets 220, B12 95 (low), serum folate 9 (normal), iron studies normal, TSH normal, anti-intrinsic factor antibody positive, MMA elevated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence intramuscular hydroxocobalamin 1 mg every second day for 2 weeks then 1 mg every 3 months long-term, monitor neurological recovery and full blood examination at 6 weeks, and screen for autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes given the intrinsic factor antibodies

Commence oral cyanocobalamin 1 mg daily for 4 months as monotherapy regardless of underlying intrinsic factor antibody positivity, with planned full blood examination and neurological reassessment at week 6 to confirm a satisfactory clinical response

Commence oral folic acid 5 mg daily as initial therapy with planned repeat B12 in 6 weeks to assess response, with parenteral B12 added only if anaemia does not improve adequately on folate monotherapy at the planned 6-week review

Refer urgently to haematology for bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy to characterise the macrocytic anaemia and rule out myelodysplastic syndrome before commencing any B12 replacement therapy, with follow-up neurology assessment within 2 weeks

Arrange transfusion of two units of packed red cells now to correct the anaemia and improve oxygen delivery, with parenteral B12 commenced after the transfusion is complete and the haemoglobin has stabilised above the threshold of 100 g/L

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis intravenous hydrocortisone in known Addison's during gastroenteritis
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 45-year-old woman with known primary adrenal insufficiency who presents with 36 hours of vomiting, watery diarrhoea, weakness and inability to keep her usual hydrocortisone 20 mg morning, 10 mg afternoon and fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily down. Her partner brought her in via ambulance after she became drowsy and complained of generalised weakness.

She is alert but mildly confused on arrival. She has not received any stress-dose steroid before arrival despite her chronic disease management plan instructing her to double her oral dose during illness and seek urgent review if vomiting prevented oral intake.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.0, HR 122, BP 78/50, RR 22, SpO2 97% room air, GCS 14
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, decreased skin turgor, hyperpigmented palmar creases and knuckles, mildly tender abdomen without peritonism, no focal neurology, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Na 122, K 6.0, glucose 3.1 mmol/L, urea 14, creatinine 142 (baseline 78), Hb 138, WCC 14.2, lactate 2.6; ECG sinus tachycardia 122; cortisol pre-treatment not yet available

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Administer oral hydrocortisone 40 mg as a stat dose with antiemetic and oral rehydration solution, with planned review in 2 hours and admission for inpatient observation if there is no improvement in observations and biochemistry at the recheck

Administer intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg stat then 50 mg six-hourly, give intravenous normal saline 1 litre stat then ongoing crystalloid resuscitation, treat hypoglycaemia with intravenous 10% dextrose, and admit to high-dependency unit

Administer intravenous dexamethasone 4 mg stat as preferred glucocorticoid as it does not interfere with subsequent cortisol assays for the diagnostic short Synacthen test, give intravenous saline, and admit to the medical ward for ongoing observation

Hold all glucocorticoid until baseline serum cortisol and ACTH results return to confirm the diagnosis of adrenal crisis, give intravenous fluid resuscitation in the interim, with cortisol assays sent before any steroid administration to avoid biochemical interference

Administer intramuscular fludrocortisone 200 micrograms stat with intravenous saline to address her hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia, with planned introduction of oral hydrocortisone once she has tolerated oral intake for 4 hours without further vomiting

subtopic_detail: Type B aortic dissection intravenous labetalol target heart rate and blood pressure
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar managing a 60-year-old hypertensive man with sudden onset severe tearing chest and interscapular pain 1 hour ago. He has poorly controlled hypertension on irbesartan 300 mg daily and amlodipine 10 mg daily. He has had no syncope, no neurology deficit, no abdominal pain, and his ECG shows sinus rhythm with left ventricular hypertrophy but no ischaemic features.

CT aortogram has demonstrated a Stanford type B dissection commencing distal to the left subclavian artery, descending to the level of the renal arteries with patent visceral vessels and no malperfusion. He has been transferred to the resuscitation cubicle with cardiothoracic surgery and intensive care on standby.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8, HR 102, BP 186/108 right arm, 124/78 left arm, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Examination: Distressed with pain, diaphoretic, no focal neurology, no abdominal tenderness, peripheral pulses present and symmetrical in lower limbs, no clinical features of cardiac tamponade
data_table.Investigations: Trop normal, FBC, UEC, coags normal, ECG sinus tachycardia 102, CXR mediastinum slightly widened, CT aortogram: Stanford type B dissection commencing distal to left subclavian and extending to renal artery level, no end-organ malperfusion, true lumen patent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate medical management?

options.text: Commence oral irbesartan 600 mg as an additional dose plus oral nifedipine modified-release 60 mg orally for blood pressure reduction, with admission to the coronary care unit for cardiac monitoring and serial troponin assessment over the next 24 hours

Administer intravenous adenosine 6 mg rapid push to slow the heart rate to a target less than 60 beats per minute and reduce shear stress on the dissection flap, with continuous cardiac monitoring and repeat doses titrated to clinical response

Commence intravenous labetalol infusion targeting a heart rate below 60 beats per minute first, then add sodium nitroprusside infusion if systolic blood pressure remains above 120 mmHg, target SBP 100-120 mmHg, opioid for pain, ICU admission

Proceed urgently to operating theatre for open surgical repair of the descending aorta given the severity of dissection and high in-hospital mortality of medically managed type B dissection presentations, with cardiopulmonary bypass team standby for the procedure

Commence intravenous heparin infusion at 18 units per kilogram per hour to prevent thrombosis within the false lumen and stabilise the dissection flap, with continuous cardiac and APTT monitoring during heparinisation in the intensive care unit

subtopic_detail: Phaeochromocytoma alpha-blockade prior to beta-blockade before adrenalectomy
stem:
You are the endocrinology registrar reviewing a 50-year-old man newly diagnosed with phaeochromocytoma after presenting with paroxysmal headaches, sweating and palpitations, with episodic systolic blood pressures up to 220 mmHg recorded by his general practitioner. Twenty-four-hour fractionated urinary metanephrines and plasma free metanephrines have confirmed the diagnosis. A 5 cm right adrenal mass has been imaged on contrast computed tomography of the abdomen, with no metastatic disease on the staging scans.

He has been referred for elective adrenalectomy and the surgical team has asked for preoperative medical optimisation. He is otherwise well, on no current medications, and has no other comorbidities.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 168/96 resting (220 systolic during paroxysms), HR 96, BMI 25
data_table.Examination: Mildly tremulous, no thyroid enlargement, normal cardiovascular examination at rest, no abdominal mass palpable
data_table.Investigations: Plasma free metanephrines and normetanephrines markedly raised, 24-hour urinary metanephrines raised, CT abdomen 5 cm right adrenal mass with classic phaeochromocytoma features and no metastases, MIBG and PET pending; ECG sinus rhythm, normal echocardiogram, normal renal function

lead_in: What is the most appropriate preoperative medical preparation?

options.text: Commence atenolol 50 mg daily for 7 days as initial preoperative beta-blockade before introducing alpha-blockade with phenoxybenzamine, to achieve dual receptor control before the planned surgical excision and avoid intraoperative haemodynamic instability

Proceed directly to adrenalectomy without preoperative medical preparation given the convenience of intraoperative haemodynamic management by experienced anaesthetics and surgical teams, with intravenous phentolamine and sodium nitroprusside available at induction

Commence amlodipine 5 mg daily titrated to blood pressure control as the primary preoperative agent and salt and fluid replacement to optimise intravascular volume, with planned surgery in 2 weeks once normotension is achieved on this regimen

Commence phenoxybenzamine 10 mg twice daily, titrate every 2 to 3 days targeting symptom control and supine BP less than 130/80 with orthostatic systolic above 90, encourage high-salt diet and oral fluids, add a beta-blocker only after established alpha-blockade for residual tachycardia

Commence metyrosine 250 mg four times daily for catecholamine synthesis inhibition for 7 days preoperatively, with planned introduction of carvedilol after the initial week of metyrosine to provide concurrent alpha and beta receptor antagonism prior to surgery

subtopic_detail: Clinically isolated syndrome optic neuritis MRI brain and spine for MS workup
stem:
You are the neurology registrar reviewing a 28-year-old woman with 5 days of progressive unilateral painful vision loss in the right eye, worsened by eye movement, with reduced colour vision and a relative afferent pupillary defect on examination. She has had no previous neurological symptoms, no recent infection, no headache outside of the painful eye movements, and is otherwise systemically well.

Fundoscopy shows a mildly swollen optic disc. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension and giant cell arteritis have been excluded clinically. There are no features of inflammatory eye disease, and she has not been exposed to ethambutol, methanol or other optic neurotoxins recently.

data_table.Examination: Right visual acuity 6/36, left 6/6; reduced colour vision right eye; relative afferent pupillary defect right; mild disc swelling right; full extraocular movements with pain on right eye motion; no other cranial nerve deficit; normal upper and lower limb power, tone and reflexes; no sensory deficit
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, ESR, CRP and B12 normal, syphilis serology negative, ANA negative; ECG normal; visual evoked potentials pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation and management plan?

options.text: Commence intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days empirically for likely optic neuritis with planned outpatient oral prednisolone taper over 3 weeks, with magnetic resonance imaging deferred to outpatient review in 2 weeks once acute treatment is complete

Arrange urgent ocular ultrasound and orbital CT to characterise optic disc oedema and any associated mass lesion compressing the optic nerve, with planned ophthalmology review the next day for visual evoked potentials and consideration of intervention

Reassure the patient that idiopathic optic neuritis usually resolves spontaneously over 2 to 4 weeks without intervention, advise outpatient ophthalmology review in 1 week and request visual evoked potentials testing without further imaging or systemic therapy

Arrange urgent contrast magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and whole spinal cord to assess for additional demyelinating lesions, refer to neurology and ophthalmology, consider intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 to 5 days to hasten visual recovery

Commence empirical ocrelizumab 600 mg intravenously now as disease-modifying therapy for presumed relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, with planned outpatient ophthalmology follow-up in 1 week to monitor visual recovery and treatment tolerability

subtopic_detail: COPD exacerbation - NIV criteria
stem: A 72-year-old woman with severe COPD (FEV1 38% predicted) is brought in with 3 days of worsening dyspnoea, increased purulent sputum and confusion that started this morning. She has been on tiotropium and combined inhaled corticosteroid plus long-acting beta agonist. She has been treated for two exacerbations in the past year. Controlled oxygen at 28% has been started with target SpO2 88 to 92%.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 37.4 degrees Celsius, HR 112, RR 30, SpO2 89% on 28% FiO2 venturi, BP 142/86 mmHg, GCS 14 (E4 V4 M6)
data_table.Examination: Use of accessory muscles, prolonged expiratory phase, scattered wheeze, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: ABG on 28% O2: pH 7.27, PaCO2 78 mmHg, PaO2 58 mmHg, HCO3 30 mmol/L; chest X-ray hyperinflation, no consolidation or pneumothorax

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer intravenous aminophylline as adjunct bronchodilation therapy now
Intubate immediately and transfer to the intensive care unit for ventilation
Increase oxygen flow to 8 L per minute via a Hudson mask to correct hypoxia
Commence non-invasive ventilation (BiPAP) with controlled oxygen titration
Switch to a heliox 70:30 oxygen mixture via a non-rebreather face mask

subtopic_detail: HFrEF - SGLT2 inhibitor addition
stem: A 64-year-old man with ischaemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 28%) attends his cardiologist for routine review. He is in sinus rhythm, NYHA class II. He is on perindopril 10 mg daily, bisoprolol 10 mg daily, spironolactone 25 mg daily and furosemide 40 mg daily. eGFR is 62 mL/min/1.73 m2. He has no diabetes. He has been stable for 6 months and is asking what else can be done.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 64, RR 14
data_table.Examination: JVP not raised, no peripheral oedema, chest clear, no third heart sound today
data_table.Investigations: Hb 138, K 4.4, Na 140, urea 7.2, creatinine 110, NT-proBNP 1100 ng/L

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next addition to his guideline-directed therapy?

options.text: Increase furosemide to 80 mg orally twice daily as the next escalation
Add digoxin 125 micrograms orally once daily to his existing regimen
Add ivabradine 5 mg orally twice daily to his existing regimen now
Add amlodipine 5 mg orally once daily to his existing regimen now
Add dapagliflozin 10 mg orally once daily to the existing regimen

subtopic_detail: AF stroke prevention
stem: A 76-year-old woman is found to have asymptomatic atrial fibrillation on a routine ECG. She has a history of hypertension on amlodipine and type 2 diabetes on metformin. She has no prior stroke or TIA. eGFR is 64 mL/min/1.73 m2. She has no bleeding history.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 134/82 mmHg, HR 78, irregular, RR 16
data_table.Examination: No murmurs, no heart failure, no carotid bruit, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: ECG atrial fibrillation rate 78, FBC normal, K 4.3, creatinine 86, HbA1c 7.1%

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate stroke-prevention therapy?

options.text: Apixaban 5 mg orally twice daily as oral anticoagulation
Aspirin 100 mg orally once daily as oral antithrombotic
Clopidogrel 75 mg orally once daily as oral antithrombotic
Warfarin orally with INR target 2.0 to 3.0 as anticoagulation
No antithrombotic therapy with annual cardiovascular review

subtopic_detail: Acute migraine - second-line
stem: A 28-year-old woman with episodic migraine without aura presents to her general practitioner. She has 2 attacks per month, each lasting up to 24 hours. Oral ibuprofen 400 mg taken at headache onset has not provided adequate relief in the past 3 attacks. She has no cardiovascular disease, no hemiplegic migraine and is not pregnant. She wants an acute-attack medication she can self-administer.

data_table.Examination: Normal neurological examination between attacks, fundi normal, BP 116/72 mmHg
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, TFTs normal; no imaging performed as no red flags

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate acute therapy?

options.text: Oral propranolol 40 mg twice daily continuously
Sumatriptan 50 mg orally at headache onset
Oxycodone 5 mg orally at headache onset
Ergotamine 2 mg sublingual tablet at headache onset
Amitriptyline 25 mg at night every night

subtopic_detail: Chronic hyponatraemia - correction rate
stem: A 78-year-old man with chronic alcoholism is admitted from a nursing home with confusion and unsteady gait. He has been on a thiazide for years. He has had no seizures. He last ate normally 4 days ago and has been on tea and biscuits. He has no focal neurology. The medical registrar asks about the safe rate of sodium correction.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 110/68 mmHg, HR 88, Temp 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Mildly confused, no peripheral oedema, mucous membranes dry, no focal neurology, no asterixis
data_table.Investigations: Na 112 mmol/L, K 3.2, urea 4.4, creatinine 92, glucose 5.0, urine osmolality 420 mOsm/kg, urine Na 50 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate sodium-correction strategy in the first 24 hours?

options.text: Aim to correct serum sodium by 20 to 25 mmol/L over the first 24 hours
Give 3% saline 100 mL intravenously over 10 minutes then recheck sodium
Aim to correct serum sodium by no more than 8 mmol/L per 24 hours
Restrict total fluid intake to 500 mL per 24 hours without other measures
Infuse intravenous 3% saline at 1 mL/kg/hour continuously for 24 hours

subtopic_detail: Intermediate-risk PE - RV strain
stem: A 58-year-old man presents with 2 days of pleuritic chest pain and dyspnoea. He returned from a long-haul flight 5 days ago. His Wells score is 6. CT pulmonary angiography confirms bilateral segmental pulmonary emboli with right ventricular enlargement. He is normotensive on arrival.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/74 mmHg, HR 112, RR 24, SpO2 92% in room air
data_table.Examination: Mild dyspnoea, JVP raised 4 cm, lungs clear, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Troponin I 65 ng/L (cut-off 14), NT-proBNP 920 ng/L, CTPA RV/LV diameter ratio 1.2, ECG sinus tachycardia and S1Q3T3

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate management?

options.text: Discharge on apixaban with general practitioner review in 7 days from now
Systemic thrombolysis using intravenous alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours
Inferior vena cava filter inserted by interventional radiology in 24 hours
Therapeutic anticoagulation with low-molecular-weight heparin and admission
Surgical pulmonary embolectomy via median sternotomy on emergency theatre

subtopic_detail: Adrenal incidentaloma workup
stem: A 56-year-old woman has an incidental 2.8 cm right adrenal mass identified on a CT abdomen done for nephrolithiasis. The CT density is 5 Hounsfield units on the unenhanced phase. She has hypertension on amlodipine and irbesartan, no episodic symptoms, no Cushingoid features, and no family history of endocrine disease.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 142/88 mmHg, HR 72, BMI 28 kg/m2
data_table.Examination: No striae, no facial plethora, no proximal myopathy, no palpable mass
data_table.Investigations: CT: right adrenal mass 2.8 cm, 5 HU non-contrast (lipid-rich); FBC, UEC, LFTs normal

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test with plasma metanephrines
24-hour urinary 5-HIAA combined with serum chromogranin A measurement
Image-guided fine-needle aspiration of the right adrenal mass this week
Repeat non-contrast CT abdomen in 6 months without biochemical testing
Right adrenalectomy without further investigation given size and density

subtopic_detail: Adult sepsis hour-1 bundle
stem: A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents to ED with 24 hours of fever, dysuria and right flank pain. He is alert but tachycardic. Initial obs show HR 124, BP 88/52 mmHg, RR 28, SpO2 96% on room air, temp 39.2 degrees Celsius. A bedside lactate is 3.4 mmol/L. He has no allergies. Renal ultrasound is being arranged. You are the receiving registrar in the resuscitation bay deciding the hour-1 plan.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 39.2 degrees Celsius, HR 124, RR 28, BP 88/52 mmHg, SpO2 96% in room air, GCS 15
data_table.Examination: Warm peripheries, capillary refill 3 seconds, right renal angle tenderness, no peritonism, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 3.4 mmol/L, WCC 18 x10^9/L, CRP 220 mg/L, creatinine 156 micromol/L (baseline 90), urinalysis 3+ leukocytes 2+ nitrites, two blood cultures sent

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate hour-1 sepsis bundle?

options.text: Cautious 500 mL crystalloid bolus, intravenous ceftriaxone and start noradrenaline if MAP remains under 65 mmHg
Oral ciprofloxacin 750 mg twice daily and 10 mL/kg of crystalloid prior to admission to a medical ward
Crystalloid 30 mL/kg over the first hour, intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam after cultures and serial lactate
Activated protein C infusion, intravenous gentamicin alone and hydrocortisone 200 mg as adjunctive therapy
Delay antibiotics until renal ultrasound has excluded obstructive uropathy and surgical drainage is planned

subtopic_detail: CAP severity scoring
stem: A 68-year-old woman presents to ED with 3 days of cough, fever and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. She lives independently and is non-smoker. She has hypertension only. CXR shows right lower lobe consolidation. She is well perfused and orientated.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 38.4 degrees Celsius, HR 96, RR 24, BP 124/76 mmHg, SpO2 92% on room air, GCS 15
data_table.Examination: Coarse crackles right base, no wheeze, no peripheral oedema, orientated to time and place
data_table.Investigations: WCC 14 x10^9/L, urea 6.8 mmol/L, CRP 188 mg/L, lactate 1.6 mmol/L, multifocal albumin 36 g/L, ABG pH 7.42 PaO2 68 mmHg on room air, blood cultures sent

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate disposition and antibiotic plan?

options.text: Admit for IV moxifloxacin monotherapy as appropriate cover for atypical and typical bacteria in CAP
Discharge on oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily and oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 5 days
Admit to ICU for intravenous ceftriaxone, azithromycin and noradrenaline support as severe CAP
Admit for IV benzylpenicillin and oral doxycycline using the moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia regimen
Admit for IV vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam covering hospital-acquired and aspiration pathogens

subtopic_detail: Uncomplicated cystitis women
stem: A 28-year-old non-pregnant woman presents to her GP with 24 hours of dysuria, urinary frequency and suprapubic discomfort. She has had two similar episodes in the past year both resolved with antibiotics. She has no fever, no flank pain and no vaginal discharge. She is not sexually active in the past 4 weeks. She has no penicillin allergy and no recent antibiotic use. Urinalysis is positive for leukocyte esterase and nitrites; midstream urine has been sent.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.8 degrees Celsius, HR 76, RR 14, BP 118/72 mmHg, SpO2 99% in room air
data_table.Examination: Mild suprapubic tenderness, no renal angle tenderness, no peritonism, no vaginal discharge
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis - leukocytes 3+, nitrites positive, blood trace, glucose negative; urine pregnancy test negative

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate empirical antibiotic?

options.text: Oral azithromycin 1 g single dose as empirical therapy covering atypical urinary pathogens
Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 3 days as effective broad-spectrum first-line cystitis therapy
Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg twice daily for 5 days as broad cover for uncomplicated cystitis
Oral cefalexin 500 mg four times daily for 5 days as a broader cephalosporin cystitis option
Oral trimethoprim 300 mg orally each night for 3 days as empirical therapy for uncomplicated cystitis

subtopic_detail: Necrotising fasciitis recognition
stem: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 9.2%) presents to ED with 36 hours of right leg pain following a minor abrasion. The pain is out of proportion to the visible skin changes.
