There is firm induration extending beyond the visible erythema and a small area of grey discolouration with a foul-smelling exudate. Blood pressure has fallen from 134/80 in triage to 92/58 mmHg after analgesia. He is alert. Bedside blood tests have returned.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 38.6 degrees Celsius, HR 122, RR 26, BP 92/58 mmHg, SpO2 97% in room air, GCS 15
data_table.Examination: Right calf erythema with central grey patch, woody induration extending proximally, severe tenderness on palpation, palpable peripheral pulses, no crepitus on examination
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22 x10^9/L, Hb 124 g/L, Na 130 mmol/L, creatinine 142 micromol/L, glucose 16 mmol/L, CRP 220 mg/L, lactate 4.2 mmol/L

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Activate emergency surgical referral for theatre and commence intravenous meropenem with clindamycin
Admit for IV flucloxacillin 2 g 6-hourly and review with the surgical team in the morning round
Arrange contrast-enhanced CT of the right leg before contacting surgery to confirm fascial involvement
Admit to general medical unit for IV vancomycin and serial wound photographs to assess progression
Commence intravenous fluid bolus only, then admit to the diabetic foot service for podiatry review

subtopic_detail: Adult bacterial meningitis empirical
stem: A 38-year-old previously well man presents to ED with 12 hours of fever, severe headache, photophobia and neck stiffness. He is drowsy but obeying commands. There is no rash. He has no penicillin allergy and no recent overseas travel. CT brain is unremarkable. You are preparing to perform a lumbar puncture but blood cultures are not yet drawn. The bedside team is asking about the order of interventions.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 39.1 degrees Celsius, HR 108, RR 22, BP 122/76 mmHg, SpO2 98% in room air, GCS 13
data_table.Examination: Neck stiffness, photophobia, no rash, no focal neurology, pupils equal and reactive, no papilloedema, alert but drowsy
data_table.Investigations: CT brain no mass lesion no haemorrhage no hydrocephalus, WCC 22 x10^9/L, CRP 240 mg/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, glucose 6.8 mmol/L

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate sequence of interventions?

options.text: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV first then blood cultures then dexamethasone then LP if no focal neurology develops
Lumbar puncture first then dexamethasone then ceftriaxone after CSF is in the lab and Gram stain returned
Blood cultures then dexamethasone 10 mg IV then ceftriaxone 2 g IV then lumbar puncture as feasible
Vancomycin and meropenem with dexamethasone after MRI brain has excluded an epidural collection
Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IM in the resuscitation area without further CT or LP because of suspected meningococcal disease

subtopic_detail: Acute HIV seroconversion testing
stem: A 27-year-old man presents to a sexual health clinic with 10 days of fever, sore throat, generalised lymphadenopathy and a non-pruritic maculopapular rash on his trunk. He had unprotected receptive anal intercourse with a new male partner 3 weeks ago. He has no past HIV testing history. He is otherwise well. He asks for the most accurate test for acute HIV at this stage of illness. Examination is consistent with mononucleosis-like illness.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 38.4 degrees Celsius, HR 96, RR 16, BP 118/74 mmHg, SpO2 99% in room air
data_table.Examination: Bilateral cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy, faint maculopapular rash on trunk, pharyngeal erythema without exudate, no oral candida, no neck stiffness
data_table.Investigations: WCC 4.8 x10^9/L with lymphocyte 1.0 x10^9/L, ALT 78 U/L, monospot pending, EBV/CMV serology pending

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate diagnostic test?

options.text: HIV RNA PCR quantitative assay to identify acute infection ahead of antibody seroconversion
Fourth-generation HIV antibody-antigen combination test alone with retest at 6 weeks if negative
Western blot HIV antibody confirmation as the gold standard for diagnosis of acute infection presentation
CD4 lymphocyte subset count alone as the most sensitive test for acute HIV at this stage of illness
Rapid point-of-care HIV antibody finger-prick test as the most appropriate initial test in this setting

subtopic_detail: Latent tuberculosis treatment
stem: A 34-year-old man recently arrived from Vietnam attends a refugee health clinic for screening. He is asymptomatic. He had BCG vaccination in childhood. His QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus is positive. CXR is normal. Sputum cannot be produced. He is not pregnant, not on immunosuppression and not living with HIV. ALT is normal. He has no household contacts of active TB and no other tuberculosis risk factors apart from being from a high-prevalence country.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.6 degrees Celsius, HR 72, RR 14, BP 118/72 mmHg, SpO2 99% in room air, BMI 22 kg/m^2
data_table.Examination: Well, no lymphadenopathy, chest clear, no scars apart from BCG, abdomen unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: QuantiFERON positive (interferon-gamma response above threshold); CXR no infiltrate, no cavitation, no hilar lymphadenopathy; ALT 28 U/L; HIV negative; hepatitis B and C negative

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure him that QuantiFERON positivity reflects prior BCG and arrange a repeat test in 2 years
Commence rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol four-drug therapy for 2 months then continue 4 months
Commence isoniazid 300 mg daily with pyridoxine 25 mg for 6 to 9 months and monitor LFTs at baseline and at 4 weeks
Refer for sputum induction and bronchoscopy to obtain microbiological samples before any treatment is considered
Commence rifampicin 600 mg daily monotherapy for 4 months as a shorter latent TB regimen for low-risk adults

subtopic_detail: STEMI reperfusion within PCI window
stem: A 58-year-old man presents to a regional emergency department with 40 minutes of crushing central chest pain radiating to the left jaw. He is a current smoker and has hypertension. He has had no previous cardiac events. The nearest 24-hour cardiac catheterisation laboratory is reached by helicopter within 90 minutes, with an expected total door-to-balloon time of 110 minutes from now. There are no contraindications to fibrinolysis.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 140/85, HR 95 sinus, RR 20, SpO2 96% on 2 L oxygen via nasal prongs, temp 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, in pain; chest clear; heart sounds normal with no murmur; peripheries cool
data_table.Investigations: ECG: ST elevation 3 mm V1 to V4 with reciprocal inferior depression; troponin pending; potassium 4.0; creatinine 80

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate reperfusion strategy?

options.text: Weight-based intravenous tenecteplase bolus immediately at the current site of presentation
Transfer immediately for primary PCI given expected door-to-balloon under 120 minutes
Loading dose aspirin and ticagrelor with conservative management given short pain duration
IV unfractionated heparin alone while organising cath lab transfer the following morning
Hospital admission for serial troponins and ECG monitoring before any reperfusion decision

subtopic_detail: AECOPD with hypercapnic respiratory failure
stem: A 72-year-old man with severe COPD on triple inhaler therapy presents to the emergency department with 3 days of increasing breathlessness and productive purulent sputum. He uses 1 L of home oxygen overnight. He has been a 60 pack-year smoker who recently quit. He is currently sitting upright and able to speak in short sentences.

data_table.Vital signs: RR 32, SpO2 84% in room air, HR 110, BP 145/85, temp 37.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tripoding, accessory muscle use, audible expiratory wheeze; chest hyperinflated with bilateral wheeze; mild ankle oedema; GCS 14
data_table.Investigations: ABG in room air: pH 7.28, pCO2 78 mmHg, pO2 52 mmHg, HCO3 28; chest x-ray: hyperinflation, no consolidation

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intubate and mechanically ventilate immediately given the degree of respiratory acidosis on ABG
High-flow oxygen via non-rebreather mask targeting SpO2 above 95 with bronchodilators and steroids
Controlled oxygen 88-92%, BiPAP NIV, nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone and antibiotics
Nebulised magnesium sulfate 2 g and IV aminophylline infusion as bronchodilator escalation therapy
IV hydrocortisone 200 mg with empiric antibiotics pending sputum culture and sensitivity results

subtopic_detail: Add SGLT2i in T2DM with established ASCVD
stem: A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 5 years attends his GP for review. His HbA1c is 8.2 percent, up from 7.5 percent 3 months ago, on metformin extended release 2 g daily. He had a percutaneous coronary intervention to the LAD 2 years ago and is on aspirin, atorvastatin, perindopril and metoprolol. He has no symptoms of hypoglycaemia and his renal function is preserved. His BMI is 31.

data_table.Examination: Cardiovascular and respiratory examination normal; lower limbs no oedema, foot pulses present, monofilament intact bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: HbA1c 8.2%, eGFR 65, ACR 4, fasting glucose 9.2, LDL 1.8, K 4.1, sodium 138; ECG sinus rhythm

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate add-on glucose-lowering therapy?

options.text: Add gliclazide modified release 60 mg daily for additional glycaemic control today
Add basal insulin glargine 10 units at night titrated to fasting glucose 4-7 mmol/L
Switch metformin to a DPP-4 inhibitor sitagliptin 100 mg daily for ease of administration
Add SGLT2 inhibitor empagliflozin 10 mg daily for cardiovascular and renal benefit
Add thiazolidinedione pioglitazone 30 mg daily for its weight-neutral glycaemic profile

subtopic_detail: Levothyroxine initiation elderly with IHD
stem: A 68-year-old woman attends her GP with 4 months of fatigue, cold intolerance, a 4 kg weight gain and constipation. She has a history of stable ischaemic heart disease (PCI 6 years ago) on aspirin, metoprolol and atorvastatin. She is otherwise well and not on any antithyroid medication. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/82, HR 60 sinus, BMI 28
data_table.Examination: Diffuse goitre; dry skin; bradycardia regular; reflexes slow to relax; no peripheral oedema; ECG sinus rhythm with no ischaemic change
data_table.Investigations: TSH 25 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free T4 8 pmol/L (10-22), TPO antibodies positive at 350; HbA1c 5.5, LFTs normal, troponin negative

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate initiation of thyroid hormone replacement?

options.text: Levothyroxine 1.6 mcg/kg daily (approximately 100 mcg) as a full replacement dose now
Combined levothyroxine 50 mcg with liothyronine 10 mcg daily for symptom control
Defer treatment and recheck TSH and free T4 in 6 weeks before commencing therapy
Carbimazole 5 mg daily given the autoimmune thyroid disease features and positive TPO
Levothyroxine 25 mcg daily for 4 weeks then up-titrate guided by TSH at 6 weekly intervals

subtopic_detail: Persisting electrocardiogram changes after the first dose of calcium
stem: A 67-year-old man with acute kidney injury received intravenous calcium gluconate five minutes ago for hyperkalaemia with a broad complex rhythm. Insulin with dextrose is now running. The rhythm strip is unchanged.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 /min, blood pressure 112/70 mmHg, SpO2 97% room air
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 7.2 mmol/L; ECG QRS 150 ms with absent P waves

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate step?

options.text: Repeat the calcium dose and continue cardiac monitoring
Add nebulised salbutamol and repeat the potassium hourly
Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate and reassess the rhythm
Arrange urgent haemodialysis through a femoral catheter
Give a further insulin bolus with dextrose cover

subtopic_detail: Refeeding syndrome recognition and management
stem: A 52-year-old man with alcohol use disorder (BMI 16, minimal oral intake for 3 weeks) was admitted 3 days ago for community-acquired pneumonia and commenced on standard hospital meals at 1800 kcal/day from day 1. Today he is more confused, weak and short of breath at rest. He has not received thiamine. He is on IV ceftriaxone and azithromycin for pneumonia.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 37.0 degrees Celsius, HR 110 sinus, BP 105/60, RR 24, SpO2 95% on 2 L nasal prongs
data_table.Examination: Cachectic, confused (AMTS 6/10), peripheral oedema bilateral ankles, fine crackles at right base; weak diffuse weakness in all limbs
data_table.Investigations: PO4 0.3 (0.8-1.5), Mg 0.5 (0.7-1.0), K 3.0, corrected Ca 2.0, Na 134, urea 4, creatinine 60, albumin 22, LFTs ALT 60 AST 90, glucose 5.2

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate priority in management?

options.text: Increase oral feeding to meet the calorie deficit and add a daily oral multivitamin supplement
IV phosphate, magnesium and potassium replacement, IV thiamine 300 mg, and reduce calories to 5-10 kcal/kg/day
Total parenteral nutrition at full calorie target to prevent further nutritional deterioration
IV thiamine 100 mg single dose with phosphate-rich oral diet and outpatient dietitian review
Cease feeding completely for 48 hours until serum electrolytes normalise then restart full diet

subtopic_detail: High-risk TIA DAPT for 21 days
stem: A 70-year-old man presents 2 hours after an episode of right hemiparesis and dysphasia lasting 30 minutes that fully resolved before arrival. He has hypertension, type 2 diabetes and is a current smoker. He is on perindopril and metformin. He has had no prior cerebrovascular events. There is no history of atrial fibrillation. ECG shows sinus rhythm.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 168/95, HR 78 sinus, BMI 28, capillary glucose 8.4
data_table.Examination: GCS 15, speech now fluent and clear, no focal weakness or facial droop, gait normal; carotid auscultation no bruit
data_table.Investigations: CT brain: no acute infarct, no haemorrhage; ABCD2 score 5; troponin negative; INR 1.0

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate management?

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg daily monotherapy with outpatient clinic review in approximately 4 weeks
Warfarin loading 5 mg daily targeting an INR 2-3 commencing today as anticoagulation now
Aspirin plus clopidogrel for 21 days, high-intensity statin and urgent stroke clinic review
IV thrombolysis with tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg given the high stroke recurrence risk profile
Direct oral anticoagulant apixaban 5 mg twice daily empirically pending further investigations

subtopic_detail: TTP recognition and urgent plasma exchange
stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with 3 days of progressive fatigue, petechial rash on her shins, intermittent confusion and a low-grade fever. She has had no recent infection, no diarrhoea, and is on no medications. She has no personal or family history of bleeding. She is not pregnant. She is alert but mildly drowsy with fluctuating attention.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 38.0 degrees Celsius, HR 100 sinus, BP 128/76, RR 18, SpO2 99% in room air
data_table.Examination: Petechial rash on shins, mild confusion (AMTS 7/10), no focal neurology, no overt bleeding, no splenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Hb 75, platelets 12, blood film schistocytes 4+, reticulocytes elevated, LDH 1500, haptoglobin undetectable, total bilirubin 60 (indirect 50), creatinine 130, PT and APTT normal, fibrinogen 3.2, DAT negative; ADAMTS13 activity sample sent

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Urgent platelet transfusion to a count above 50 and IV ceftriaxone empiric sepsis cover today
IV immunoglobulin 1 g/kg over 2 days for presumed immune thrombocytopenic purpura disorder
Urgent haemodialysis given acute kidney injury with electrolyte derangement and uraemia present
Urgent therapeutic plasma exchange and IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily while ADAMTS13 pending
Therapeutic anticoagulation with unfractionated heparin for thrombotic microangiopathy syndrome

subtopic_detail: Clostridioides difficile first non-severe episode
stem: A 68-year-old woman presents to ED with 4 days of watery non-bloody diarrhoea 6 times daily after a 7-day course of oral amoxicillin-clavulanate for cellulitis ended 10 days ago. She is haemodynamically stable, mildly dehydrated, and tolerating oral fluids. She has no abdominal distension, no peritonism and no ileus. She takes a proton pump inhibitor for reflux and lives independently with her husband at home.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 128/76, HR 92, RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air, Temp 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Mild lower abdominal tenderness without guarding; bowel sounds present; mucous membranes a little dry
data_table.Investigations: WCC 11.4 x10^9/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L (baseline 70), lactate 1.4 mmol/L, CRP 32 mg/L, stool PCR positive for Clostridioides difficile toxin B gene

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate antimicrobial choice?

options.text: Intravenous metronidazole 500 mg eight hourly for 10 days alongside ongoing oral PPI therapy to suppress gastric acid recurrence
Oral loperamide 4 mg followed by 2 mg after each loose stool and no antibiotic therapy initiated until repeat testing in 48 hours
Oral rifaximin 400 mg three times daily for 14 days as the first-line agent for community-acquired Clostridioides difficile infection in adults
Faecal microbiota transplant via colonoscopy as the first-line approach for an initial non-severe Clostridioides difficile episode in this patient
Oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily for 10 days with cessation of the inciting antibiotic and ongoing oral rehydration support

subtopic_detail: Atrial flutter haemodynamically stable rate control
stem: A 72-year-old man with hypertension and reflux presents to ED with 6 hours of palpitations and mild exertional dyspnoea. He has no chest pain, no syncope, no heart failure symptoms and a known LV ejection fraction of 58 percent on a recent transthoracic echocardiogram. His CHA2DS2-VA score is 3. He is otherwise well, has no chronic kidney disease and weighs 84 kg. There is no obvious precipitant such as alcohol or recent infection.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 142/86, HR 138 irregularly regular pattern on monitor, RR 18, SpO2 97% room air
data_table.Examination: Clear lungs, no peripheral oedema, no carotid bruit
data_table.Investigations: ECG shows sawtooth flutter waves with 2:1 AV conduction, ventricular rate 138; troponin negative; TSH 1.4 mU/L; creatinine 78 micromol/L; potassium 4.1 mmol/L

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate initial rate-control choice?

options.text: Oral metoprolol tartrate 25 mg twice daily commenced now with cardiology follow-up for outpatient anticoagulation decision after CHA2DS2-VA review
Intravenous adenosine 6 mg rapid push then 12 mg as the first-line agent to convert flutter rhythm to sinus rhythm in the emergency department
Intravenous amiodarone 300 mg over 1 hour then 900 mg over 24 hours as the first-line agent for rate control in stable atrial flutter
Immediate synchronised DC cardioversion under sedation despite haemodynamic stability and a duration of arrhythmia under 12 hours without anticoagulation
Oral digoxin 250 micrograms daily as monotherapy for rate control in this active 72-year-old with preserved left ventricular ejection fraction and reflux

subtopic_detail: Acute gallstone pancreatitis early management
stem: A 54-year-old woman presents to ED with 8 hours of severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, with vomiting. She has no fever, no jaundice and no haemodynamic instability. Her lipase is 8 times the upper limit of normal and her ALT is twice normal. An abdominal ultrasound shows gallstones in a non-distended gallbladder, a normal-calibre common bile duct without stones, and no choledocholithiasis. She is haemodynamically stable and tolerates small sips of water in ED.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/82, HR 96, RR 18, SpO2 97% on room air, Temp 37.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Epigastric tenderness without peritonism, no guarding; bowel sounds normal; no Cullen or Grey Turner signs
data_table.Investigations: Lipase 1880 U/L, ALT 92 U/L, bilirubin 18 micromol/L, GGT 124 U/L, lactate 1.6 mmol/L, calcium 2.32 mmol/L, urea 5.2 mmol/L, CRP 24 mg/L; ultrasound as described above

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate initial in-hospital management plan?

options.text: Urgent endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography within 24 hours regardless of jaundice status or imaging evidence of choledocholithiasis identified
Admit, restrict to nil by mouth for 5 to 7 days, total parenteral nutrition from day 1 and re-image with CT to grade severity at 24 to 48 hours
Discharge home with oral analgesia and elective outpatient cholecystectomy in 6 weeks regardless of ongoing pain, hydration status or oral tolerance during the admission today
Commence empirical intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g six hourly from admission to prevent peripancreatic infection in this patient with mild gallstone pancreatitis today
Admit for intravenous Hartmann's resuscitation, parenteral analgesia, early oral or enteral feeding within 24 to 48 hours and same-admission laparoscopic cholecystectomy

subtopic_detail: Mild diabetic foot infection outpatient management
stem: A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 12 years presents to his GP with a 3-day history of a warm, mildly painful 2 cm ulcer over the second metatarsal head with surrounding erythema extending 1 cm from the wound. He has no fever, no streaking lymphangitis and a palpable dorsalis pedis pulse. There is no probe-to-bone and no exposed tendon or capsule. He has no penicillin allergy and his HbA1c is 7.2 percent. He has full ankle range of motion.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/82, HR 80, Temp 36.9 degrees Celsius, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: 2 cm shallow plantar ulcer; surrounding cellulitis 1 cm wide; pedal pulses palpable; no probe-to-bone; sensation diminished to 10 g monofilament at first metatarsal head bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: WCC 8.4 x10^9/L, CRP 18 mg/L, HbA1c 7.2%, creatinine 88 micromol/L, plain foot X-ray negative for osteomyelitis

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate antimicrobial regimen?

options.text: Oral flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily for 7 days, daily dressing changes, off-loading and review at 5 to 7 days with high-risk foot service input as needed
Intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g six hourly for 7 days in hospital with vascular and orthopaedic review on admission to manage anaerobic and Pseudomonas cover today
Topical mupirocin 2 percent ointment three times daily for 7 days without any systemic antibiotic therapy initiated at this presentation in the practice today
Oral metronidazole 400 mg three times daily for 7 days as the sole antibiotic agent to cover anaerobic skin flora colonising the diabetic ulcer base today
Oral cefalexin 500 mg four times daily for 28 days plus oral clindamycin 450 mg eight hourly for 28 days for a prolonged course of dual-agent therapy

subtopic_detail: Uncomplicated type B aortic dissection
stem: A 64-year-old man presents to ED with 2 hours of sudden tearing interscapular pain radiating to the lower back. His BP is 178/108 in the right arm and 174/106 in the left arm. There is no neurological deficit, no limb ischaemia and no mesenteric ischaemia features. A CT aortogram shows a dissection flap originating distal to the left subclavian artery extending into the proximal abdominal aorta, with no aortic rupture or visceral malperfusion. He has known hypertension on irregular ramipril.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 178/108, HR 92, RR 18, SpO2 98% on room air, Temp 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Equal peripheral pulses, no neurological deficit, soft non-tender abdomen
data_table.Investigations: Troponin negative, lactate 1.4 mmol/L, creatinine 92 micromol/L; CT angiogram as described; ECG no ischaemic changes; chest X-ray widened mediastinum

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate initial pharmacological priority?

options.text: Sublingual glyceryl trinitrate 600 micrograms followed by oral amlodipine 10 mg as the priority agent for blood pressure control in this presentation today
Intravenous fluid loading with 1 litre of 0.9 percent saline followed by oral metoprolol tartrate 50 mg as initial management in this acute aortic syndrome presentation today
Emergent transfer for open thoracotomy and graft repair of the descending aorta as the priority intervention for this uncomplicated type B aortic dissection patient today
Intravenous unfractionated heparin loading at 80 units/kg then a continuous infusion to prevent dissection flap thrombosis and downstream ischaemia in this man today
Intravenous esmolol or labetalol infusion titrated to heart rate under 60 and systolic BP under 120 mmHg, plus parenteral analgesia and urgent vascular surgery review

subtopic_detail: Severe acute ulcerative colitis with Truelove-Witts criteria
stem: A 28-year-old man with a 3-year history of ulcerative colitis on oral mesalazine presents with 7 days of worsening bloody diarrhoea now occurring 10 times per day with marked nocturnal symptoms. He has crampy abdominal pain and feels systemically unwell. He has no recent travel, no recent antibiotics, and is up to date with vaccinations. There is no toxic megacolon on plain abdominal X-ray and no peritonism on examination today in the ward bed area.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 110/70, HR 108, RR 18, Temp 38.1 degrees Celsius, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen with diffuse mild tenderness, no guarding, no rebound; bowel sounds present
data_table.Investigations: Hb 102 g/L, WCC 14.2 x10^9/L, platelets 480 x10^9/L, CRP 84 mg/L, albumin 28 g/L; stool C difficile PCR negative, faecal calprotectin elevated; plain abdominal X-ray no megacolon

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Admit for intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg six hourly, VTE prophylaxis with enoxaparin, and stool tests including Clostridioides difficile PCR with daily reassessment of response
Continue oral mesalazine 4 g daily and add oral budesonide 9 mg daily with outpatient gastroenterology review in 2 weeks once symptoms have plateaued at the current intensity
Commence empirical oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily and oral metronidazole 400 mg three times daily for 7 days to cover bacterial overgrowth and travel-related pathogens today
Commence subcutaneous adalimumab 160 mg loading dose today and 80 mg in 2 weeks as the first-line biologic agent without starting any intravenous corticosteroid therapy beforehand
Plan urgent total colectomy within 24 hours of admission regardless of corticosteroid response in this patient with acute severe ulcerative colitis presentation now today

subtopic_detail: Vitamin B12 deficiency with neurological features
stem: A 64-year-old woman presents to her GP with 3 months of progressive fatigue, paraesthesiae of the toes and increasing unsteadiness when walking in the dark. She has type 1 diabetes on insulin and a 20-year history of metformin use was stopped earlier this year. She has no history of pernicious anaemia, no recent bowel surgery and no vegan dietary restriction. She has no recent change in medications and no history of alcohol misuse documented in her file.

data_table.Examination: Reduced vibration sense at the great toes bilaterally; impaired joint position sense; positive Romberg; normal cranial nerves; brisk knee reflexes with absent ankle reflexes
data_table.Investigations: Hb 102 g/L, MCV 108 fL, platelets 220 x10^9/L, WCC 4.6 x10^9/L; serum B12 78 pmol/L (reference > 200 pmol/L); folate 14 nmol/L; TSH 1.4 mU/L; anti-intrinsic factor antibody positive

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Intramuscular hydroxocobalamin 1000 micrograms every other day for 1 to 2 weeks until neurological progression halts, then maintenance every 3 months for life
Oral cyanocobalamin 1 mg daily for life without intramuscular loading therapy as the first-line treatment of vitamin B12 deficiency with neurological signs in this Australian outpatient
Oral folic acid 5 mg daily for 4 months alone, repeating macrocytic anaemia indices in 4 to 6 weeks, with no B12 supplementation initiated in this presentation in primary care today
Pack-red-cell transfusion of 2 units in the day ward as the first-line therapy for symptomatic macrocytic anaemia at a haemoglobin of 102 g/L in this older woman today in the GP rooms
Recommence metformin 500 mg twice daily and add iron polymaltose 105 mg once daily to address the macrocytic anaemia she has developed since stopping metformin earlier this year today

subtopic_detail: Hypercalcaemia of malignancy acute management
stem: A 65-year-old woman with newly diagnosed metastatic breast cancer presents to ED with 5 days of confusion, polyuria, polydipsia and constipation. She is no longer eating or drinking well. She has no chronic kidney disease, no current bisphosphonate use, no known QT prolongation, no atrial fibrillation, and is not currently on diuretics. Her dental review for jaw clearance was unremarkable last month, and there is no evidence of osteonecrosis of the jaw.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 112/68, HR 102, RR 18, Temp 36.7 degrees Celsius, SpO2 98% on room air
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, GCS 14 (confused), no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 3.4 mmol/L, phosphate 0.7 mmol/L, albumin 32 g/L, creatinine 124 micromol/L (baseline 78), Mg 0.78 mmol/L; PTH suppressed; PTHrP elevated; ECG QTc 380 ms

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate initial management plan?

options.text: Intravenous furosemide 40 mg eight hourly without prior fluid resuscitation, with hourly monitoring of urine output and serum electrolytes in this woman to forcibly diurese calcium quickly
Aggressive intravenous saline rehydration with 3 to 4 litres in the first 24 hours and intravenous zoledronic acid 4 mg once renal function permits, plus calcitonin if symptomatic in the meantime

Urgent haemodialysis as the first intervention before any intravenous fluid challenge or pharmacological calcium-lowering therapy is administered in this hypercalcaemia of malignancy presentation today
Subcutaneous denosumab 120 mg as the immediate first-line therapy for hypercalcaemia of malignancy in this woman with otherwise normal renal function and no prior antiresorptive therapy
Oral cinacalcet 30 mg twice daily commenced from admission as the immediate first-line treatment for hypercalcaemia of malignancy in this woman before any intravenous saline rehydration begins

subtopic_detail: Hereditary angioedema with laryngeal involvement
stem: A 34-year-old man presents to ED with acute swelling of the lips and tongue and a hoarse voice that started 90 minutes ago. He has had four similar previous episodes of non-pruritic, non-urticarial facial swelling, two with abdominal cramping pain that required admission. His father has the same problem. He is not on any new medications, has had no insect stings, no new foods and no contact with latex. Standard intramuscular adrenaline and intravenous antihistamines have had minimal effect.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/82, HR 102, RR 22, SpO2 96% on 4 L nasal prongs, Temp 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tongue and lip oedema, hoarse voice, no urticaria, no wheeze, no hypotension
data_table.Investigations: Tryptase pending; previous serology: C4 0.04 g/L (low), C1 esterase inhibitor functional activity 22 percent of normal (low) on stored bloods; FBC and UEC normal today

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next therapeutic agent?

options.text: A further dose of intramuscular adrenaline 500 micrograms with an intravenous adrenaline infusion at low dose as the priority therapy for refractory angioedema in this patient

Intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg, intravenous chlorphenamine 10 mg, and nebulised salbutamol 5 mg as the priority therapy for this severe refractory angioedema episode in the emergency department today
Intravenous C1 esterase inhibitor concentrate (20 IU/kg) or subcutaneous icatibant 30 mg as targeted bradykinin pathway therapy with airway-ready ENT and anaesthetic backup
Oral danazol 200 mg three times daily commenced now as acute therapy for this hereditary angioedema attack, with intravenous antihistamines and observation in the short stay unit afterwards
Endotracheal intubation under general anaesthesia and observation in the intensive care unit without administering any specific pharmacological angioedema-directed therapy in the meantime

subtopic_detail: Phaeochromocytoma crisis preoperative blockade
stem: A 48-year-old woman presents to ED with episodic palpitations, sweating and severe headaches over 6 months, today with BP 224/128, headache and chest pain. Imaging in the last week showed a 4 cm right adrenal lesion with characteristic features on MRI. 24-hour fractionated urinary metanephrines were elevated at 5 times the upper limit of normal. She has no asthma, no diabetes, no current beta blocker and no contraindications to alpha or beta blockade. She is haemodynamically tachycardic in ED.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 224/128, HR 124, RR 18, Temp 36.7 degrees Celsius, SpO2 98% on room air
data_table.Examination: Pale, sweating, no focal neurological deficit, no signs of heart failure
data_table.Investigations: Troponin negative, ECG sinus tachycardia, CT brain normal; 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines 5 x ULN one week ago

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next pharmacological priority?

options.text: Intravenous metoprolol 5 mg increments as the priority agent to immediately bring the resting heart rate to under 80 in this woman with a hypertensive crisis presentation today
Sublingual nifedipine 10 mg as the priority agent to rapidly drop blood pressure into the normotensive range in this woman with hypertensive crisis in the emergency department in front of you

Intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g bolus then 1 g per hour as the first-line agent to provide vasodilation and antiarrhythmic effect in this woman with severe catecholamine excess and hypertension today
Commence alpha blockade with intravenous phentolamine boluses now and transition to oral phenoxybenzamine over the next 7 to 14 days before adding any beta blocker for sinus tachycardia
Refer for urgent laparoscopic adrenalectomy within 24 hours without any pharmacological optimisation in this woman with biochemically confirmed phaeochromocytoma and current hypertensive crisis

subtopic_detail: Empiric antibiotic therapy for suspected infective endocarditis in an IVDU
stem: A 32-year-old man with active intravenous heroin use presents with 5 days of fevers, rigors and pleuritic chest pain. He is haemodynamically stable but unwell. Three sets of peripheral blood cultures have been drawn from separate sites. Bedside transthoracic echo shows a 9 mm mobile vegetation on the tricuspid valve with mild tricuspid regurgitation. Chest imaging shows multiple peripheral nodular opacities consistent with septic pulmonary emboli.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 112/68, HR 108, RR 22, SpO2 94% on room air, Temp 38.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Multiple needle track marks both antecubital fossae; soft systolic murmur at lower left sternal edge increasing on inspiration; no peripheral stigmata of left-sided IE
data_table.Investigations: WCC 16.4 x10^9/L, CRP 184 mg/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L, lactate 1.6 mmol/L; troponin negative; ECG sinus tachycardia

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate initial antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin with intravenous gentamicin empirically while cultures are pending, with daily levels and renal function checks
Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily as monotherapy, given its broad gram-negative cover and convenient once-daily administration in this presentation
Defer all antibiotics for 48 hours to allow blood cultures to declare a pathogen before any empirical antibiotic exposure
Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily with outpatient cardiology follow-up arranged for the following week
Intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.8 g six-hourly as a single agent based on streptococcal cover for community-acquired endocarditis

subtopic_detail: Post-exposure prophylaxis after occupational HIV needlestick
stem: A 29-year-old surgical resident sustains a deep hollow-needle injury during arterial line placement in a known HIV-positive patient with an unsuppressed viral load on adherence-poor antiretrovirals. The injury was 40 minutes ago. The resident is healthy, on no medications and not pregnant. She has had a single hepatitis B vaccination course with documented anti-HBs above 100 mIU/mL six months ago. Her last hepatitis C and HIV screens at occupational health 3 months ago were negative.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72, HR 84, Temp 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Wound at left index finger pulp, bleeding milked and wound irrigated with saline
data_table.Investigations: Source patient HIV RNA above 100,000 copies/mL on last clinic visit; source HCV antibody negative, HBsAg negative

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Send source patient and worker baseline HIV serology and arrange to start any prophylaxis in the morning once the laboratory has reported results
Commence tenofovir disoproxil with emtricitabine and dolutegravir as a 28-day three-drug course now and arrange baseline and follow-up testing in parallel
Give a single 50 mg dose of dolutegravir as a pragmatic monotherapy prophylaxis until source results return at the next clinic visit
Test only the exposed healthcare worker now and defer any prophylaxis until her own baseline serology is available the following day
Reassure the worker that her hepatitis B vaccine response covers her, and arrange follow-up serology at 3 months without any antiretroviral therapy

subtopic_detail: Latent tuberculosis treatment in an asymptomatic new migrant
stem: A 28-year-old man newly arrived from a high TB prevalence country attends a refugee health clinic for screening. He has no respiratory or systemic symptoms, no history of treated TB and no known contact with active TB. He is HIV-negative, his BMI is 22 and he has no liver disease. Quantiferon-Gold Plus is positive. Chest radiograph and clinical examination are unremarkable. Sputum induction and AFB testing have not been performed.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/78, HR 72, Temp 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: No lymphadenopathy, chest clear to auscultation
data_table.Investigations: QFT-Plus positive; CXR no infiltrate, cavitation or hilar adenopathy; ALT 22 U/L, AST 18 U/L, bilirubin 8 micromol/L; HIV serology negative; HbA1c 5.2%

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Commence a 6-month rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol regimen empirically as treatment for presumed active pulmonary tuberculosis
Provide no treatment at this stage and arrange a repeat Quantiferon assay in 12 months as routine follow-up for an asymptomatic positive result
Offer 9 months of daily isoniazid with pyridoxine, or alternatively 4 months of daily rifampicin, with monthly clinical and liver function review during treatment
Collect three early-morning sputum samples for AFB smear and culture before deciding on any preventive or active treatment regimen for this man
Repeat the Quantiferon-Gold Plus assay in 4 weeks before any decision is made, on the basis that early conversion windows may produce uncertain results

subtopic_detail: Hour-1 sepsis bundle in suspected urosepsis
stem: A 68-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes is brought to ED with 24 hours of fevers, rigors and worsening confusion. She has been treated by her GP for a urinary tract infection in the past week. On arrival she is tachypnoeic and hypotensive. Bedside venous blood gas shows pH 7.30 with lactate 4.2 mmol/L. Urinalysis shows leucocyte esterase, nitrites and blood. She has no documented allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 84/52, HR 124, RR 28, SpO2 95% on room air, Temp 38.9 degrees Celsius, GCS 14
data_table.Examination: Cool peripheries with prolonged capillary refill, mild left renal angle tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 4.2 mmol/L, WCC 18.2 x10^9/L, creatinine 162 micromol/L (baseline 78), glucose 14.4 mmol/L; cultures and lipase pending

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Restrict fluids to a single 250 mL crystalloid bolus to avoid pulmonary oedema, then reassess clinically in 60 minutes before any further therapy
Withhold all antibiotics until blood and urine cultures have been processed by the laboratory, to optimise the diagnostic yield from microbiology
Commence noradrenaline by peripheral line at 0.1 microgram/kg/min before any crystalloid resuscitation, prioritising mean arterial pressure restoration first
Crystalloid 30 mL/kg over the first hour, intravenous gentamicin plus piperacillin-tazobactam after blood and urine cultures, serial lactates and source imaging within the hour
Administer intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg as the immediate first measure for circulatory collapse, plus a single dose of intravenous sodium bicarbonate to correct acidosis

subtopic_detail: Empiric therapy for community-acquired bacterial meningitis
stem: A 34-year-old man presents to ED with 12 hours of severe headache, photophobia, neck stiffness and a single rigor. He has no recent travel, no immunosuppression and is on no regular medications. He is alert with no focal neurology. There is no rash. CT brain is reported normal. Lumbar puncture is being prepared by the ED registrar.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/82, HR 108, RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air, Temp 39.0 degrees Celsius, GCS 15
data_table.Examination: Kernig and Brudzinski signs positive, no rash, no papilloedema
data_table.Investigations: WCC 17.4 x10^9/L, CRP 142 mg/L, lactate 1.9 mmol/L, platelets 198 x10^9/L, INR 1.0; CT brain unremarkable

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate step?

options.text: Proceed straight to lumbar puncture with full opening pressure and CSF cell count, then hold all empirical antibiotics pending the laboratory report
Administer intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g alone without dexamethasone, on the basis that steroids increase the risk of iatrogenic immunosuppression in young adults
Start empirical intravenous aciclovir 10 mg/kg alone for presumed herpes simplex encephalitis, with bacterial cover deferred pending CSF PCR results
Defer all therapy until a contrast-enhanced MRI brain has been obtained and reviewed by a neurology registrar to characterise any meningeal enhancement
Give intravenous dexamethasone 10 mg with intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g now after a single set of blood cultures, then proceed to lumbar puncture

subtopic_detail: Oseltamivir initiation in frail nursing home resident with confirmed influenza A
stem: An 84-year-old woman in residential aged care develops fevers, cough and lethargy 36 hours ago, during a documented influenza outbreak in her facility. Point-of-care PCR is positive for influenza A. She has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and ischaemic heart disease but no liver or significant renal disease (eGFR 58). She has been vaccinated against influenza this season.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/78, HR 96, RR 22, SpO2 91% on room air, Temp 38.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Mildly tachypnoeic, scattered wheeze, no focal consolidation; alert and orientated
data_table.Investigations: Influenza A PCR positive; CXR mild bibasal atelectasis, no consolidation; troponin negative; creatinine 96 micromol/L

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate antiviral plan?

options.text: Oral oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days, started today, alongside symptomatic measures and watchful escalation for hypoxia
Oral oseltamivir 150 mg twice daily for 10 days as an extended high-dose regimen for an outbreak setting in residential aged care
Withhold all antiviral therapy and provide only supportive care, given that symptom onset was more than 24 hours ago in a vaccinated individual
Intravenous peramivir as the first-line antiviral on the basis of mild renal impairment and the convenience of single-dose intravenous therapy
Oral amantadine 100 mg twice daily for 5 days as first-line cover against an A subtype influenza outbreak in this residential setting

subtopic_detail: Uncomplicated lower limb cellulitis empirical therapy
stem: A 46-year-old man presents with a 36-hour history of a red, hot, painful lower leg following minor trauma. He is otherwise well, with no diabetes, no immunosuppression and no documented penicillin allergy. There is no fluctuant collection, no necrosis and no crepitus. The leg has well-demarcated erythema below the knee with associated tenderness. He is haemodynamically stable and afebrile.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/76, HR 80, RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air, Temp 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Unilateral right calf erythema with central warmth, no fluctuance or abscess, intact distal pulses and sensation
data_table.Investigations: WCC 11.4 x10^9/L, CRP 38 mg/L; ultrasound shows no abscess or DVT; HbA1c 5.3%

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate first-line antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral cefalexin 500 mg six-hourly for 7 days as a first-choice agent because of its broader gram-negative cover compared to flucloxacillin
Oral di/flucloxacillin 500 mg six-hourly for 5 days as first-line outpatient therapy for non-severe lower limb cellulitis in this patient
Intravenous vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading then maintenance per trough level for empirical MRSA cover in a community-acquired skin infection presentation
Topical mupirocin to the affected area three times daily plus oral analgesia, without any systemic antibiotic therapy initiated at this assessment
Oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily as monotherapy given anaerobic activity and a once-daily option, with no addition of antistreptococcal cover at this time

subtopic_detail: Uncomplicated lower UTI in a non-pregnant adult woman
stem: A 34-year-old non-pregnant woman presents with 48 hours of urinary frequency, dysuria and suprapubic discomfort. She has no fevers, flank pain, vaginal symptoms or systemic features. She has no significant past medical history, takes no regular medications and has no known drug allergies. There is no recent antibiotic exposure. Bedside urinalysis shows leucocyte esterase and nitrites positive.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/72, HR 78, Temp 37.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Suprapubic tenderness only; no flank tenderness, no vaginal discharge
data_table.Investigations: Bedside urinalysis: leucocytes +++, nitrites positive, blood +; midstream urine sent; not pregnant on serum beta-hCG

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 3 days as empirical first-line therapy in this uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection presentation
Single 3 g oral dose of fosfomycin as the empirical first-line agent without any further courses required for treatment of this uncomplicated lower UTI
Oral trimethoprim 300 mg once daily for 3 days as empirical first-line therapy in this non-pregnant adult woman with uncomplicated lower UTI
Intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily for 7 days as empirical first-line therapy for any culture-positive urinary tract infection in adults regardless of severity
Oral amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 14 days as a long course of empirical therapy in this uncomplicated lower UTI presentation

subtopic_detail: Pharmacotherapy initiation after low-trauma vertebral fracture
stem: A 72-year-old post-menopausal woman presents with sudden mid-thoracic back pain after a minor stumble. Imaging confirms a wedge compression fracture of T7 without neurological deficit. DXA shows lumbar spine T-score -2.8 and femoral neck T-score -2.4. Renal function and dental status are normal. She is not currently on any antiresorptive or anabolic therapy and has no contraindication to oral bisphosphonates. Calcium and vitamin D intake are documented as low.

data_table.Examination: Localised T7 tenderness, no spinal cord features; vitamin D 38 nmol/L
data_table.Investigations: Calcium corrected 2.32 mmol/L, phosphate 1.0 mmol/L, eGFR 76, magnesium 0.84 mmol/L, TSH 1.8 mIU/L, PTH 4.2 pmol/L

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate pharmacological plan?

options.text: Oral calcium 1200 mg daily and vitamin D 1000 IU daily alone, deferring any antiresorptive agent until a second fracture occurs in the next year
Subcutaneous denosumab 60 mg every 6 months without prior bisphosphonate trial and without any transition plan if it is later discontinued
Oestrogen replacement therapy as first-line antifracture therapy in a 72-year-old woman more than 20 years post-menopause with established osteoporosis
Oral weekly alendronate 70 mg with daily calcium 1300 mg and vitamin D 1000 IU supplementation, after dental review and adherence counselling for upright dosing
Daily subcutaneous teriparatide 20 micrograms as initial anabolic therapy without any prior antiresorptive trial in this established post-menopausal osteoporosis

subtopic_detail: Anticoagulation duration after provoked DVT post-orthopaedic surgery
stem: A 38-year-old man develops unilateral left calf swelling 12 days after open reduction internal fixation of an ankle fracture. He has been weight-bearing as tolerated in a moon-boot. Compression duplex ultrasound confirms a non-occlusive popliteal vein deep vein thrombosis. He has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism, no malignancy, no thrombophilia screen abnormality and no active bleeding. He is otherwise healthy on no regular medications.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/74, HR 78, SpO2 98% on room air
data_table.Examination: Left calf 3 cm larger than right, mild tenderness, pulses intact, no respiratory features
data_table.Investigations: Hb 142 g/L, platelets 232 x10^9/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L, LFTs normal, INR 1.0; ECG normal

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate anticoagulation plan?

options.text: Lifelong oral anticoagulation with warfarin titrated to INR 2.0 to 3.0 as definitive therapy for any first proximal deep vein thrombosis episode
Six weeks of oral apixaban 5 mg twice daily without an initial loading dose and then cessation of all anticoagulation with no further review needed
Twelve months of oral apixaban then transition to warfarin titrated to INR 2.0 to 3.0 indefinitely for ongoing secondary prevention of recurrent VTE in this patient
Withhold all anticoagulation in favour of an inferior vena cava filter alone on the basis that this DVT has been provoked by a recent surgical procedure
Oral apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily for a total of 3 months, then stop and counsel about recurrence risk and prevention

subtopic_detail: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state with marked sodium derangement
stem: A 78-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is brought to ED with 5 days of progressive lethargy and reduced oral intake during a urinary tract infection. He has been incrementally less responsive over 24 hours. He is on metformin and gliclazide; he ran out of insulin three weeks ago. He is dry on examination with a tongue furrow and reduced skin turgor. There is no Kussmaul breathing and no significant ketonuria.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 102/64, HR 112, RR 20, SpO2 96% on room air, Temp 37.6 degrees Celsius, GCS 12
data_table.Examination: Markedly dehydrated mucous membranes, no air hunger, lung bases clear
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 52 mmol/L, Na 152 mmol/L, K 4.6 mmol/L, urea 22 mmol/L, creatinine 168 micromol/L, calculated osmolality 358 mOsm/kg, capillary ketones 0.5 mmol/L, pH 7.34, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, urinary nitrites positive

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride at 15 mL/kg over 1 hour, then insulin at 0.05 units/kg/hour after fluid response, with potassium replacement and capped corrected sodium fall
Intravenous 0.45 percent sodium chloride at 1 litre per hour for the first 4 hours with a concurrent insulin bolus of 0.1 units/kg, no potassium addition initially
Intravenous insulin bolus 20 units stat followed by 0.1 units/kg/hour insulin infusion and DKA-style high-dose insulin therapy without prior fluid resuscitation
Hypertonic 3 percent saline 100 mL boluses with reassessment for cerebral oedema and ongoing infusion to correct the hyperosmolar state efficiently
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol over 30 minutes as initial therapy to correct acidaemia and an empirical insulin infusion at 0.2 units/kg/hour

subtopic_detail: Necrotising soft tissue infection in a person with diabetes
stem: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents with rapidly worsening left thigh pain and swelling 36 hours after a minor abrasion. The pain is now out of proportion to visible skin findings. There is dusky discolouration with crepitus on palpation. He is febrile, tachycardic and hypotensive. He has had two episodes of vomiting and is becoming confused. Bedside blood gas shows lactate 5.8 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 88/52, HR 132, RR 26, SpO2 96% on room air, Temp 39.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Left thigh dusky violaceous discolouration, palpable crepitus, exquisite tenderness, anaesthesia in the centre of the lesion
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22 x10^9/L, CRP 318 mg/L, Na 132 mmol/L, glucose 18 mmol/L, creatinine 168 micromol/L, lactate 5.8 mmol/L; LRINEC score calculated at 9

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Oral cefalexin 500 mg six-hourly with discharge home for 24-hour reassessment by the community ambulatory care nurse-led wound clinic and a GP review the following morning
Immediate resuscitation, intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam plus clindamycin plus vancomycin, blood cultures, urgent surgical consult for theatre-based debridement
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy as the sole initial modality, with antibiotic therapy and surgical debridement deferred until completion of two sessions
Topical iodine dressings and limb elevation with intravenous flucloxacillin monotherapy, with surgical review deferred until cultures and imaging confirm a clear diagnosis
Single dose intravenous vancomycin then discharge home with oral antibiotics, with a community wound nurse review arranged for the following morning

subtopic_detail: Workup of primary aldosteronism in resistant hypertension with hypokalaemia
stem: A 47-year-old woman presents with hypertension refractory to three agents (ACE inhibitor, calcium channel blocker and thiazide) at maximal doses. She has incidentally been found to be hypokalaemic on three separate occasions. She has no family history of hypertension under age 40. She has no episodic features of catecholamine excess. She is not pregnant. A morning aldosterone-to-renin ratio is markedly elevated.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 168/104 (averaged over 3 readings), HR 76
data_table.Examination: No abdominal bruit, no Cushingoid features, normal funduscopy
data_table.Investigations: K 3.2 mmol/L, Na 142 mmol/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L; aldosterone 720 pmol/L, direct renin concentration 5 mIU/L, ARR markedly elevated; 24-hour urinary metanephrines normal; HbA1c 5.4%

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step in the workup?

options.text: Cease all antihypertensive agents for 6 weeks with no further investigations performed in the interim period for this patient and arrange a remote phone review
Proceed directly to laparoscopic adrenalectomy on the basis of the markedly elevated screening aldosterone-to-renin ratio alone without further testing
Withdraw interfering agents per protocol, repeat the ARR, perform a confirmatory test such as saline suppression or fludrocortisone suppression, then adrenal CT and adrenal vein sampling
Empirical lifelong spironolactone 25 mg daily without any confirmatory diagnostic testing for primary aldosteronism in this patient with resistant hypertension
Send 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines and plasma metanephrines as the next step to investigate this hypertension as an endocrine secondary cause

subtopic_detail: Pituitary apoplexy with ophthalmoplegia and adrenal insufficiency
stem: A 58-year-old man presents with sudden severe occipital headache, vomiting and binocular diplopia. He has no history of head trauma. Pupillary examination shows a dilated, poorly reactive left pupil and ptosis. He is hypotensive and lethargic. MRI brain shows a 22 mm pituitary macroadenoma with central haemorrhagic transformation. He is on no regular medications. There is no family history of intracranial bleeding.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 88/56, HR 108, Temp 36.4 degrees Celsius, GCS 14
data_table.Examination: Left third nerve palsy with dilated pupil and ptosis, bitemporal visual field defect on confrontation
data_table.Investigations: Na 128 mmol/L, K 4.0 mmol/L, glucose 3.2 mmol/L, cortisol (random) 64 nmol/L, TSH 0.4 mIU/L, free T4 8 pmol/L, prolactin 12 microgram/L; MRI confirms haemorrhagic macroadenoma

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous hydralazine to reduce BP and prevent rebleeding without any concurrent corticosteroid because the diagnosis remains uncertain in this acute setting
Conservative outpatient management with serial visual field testing in 4 weeks and repeat MRI in 3 months for this acute neuro-ophthalmic presentation in a stable patient
A single dose of intravenous dexamethasone 4 mg only for cerebral oedema, with no subsequent endocrine replacement and no neurosurgical referral arranged
Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately then 200 mg per 24 hours, fluid resuscitation, urgent neurosurgical and endocrine review for possible transsphenoidal decompression
Intravenous mannitol 1 g/kg as immediate osmotic therapy alone for the haemorrhagic mass with no corticosteroid replacement or surgical referral arranged at this point

subtopic_detail: Early disease-modifying therapy in seropositive rheumatoid arthritis
stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with 4 months of symmetrical small joint pain and morning stiffness lasting 2 hours. She has bilateral MCP and PIP synovitis. Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP are positive. Hand radiographs show early periarticular osteopenia without erosions. She is otherwise well, on no regular medications, not planning pregnancy in the next 18 months and has no liver or lung disease. DAS28 is calculated at 5.4.

data_table.Examination: Synovitis at 8 MCP and 6 PIP joints, two tender swollen wrists, no nodules; ESR 48 mm/hour
data_table.Investigations: RF 86 IU/mL, anti-CCP 320 U/mL, ANA negative, ALT 22 U/L, eGFR 88, hepatitis B and C serology negative, CXR clear, QFT-Plus negative

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate initial pharmacological plan?

options.text: Long-term oral prednisolone 10 mg daily as monotherapy with no addition of any conventional or biologic disease-modifying antirheumatic agent now or in the foreseeable future
Naproxen 500 mg twice daily as monotherapy with no escalation plan and no addition of any conventional or biologic disease-modifying antirheumatic agent at any later stage
Defer disease-modifying therapy for 12 months while observing for spontaneous remission and using analgesia as required during the wait-and-watch interval
Hydroxychloroquine 5 mg/kg daily as monotherapy as the sole first-line disease-modifying agent in this seropositive, high-disease-activity rheumatoid arthritis presentation
Methotrexate 10 mg weekly with folic acid, a tapering bridging course of oral prednisolone, baseline screening completed, plus a treat-to-target plan with biologic step-up if no remission

subtopic_detail: Suspected giant cell arteritis with new headache and jaw claudication
stem: An 81-year-old woman presents with 3 weeks of new bitemporal headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication when chewing and one episode of transient visual blurring in the right eye 12 hours ago. She has no diabetes, no peptic ulcer disease and no infection. There is no rash and no symptoms of polymyalgia at presentation. Her visual acuity is normal today. There is tenderness over both temporal arteries with reduced pulsatility on the right.

data_table.Examination: Tender thickened right temporal artery, reduced pulse; visual acuity 6/6 bilaterally, fundi normal
data_table.Investigations: ESR 92 mm/hour, CRP 124 mg/L, Hb 108 g/L, platelets 462 x10^9/L, ALT 24 U/L

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 60 mg daily today and arrange urgent temporal artery biopsy within 7 to 14 days, plus aspirin 100 mg daily and bone and gastric protection
Defer corticosteroid therapy until temporal artery biopsy has been performed and reviewed, even if biopsy is not arranged for several days into the working week
Apply topical ophthalmic prednisolone drops alone to the right eye with no systemic corticosteroid therapy until the biopsy result has been reviewed by the rheumatology team
Oral naproxen 500 mg twice daily as monotherapy for the headache with reassessment of inflammatory markers and clinical features in 4 weeks at the next planned review
Initiate subcutaneous tocilizumab as monotherapy without any concurrent oral corticosteroid therapy at the first visit before any biopsy is arranged or organised

subtopic_detail: Myasthenic crisis with bulbar and respiratory failure
stem: A 56-year-old woman with seropositive myasthenia gravis on pyridostigmine and azathioprine presents with worsening generalised weakness over 5 days following a chest infection. She now has dysphagia, dysphonia and dyspnoea. She has no fevers today. Her forced vital capacity has dropped from a baseline of 3.4 L to 0.9 L. Negative inspiratory force is reduced. She is unable to count to 20 in a single breath.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/76, HR 108, RR 26, SpO2 93% on room air
data_table.Examination: Bilateral ptosis, paradoxical breathing, weak cough, gag reflex reduced
data_table.Investigations: FVC 0.9 L, NIF -22 cmH2O, anti-AChR antibody historically positive, CXR right basal opacity, ABG shows hypercapnia (pCO2 56 mmHg)

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Increase pyridostigmine fivefold and discharge home with a community nurse review after 24 hours, recommending early follow-up with the treating neurologist
ICU admission, prepare for non-invasive then invasive ventilation, treat the precipitating chest infection, and initiate intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange
Edrophonium intravenous bolus 10 mg as a diagnostic test before any further therapy is considered, with no ICU referral and no escalation of monitoring in this presentation
Oral prednisone titrated outpatient over 6 weeks as the only adjustment, with reassurance and home spirometry monitoring rather than admission for ventilatory support and immunomodulation
Single dose intravenous lorazepam 2 mg for anxiety and supportive observation only on the general ward, with no airway escalation arranged or planned at this current encounter

subtopic_detail: Clinically isolated syndrome with MRI dissemination meeting McDonald criteria
stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with a 7-day history of painful loss of vision in the right eye and impaired colour perception. Examination confirms right optic neuritis with a relative afferent pupillary defect. She has no prior episodes of neurological symptoms. MRI brain and orbits show right optic nerve enhancement plus three periventricular T2 lesions and one juxtacortical lesion. Both gadolinium-enhancing and non-enhancing lesions are present. CSF shows two unique oligoclonal bands.

data_table.Examination: Right visual acuity 6/24, RAPD present, normal fundi; remainder of cranial nerves and limbs normal
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain: dissemination in space (periventricular plus juxtacortical) and time (enhancing plus non-enhancing) present; CSF oligoclonal bands positive; aquaporin-4 and MOG antibodies negative

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Withhold all disease-modifying therapy and reassess in 12 months with a repeat clinical examination and follow-up MRI, with no further specific action between visits
Apply five sessions of plasma exchange immediately for this first attack of optic neuritis without any further investigations or commencement of long-term disease-modifying therapy at this point
Apply the McDonald 2017 criteria, diagnose relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, treat the acute attack with high-dose methylprednisolone, and initiate disease-modifying therapy
Steroid pulse for the attack and immediate cessation of all follow-up plans with no specific disease-modifying therapy initiated and no further specialist review arranged at this time
Wait for a second clinical attack before any treatment is initiated, with no acute corticosteroid for the current optic neuritis and no follow-up MRI planned at this time

subtopic_detail: Acute chest syndrome in adult sickle cell disease
stem: A 27-year-old man with homozygous sickle cell disease (HbSS) presents with 24 hours of fever, productive cough and pleuritic chest pain. He has been admitted twice in the last year for vaso-occlusive crises. His usual hydroxycarbamide has been taken regularly. Chest radiograph now shows a new right lower lobe infiltrate. Pulse oximetry shows hypoxia on room air. He has no penicillin allergy. He has had pneumococcal and meningococcal vaccinations.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 122/74, HR 116, RR 26, SpO2 90% on room air, Temp 38.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Right basal crackles and dullness to percussion; mild jaundice; spleen not palpable
data_table.Investigations: Hb 76 g/L (baseline 92), reticulocytes 11 percent, WCC 14.6 x10^9/L, platelets 388 x10^9/L, LDH 720 U/L, bilirubin 56 micromol/L; CXR confirms right lower lobe infiltrate

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate management bundle?

options.text: Exchange transfusion is contraindicated in adults with sickle cell disease, and management is limited to oxygen, analgesia and oral antibiotics on the general ward only
NSAIDs as sole analgesia, no antibiotic cover and observation alone with no transfusion or escalation, given hydroxycarbamide adherence is documented in this patient with sickle cell disease
Continuous positive airway pressure as the only intervention without any antibiotic therapy, opioid analgesia, transfusion plan or incentive spirometry while admitted on the medical ward
Oxygen, intravenous fluids at maintenance, opioid analgesia, intravenous ceftriaxone plus oral azithromycin, incentive spirometry, simple top-up or exchange transfusion, haematology and ICU review

Single high-dose acute hydroxycarbamide bolus as the immediate therapy without any other measures, on the basis that hydroxycarbamide is the cornerstone of long-term disease modification in this patient

subtopic_detail: Reversal of apixaban-associated intracerebral haemorrhage
stem: A 72-year-old man with non-valvular atrial fibrillation on apixaban 5 mg twice daily for stroke prevention is brought to ED with sudden dense left hemiparesis 90 minutes after his most recent dose. CT brain shows a 22 mL right basal ganglia haematoma without intraventricular extension or imminent herniation. His baseline INR was 1.0; he is on no antiplatelet therapy. He has no documented liver or significant renal disease. He is haemodynamically stable.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 178/102, HR 88, GCS 13, NIHSS 14
data_table.Examination: Left-sided hemiparesis affecting face, arm and leg; dysarthria; no signs of herniation
data_table.Investigations: CT brain: 22 mL right basal ganglia ICH, no IVH; platelets 218 x10^9/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L, INR 1.1, anti-Xa raised (consistent with on-therapy DOAC)

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate first-line reversal strategy?

options.text: Transfusion of 4 units of fresh frozen plasma alone with no additional agent, expecting correction within 60 minutes of the start of transfusion in this DOAC-associated intracranial haemorrhage
Vitamin K 10 mg intravenously alone without any other agent, expecting full reversal of apixaban anticoagulant effect within 6 to 12 hours after administration in this patient

Tranexamic acid 1 g intravenous infusion as the sole haemostatic agent with no specific DOAC reversal, no factor concentrate and no further intervention beyond supportive care for this DOAC-associated intracranial haemorrhage

Defer reversal for 12 hours to allow natural drug clearance, with neurosurgical reassessment only if clinical deterioration occurs and no additional haemostatic intervention is undertaken now in this patient
Andexanet alfa if available, otherwise 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate 50 IU/kg with BP control, neurosurgical referral and reversal of any concurrent antiplatelet therapy

subtopic_detail: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax: ambulatory device versus chest drain
stem: A 22-year-old tall thin male non-smoker presents with sudden onset right-sided pleuritic chest pain and mild dyspnoea over the past 6 hours. He has no past medical history and is on no medications. He is haemodynamically stable. Chest radiograph shows a 3.5 cm rim of air at the level of the hilum with no shift of the trachea or mediastinum. He has no history of underlying lung disease.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/78, HR 92, RR 20, SpO2 97% room air, T 36.7
data_table.Examination: Reduced air entry and hyperresonance over the right hemithorax, trachea midline, no surgical emphysema
data_table.Investigations: CXR right-sided pneumothorax with 3.5 cm rim of air at hilum; no rib fractures; no underlying lung disease

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Observation only on supplemental high flow oxygen for 24 hours without aspiration or drain
Insertion of an ambulatory pneumothorax drain with Heimlich valve and discharge planning
Needle thoracocentesis at the second intercostal space midclavicular line without imaging review
Insertion of a 28 French chest drain and admission to the high dependency unit for 5 days
Referral for video-assisted thoracoscopic surgical pleurodesis on the first presentation now

subtopic_detail: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax with moderate rim
stem: A 23-year-old tall thin male non-smoker presents with 6 hours of right-sided pleuritic chest pain and mild breathlessness at rest. He has no preceding trauma. He has had no prior episodes, no underlying lung disease, and no recent travel. He is haemodynamically stable. He has no asthma history and lives 30 minutes from the hospital.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 98, RR 22, T 36.7, BP 124/76, SpO2 94% room air
data_table.Examination: Reduced breath sounds and hyperresonance on the right; trachea midline; no surgical emphysema
data_table.Investigations: Erect chest x-ray: right pneumothorax with rim of 3 cm at the hilum, no mediastinal shift; computed tomography not performed; no contralateral lung disease

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Insert an 8 to 14 French intercostal catheter into the safe triangle with underwater seal drainage and admit for observation
Aspirate with a 16-gauge cannula at the second intercostal space midclavicular line and discharge if successful
Provide oxygen by face mask and observe for 24 hours without any active intervention before considering drainage
Refer for urgent video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery and pleurodesis on this first presentation today
Perform emergent needle decompression at the second intercostal space midclavicular line immediately without further imaging

subtopic_detail: Lower limb cellulitis empirical antibiotic choice
stem: A 58-year-old presents with 24 hours of right calf erythema, warmth, and tenderness extending from the ankle to the knee with associated low-grade fever. He has type 2 diabetes managed with metformin and no known drug allergies. There is no obvious break in the skin and no fluctuance or crepitus. Both legs are otherwise clinically equal in size with no calf tenderness on Homan's manoeuvre.

data_table.Examination: Right calf 2 cm of advancing erythema with warmth and tenderness; no skin necrosis, no crepitus, no lymphangitic streaking; pulses normal; sensation intact
data_table.Investigations: FBC WCC 12.5 with neutrophilia; CRP 84; eGFR 78; HbA1c 7.6; venous duplex Doppler not yet performed but clinically deep vein thrombosis low likelihood

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial antibiotic plan?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily for 7 days with same-day general practitioner review of mark and limb elevation
Oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg twice daily for 10 days as first-line treatment for community-acquired soft tissue infection
Intravenous vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading dose then 15 mg/kg twice daily as initial empirical therapy until culture results return
Oral clindamycin 450 mg three times daily for 7 days as first-line for non-purulent cellulitis in this presentation
Oral flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily for 5 days, with marked limb edge for surveillance and review at 48 hours

subtopic_detail: Aldosterone-renin ratio screening in resistant hypertension
stem: A 46-year-old has stage 2 hypertension uncontrolled despite three antihypertensives at full dose: perindopril 8 mg, indapamide 2.5 mg, and amlodipine 10 mg. Home BP averages 158/96. Potassium is 3.2 mmol/L without a diuretic dose change. He has no kidney disease, no obstructive sleep apnoea, and no use of liquorice or nasal decongestants. The endocrinologist plans to investigate for primary hyperaldosteronism.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 158/96 average home readings; HR 78
data_table.Examination: BMI 31, no Cushingoid features, no abdominal bruit, normal fundi
data_table.Investigations: Na 142, K 3.2, eGFR 82, plasma renin and aldosterone not yet drawn, urine albumin-creatinine ratio 2.5 mg/mmol

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate preparation before drawing the aldosterone-renin ratio?

options.text: Continue all current antihypertensive agents unchanged and draw the aldosterone-renin ratio in the morning after 8 hours of overnight recumbency
Stop all antihypertensive medications for 4 weeks and treat hypertension only with hydralazine plus metoprolol during the washout period before testing
Replace potassium above 4.0 mmol/L, stop any mineralocorticoid antagonist for 4 weeks, and substitute prazosin, hydralazine, moxonidine, or verapamil for sampling
Draw aldosterone-renin ratio in the supine position at midnight to maximise diagnostic sensitivity and avoid morning circadian effects
Restrict dietary sodium to under 80 mmol daily for 2 weeks before sampling to suppress aldosterone secretion and enhance test specificity

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis recognition and emergency management
stem: A 38-year-old with primary adrenal insufficiency on hydrocortisone 20 mg and fludrocortisone 0.1 mg daily presents to the emergency department after 36 hours of vomiting and diarrhoea from gastroenteritis. She has been unable to keep down her morning hydrocortisone. She feels dizzy on standing and has had no urine output today.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 124, RR 22, T 37.1, BP 86/52 lying, SpO2 99%
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, cool peripheries, capillary refill 4 seconds, no focal abdominal signs
data_table.Investigations: Na 128, K 5.6, glucose 3.8, creatinine 132, urea 14, venous blood gas pH 7.31, bicarbonate 18, lactate 2.6

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate first action?

options.text: Administer oral hydrocortisone 40 mg now and admit to the short-stay unit for observation and oral rehydration over 6 hours
Administer intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg and 1 L of sodium chloride 0.9% over 1 hour, then admit for ongoing hydrocortisone 200 mg over 24 hours
Administer intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg and 500 mL of 5% dextrose over 1 hour as first-line treatment for adrenal crisis
Administer oral fludrocortisone 0.2 mg and intravenous 5% dextrose at 100 mL/hour to correct hypoglycaemia and electrolyte imbalance
Defer steroid until plasma cortisol level returns within 2 hours and initiate intravenous antibiotics empirically before any hormonal intervention

subtopic_detail: Phaeochromocytoma preoperative blockade sequencing
stem: A 41-year-old has biochemically confirmed phaeochromocytoma with plasma metanephrines 12-fold elevated and a 5 cm right adrenal mass with avid uptake on MIBG. He is referred to the endocrine team for preoperative optimisation. He has paroxysmal palpitations, headaches, and pallor 3 to 4 times weekly. His BP swings between 165/96 during episodes and 138/78 at rest. He has no other comorbidity.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96 sinus rhythm, BP 152/92 at rest, no orthostatic drop yet
data_table.Examination: BMI 22, no abdominal mass palpable, no carotid bruit
data_table.Investigations: Plasma metanephrines elevated; MIBG positive at the right adrenal; CT confirms 5 cm right adrenal mass; ECG sinus rhythm, no left ventricular hypertrophy

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate preoperative blockade plan?

options.text: Start metoprolol 25 mg twice daily today and titrate to heart rate under 80 over 2 weeks before initiating alpha blockade
Start oral amlodipine 5 mg daily and refer for elective adrenalectomy in 5 to 7 days without preoperative alpha or beta blockade
Recommend immediate adrenalectomy without preoperative blockade because anaesthetic alpha and beta agents can be titrated intraoperatively
Start phenoxybenzamine 10 mg twice daily, titrate with high-sodium diet, then add beta-blocker if reflex tachycardia develops, with surgery at 10 to 14 days
Start labetalol 100 mg twice daily as a single agent for combined alpha and beta blockade to streamline preoperative preparation

subtopic_detail: Massive pulmonary embolism with haemodynamic compromise
stem: A 62-year-old presents collapsed 90 minutes after returning from a 24-hour flight. She remains haemodynamically unstable on arrival. She has no prior bleeding history, no recent surgery, no head injury, no current anticoagulation, and no known coagulopathy. She is alert and able to consent. The on-call respiratory and cardiology teams have reviewed and agree she has massive pulmonary embolism.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132, RR 32, T 36.9, BP 78/48, SpO2 86% on 15 L/min non-rebreather mask
data_table.Examination: Cool peripheries, raised jugular venous pressure, prominent right ventricular heave, no audible third heart sound, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Bedside echocardiogram shows severe right ventricular dilatation with septal flattening; troponin elevated; CT pulmonary angiogram shows bilateral central pulmonary emboli; lactate 4.2

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Administer intravenous alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours then commence unfractionated heparin once activated partial thromboplastin time normalises
