Initiate therapeutic enoxaparin 1.5 mg/kg subcutaneously twice daily and admit to the medical assessment unit for monitoring with cardiology review tomorrow
Insert an inferior vena cava filter immediately as definitive therapy without anticoagulation or reperfusion treatment
Commence non-invasive ventilation with bilevel positive airway pressure and reassess for thrombolysis if not improving after 4 hours of trial
Refer to interventional radiology for outpatient catheter-directed thrombolysis within the next 7 to 10 days after stabilisation on heparin alone

subtopic_detail: Suspected osteomyelitis underlying a diabetic foot ulcer
stem: A 64-year-old has had a chronic 2 cm plantar ulcer over the first metatarsal head for 8 weeks with surrounding cellulitis and ongoing serous discharge. He has type 2 diabetes for 18 years, HbA1c 8.6, peripheral neuropathy, and palpable pulses. Probe-to-bone with a sterile probe is positive today through the ulcer. There is no acute necrosis.

data_table.Examination: 2 cm plantar ulcer over first metatarsal head with sloughy base; positive probe-to-bone; surrounding 3 cm cellulitis without crepitus; ankle-brachial index 1.0; sensation to 10 g monofilament absent in forefoot
data_table.Investigations: WCC 11.8; CRP 56; ESR 78; HbA1c 8.6; foot x-ray shows cortical erosion of first metatarsal head; MRI not yet performed; previous wound swab grew Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus agalactiae

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue outpatient oral cefalexin 500 mg four times daily for a further 4 weeks and review at the diabetic foot clinic in 6 weeks
Order an outpatient bone biopsy in 8 weeks while continuing topical wound dressings and routine podiatry review every 2 weeks
Treat empirically with oral metronidazole 400 mg three times daily as monotherapy for 6 weeks and review at the wound clinic monthly
Proceed directly to mid-foot amputation today without further investigation or culture-directed antimicrobial therapy as definitive treatment
Admit for orthopaedic and infectious diseases input, bone biopsy with histology and culture, and 6 weeks of culture-directed intravenous then oral antibiotic therapy

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis on chronic steroid replacement
stem: A 56-year-old woman with Addison's disease on hydrocortisone 10 mg morning and 5 mg afternoon plus fludrocortisone 100 mcg daily is brought to ED by her partner. She has had 24 hours of fevers, cough and progressive lethargy. This morning she vomited her hydrocortisone dose. On arrival she is hypotensive and confused. Her medic-alert bracelet identifies the diagnosis.

data_table.Examination: Confused (GCS 14), warm peripheries, RR 26, no neck stiffness, right basal crackles; capillary refill 3 s
data_table.Investigations: Na 128 mmol/L, K 5.6 mmol/L, glucose 3.4 mmol/L, urea 9.2, creatinine 124, lactate 3.8, CRP 198 mg/L; CXR right lower lobe consolidation

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Double her usual oral hydrocortisone dose and observe in ED with intravenous saline overnight
Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg stat plus crystalloid resuscitation and empirical antibiotics
Start IV dexamethasone 4 mg with stim test scheduled before any glucocorticoid replacement therapy
Administer noradrenaline infusion targeting MAP 65 before any steroid replacement is given
Withhold steroid dosing pending confirmation of sepsis source by chest CT before treatment starts

subtopic_detail: Latent tuberculosis treatment selection
stem: You are an infectious diseases registrar reviewing a 34-year-old man from a high-prevalence country who arrived in Australia 18 months ago. He is screened before commencing infliximab for severe rheumatoid arthritis. He is asymptomatic, with no cough, fever, or weight loss. His QuantiFERON-Plus assay is positive. Chest X-ray is normal. There are no apical changes or calcified granulomas. He drinks no alcohol, has no past liver disease, and his ALT and AST are normal. He has no household contacts known to have active tuberculosis. He is keen to start his rheumatology treatment as soon as possible.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78 bpm, BP 124/76 mmHg, Temp 36.7 degrees C, BMI 25 kg/m2
data_table.Examination: Cardiorespiratory examination unremarkable, mild synovitis of the MCP joints
data_table.Investigations: QFT-Plus positive, CXR normal, ALT 22 U/L, AST 24 U/L, HIV non-reactive, HepBsAg negative, HepC negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment for his latent tuberculosis infection?

options.text: Sputum induction for acid-fast bacilli smear and culture before any latent treatment is started
Defer treatment and commence infliximab immediately given normal chest imaging and no symptoms
Four-drug RIPE therapy (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) for 2 months then dual therapy for 4 months
Single-dose intramuscular BCG vaccination as protective immunisation prior to biologic therapy
Isoniazid 300 mg orally daily with pyridoxine 25 mg daily for 6 months and monthly clinical and LFT review

subtopic_detail: VTE anticoagulation duration
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 56-year-old man at a 3-month follow-up after an unprovoked proximal deep vein thrombosis of the right popliteal vein. He has been treated with apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily for 3 months and is well. He has had no further symptoms. He has no personal or family history of VTE.

He has no history of cancer, has lost no weight, and a malignancy screen at presentation was unremarkable. There is no thrombophilia identified on a basic screen. His mild hypertension is well controlled. He has no bleeding history.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/82 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, BMI 27 kg/m2
data_table.Examination: No leg swelling, no calf tenderness, no signs of post-thrombotic syndrome, no bruising
data_table.Investigations: Hb 142 g/L, platelets 235 x10^9/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L, eGFR > 60 mL/min/1.73m2, ALT 24 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing anticoagulation plan?

options.text: Switch to warfarin with target INR 2.0 to 3.0 indefinitely as the most cost-effective long-term option
Stop apixaban at 3 months given the patient has completed standard treatment and is asymptomatic
Switch to aspirin 100 mg daily as long-term secondary prevention with no further anticoagulant
Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily indefinitely without reducing the dose for extended therapy
Continue apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily indefinitely with annual bleeding-risk review and renal monitoring

subtopic_detail: Septic shock hour-1 bundle
stem:
You are the medical registrar at a metropolitan emergency department. A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents with 3 days of dysuria, rigors, and now confusion. He has been brought in by his wife. He is alert but confused, peripherally cool, and tachypnoeic. Capillary refill is 4 seconds. He weighs 80 kg. He has no known allergies. He has no known kidney disease.

Intravenous access has been established. A urinalysis is positive for nitrites and leucocytes. A point-of-care lactate has been performed and blood cultures sent. He has received no antibiotics today.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 124 bpm, BP 86/52 mmHg, RR 28, Temp 39.4 degrees C, SpO2 95% room air
data_table.Examination: Drowsy GCS 13, mottled lower limbs, suprapubic tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 4.2 mmol/L, glucose 12 mmol/L, creatinine 158 micromol/L, WCC 18 x10^9/L, CRP 220 mg/L, urinalysis nitrites and leucocytes positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate first-hour intervention?

options.text: Commence intravenous fluid resuscitation at 1 L over 30 minutes then reassess before further bolus
Defer antibiotics until urine culture and blood culture results are available to allow targeted therapy
Administer intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g and commence 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid resuscitation
Commence noradrenaline infusion via peripheral cannula without fluid resuscitation
Administer intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg as first-line therapy for hypotension before fluids

subtopic_detail: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax
stem:
You are the emergency registrar reviewing a 22-year-old previously well thin man with sudden onset right-sided pleuritic chest pain and mild breathlessness 4 hours ago. He has never smoked and has no past medical history. He has no trauma, no fever, and no preceding illness. On examination he has reduced breath sounds on the right with normal trachea midline. Vital signs are stable.

Chest X-ray confirms a moderate right primary pneumothorax with an interpleural distance of 3 cm at the hilum and no mediastinal shift. There is no underlying lung disease on imaging.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88 bpm, BP 122/76 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 97% room air, Temp 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Trachea midline, reduced right breath sounds, hyper-resonant percussion right, no surgical emphysema
data_table.Investigations: CXR: right pneumothorax interpleural distance 3 cm at hilum, no shift, no underlying disease

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Urgent video-assisted thoracoscopic pleurodesis as definitive surgical management for first presentation
Insertion of a 28F intercostal catheter as the first procedure for any visible primary pneumothorax
Observation only with high-flow oxygen by mask and reassessment with serial chest X-rays at 24 hours
Needle aspiration of the right pleural space with a 14 to 16 gauge cannula and post-procedure chest X-ray
Discharge home with analgesia and outpatient review in 2 weeks with repeat chest X-ray then

subtopic_detail: Infective endocarditis empiric therapy
stem: You are the general medical registrar admitting a 58-year-old woman with 3 weeks of low-grade fever, weight loss, and night sweats. She has a known bioprosthetic aortic valve replaced 14 months ago for severe aortic stenosis. Today she has developed a new soft early diastolic murmur on the left sternal edge. There are no embolic phenomena on examination. Three sets of blood cultures have been drawn from separate sites and a transthoracic echocardiogram has been ordered. There are no penicillin allergies. The team plans empirical antibiotics while awaiting culture and echocardiographic results.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96 bpm, BP 124/68 mmHg, Temp 38.4 degrees C, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Examination: New aortic regurgitation murmur, no Janeway lesions, no Osler nodes, no splinter haemorrhages
data_table.Investigations: CRP 88 mg/L, WCC 12 x10^9/L, Hb 108 g/L (normocytic), creatinine 84 micromol/L, ECG sinus rhythm with no new conduction delay

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone monotherapy as broad-spectrum cover for streptococci and HACEK organisms
Intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin combination for streptococcal native valve endocarditis cover
Intravenous flucloxacillin monotherapy at high dose for community-acquired Staphylococcus aureus cover
Intravenous vancomycin, gentamicin, and rifampicin combination for early prosthetic valve infective endocarditis cover
Defer empirical antibiotics until echocardiographic vegetation is demonstrated to avoid unnecessary therapy

subtopic_detail: Hypertensive emergency with end-organ damage
stem:
You are the medical registrar at a metropolitan emergency department. A 54-year-old man presents with severe headache, blurred vision, and a few hours of dyspnoea. He has poorly controlled essential hypertension on irregular amlodipine. He has no chest pain. He has been working long hours and has not taken his medication for 1 week. Fundoscopy reveals papilloedema and flame haemorrhages.

CXR shows pulmonary oedema. Troponin is mildly elevated and ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy with strain. There is no evidence of aortic dissection on the bedside ultrasound. The consultant asks for your initial intravenous antihypertensive plan.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 110 bpm, BP 232/142 mmHg, RR 26, SpO2 91% room air
data_table.Examination: Bibasal crackles, JVP 4 cm elevated, papilloedema, flame haemorrhages, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Troponin I 0.08 micrograms/L (peak), creatinine 138 micromol/L, eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73m2, urinalysis 2+ blood 2+ protein, CXR pulmonary oedema, ECG sinus tachycardia with LVH

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial intravenous antihypertensive strategy?

options.text: Intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion titrated to reduce mean arterial pressure by approximately 25% over the first hour
Oral nifedipine 20 mg immediate release with target normotension within 30 minutes of administration
Intravenous esmolol bolus and infusion as monotherapy with target systolic BP under 120 mmHg in 30 minutes
Intravenous hydralazine 10 mg bolus repeated every 20 minutes until systolic BP under 140 mmHg
Oral captopril 25 mg sublingually as rapid renin-angiotensin blockade for malignant hypertension

subtopic_detail: Phaeochromocytoma crisis management
stem: You are the medical registrar called to the high dependency unit. A 48-year-old woman was admitted yesterday for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. During induction of anaesthesia 30 minutes ago she developed extreme hypertension and tachycardia followed by an episode of hypotension. She has now been transferred to the high dependency unit. She had been investigated 6 months ago for episodic headache, sweating, and palpitations but did not attend her endocrine appointment. The surgical team and the anaesthetist suspect an undiagnosed endocrine tumour. Plasma fractionated metanephrines have been sent. She is currently haemodynamically labile.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138 bpm (sinus), BP currently 192/118 mmHg fluctuating, RR 22, Temp 37.1 degrees C, SpO2 97% room air
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, no focal neurology, no goitre, no abdominal mass palpable, no signs of NF1 stigmata
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia, troponin 0.04 micrograms/L, glucose 11 mmol/L, plasma free metanephrines pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate antihypertensive strategy?

options.text: Commence intravenous phentolamine and fluid resuscitation, with a beta-blocker added only after alpha-blockade
Commence intravenous metoprolol bolus to control the heart rate and reduce myocardial oxygen demand
Commence intravenous labetalol infusion as combined alpha and beta blockade for catecholamine crisis
Commence intravenous amiodarone 300 mg bolus over 20 minutes to suppress sinus tachycardia
Commence intravenous magnesium sulfate 5 g loading dose with cessation of the surgical procedure

subtopic_detail: DVT diagnosis Wells score
stem: You are the general medicine RMO assessing a 58-year-old woman presenting with three days of left calf swelling and tenderness. She returned from a 14-hour flight a week ago. She has hypertension on perindopril, no prior VTE, and no active cancer. Examination reveals a swollen tender left calf with 3 cm circumference difference compared to the right and pitting oedema confined to the symptomatic leg.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/82, HR 84, RR 16, SpO2 98% room air, T 36.6
data_table.Examination: Left calf swollen with 3 cm circumference difference at 10 cm below tibial tuberosity, tender along deep venous distribution, pitting oedema confined to symptomatic leg, no superficial varicosities
data_table.Investigations: Not yet performed
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 5 mg, paracetamol PRN

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Arrange an MRI venogram of the lower limb to fully characterise venous involvement and exclude alternative diagnoses including muscular and lymphatic pathology
Send a D-dimer level as the first step regardless of pretest probability because a negative result rules out deep vein thrombosis in all patient groups including this one
Arrange CT venography of the lower limb as the most sensitive imaging test for proximal and distal vein involvement before initiating any further intervention
Commence therapeutic anticoagulation with apixaban and arrange ultrasound for confirmation if symptoms have not resolved over the next seven to ten days
Compression duplex ultrasound of the proximal leg veins given her Wells score makes DVT likely and pretest probability favours imaging over D-dimer

subtopic_detail: Adult anaphylaxis adrenaline timing
stem: You are the ED RMO called to a 38-year-old man who developed widespread urticaria, throat tightness, and wheeze 15 minutes after eating prawns at a work lunch. He has previously had mild oral itching with shellfish. There has been no previous severe reaction. The triage nurse has placed IV access and is preparing equipment.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 92/58, HR 124, RR 26, SpO2 92% room air, T 36.8
data_table.Examination: Generalised urticaria, audible wheeze, mild lip swelling, no stridor, alert
data_table.Investigations: Not applicable for immediate management
data_table.Medications: Nil regular

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Administer intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg as the first intervention for the systemic inflammatory response before any other pharmacological intervention is undertaken
Administer intramuscular adrenaline 0.5 mg into the anterolateral thigh and position the patient supine while preparing further supportive measures
Administer intravenous promethazine 25 mg to manage the urticarial component and reassess the need for adrenaline once the antihistamine has been completed
Administer nebulised salbutamol 5 mg as the first treatment for the bronchospasm and reassess oxygen requirements before considering further pharmacological intervention
Administer intravenous adrenaline infusion at 0.05 micrograms/kg/min titrated to blood pressure response without prior intramuscular dose of adrenaline at all

subtopic_detail: Hypertensive emergency BP targets
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 64-year-old man brought to ED with sudden severe headache, vomiting, and confusion. He has known hypertension and stopped his perindopril two months ago. CT brain shows a small right basal ganglia haemorrhage. His GCS is 14, no focal neurology beyond mild left arm weakness, and he is haemodynamically stable. The stroke registrar is on the way.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 218/124 confirmed on repeated manual measurement, HR 78, RR 16, SpO2 97%, T 36.8
data_table.Examination: GCS 14 (E4 V4 M6), mild left arm weakness 4/5, no neglect, fundi show grade III changes
data_table.Investigations: CT brain: 12 mL right basal ganglia haemorrhage, no IVH, no mass effect; sodium 138, potassium 4.0, creatinine 92
data_table.Medications: Recently stopped perindopril 10 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, aspirin 100 mg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management of his blood pressure?

options.text: Commence intravenous nitroprusside infusion with target systolic blood pressure of 100 mmHg within the first thirty minutes to minimise the risk of further bleeding
Commence oral nifedipine 20 mg immediate release with reassessment every fifteen minutes for further dose titration as needed for ongoing severely elevated blood pressure
Resume oral perindopril at 10 mg daily and arrange admission for monitoring without intravenous antihypertensive therapy given the established mild blood pressure background
Commence intravenous labetalol with a systolic blood pressure target of 140 mmHg within the first hour as per current intracerebral haemorrhage guidance
Permit permissive hypertension with no antihypertensive therapy in the first six hours to maintain cerebral perfusion pressure and avoid worsening neurological status

subtopic_detail: Acute HIV seroconversion recognition
stem: You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 32-year-old man with two weeks of fever, sore throat, fatigue, and a faint maculopapular rash on his trunk and arms. He had unprotected receptive anal intercourse with a new male partner six weeks ago. Initial fourth-generation HIV test was negative two days into symptoms. He is now on day 14 of symptoms and feels worse rather than better.

data_table.Examination: Cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy, faint trunk and limb maculopapular rash, pharyngeal injection without exudate
data_table.Investigations: FBC: lymphopenia with platelets 110, ALT 96; EBV and CMV serology pending; rapid Strep negative
data_table.Medications: Nil

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Send HIV RNA viral load by PCR and repeat fourth-generation antigen/antibody combination test with infectious diseases involvement and PEP discussion review
Repeat fourth-generation HIV serology in three months and provide reassurance that the initial negative result effectively excludes acute HIV infection in this patient
Commence oral aciclovir empirically for primary Herpes simplex virus seroconversion and arrange swabs of any oral lesions detected on careful examination of the patient
Treat empirically for streptococcal pharyngitis with oral phenoxymethylpenicillin and arrange outpatient review by the immunology service in two to three weeks
Arrange a heterophile antibody (Monospot) test alone to confirm Epstein-Barr virus mononucleosis as the most likely diagnosis given the clinical presentation here today

subtopic_detail: Latent tuberculosis treatment decision
stem: You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 28-year-old woman recently arrived from Vietnam who is being screened by the local refugee health clinic. She is asymptomatic. Her QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus is positive. Chest X-ray is normal. She is HIV negative, hepatitis B and C negative, and has no immunosuppression. She plans to start a medical degree next year and wants to know whether treatment is needed now.

data_table.Examination: Unremarkable; no lymphadenopathy, normal chest
data_table.Investigations: QFT-Plus positive, chest X-ray clear, sputum AFB not sent (asymptomatic), HIV negative, HBV and HCV negative, ALT 22
data_table.Medications: Nil

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her latent TB infection?

options.text: Repeat QFT-Plus in three months to confirm true positive status and exclude transient interferon-gamma release as an alternative explanation for the result obtained
Commence isoniazid monotherapy for nine months (9H) with monthly review and liver function monitoring after baseline aminotransferase establishment in this woman
Defer treatment until completion of her medical degree and screen with annual QFT-Plus testing until she demonstrates evidence of active infection or symptoms suggesting reactivation
Commence rifampicin and isoniazid (3HR) for three months with monthly liver function tests and counsel about hepatotoxicity and drug interactions
Arrange CT chest to exclude subclinical active disease prior to commencing any latent infection treatment regimen given the high prevalence in her country of origin

subtopic_detail: Parkinsonism red flags atypical features
stem: You are the geriatrics registrar reviewing a 68-year-old man who was started on levodopa eight months ago for presumed Parkinson disease. He has had limited symptomatic response, frequent backward falls, and now describes difficulty looking down at his food. His wife reports increasing speech difficulties and emotional lability. There is mild axial rigidity but limb tone is relatively preserved on examination.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/78 supine, 128/76 standing (no postural drop), HR 76
data_table.Examination: Limited downgaze palsy, axial rigidity greater than limb rigidity, postural instability with backward falls on pull test, hypomimia, no resting tremor, no asymmetry
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain shows midbrain atrophy with hummingbird sign; cognitive screen MoCA 22/30 with executive dysfunction
data_table.Medications: Levodopa/carbidopa 100/25 four times daily (limited response)

lead_in: Which feature most strongly suggests an atypical parkinsonian syndrome?

options.text: Slow shuffling gait with reduced arm swing developing gradually over four years without falls, gaze restriction, or autonomic dysfunction during follow-up assessment
Resting tremor with asymmetric onset and a good response to levodopa during the initial six months of treatment after the diagnosis was confirmed by movement disorders
Vertical supranuclear gaze palsy with early postural instability, axial rigidity greater than limb rigidity, and poor levodopa response
Mild bradykinesia with bilateral involvement after seven years of levodopa therapy and emergence of dyskinesias with peak-dose involuntary movements over time as therapy progresses
Mild hyposmia preceding motor symptoms by several years and REM sleep behaviour disorder with vivid dream enactment occurring during the night with bed partner

subtopic_detail: Guillain-Barre syndrome workup and treatment
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 45-year-old man with five days of ascending lower limb weakness following a self-limited diarrhoeal illness two weeks ago. He now has difficulty climbing stairs and walking. He has noticed mild hand weakness today. He has no bladder or bowel changes. He is otherwise well with no chronic medical conditions.

data_table.Examination: Lower limb power 3/5 proximally, 4/5 distally, areflexia at knees and ankles, upper limb power 5/5 proximally, 4+/5 distally, sensation intact, no fasciculations
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs normal, B12 and TSH normal, MRI spine normal, CSF cell count 2, CSF protein 1.4 g/L, FVC 3.2 L (predicted 4.1 L), Negative inspiratory force minus 60 cmH2O
data_table.Medications: Nil regular

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone 1 gram daily for five days as the standard initial management of demyelinating neuropathies in adult populations across all settings
Commence intravenous immunoglobulin 0.4 g/kg daily for five days with respiratory monitoring including four-hourly FVC and admission to a monitored bed
Arrange outpatient nerve conduction studies and review in two weeks given preserved walking and absence of any bladder or bowel involvement at this stage
Commence empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics for presumed post-infectious sepsis given recent diarrhoeal illness and arrange admission to general medical ward overnight
Arrange physiotherapy rehabilitation with discharge home as walking remains preserved and respiratory function is currently within reasonable safety margins on assessment

subtopic_detail: Phaeochromocytoma crisis perioperative management
stem: You are the medical registrar called to a 42-year-old woman admitted yesterday for elective cholecystectomy. She has had episodic palpitations, sweating, and headaches for six months attributed to anxiety. During induction of anaesthesia she developed sudden severe hypertension to 240/140 with arrhythmia. The surgery is now cancelled. She is in ICU. Plasma metanephrines drawn today are markedly elevated.

data_table.Vital signs: BP swings 220/130 to 90/50, HR 130 with ectopics, T 37.8, SpO2 96% on intubation
data_table.Examination: Sedated, diaphoretic, ECG shows multiple VEBs and ischaemic changes
data_table.Investigations: Plasma free metanephrines 8.4 nmol/L (normal under 0.6), normetanephrines 12.6 nmol/L (normal under 1.0), troponin rising, CT abdomen shows 4.5 cm right adrenal mass
data_table.Medications: ICU sedation; was on no antihypertensives prior to admission

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate pharmacological strategy?

options.text: Commence intravenous amiodarone for the ventricular arrhythmias before any other antihypertensive therapy and arrange transfer to cardiology service for further management
Commence intravenous metoprolol immediately to control the tachycardia and arrhythmia before introducing alpha-blockade after the heart rate has been adequately controlled
Proceed to emergency adrenalectomy while she remains anaesthetised to definitively address the source of catecholamines without further preoperative pharmacological preparation
Commence intravenous nitroprusside infusion as monotherapy to control blood pressure with titration to mean arterial pressure target without specific alpha or beta blockade
Commence intravenous phentolamine and titrated phenoxybenzamine, withhold any beta-blockade until alpha-blockade is established, and plan delayed surgical resection

subtopic_detail: Sepsis hour-1 bundle
stem: You are the medical registrar admitting a 67-year-old man via ED with two days of dysuria, rigors, and confusion. He has a background of type 2 diabetes on metformin. On arrival he is tachycardic, tachypnoeic, hypotensive, confused and mottled. Urinalysis shows nitrites and leukocytes. He has received 500 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride en route. Initial bloods include a lactate of 4.8 mmol/L.

data_table.Examination: Mottled extremities, dry mucous membranes, mild suprapubic tenderness
data_table.Investigations: VBG: lactate 4.8, pH 7.30, HCO3 18, glucose 11.2; FBC: WCC 18.4, Hb 138, plt 122; EUC: Cr 168 (baseline 92); CRP 240; urine: nitrites/leukocytes/blood positive
data_table.Medications: Metformin 1 g twice daily

lead_in: Which intervention is the highest priority within the next hour?

options.text: Insert central venous catheter for CVP monitoring before commencing fluid resuscitation now
CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast to identify the source before any antibiotic is given
Start IV noradrenaline immediately at 0.05 mcg/kg/min before completion of fluid resuscitation
IV crystalloid 30 mL/kg with blood cultures then IV antibiotics within the first hour now
Administer IV hydrocortisone 200 mg before commencement of fluid resuscitation now

subtopic_detail: Bacterial meningitis empiric therapy
stem: You are the medical registrar admitting a 56-year-old previously well man with 12 hours of severe headache, neck stiffness, fever and confusion. He has no rash. He has had no recent travel, no animal exposure and no immunosuppression. The ED has obtained IV access and is preparing to do an LP. He has no focal neurology and no papilloedema on fundoscopy.

data_table.Examination: Neck stiff to passive flexion, Kernig and Brudzinski positive, no rash, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: WCC 16.8, CRP 280, glucose 8.2, lactate 2.1, blood cultures sent; LP pending
data_table.Medications: Nil regular

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antimicrobial therapy?

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 2 g 12 hourly with IV benzylpenicillin 1.8 g 4 hourly to cover Listeria empirically
IV benzylpenicillin 1.8 g 4 hourly with IV dexamethasone 10 mg 6 hourly given for 4 days
IV cefotaxime 2 g 6 hourly with vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading dose IV ceftriaxone alternative
IV meropenem 2 g 8 hourly with IV dexamethasone 10 mg 6 hourly until cultures available
IV ceftriaxone 2 g 12 hourly with IV dexamethasone 10 mg 6 hourly given before or with antibiotic

subtopic_detail: Pyelonephritis admission threshold
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 38-year-old woman with 36 hours of right loin pain, fever, rigors and dysuria. She has not vomited and is tolerating oral fluids. She is haemodynamically stable. Urinalysis shows nitrites and leukocytes. She has no diabetes, no urological history and is not pregnant. She has had no recent hospitalisation or instrumentation. She lives within 10 minutes of the hospital and has a partner at home.

data_table.Examination: Right renal angle tenderness, no peritonism, no costovertebral mass
data_table.Investigations: WCC 14.2, CRP 96, EUC: Cr 78, lactate 1.8; urinalysis: nitrites/leukocytes/blood
data_table.Medications: Nil

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 7 days with ED safety net and 48 hour GP review
Oral cefalexin 500 mg four times daily for 10 days with GP review in 48 hours and clear safety net
Admit for IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg single dose then oral switch to amoxicillin-clavulanate after
Admit for IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g 8 hourly for 7 days as the broad-spectrum cover
Oral nitrofurantoin 100 mg four times daily for 7 days with ED safety net and 48 hour review

subtopic_detail: Necrotising fasciitis vs cellulitis
stem: You are the surgical registrar called by ED to review a 52-year-old man with worsening leg redness over 18 hours. He has type 2 diabetes on metformin. He describes pain out of proportion to the visible erythema. He had a fall three days ago with a small abrasion on the calf. On examination there is a 15 cm area of erythema and tense induration with grey discolouration of a 4 cm central patch. He cannot weight-bear. His observations are tachycardic and febrile.

data_table.Examination: Calf erythema with central dusky discolouration, exquisite tenderness extending beyond visible margin, tense induration, no crepitus yet
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22.6, Hb 132, CRP 320, Na 132, glucose 14.4, Cr 142 (baseline 88), CK 1840, lactate 3.4; X-ray: no gas in tissues
data_table.Medications: Metformin 1 g BD

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: IV flucloxacillin 2 g 6 hourly with limb elevation and review at 24 hours for response
Urgent surgical debridement with broad-spectrum antibiotics including clindamycin for toxin
MRI of the leg with contrast urgently to confirm necrotising fasciitis before any surgery
Compute LRINEC score and admit for IV ceftriaxone if score is 6 or higher with review
IV vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading and admit under medical team for further investigations

subtopic_detail: Phaeochromocytoma alpha then beta blockade
stem: You are the endocrinology registrar reviewing a 48-year-old woman with confirmed phaeochromocytoma on 24 hour fractionated metanephrines (urinary metanephrine 12 times upper limit) and a 4 cm right adrenal mass on CT. She has episodic hypertension peaking at 198/118 mmHg with palpitations, sweating and headaches. She is on no antihypertensive. She is scheduled for laparoscopic adrenalectomy in 14 days.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 168/104 supine, 144/92 standing, HR 88 supine, 110 standing
data_table.Examination: Mild orthostatic symptoms, no tremor, no goitre
data_table.Investigations: 24 hour fractionated metanephrines: metanephrine 12 x ULN; CT abdomen: 4 cm right adrenal mass; ECG: sinus rhythm, no LVH
data_table.Medications: Nil

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate pharmacological preparation?

options.text: Amlodipine 5 mg daily and salt restriction with surgical referral in seven to fourteen days
Metoprolol 25 mg twice daily for heart rate control then add alpha blocker once stable
Phenoxybenzamine 10 mg twice daily titrated up over 7 to 14 days then add beta blocker if HR high
Combined alpha-beta blocker labetalol 200 mg twice daily as single agent control of BP and HR
Spironolactone 25 mg daily to address presumed primary aldosteronism with adrenal mass first

subtopic_detail: Multiple sclerosis McDonald 2024 criteria
stem: You are the neurology registrar reviewing a 31-year-old woman with subacute optic neuritis confirmed by ophthalmology three weeks ago, now recovered with steroid. MRI brain today shows 3 periventricular and 2 juxtacortical T2 hyperintense lesions, one of which enhances with gadolinium. MRI spine shows 1 cervical cord lesion without enhancement. CSF (LP performed yesterday) shows oligoclonal bands present (CSF-specific). She has no prior neurological symptoms. There is no fever or recent infection.

data_table.Examination: Visual acuity 6/9 right, 6/6 left (recovered from 6/24); afferent pupillary defect right; remainder normal
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain: 5 T2 lesions (3 periventricular, 2 juxtacortical), 1 gadolinium-enhancing; MRI spine: 1 cervical T2 lesion; CSF: oligoclonal bands positive (CSF-specific)
data_table.Medications: Nil

lead_in: Which McDonald 2024 criterion is met to confirm a diagnosis of multiple sclerosis?

options.text: Diagnosis cannot be made until a second clinical attack confirms dissemination in time
Dissemination in space and time both met clinically without need for paraclinical evidence
Dissemination in time is met by simultaneous enhancing and non-enhancing lesions on MRI scan
Dissemination in space met clinically; oligoclonal bands substitute for dissemination in time
Diagnosis requires evoked potentials abnormality in addition to current criteria for confirmation

subtopic_detail: Mixed shock recognition
stem:
You are the ICU registrar called to a 72-year-old man on the cardiology ward, day 4 after anterior STEMI treated by primary PCI to LAD, now in shock. He has developed fever and worsening dyspnoea over 6 hours. Bedside echo shows anterior wall hypokinesis (similar to admission), LVEF 35%, no new tamponade, no new VSD, no severe MR. CXR shows new bilateral infiltrates.

Sputum is purulent. Lactate has risen from 1.4 to 3.8 over 6 hours. Cardiac index by non-invasive estimation is 2.0 L/min/m2. Mixed venous saturation by central line is 76%.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 84/52 (was 118/70 yesterday), HR 118, T 38.7, RR 28, SpO2 88% on 6 L/min, GCS 14
data_table.Examination: Warm peripheries despite hypotension, no peripheral oedema, no new murmur
data_table.Investigations: CXR: bilateral lower zone infiltrates new; troponin stable from yesterday; CRP 280; WCC 19; lactate 3.8; ScvO2 76%; CI 2.0
data_table.Medications: Aspirin, ticagrelor, atorvastatin, bisoprolol, ramipril, furosemide

lead_in: What is the most likely shock pattern and most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Cardiogenic shock from reinfarction; activate cath lab for repeat PCI within ninety minutes
Cardiogenic shock from late stunning post-STEMI; start dobutamine and arrange repeat angiography
Hypovolaemic shock from gastrointestinal bleed on dual antiplatelet; transfuse and pause DAPT
Obstructive shock from PE post-myocardial infarction; CT pulmonary angiogram and anticoagulate
Septic shock from hospital-acquired pneumonia; IV fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics now

subtopic_detail: DOAC choice in AF with renal impairment
stem: You are the cardiology registrar reviewing a 78-year-old woman with newly diagnosed permanent atrial fibrillation found on ambulatory monitoring after dizziness. She has type 2 diabetes, hypertension, prior TIA 2 years ago, and is taking metformin, perindopril, and aspirin. Her CHA2DS2-VA score is 5. Her creatinine clearance (Cockcroft-Gault) is 38 mL/min. She has no history of GI bleeding, no liver disease, no drug interactions, and weighs 62 kg. She has reasonable oral intake and good adherence to medications historically.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/82, HR 88 irregular, T 36.7
data_table.Examination: Irregularly irregular pulse, no murmurs, no signs of heart failure, no carotid bruits
data_table.Investigations: ECG: AF rate 88, no ischaemic changes; FBC: Hb 124, plt 240; EUC: Cr 132, eGFR 38, CrCl 38; LFTs normal; HbA1c 7.2%
data_table.Medications: Metformin 1 g BD, perindopril 5 mg daily, aspirin 100 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation choice?

options.text: Continue aspirin 100 mg daily without anticoagulation given her age and the bleeding risk this carries
Warfarin with INR target 2.0 to 3.0 monitored monthly because DOACs are contraindicated below CrCl 50
Apixaban 5 mg twice daily continued with aspirin 100 mg daily for secondary prevention of stroke and TIA
Apixaban 5 mg twice daily with cessation of aspirin in view of bleeding risk on combined antithrombotic therapy
Dabigatran 150 mg twice daily with cessation of aspirin once anticoagulation is established at steady state

subtopic_detail: Community-acquired pneumonia outpatient antibiotic
stem: You are the GP registrar reviewing a previously well 44-year-old man with 4 days of productive cough with green sputum, fevers to 38.6, and pleuritic right-sided chest pain. He has no known comorbidities, takes no regular medications, and has no penicillin allergy. He is tolerating oral fluids and food. CXR shows right lower lobe consolidation. His SMART-COP score is 1 (multilobar = 0, albumin not done, RR 22 = 0, tachycardia 96 = 0, confusion 0, oxygen 0, pH not done; only SBP 95 which is 1 from threshold; actually SBP 118 so 0). Current vitals are within near-normal range otherwise.

data_table.Examination: Bronchial breath sounds right base with crepitations, dullness to percussion, no signs of effusion, no tracheal deviation, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: CXR: right lower lobe consolidation; no bloods needed in primary care setting; SMART-COP estimated score 0; not assessing for severe pneumonia by Australian guideline
data_table.Medications: Nil

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily for 5 days with safety net and review in 48 hours
Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily plus doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days
Admission for IV benzylpenicillin 1.2 g 6 hourly plus IV doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days
Oral azithromycin 500 mg daily for 3 days as monotherapy targeting atypical pneumonia pathogens primarily
Oral moxifloxacin 400 mg daily for 7 days as monotherapy covering typical and atypical organisms equally

subtopic_detail: Osteoporosis first-line therapy choice
stem:
You are the GP registrar reviewing a 68-year-old postmenopausal woman with a recent low-trauma fracture of the left distal radius from a fall at standing height. She has no other fractures and no back pain. DXA scan today: lumbar spine T-score -2.8, total hip T-score -2.5, femoral neck T-score -2.7. Vitamin D is 78 nmol/L (adequate). Calcium and PTH normal.

eGFR 64 (mildly reduced). No history of dental disease, no planned dental procedures, no oesophageal disease, and no upper GI symptoms. She is otherwise healthy.

data_table.Examination: Healing distal radius fracture in cast, no kyphosis, no other tender vertebrae
data_table.Investigations: DXA: LS T -2.8, hip T -2.5, FN T -2.7; vitamin D 78; calcium 2.32; PTH 4.2; eGFR 64; TSH 1.8; coeliac screen negative; FBC normal; SPEP normal
data_table.Medications: Colecalciferol 1000 IU daily; calcium dietary

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line osteoporosis therapy?

options.text: Annual IV zoledronic acid 5 mg infusion as first-line therapy without trial of oral therapy initially
Subcutaneous denosumab 60 mg every 6 months for postmenopausal osteoporosis with vertebral fracture prevention
Subcutaneous teriparatide 20 mcg daily for 18 months as anabolic therapy for severe postmenopausal osteoporosis
Oral raloxifene 60 mg daily as selective oestrogen receptor modulator for postmenopausal osteoporosis treatment
Oral alendronate 70 mg weekly with calcium and vitamin D continued and 3-yearly DXA monitoring arranged

subtopic_detail: Adult acute asthma severity assessment
stem: You are the ED registrar reviewing a 28-year-old woman with known mild asthma on PRN salbutamol who presents with 12 hours of worsening dyspnoea, wheeze, and cough after a viral URTI. She has used salbutamol 6 puffs hourly without sustained improvement. She is sitting forward, speaking in short phrases of 4 to 5 words. She has not been intubated or admitted to ICU for asthma previously and has had no prior systemic steroid course this year. There are no triggers other than the recent URTI.

data_table.Examination: Sitting forward, accessory muscle use, audible wheeze, prolonged expiratory phase, equal air entry, no focal consolidation, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: PEF 38% of predicted before treatment; arterial blood gas: pH 7.40, PaCO2 38, PaO2 64, HCO3 22; CXR: clear, no consolidation, no pneumothorax
data_table.Medications: Salbutamol MDI as needed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Salbutamol 5 mg + ipratropium 500 mcg nebulised, oxygen to maintain SpO2 93 to 95, oral prednisolone 50 mg now
High-flow nasal oxygen at 60 L/min FiO2 1.0 then salbutamol 6 puffs via spacer hourly with reassessment in 1 hour
Intramuscular adrenaline 0.5 mg as initial pharmacotherapy for severe airway obstruction without delay for cannulation
Intubation and mechanical ventilation immediately under rapid sequence induction without pre-treatment trial
IV magnesium sulfate 2 g infusion over 20 minutes as first-line bronchodilator without nebulised therapy first

subtopic_detail: Acute aortic dissection initial medical therapy
stem: You are the ED registrar reviewing a 62-year-old man who presents with sudden onset tearing interscapular chest and back pain 90 minutes ago, radiating to the abdomen. He has long-standing poorly controlled hypertension. He looks unwell and diaphoretic. He is hypertensive with 30 mmHg difference between arms. CT aortogram shows a type B (descending) aortic dissection extending from the left subclavian origin to the iliac bifurcation, with no malperfusion of visceral or renal branches and no rupture or haemothorax. He is haemodynamically stable.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 192/108 right arm, 162/96 left arm, HR 96, RR 22, SpO2 96% RA, T 36.8
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, equal but reduced left radial pulse, tender thoracic spine, abdomen soft, no peritonism, neurologically intact
data_table.Investigations: ECG: sinus rhythm, no ischaemic changes; CXR: mediastinal widening; CT aortogram: type B dissection L subclavian to iliac bifurcation, no malperfusion, no rupture; troponin negative; D-dimer markedly raised
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 5 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily (poor adherence)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate medical therapy?

options.text: IV labetalol infusion titrated to systolic BP 100 to 120 mmHg and heart rate under 60 with continuous arterial line
IV hydralazine 10 mg boluses repeated every 30 minutes targeting systolic blood pressure 130 mmHg ongoing
IV sodium nitroprusside infusion targeting systolic blood pressure 110 mmHg without beta blockade now
Urgent surgical consultation with view to endovascular stent grafting now before pharmacological BP control
IV sublingual nifedipine 10 mg titrated to systolic blood pressure 130 with reassessment every 15 minutes

subtopic_detail: Hypertensive emergency target BP reduction
stem: You are the ED registrar reviewing a 58-year-old woman with severe headache, blurred vision, and nausea over 4 hours. She has known hypertension on irbesartan with poor adherence. Examination shows BP 226/132, papilloedema, and grade 3 hypertensive retinopathy. She has no focal neurological deficit. Urinalysis: protein +++, blood +. Bloods show acute kidney injury (Cr 168 from baseline 88), microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia features (schistocytes, low platelets, raised LDH), but troponin and ECG are normal. CT brain shows no acute stroke, no haemorrhage. She is alert and oriented.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 226/132 (both arms), HR 104, T 36.7, RR 18, SpO2 98% RA
data_table.Examination: Bilateral papilloedema, flame haemorrhages and cotton-wool spots on fundoscopy, no focal neurology, no chest pain, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Cr 168 (baseline 88), eGFR 32, Hb 96 with schistocytes on film, plt 88, LDH 1240, haptoglobin <0.1, urinalysis: protein +++, blood +; ECG and troponin normal; CT brain clear
data_table.Medications: Irbesartan 300 mg daily (poor adherence)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate BP target and rate of reduction over the first hour?

options.text: Reduce blood pressure to 200/110 over the first hour using sublingual nifedipine to avoid IV access and admission
Reduce blood pressure to 140/90 within the first 30 minutes using IV labetalol bolus and continuous infusion
Reduce blood pressure to under 110/70 within 6 hours using IV sodium nitroprusside continuous infusion
Reduce blood pressure to under 180/110 over 24 hours using oral amlodipine and oral hydralazine combination
Reduce mean arterial pressure by no more than 20 to 25% over the first hour with IV labetalol or IV nicardipine titrated

subtopic_detail: Pleural effusion Light criteria interpretation
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 64-year-old man with progressive dyspnoea over 6 weeks and 4 kg weight loss. He has a 30 pack-year smoking history and worked in shipbuilding in his 20s. CXR shows a large right pleural effusion. Diagnostic thoracentesis yields straw-coloured fluid. Results: pleural protein 35 g/L, serum protein 62 g/L; pleural LDH 280 U/L, serum LDH 220 U/L (ULN serum 230). Pleural glucose 4.0 mmol/L. Pleural pH 7.34. Cytology and TB culture pending. CT chest reports right pleural thickening with nodularity.

data_table.Examination: Dullness to percussion right base to mid-zone, absent breath sounds right base, reduced vocal resonance, no clubbing, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Pleural fluid: protein 35 g/L, LDH 280 U/L, glucose 4.0, pH 7.34; serum: protein 62 g/L, LDH 220 U/L, albumin 32; FBC normal; CT chest: right pleural thickening with nodularity, no parenchymal lesion
data_table.Medications: Nil regular

lead_in: How should this pleural effusion be characterised and what is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Transudative effusion most likely due to congestive cardiac failure; manage with diuretic and outpatient review
Exudative effusion meeting Light criteria; arrange CT-guided pleural biopsy or thoracoscopy for mesothelioma exclusion
Empyema with pleural pH below 7.20; insert chest drain urgently and treat with IV antibiotics for 2 weeks
Parapneumonic effusion most likely; commence IV ceftriaxone and review CT pulmonary angiogram for embolus too
Chylothorax related to thoracic duct injury; arrange lymphangiogram and dietary fat restriction with octreotide

subtopic_detail: Adult uncomplicated UTI - antibiotic selection in Australian practice
stem: A 28-year-old woman presents to general practice with a 2-day history of dysuria, urinary frequency, and suprapubic discomfort. She is otherwise well with no fever, loin pain, or nausea. She has no history of recurrent UTIs, urinary tract abnormalities, or immunosuppression. She is not pregnant. Urine dipstick shows nitrites positive and leucocytes positive.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 74, BP 118/72 mmHg, Temp 36.8 degrees C, no costovertebral angle tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick: nitrites positive, leucocytes ++, blood trace, mid-stream urine sent for culture

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empiric antibiotic?

options.text: Trimethoprim 300 mg once daily for 3 days as a single oral course
Amoxicillin-clavulanate 500/125 mg three times daily for 5 days
Ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 3 days as first-line therapy
Cefalexin 500 mg twice daily for 5 days as an empiric course
Nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for 5 days as first-line agent

subtopic_detail: Osteoporosis - FRAX assessment and bisphosphonate initiation
stem: A 68-year-old postmenopausal woman is referred after a low-trauma distal radius fracture from a fall from standing height. She has no history of previous fractures. Her BMI is 22. She takes no regular medications. She does not smoke and drinks 2 standard drinks per week. Family history is notable for her mother sustaining a hip fracture at age 72.

data_table.Investigations: DXA: lumbar spine T-score -2.6, femoral neck T-score -2.3, vitamin D 52 nmol/L (ref >50), calcium 2.35 mmol/L (ref 2.10-2.60), eGFR 72 mL/min/1.73m2, TSH 2.8 mIU/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Calcium and vitamin D supplementation alone with repeat DXA in 2 years
Oral alendronate 70 mg weekly with calcium, vitamin D, and falls prevention
Denosumab 60 mg subcutaneous injection every 6 months as first-line
Raloxifene 60 mg daily as a selective oestrogen receptor modulator
Teriparatide 20 microg daily subcutaneous injection for 18 months

subtopic_detail: Peripheral neuropathy - systematic workup for sensorimotor neuropathy
stem: A 62-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of progressive numbness and tingling in both feet, now extending to mid-calf bilaterally. He also describes a burning sensation worse at night. He has difficulty with balance in the dark. On examination he has reduced pinprick and vibration sense to the mid-calf bilaterally, absent ankle reflexes, and intact knee reflexes. Motor power is full in all muscle groups.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 76, BP 142/88 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Reduced pinprick and vibration to mid-calf bilaterally, absent ankle jerks, knee jerks present, Romberg positive, normal motor power, no muscle wasting
data_table.Investigations: Hb 136 g/L, MCV 98 fL, WCC 7.2 x10^9/L, creatinine 82 micromol/L

lead_in: Which combination of investigations is most appropriate for the initial workup?

options.text: Nerve conduction studies and electromyography as the sole investigation
MRI of the lumbar spine to exclude radiculopathy as the primary cause
Fasting glucose, HbA1c, B12, folate, TFTs, and serum protein electrophoresis
Anti-ganglioside antibodies and CSF analysis for inflammatory neuropathy
Genetic testing for Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease and hereditary neuropathies

subtopic_detail: Fibromyalgia - diagnosis and initial management approach
stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with widespread musculoskeletal pain for over 6 months affecting her neck, shoulders, lower back, and thighs. She also reports persistent fatigue, non-restorative sleep, and difficulty concentrating. She has seen multiple specialists and had extensive investigations, all of which have been normal. On examination she has diffuse tenderness to palpation at multiple sites but no joint swelling, synovitis, or objective neurological deficit.

data_table.Investigations: ESR 8 mm/hr, CRP 3 mg/L, ANA negative, RF negative, anti-CCP negative, TSH 2.5 mIU/L, vitamin D 68 nmol/L, Hb 135 g/L, creatinine 62 micromol/L, CK 85 U/L (normal)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management approach?

options.text: Commence prednisolone 25 mg daily for a therapeutic trial of steroids
Repeat ANA and rheumatoid factor testing with a full autoimmune panel
Regular opioid analgesia with oxycodone 5 mg as needed for pain control
Patient education, graded exercise program, and sleep hygiene optimisation
Pregabalin 75 mg twice daily as first-line monotherapy for pain control

subtopic_detail: Colorectal cancer screening - positive iFOBT and urgent colonoscopy
stem: A 58-year-old man with no symptoms visits his GP after receiving a positive immunochemical faecal occult blood test (iFOBT) result from the National Bowel Cancer Screening Program. He is asymptomatic with no abdominal pain, change in bowel habit, rectal bleeding, or weight loss. He has no family history of colorectal cancer or polyps. His last colonoscopy was 10 years ago and was normal.

data_table.Investigations: NBCSP iFOBT: positive (haemoglobin detected above threshold), Hb 142 g/L, ferritin 45 microg/L, LFTs normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat iFOBT in 3 months to confirm the positive result
CT colonography as a less invasive alternative to colonoscopy
Reassurance as the patient is asymptomatic with a normal haemoglobin
Flexible sigmoidoscopy to evaluate the left colon and rectum only
Referral for colonoscopy within 30 days of the positive result

subtopic_detail: Iron deficiency anaemia in older man - mandatory GI investigation
stem: A 72-year-old man presents with progressive fatigue over 3 months. He denies haematemesis, melaena, or overt rectal bleeding. He takes no NSAIDs or anticoagulants. He has no history of coeliac disease. His diet includes regular meat and vegetables. He has not had previous GI investigations.

data_table.Investigations: Hb 95 g/L (ref 130-170), MCV 72 fL, ferritin 8 microg/L (ref 30-300), transferrin saturation 8% (ref 16-50), reticulocyte count 1.0%, B12 350 pmol/L, folate 18 nmol/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L, coeliac serology negative

lead_in: What is the most important next investigation?

options.text: Trial of oral iron supplementation and recheck haemoglobin in 8 weeks
Upper GI endoscopy alone to assess for gastric and duodenal pathology
CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast as a non-invasive screening tool
Colonoscopy with concurrent upper GI endoscopy if colonoscopy is normal
Faecal calprotectin to assess for occult inflammatory bowel disease

subtopic_detail: Melanoma recognition - ABCDE criteria and urgent excision biopsy
stem: A 55-year-old fair-skinned man presents with a changing mole on his left upper back that his partner noticed. The lesion has been present for years but has grown over the past 4 months and recently developed an irregular dark area. He has a history of multiple sunburns in childhood and outdoor work for 20 years. On examination the lesion is 12 mm in diameter with irregular borders, colour variation (tan, dark brown, and black areas), and asymmetry.

data_table.Examination: Left upper back: 12 mm pigmented lesion, asymmetric, irregular border, colour variation (tan, dark brown, black), no ulceration, no satellite lesions, no palpable axillary lymphadenopathy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Excision biopsy of the entire lesion with a 2 mm clinical margin
Punch biopsy of the darkest area for initial histological assessment
Dermoscopic monitoring with serial photography in 3 months
Wide local excision with 1 cm margin as definitive primary treatment
Referral to dermatology for assessment within the next 4 to 6 weeks

subtopic_detail: Primary hyperaldosteronism - ARR screening and confirmatory testing
stem: A 42-year-old woman is referred for investigation of resistant hypertension requiring three antihypertensives (amlodipine, perindopril, and indapamide). Her blood pressure remains 158/96 mmHg despite adherence. Routine bloods reveal persistent hypokalaemia at 3.1 mmol/L on two occasions despite not taking diuretics at the time of testing. She has no family history of endocrine disease. Secondary causes of hypertension including renal artery stenosis and phaeochromocytoma have been excluded.

data_table.Investigations: K+ 3.1 mmol/L (ref 3.5-5.0), Na+ 143 mmol/L, creatinine 68 micromol/L, eGFR >90, morning aldosterone 680 pmol/L (ref <440), plasma renin activity <0.5 mIU/L (suppressed)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Proceed directly to adrenal CT to localise an aldosterone-producing adenoma
Confirmatory saline infusion test after appropriate medication washout
Adrenal venous sampling as the definitive lateralisation investigation
24-hour urinary aldosterone and cortisol on a high-sodium diet
Commence spironolactone 50 mg daily as both diagnostic and therapeutic trial

subtopic_detail: Prolactinoma - cabergoline as first-line medical management
stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with 8 months of amenorrhoea and bilateral galactorrhoea. She is not pregnant and not taking any medications known to elevate prolactin. Visual fields are normal on confrontation testing. MRI of the pituitary shows a 14 mm pituitary adenoma with displacement of the optic chiasm but no chiasmal compression.

data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 8500 mIU/L (ref <500), TSH 2.2 mIU/L, free T4 14 pmol/L, cortisol (0800h) 380 nmol/L (ref 140-500), IGF-1 normal for age, formal visual field testing: full fields bilaterally, MRI: 14 mm pituitary adenoma, no cavernous sinus invasion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Transsphenoidal surgery for adenoma resection as first-line treatment
Bromocriptine 2.5 mg daily as the preferred dopamine agonist
Cabergoline 0.25 mg twice weekly with dose titration to normalise prolactin
Stereotactic radiosurgery targeting the adenoma for tumour control
Observation with serial MRI and prolactin monitoring every 6 months

subtopic_detail: Primary hyperparathyroidism - calcium workup and surgical indications
stem: A 56-year-old woman has persistent hypercalcaemia found incidentally on two blood tests 3 months apart. She is mostly asymptomatic but reports mild fatigue and constipation. She has no history of malignancy. She takes no calcium supplements, thiazide diuretics, or lithium. DXA scan shows a T-score of -2.7 at the distal one-third radius.

data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.82 mmol/L (ref 2.10-2.60), phosphate 0.72 mmol/L (ref 0.80-1.50, low), PTH 12.5 pmol/L (ref 1.5-6.5, elevated), 25-OH vitamin D 62 nmol/L, creatinine 72 micromol/L, eGFR 82, 24-hour urine calcium 8.5 mmol/day (ref 2.5-7.5, elevated), ALP 98 U/L (mildly elevated)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Referral for parathyroidectomy given meeting surgical criteria
Cinacalcet 30 mg twice daily to normalise calcium levels medically
Annual monitoring of calcium and DXA without surgical intervention
Oral bisphosphonate therapy to address osteoporosis without surgery
Thiazide diuretic to reduce urinary calcium excretion and prevent stones

subtopic_detail: Multiple sclerosis - clinically isolated syndrome workup and management
stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with a 5-day history of progressive blurring and pain on eye movement in her left eye. Visual acuity is 6/36 in the left eye and 6/6 in the right. She has a left relative afferent pupillary defect. Colour vision is impaired in the left eye. Fundoscopy shows a mildly swollen optic disc on the left. The remainder of her neurological examination is normal. She has no prior neurological symptoms.

data_table.Investigations: MRI brain: left optic nerve enhancement with gadolinium, plus 4 periventricular T2/FLAIR white matter lesions (3 ovoid, perpendicular to the corpus callosum), 1 juxtacortical lesion, and 1 infratentorial lesion. MRI spine: no spinal cord lesions. CSF: oligoclonal bands present (absent in serum), mildly elevated protein

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management approach?

options.text: Observation only as she has had a single clinical episode without recurrence
IV methylprednisolone for acute episode then commence disease-modifying therapy
Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg tapering course for optic neuritis treatment
Repeat MRI in 6 months to demonstrate dissemination in time for diagnosis
Plasma exchange for the acute optic neuritis with ongoing visual loss

subtopic_detail: B12 deficiency with subacute combined degeneration - urgent replacement
stem: A 65-year-old woman with a history of autoimmune gastritis presents with a 3-month history of progressive unsteadiness, tingling in both hands and feet, and difficulty buttoning her shirt. On examination she has reduced vibration and proprioception in the hands and feet, brisk knee reflexes with absent ankle reflexes, bilateral extensor plantar responses, and a wide-based ataxic gait. Romberg test is positive.

data_table.Investigations: Hb 98 g/L, MCV 112 fL, reticulocyte count 0.8%, blood film: hypersegmented neutrophils and macro-ovalocytes, B12 68 pmol/L (ref >150, severely deficient), folate 22 nmol/L (normal), homocysteine 45 micromol/L (elevated, ref <15), methylmalonic acid 1.8 micromol/L (elevated, ref <0.4), intrinsic factor antibodies positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral cyanocobalamin 1000 microg daily as adequate replacement therapy
Folic acid 5 mg daily with oral B12 supplementation to address anaemia
IM hydroxocobalamin 1000 microg on alternate days for 2 weeks then maintenance
Packed red cell transfusion followed by oral iron and B12 supplementation
Referral for MRI spine before commencing treatment to confirm the diagnosis

subtopic_detail: Haemochromatosis - HFE genotyping and venesection initiation
stem: A 45-year-old man of Northern European descent presents with fatigue, arthralgia affecting the 2nd and 3rd metacarpophalangeal joints bilaterally, and mildly abnormal liver function tests found incidentally. He drinks 6 standard drinks per week. On examination he has a mildly enlarged liver but no stigmata of chronic liver disease. His fasting transferrin saturation is markedly elevated on two separate occasions.

data_table.Investigations: Ferritin 1850 microg/L (ref 30-300), transferrin saturation 82% (ref 16-50, confirmed on repeat fasting sample), ALT 62 U/L, AST 55 U/L, GGT 48 U/L, ALP 72 U/L, albumin 38 g/L, Hb 158 g/L, platelets 195 x10^9/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Liver biopsy with Perls staining to quantify hepatic iron concentration
MRI liver with T2* quantification to measure hepatic iron content
Serum hepcidin level to assess iron regulatory hormone function
HFE gene mutation analysis for C282Y and H63D polymorphisms
Abdominal ultrasound to assess for hepatocellular carcinoma screening

subtopic_detail: Sepsis initial management
stem: A 62-year-old man presents to the emergency department with rigors, confusion, and productive cough for 2 days. He has a history of type 2 diabetes and COPD. He was found by his wife lying on the couch, disoriented and unable to stand. He has not been taking fluids for the past 24 hours.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118 bpm, BP 82/48 mmHg, RR 28, Temp 38.9 degrees C, SpO2 91% on room air, GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6)
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22.4 x10^9/L (neutrophils 19.8), CRP 284 mg/L, lactate 4.8 mmol/L, creatinine 168 micromol/L (baseline 92), glucose 18.2 mmol/L, chest X-ray - right lower lobe consolidation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Obtain blood cultures from 2 peripheral sites, commence IV ceftriaxone 1 g plus azithromycin 500 mg, administer 30 mL/kg IV crystalloid, and remeasure lactate
Commence IV flucloxacillin 2 g and gentamicin 5 mg/kg, obtain blood cultures, and arrange CT chest with contrast urgently
Administer IV normal saline 500 mL over 2 hours, commence oral amoxicillin 1 g, and observe in the emergency short stay unit
Immediately commence noradrenaline infusion via peripheral cannula while arranging central venous access and ICU admission
Obtain sputum culture, commence IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g, and arrange urgent bronchoscopy for directed therapy

subtopic_detail: Cushing syndrome diagnostic workup
stem: A 42-year-old woman is referred by her GP for evaluation of suspected Cushing syndrome. She has had progressive weight gain of 15 kg over 18 months, predominantly truncal, with new-onset proximal muscle weakness, easy bruising, and wide purple striae on her abdomen. She developed type 2 diabetes 6 months ago requiring insulin and hypertension requiring 3 antihypertensives. She takes no exogenous glucocorticoids.

data_table.Investigations: HbA1c 68 mmol/mol, fasting glucose 11.2 mmol/L, potassium 3.0 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial biochemical investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Random morning serum cortisol level to screen for elevated basal cortisol production in this patient
Overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test with measurement of 8 am serum cortisol the following morning
MRI of the pituitary gland with gadolinium to identify a pituitary adenoma as the source of excess cortisol
Plasma ACTH level to distinguish between ACTH-dependent and ACTH-independent causes of hypercortisolism
High-dose 8 mg dexamethasone suppression test to differentiate pituitary from ectopic ACTH secretion directly

subtopic_detail: VTE anticoagulation duration
stem: A 48-year-old man was diagnosed with an unprovoked left leg proximal deep vein thrombosis 3 months ago and commenced on rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily for 3 weeks followed by 20 mg daily. He has had no bleeding complications. He has no identifiable risk factors - no recent immobilisation, surgery, travel, malignancy, or thrombophilia on testing. His BMI is 24 kg/m2 and he is otherwise well.

data_table.Investigations: Compression ultrasound - residual non-compressible thrombus in the left popliteal vein but improving. FBC, UEC, LFTs normal. Cancer screening up to date and negative. Thrombophilia screen - negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate recommendation regarding anticoagulation duration?

options.text: Cease anticoagulation now as 3 months is the standard recommended duration for all proximal DVT events
Continue warfarin with target INR 2-3 indefinitely, as warfarin is the preferred agent for long-term prevention
Continue rivaroxaban at a reduced dose of 10 mg daily for extended secondary prevention, with annual review of bleeding risk
Cease anticoagulation and commence aspirin 100 mg daily for long-term secondary prevention of recurrent VTE
Cease anticoagulation at 6 months and perform D-dimer testing 4 weeks later to guide need for extended therapy

subtopic_detail: Adult bacterial meningitis
stem: A 58-year-old man presents with 18 hours of worsening headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, and confusion. His wife reports he was well yesterday morning. He has a history of splenectomy following a motor vehicle accident 15 years ago and receives annual influenza and pneumococcal vaccinations, though he is unsure if his pneumococcal vaccine is current.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 112 bpm, BP 138/82 mmHg, RR 22, Temp 39.4 degrees C, GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5)
data_table.Investigations: WCC 24.6 x10^9/L, CRP 312 mg/L, platelets 168 x10^9/L. CT brain normal. CSF - opening pressure 32 cmH2O, WCC 2400/microL (95% neutrophils), protein 4.2 g/L, glucose 0.8 mmol/L (serum glucose 7.2), Gram stain - Gram-positive diplococci

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antimicrobial and adjunctive therapy?

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 2 g 12-hourly alone, with repeat lumbar puncture in 48 hours to confirm sterilisation of the CSF
IV benzylpenicillin 2.4 g 4-hourly with adjunctive IV dexamethasone 10 mg 6-hourly for 4 days starting immediately
IV meropenem 2 g 8-hourly with IV dexamethasone 10 mg 6-hourly for 4 days commenced before the first antibiotic dose
IV dexamethasone 10 mg immediately, then IV ceftriaxone 2 g 12-hourly plus IV vancomycin, dexamethasone continued for 4 days
IV ceftriaxone 2 g 12-hourly plus IV ampicillin 2 g 4-hourly for Listeria coverage, with dexamethasone 10 mg 6-hourly for 4 days

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis management
stem: A 55-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by ambulance after being found confused and hypotensive at home. She has a known history of Addison disease diagnosed 8 years ago and takes hydrocortisone 10 mg morning / 5 mg afternoon and fludrocortisone 100 mcg daily. Her partner reports she developed gastroenteritis 3 days ago with vomiting and diarrhoea and was unable to keep her tablets down. She did not have an emergency injection kit at home.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 124 bpm, BP 72/44 mmHg, RR 24, Temp 38.2 degrees C, GCS 11 (E3 V3 M5)
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 122 mmol/L, potassium 6.4 mmol/L, glucose 2.8 mmol/L, urea 14.8 mmol/L, creatinine 148 micromol/L, cortisol 28 nmol/L, TSH 4.8 mIU/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Resume oral hydrocortisone at double the usual dose with oral fludrocortisone and IV fluid support for rehydration of the patient
IV dexamethasone 4 mg as the preferred glucocorticoid in adrenal crisis because of its longer duration of action than hydrocortisone
IV hydrocortisone 50 mg stat, IV normal saline with 5% dextrose, and commence vasopressors immediately before fluid loading is complete
Administer IV fludrocortisone equivalent for the mineralocorticoid deficiency as the primary treatment with IV fluid support for volume
IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat then 50 mg 6-hourly, rapid IV 0.9% sodium chloride bolus, IV dextrose, and treat the precipitating cause

subtopic_detail: Sepsis hour-1 bundle priorities
stem: A 68-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by ambulance from a residential aged care facility. Staff report she has been increasingly confused over the past 6 hours with a productive cough and reduced oral intake for 2 days. She has a background of type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and mild cognitive impairment. Her regular medications include metformin, perindopril, and donepezil.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.9, HR 118, BP 88/52, RR 28, SpO2 91% on room air, GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6)
data_table.Examination: Coarse crackles right lower zone, capillary refill 4 seconds peripherally, dry mucous membranes, no neck stiffness
data_table.Investigations: WCC 19.4 x10^9/L (neutrophils 16.8), CRP 312 mg/L, lactate 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 168 micromol/L (baseline 82), glucose 14.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management priority?

options.text: Obtain chest X-ray to confirm pneumonia before initiating therapy
Administer IV noradrenaline via peripheral access to restore perfusion
Obtain blood cultures then commence IV antibiotics and 30 mL/kg crystalloid
Insert an indwelling catheter and commence a fluid balance chart first
Commence oral amoxicillin-clavulanate and reassess after 500 mL saline

subtopic_detail: First-line vasopressor in septic shock
stem: A 55-year-old man with community-acquired pneumonia is being resuscitated in the emergency department. He was commenced on IV ceftriaxone and azithromycin 40 minutes ago. He has received 2 litres of IV Hartmann solution (approximately 30 mL/kg). Despite this, his blood pressure remains 78/48 mmHg with a heart rate of 124 bpm. His lactate has risen from 3.8 to 5.1 mmol/L over the past 30 minutes. Central venous access has been established.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.1, HR 124, BP 78/48, RR 26, SpO2 94% on 6 L/min via Hudson mask
data_table.Examination: Warm peripheries, bounding pulses, capillary refill 3 seconds centrally, mottled knees
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 5.1 mmol/L (was 3.8 mmol/L 30 minutes ago), urine output 10 mL in the past hour

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in haemodynamic management?

options.text: Commence IV adrenaline infusion at 0.05 mcg/kg/min via central line
Commence IV noradrenaline infusion at 0.05 mcg/kg/min via central line
Administer a further 2 litres of IV crystalloid before considering vasopressors
Commence IV vasopressin infusion at 0.03 units/min via central line
Commence IV phenylephrine infusion at 0.5 mcg/kg/min via central line

subtopic_detail: Migraine prophylaxis selection with comorbidities
stem: A 34-year-old woman presents to her GP requesting preventive treatment for migraines. She experiences 7-8 migraines per month, each lasting 12-24 hours, significantly impairing her ability to work. Acute triptans provide partial relief. She has a history of recurrent nephrolithiasis with two calcium oxalate stones requiring lithotripsy in the past 3 years. She also has a BMI of 22 and no history of depression or anxiety. She is using reliable contraception.

data_table.Examination: Normal neurological examination, no papilloedema
data_table.Investigations: Normal renal function, eGFR >90 mL/min

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line prophylactic agent?

options.text: Topiramate 25 mg daily, titrating to 50-100 mg daily over 4 weeks
Amitriptyline 10 mg nocte, titrating to 25-50 mg over 4 weeks
Sodium valproate 200 mg twice daily, titrating to 400-600 mg daily
Propranolol 20 mg twice daily, titrating to 40-80 mg twice daily
Pizotifen 0.5 mg nocte, titrating to 1.5 mg daily over 2 weeks

subtopic_detail: Abortive treatment for attacks away from oxygen
stem: A 34-year-old man with known cluster headache has attacks at work that peak within ten minutes. Home oxygen aborts them, but he cannot take a cylinder to the office and needs treatment he can carry.

data_table.Attacks: Three daily, 30 to 60 minutes, right periorbital with lacrimation
data_table.Background: No regular medicines; cardiovascular examination normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate acute treatment?

options.text: Sumatriptan 6 mg subcutaneously at the onset of an attack
Sumatriptan 100 mg orally at the onset of an attack
Prednisolone 50 mg orally each morning during the cluster bout
Indometacin 25 mg orally three times daily during the bout
Oxycodone 5 mg orally as required for severe attacks

subtopic_detail: GCA immediate management before biopsy
stem: A 74-year-old woman presents to her GP with a 3-week history of new-onset left-sided temporal headache, jaw claudication when chewing, and scalp tenderness when brushing her hair. She noticed blurred vision in her left eye for 10 minutes yesterday that resolved spontaneously. She has a history of polymyalgia rheumatica treated with prednisolone 5 mg daily for the past 8 months. She takes alendronate and calcium-vitamin D supplementation.

data_table.Examination: Tender, thickened, non-pulsatile left temporal artery, visual acuity 6/9 left and 6/6 right, no RAPD, normal fundoscopy bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: ESR 68 mm/hr, CRP 54 mg/L, platelets 412 x10^9/L, Hb 118 g/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Arrange urgent temporal artery biopsy within 24 hours before starting therapy
Increase prednisolone from 5 mg to 15 mg daily and arrange outpatient biopsy
Commence tocilizumab subcutaneous injection and arrange temporal artery biopsy
Arrange urgent CT angiography of the temporal arteries before initiating treatment
Commence prednisolone 60 mg daily and arrange temporal artery biopsy within 2 weeks

subtopic_detail: Parkinson's disease initial therapy selection
stem: A 51-year-old software engineer presents to a movement disorder clinic following a neurology referral. He was diagnosed with early Parkinson's disease 4 months ago based on unilateral rest tremor, bradykinesia, and cogwheel rigidity affecting his right arm. His symptoms are mild and do not significantly impact his daily activities or work. He is otherwise well with no cognitive concerns. He wishes to delay the onset of motor complications for as long as possible while maintaining function.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 68, BP 128/78 lying, 124/76 standing
data_table.Examination: Right upper limb rest tremor, mild right-sided bradykinesia on finger tapping, cogwheel rigidity right wrist, normal gait, MMSE 30/30
data_table.Investigations: Nil recent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Levodopa-carbidopa 100/25 mg three times daily from treatment outset
Rasagiline 1 mg daily as monotherapy with regular review of motor function
Benzhexol 2 mg three times daily for predominant tremor symptom control
Pramipexole 0.125 mg three times daily, titrating over 4-6 weeks
Amantadine 100 mg twice daily for early symptomatic management

subtopic_detail: Lewy body dementia medication safety
stem: An 76-year-old retired teacher is brought to her GP by her husband. Over the past 9 months she has developed progressive forgetfulness, recurrent vivid visual hallucinations of small children in the house, and marked fluctuations in her alertness throughout the day. She has also developed a shuffling gait and her husband reports she acts out her dreams at night. Her hallucinations are distressing and she is requesting treatment. She takes perindopril for hypertension.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 62, BP 134/72 lying, 108/64 standing
data_table.Examination: Bilateral mild upper limb cogwheel rigidity, reduced arm swing bilaterally, shuffling gait with short steps, MMSE 22/30, no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TFTs, B12, folate all within normal limits, MRI brain shows mild generalised atrophy with preserved medial temporal lobes
